News.title: Huge blaze erupts in city centre building as residents evacuated and 12 engines rush to battle fire
News.content:
Next

A HUGE blaze erupted in a UK city centre with residents being forced to evacuate from their homes.

Twelve fire engines rushed to Market Street in the heart of Nottingham just after 10pm last night.



A crowd of around 40 people gathered outside a residential property, watching the thick smoke rise into the night sky and a fire brightly burning.

Nearby residents were evacuated from the area as emergency crews worked to contain the fire.



Multiple fire engines parked on the streets as crews unravelled water hoses and block off the area.

It is not known what caused the incident or whether anyone was injured.

Nottingham Fire and Rescue have told people to avoid the area and bus routes in and out of the area are said to be affected.

Upper Parliament Street, Lower Parliament Street, Market Street, King Street and Queen Street have been closed.

A spokesperson said: “We currently have 12 fire engines attending a fire at a residential property on Market Street, Nottingham.

“Roads are closed on Upper Parliament Street, Lower Parliament Street, Market Street, King Street and Queen Street.



“The NET Nottingham Tram has been stopped in both directions between Theatre Royal and Market Square.

“Please continue to avoid the area whilst we work to resolve this incident.”

News.title: Terrifying moment thug strangles policewoman & punches her in the face during heinous attack against two female officers
News.content:
Next

THIS is the terrifying moment a thug strangles a policewoman and punches her in the face during a horrific attack.

Police were called to a hotel in Capel St Mary, Suffolk on July 29 after Xander Butler, 23, smashed a window and damaged his hotel room.



Two police officers responded to the report, with disturbing bodycam footage showing how Xander flew into a fit of a rage as he opened the door to the cops.

After being told to stay back, Xander lunges at one of the cops, grabbing her by the neck and begins to choke her.



The thug then throws her on to the floor of the hotel corridor as the other cop tries to grab hold of him.

He appears to kick and punch the officer multiple times while she’s on the ground until the other cop gets in between the two.



She pulls the officer up onto her feet – at which point the cop whips out her Taser.

Xander then appears to panic and kneels down by a wall with his hands behind his head.



Pointing the Taser at him, the cop shouts: “Stay where you are. Get down now. Put your hands above your head.”

He fails to follow her instructions, so she discharges the Taser and Xander is detained and arrested.

Xander was sentenced to 16 months in prison at Ipswich Crown Court on Thursday after pleading guilty to intentional strangulation, assault by beating of an emergency worker and criminal damage.



The policewoman who was strangled suffered facial swelling, bruising, jaw pain and a head injury, requiring hospital assessment and X-rays as a result of the attack.

The other officer escaped with minor injuries, but both cops described feeling frightened and emotionally distressed following the incident.

In her victim impact statement for the court, one of the officers wrote: “I do not think I will ever be able to fully describe how I felt in that moment.

“I was terrified. I genuinely feared for my life.

“As the attack unfolded, my thoughts immediately turned to my family and loved ones.



“I thought about the possibility that I might never see them again and the devastating impact that would have on those I could have left behind.

“No one should go to work believing there is a chance they may not come home at the end of their shift.”

Sergeant Alasdair Nicol, South West Response Team said: “This was one of the worst assaults on police officers I have seen.

“It is important to remember police officers are normal people doing the abnormal.

“Butler’s abhorrent actions against two of my colleagues has again highlighted the unacceptable levels of violence that officers around the country are facing on a daily basis.



“The officers’ actions have no doubt prevented Butler from causing significant harm to others.

“However, in doing so, they have had to put themselves in harm’s way for the sake of others.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Let me be clear. If you actively choose to attack police constables, you can expect a robust response as demonstrated in this matter.

“We will pursue offenders and make use of every appropriate power available to ensure they are brought to justice.”

News.title: Anti-migrant group use computer-generated radio broadcast to threaten ‘severe consequences’ for letting migrants into UK
News.content:
Next

ANTI-migrant protesters used a computer- generated radio broadcast to threaten “severe consequences” for letting small boats into the UK.

An anonymous transmission from so-called UK Patriots was broadcast to shipping near Portsmouth at about 8.50pm on Sunday.



The message, in an AI-generated American voice, threatened to “target commercial shipping and the homes of anyone that aids illegal migrants to enter the UK”.

The message said: “I represent the Patriots of the UK.



“Any attempt to allow vessels carrying illegal migrants to enter the port of Portsmouth will have severe consequences.

“We will target commercial shipping and also the homes of anyone that aids illegal migrants to enter the UK.

“You have been warned.”

It was received as Border Force brought about 140 migrants into Gosport in Portsmouth Harbour, sparking demonstrations that led to 12 arrests.

Assistant Chief Constable Simon Dodds said: “Violence and criminal damage have no part in peaceful protest, our position on this has been clear that we will investigate thoroughly and take robust action against anyone responsible.

“Last night saw a number of incidents that were clearly not peaceful protest, rather violent public disorder, and this will not be tolerated as we work to keep our wider communities in Hampshire and on the Isle of Wight safe.



“Our officers did not deserve to be assaulted as they worked incredibly diligently on Sunday to ensure the safety of everyone in the area.

“Neither do they, or anyone from our partner agencies, deserve to be singled out online or subjected to abuse via social media.”

News.title: TV licence fee dodgers are as bad as shoplifters, fumes BBC veteran John ­Simpson, 82
News.content:
Next

BBC veteran John ­Simpson says TV licence fee dodgers are as bad as shoplifters.

The BBC News world affairs editor fears they will help kill off the current model of funding the Beeb.



John spoke out as increasing numbers of viewers, particularly the young, do not pay as they get most content though streaming services such as Netflix, Amazon and YouTube.

He said: “If people can decide they simply don’t want to pay, which they’re increasingly doing, we’ve had it, we’re finished.



“Don’t tell me these people don’t watch the BBC.

“Of course they do. For me that’s just like shoplifting.”

The BBC annual report shows the number paying the £180 licence fee fell by 500,000 last year.

Regulator Ofcom reports about half of 16 to 24-year-olds do not watch live TV and nearly all prefer streaming services.

In January it was revealed that, for the first time, the BBC had been overtaken by YouTube — when for two months its audience was larger than for all the corporation’s channels.

John’s comments in Radio Times came as he promoted his new show, John Simpson: 60 Years at the BBC.



He said the best alternative to the fee was a mandatory household levy, collected and administered by an organisation independent of the Government and BBC.

Ministers have already rejected the idea but John, 82. said: “That to me is the right way of doing it. Everybody pays for it.”

News.title: Staggering number of cups of coffee the average Brit drinks in their lifetime revealed
News.content:
Next

THE average Brit drinks nearly 57,000 cups of coffee during their adult life.

And seven per cent told a survey they drink five or more cups a day.



The typical coffee drinker spends more than 92 hours a year — nearly four full days — making and enjoying coffee.

On average, they neck 8,000 americanos, 6,000 lattes and 5,800 flat whites in their lifetime.



Most reach for their first brew of the day between 7am and 8am, research for coffee firm Lavazza revealed.

Forty per cent of the 2,000 people polled said they would not dream of skipping their morning brew, with 16 per cent claiming it is a non-negotiable part of their breakfast routine.

And 43 per cent insisted their morning coffee is one of the best parts of their day — with 18 per cent saying it was even more important than taking a shower.

The research found 28 per cent think sugary syrups in coffee should be banned.

And 23 per cent consider very milky coffee a no-go.

Emanuele Pellegrino, of Lavazza, said: “Clearly, we are a nation of coffee lovers.



“But whether people prefer their coffee short and intense, long and smooth or with milk, what matters is being able to enjoy quality coffee exactly the way you like it at home.”

The company is launching Tabli — packaging-free pods of compressed coffee designed to fit its new range of machines.

News.title: Tory leader Kemi Badenoch is banking on one thing with her £10bn Iron Dome plan – is she on to a winner?
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

POLITICS FIX Tory leader Kemi Badenoch is banking on one thing with her £10bn Iron Dome plan – is she on to a winner?







Next

KEEPING the country safe is the first duty of any government – but Kemi Badenoch says Labour is failing “this most basic task”.

The Tory leader will spend today trying to burnish her credentials on defence and claim Andy Burnham is unwilling to invest in the military.



She has grabbed the headlines by pledging to build an Iron Dome capable of shooting down missiles targeting Britain.

Modelled on Israel’s world-beating air defence system, it will cost £10billion and be funded by slashing spending on benefits.



By putting defence front and centre of her party conference, Badenoch hopes to put the issue up in lights and draw a clear dividing line with Labour.

Her framing is simple: Burnham’s reluctance to cut welfare means he is forced to scrimp on our national security.



Is Badenoch on to a winner?

Previous governments have also penny-pinched on defence and diverted cash to other public services.

Ploughing billions into a military that you hopefully never have to use is no mean feat.

But Badenoch is banking on voters realising the world is a vastly more dangerous place, with hostile powers flexing their muscles.



She also hopes to punch a political bruise, given John Healey quit as Defence Secretary over a lack of funding he is now failing to plug as Chancellor.

Speaking of Healey, he also has a new headache in the form of the Sun’s own star columnist Jeremy Clarkson.

The telly legend made a surprise appearance at the Conservative conference to barrack Labour over punitive business taxes.

News.title: Putin picked ‘General Armageddon’ to ‘starve Ukraine into submission & annihilate civilians’ after brutal Syria tactics
News.content:
Next

VLADIMIR Putin is set to deploy his General Armageddon, known as the “Butcher of Syria”, to starve Ukraine into submission, experts have warned.

Bloodthirsty Sergei Surovikin, 59, will “try and break the will of the population” as Mad Vlad “takes the gloves off”, a former senior British military commander has revealed.



Surovikin, one of Russia’s cruellest commanders, is reportedly back in Moscow after being banished to command Russian troops in Algeria.

Retired Major-General Chip Chapman told The Sun that sick Surovikin will likely deploy evil tactics to try to crush the spirits of the Ukrainian population as Russian forces flail on the front lines.



He endorsed using nuclear weapons early on in Putin’s brutal invasion of Ukraine and headed up the tyrant’s entire invading forces from October 2022 to January 2023.

But after plotting a coup led by Wagner warlord Yevgeny Prigozhin that summer Surovikin was exiled to North Africa.

Major-General Chapman said Surovikin “is absolutely the right guy” to carry out the twisted tactics.

He said: “Surovikin first came to my attention in Syria.



“He was known there as the butcher of Syria and it was Surovikin who really formulated the campaign plan in 2017 which enabled the tide turning in favour of Assad because of his approach to really annihilating life in cities.”

Surovikin oversaw the obliteration of Aleppo as commander of Russia‘s aerospace unit, when Putin intervened in the country in 2015 on the side of the tyrant President Bashar al-Assad.

Under his command, Russian forces reportedly covered up the use of nerve agent sarin before a deadly chemical attack that killed 80.



Major-General Chapman said: “If you can’t succeed on the front line, what do you try and do?

“You try and break the will of the population in the same way that the Russians and Syrians did that to the opposition by making cities uninhabitable.

“That is all the basic infrastructure of life, water, sewage, clinics, bakeries, all the things that they hit in Syria look to be on the target list in Kyiv and certainly eastern Ukraine at the moment.”

Surovikin’s soldiers have repeatedly been accused of violence against civilians.

He commanded dozens of air and ground attacks on innocent people in Syria, targeting civilian objects and infrastructure, according to a 2020 Human Rights Watch report.



The report said his forces struck Syrian “homes, schools, healthcare facilities, and markets – the places where people live, work, and study”.

Russian military commentator Colonel Viktor Baranets confirmed Surovikin’s move back to Moscow, saying: “Generals like this don’t lie around on the sofa.

It has sparked fears that he could turn his illegal targeting of civilians to Ukraine as the country heads into yet another winter under Russian bombardment.

Some have suggested General Armageddon could spearhead operations to seize the Ukrainian stronghold cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, where Russian forces continue to lose ground.

Others have speculated is that he could command a new offensive on Kyiv through to occupied Chernihiv.



Major-General Chapman said: “Do I think that he could energise the close battle which is taking place on the front line? No I don’t.

“But do I think he could energise that deep battle in terms of the destruction that could go on in Kyiv and other cities? Yes he could and that’s the whole point of it.

“Indeed the UN I think in 2024 when they looked at his approach in Syria talked about him as using starvation until submission.

“Now we’re seeing food distribution points, food warehouses being attacked now along with all those the fabric of the electricity grid for example.”

And Major-General Chapman warned that Putin is taking the “gloves off” “in terms of their approach to the laws of war”.



He said: “Any sort of Geneva Convention type laws of conflict seem to be going out the window.

“Many would argue that they already went out of the window, which is why we shouldn’t forget that Putin is still a criminal in the eyes of the International Criminal Court.”

It comes as stark new figures show how Putin is increasingly targeting civilians in Ukraine.

The UN Human Rights Office said an average of more than 400 civilians were killed or wounded every week in Ukraine during the first eight months of 2026.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

This is a 55 per cent increase from the same period in 2025.



A total of 15,280 civilians were killed or injured during the first eight months of the year, according to the report.

News.title: Shocking moment thug kicks man, 41, in front of van in random broad daylight attack – as he’s set to be FREED from jail
News.content:
Next

THIS is the shocking moment a thug kicks a man into the path of a van in a random broad daylight attack – as he’s set to be freed from prison.

James Hatcher, 41, was walking down Brighton Road in South Croydon, London, on August 16, 2025, when he was attacked and could have died.



James now said he felt “devastated” after he got a letter telling him that his attacker is eligible for early release.

Paramedics were called to the scene, and James was taken by ambulance to St George’s Hospital with life-threatening injuries, including a bleed on the brain and broken legs, ribs, jaw and pelvis.



James was placed in an induced coma and underwent multiple life-saving operations before waking up six days later.

He had to relearn how to walk and, more than a year after the attack, is still undergoing physiotherapy to help with his mobility.

On June 4, 2026, James’ attacker, Salman Kamraman Karim, was found guilty of grievous bodily harm with intent at Croydon Crown Court and sentenced to 11 years in prison.

But on July 20, 2026, James received a letter from the Ministry of Justice saying that Karim was eligible for early release – just a few months into his sentence.



James, a tower crane operator, from Croydon, said: “It is sickening that he is eligible for early release.

“He got sentenced in June, and I am being told that he is eligible for early release.

“If it weren’t for the air ambulance staff, I would not be alive today.”



After getting his hair cut, James waited for the bus home, but due to delays, he decided to walk instead.

James had his noise-cancelling headphones in as he walked down Brighton Road when a man kicked him in front of an oncoming van.

“It was a really nice day. I had my haircut, and the bus wasn’t due for a while, so I decided to walk,” James said.

“I was walking along the road when a man came out of the vape shop and kicked me in front of an oncoming van.

“I hit the floor straight away; there was a crowd of people who circled me before the police came and shut the road.”



The van driver spoke to officers at the scene and was not arrested, but a few days later, the Metropolitan Police arrested and charged Karim.

Due to other 999 call-outs, an ambulance couldn’t get to James for 30 minutes, he claimed, so the London Air Ambulance team arrived nine minutes later.

James was treated at the scene before an ambulance was available to blue-light him to St George’s Hospital.

He said: “I broke my legs, my pelvis, ribs, wrist, jaw and had a punctured lung – I had life-threatening injuries.

“I also had a bleed on the brain.



“I was placed in a coma for six days, and underwent multiple operations before I came around.”

On August 21, 2025, James woke from his coma, having no idea where he was.

When he woke up, James said he “couldn’t feel his legs” and realised he was lucky to be alive.

James said: “I came around and had no idea where I was.

“I was then told what happened to me. I just thought, ‘shit’, I am lucky to be alive.



“I didn’t think about it too much and wanted to focus on the recovery.”

James spent six weeks in hospital, where he had to relearn how to walk.

He was released from hospital in November 2025, but to this day, James said he still struggles with his mobility and is still unable to work.

At first, James said he learned to sit up from his chair, before gradually learning to walk down the hospital corridors.

“I still have to go physio now,” James said.



“At first I couldn’t feel either of my legs; they were really numb. But slowly but surely they came back, and I was able to move them.

“I go to group physio once a week now.”

During the trial, at Croydon Crown Court, Karim was convicted of causing grievous bodily harm and acquitted of attempted murder.

On June 4, 2026, Karim was sentenced to 11 years in prison.

At the trial, James didn’t want to see Karim’s face, but he decided to attend the sentencing and face down his attacker.



James said: “I was on my crutches; it was horrible to see him.

“I was looking him straight in the eyes, thinking, ‘you piece of s**t’.

“11 years was not a long enough punishment in my opinion; I could have died.”

On July 20, 2026, James received a letter from the Ministry of Justice saying that Karim was eligible for early release.

James said he is horrified that Karim is eligible, just over a year after the attack, when he is still dealing with the effects of what happened.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“I am still feeling the effects of what he did to me,” James said.

“I am unable to work; the fact that he is eligible for early release really hurts me.”

News.title: What prompted the US bombers to leave RAF Fairford?
News.content:
The unexpected mass withdrawal of America's heavy bombers happened so suddenly on Sunday that it has got everyone wondering what prompted it.

An "abundance of caution," says US Vice-President JD Vance, adding that Washington felt Iran was doing what it has "done for 49 years... which is engage in acts of terrorism against the US and against a lot of other people".

An abundance of panic is how others have seen it.

For the last seven months, America's B-1 Lancer bombers and other aircraft have been operating out of Fairford to strike the Iranian missile launch sites.

In July, Iran threatened any country that provided the US with such a facility would be considered a "legitimate target".

Then on 27 September, a major incident was declared when five British men were arrested and later bailed after being seen acting suspiciously with their three white vans in the dead of night close to the airbase perimeter.

At the weekend, a UK-Iranian dual national was arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts. He was also released on bail.

Twelve valuable and strategically important B-1 bombers have now departed en masse and seemingly in such a rush that, reportedly, the air-to-air refuelling aircraft needed to get them back across the Atlantic to their home bases in the continental US were still being fuelled up while the B-1 Lancer crews were being ordered to scramble to take off.

So something was considered urgent and dangerous enough to prompt this.

News.title: Author and former politician Jeffrey Archer dies aged 86
News.content:
Archer was born in north London on 15 April 1940 but would quickly move to Weston-super-Mare in Somerset, where his family bought a house from John Cleese's mother.

In 1969, Archer was elected MP for the Lincolnshire constituency of Louth.

He served as an MP for five years before becoming Conservative Party deputy chairman.

His political career was paused in 2001 when he was jailed for four years for perjury and perverting the course of justice.

He was found to have lied in libel action he had brought against The Star newspaper, in which he was awarded Â£500,000 in damages.

He was released in 2003 and returned to the House of Lords until he retired in 2024.

His last book, Adam and Eve, is set to be released this week, HarperCollins said, describing him as a "master storyteller" whose readers "meant everything to him".

The publisher added that the author had been at the Leicester Square Theatre in London on Sunday, signing books for fans with broadcaster Gyles Brandreth.

Writing on X, Brandreth said: "Just yesterday I did a show with Jeffrey Archer to celebrate his new novel â he said it was to be his last.

"He was in the most wonderful, ebullient form and had such a great reception from a packed house. He was funny, engaging and self-deprecating â a great storyteller to the last."

Last week, Archer also returned to his former school to promote his last book.

"It's wonderful to come back. What I got a real thrill about when I was walking towards the library is seeing the young boys and girls and thinking, 'that's the next generation'," Archer said at Wellington School.

Archer was due to attend the Cheltenham Festival on Saturday to discuss his final novel.

He and his wife Mary had celebrated their 60th wedding anniversary this year, HarperCollins said.

The pair have two sons and five grandchildren.

News.title: Tories pledge £10bn 'Britannia Shield' air defence system
News.content:
The Conservatives have pledged to invest Â£10bn in a new missile and drone defence system to defend the UK if voted into government at the next election.

The so-called "Britannia Shield" would provide an integrated network of radar, command and control systems, as well as interceptor missiles, the party said.

In a speech at the Conservative Party conference on Tuesday, shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge will describe the pledge as "the most significant upgrade to UK air defence for generations".

In response, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the Tories had an "abysmal record" of defending Britain during their 14 years in power, adding: "They owe Britain an apology, not another lecture."

The Tories described their plans as "a British 'Iron Dome'", a reference to Israel's elaborate air defence system.

The party said it would be capable of defending the UK's critical national infrastructure, military bases and sovereign territories from sophisticated threats.

It added that the proposal would strengthen the UK's air defence systems at a time when Nato allies have warned they are facing repeated Russian drone incursions.

The party also cited a report from the defence committee of MPs last November which said the UK was lagging behind its European counterparts in having a plan to defend itself and overseas territories from a military attack.

News.title: Temperatures set to fall as rain and cloud sweep across UK
News.content:
After weeks of unusually warm weather, autumn is finally set to make its presence felt on Tuesday as cooler air sweeps across the UK from the north-west.

Temperatures will plunge from the low 20s to the mid-teens. Wednesday could be the first day since June when temperatures stay below 20C across the whole of the country.

A spell of rain and stronger winds will accompany the colder air, adding to the autumnal feel.

But the cooler spell is not expected to last, with temperatures set to rise towards average over the weekend.

News.title: Europe is pouring billions into space. Can Glasgow's satellite industry keep up?
News.content:
In 2005, a young space engineer called Craig Clark moved back to his home city of Glasgow. He'd graduated from university just over a decade before, but the only jobs he could find were south of the border. Now Craig wanted to start a company of his own. He called it Clyde Space.

I went to school not far from the River Clyde, where the city's shipbuilding heritage was forged, and knew Glasgow had once been an industrial powerhouse. When I was a child, "Clyde-built" really meant something: craftsmanship and engineering excellence. There was a saying that I grew up with: "The Clyde made Glasgow and Glasgow made the Clyde."

What I hadn't realised until recently was that, in a different guise, that tradition is still alive. Two decades later, Glasgow is a European leader in building small satellites.

Many of those built here are known as CubeSats. Their basic building block measures just 10cm by 10cm by 10cm - think of something about the size of a Rubik's Cube. They are much smaller, cheaper and quicker to develop than the huge contraptions that you might picture when you think of satellites.

News.title: King's funding for Andrew not to be used for legal action against police
News.content:
Mountbatten-Windsor has consistently denied any wrongdoing linked to his association with Epstein.

The former Prince Andrew is not a working royal - so Buckingham Palace no longer speaks on his behalf and is not involved in his legal battle.

But a royal source said the King's financial support for his brother should not be directed towards paying for the judicial review that Mountbatten-Windsor is seeking.

It's not been disclosed how much the King gives to Mountbatten-Windsor, but the funding for his brother was part of the arrangement when the former Prince Andrew was moved from his previous home at Royal Lodge in Windsor.

This allowance for Mountbatten-Windsor is not from the Sovereign Grant, which is the Â£138m in public funding for the monarchy.

It is drawn from the King's private money, which includes his income from the Duchy of Lancaster, private estates and his own investments and inheritances.

At the time of Mountbatten-Windsor's arrest, the King said the "law must take its course", and the Palace is now distancing itself from the former Duke of York's legal pushback.

Mountbatten-Windsor's lawyers are understood to be challenging Thames Valley Police and the Central Criminal Court over the lawfulness of warrants used for searches of Sandringham and Royal Lodge - in what has been Andrew's first public response since his arrest earlier this year.

Thames Valley Police has confirmed it is "engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained from the Central Criminal Court".

It added: "As these legal proceedings are currently ongoing, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further."

Mountbatten-Windsor, who lost his titles as a prince and Duke of York over his connections to the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, wants a judicial review to consider the legality of the search warrants.

A court hearing on Thursday afternoon will be part of Mountbatten-Windsor's bid to quash the warrants.

News.title: MPs call for investigation after Lutnick-Epstein whistleblower dies
News.content:
The treatment of whistleblowers by the UK's financial watchdog must be investigated following the death of a British trader who exposed evidence of links between US commerce secretary Howard Lutnick and Jeffrey Epstein, MPs have said.

Simon Andriesz, a former senior employee of BGC Partners - the international firm of financial brokers founded and run by Lutnick before his appointment by US President Donald Trump - died last month in Thailand.

Earlier this year, Andriesz raised concerns with the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), the FBI and other watchdogs about evidence he had uncovered of business links between Epstein and Lutnick. It cast doubt on Lutnick's public statements about his associations with the late sex offender.

A group of UK MPs have now said his death raises "deeply troubling questions" about the way whistleblowers can be treated when they approach the FCA - the financial regulator - with concerns about wrongdoing and subsequent retaliation.

Andriesz's family said he had taken his own life on 23 September, and that there was no suggestion of foul play.

News.title: I won't accept exclusion, says Polanski after criticism of Zionism motion
News.content:
Nine Labour MPs have also referred the party to Sussex Police, asking the force to investigate whether alleged "possible antisemitic offences" at the conference merit a criminal investigation.

Sussex Police has been contacted for comment.

It is the latest development in a backlash to the policy motion, which was put forward by a group of activists at the party's conference in Brighton and endorsed by 1,022 votes to 813.

"The real, material, manifestation of Zionism has been the historic and ongoing dehumanisation, displacement, dispossession, disenfranchisement and destruction of Palestinians," it said.

The motion has exposed divisions between the party's newly enlarged membership base under leader Zack Polanski and its MPs elected at the last general election.

Polanski did not take part in the vote on Sunday and four of the party's five MPs opposed it.

Israel's foreign ministry responded by banning Polanski from entering the country, while some Jewish groups have described it as an "attack on the Jewish community".

In his first comments since the motion was passed, having declined interviews on Monday, Polanski released a lengthy statement saying he "take[s] seriously my responsibility to make sure everyone feels safe and welcome in our party".

He added: "As leader I will not accept any exclusion, or refusal to engage with anyone, because of the religious or communal body they are part of."

He said his party and its leadership stood for "deeply held values of compassion, fairness and equality for all".

Polanski, who is Jewish, added that "antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state are, and must always be, completely distinct".

News.title: Prisoner took his own life after terror order had 'substantial impact' on mental state, inquest finds
News.content:
Prior to being jailed in February 2020 for breaching the TPIM order, Uddin had served a sentence for racially or religiously aggravated harassment.

TPIMs allow the authorities to control people whom the government believes are involved in terrorism, but who are not facing criminal charges. The home secretary acts on advice from MI5 when imposing TPIMs.

Subjects of TPIMs face measures such as wearing an electronic tag, curfews, relocation to a different part of the country, bans on internet use, controls on finances, and limits on who they can meet and where they can go.

Breaches can result in a terrorism conviction and prison sentence. TPIMs can currently last up to five years, up from a maximum of two years when Uddin was under one.

Uddin breached the measures 12 times by withdrawing more money than he was permitted. The inquest heard he largely spent it on drugs. He had over 20 previous criminal convictions - none of which were for terrorism offences.

The inquest, which was the first ever to consider the impact of TPIMs, heard that Uddin believed the order was originally imposed because he had made reckless statements while under the influence of drugs, but that he insisted he was not a terrorist.

It is understood he was alleged to have made verbal threats and associated with people regarded by MI5 as being involved in terrorist activity.

Coroner Bernard Richmond KC said Uddin was "loved and loving" but was "not someone without his troubles" and these revolved around his drug use.

The coroner said he will be issuing a report to the government out of concern about a risk to other people under the terrorism control measures.

When the TPIM was first imposed on Uddin in January 2020, he was forcibly relocated to the West Midlands after being arrested at the prison gates in front of his sister who had come to meet him on release.

The full reasons for a person being on a TPIM are typically kept secret, even from the person subject to the TPIM, because they are based on MI5 intelligence.

The inquest heard that Uddin feared the TPIM would be re-imposed when he left prison early in 2022, and that he would again breach it due to drugs.

Today the inquest jury concluded the following:

"We are satisfied that the imposition of the original TPIM and its unusually restrictive nature had a substantial impact on the mental state of Akhtar Uddin."

"We are satisfied that the fear of a likely reimposition of such a restrictive TPIM, and its possibly never-ending nature, had a significant impact on the mental state of Akhtar in prison."

"We are satisfied, as a result of the consistent evidence that prison services were unaware of TPIM restrictions and their likely impact on Akhtar, there was a failure to provide support most suitably targeted to Akhtar's specific needs and situations."

A governor at HMP Wandsworth accepted in evidence that lack of knowledge of TPIMs by prison staff had resulted in "unintentionally cruel" treatment of Uddin.

Giving evidence, Uddin's sister Jasmine said that, in the weeks before his death, he had described "counter terrorism officers" questioning him in prison and saying he would never get off the TPIM.

A statement from Uddin's family, issued by their solicitors Birnberg Peirce, said they welcomed the inquest's findings.

"Although nothing can bring back their loving son, brother and uncle, they hope that this will make a real difference to those who are currently at the mercy of this inhumane regime."

His former solicitor, Amer Ahmad, had told Uddin in autumn 2021 there were "highly limited prospects" that he would succeed in having the TPIM legally overturned, the inquest heard.

Dr Richard Latham, an NHS consultant forensic psychiatrist, appeared as an expert witness for the coroner and concluded that Uddin had an undiagnosed "personality disorder", associated "psychological problems and vulnerabilities", and this resulted in impulsiveness, grievance and paranoia.

He said Uddin probably assumed the worst about the TPIM in future, and that this prospect would have created "distress and a sense of hopelessness".

Dr Latham added TPIMs are intended to create a "degree of isolation," but that plays on psychological vulnerability and can create "emotional isolation".

Questioned by Jesse Nicholls, representing the bereaved family, Dr Latham said Uddin "felt a sense of injustice" about being branded a terrorist.

The inquest heard there was little or no awareness by staff in HMP Wandsworth of TPIMs. The coroner said "very few people, if any" knew about Uddin's TPIM, the revocation, or potential re-imposition.

In the absence of jurors, the coroner said there was much assessment by the state of Uddin's potential risk to others, but he had seen "nothing" showing any assessment of risks to him. He said there is a "paucity of support for people subject to TPIMs" and there is a potential risk to other people subjected to them.

For this reason, he added, he would be writing a preventing future deaths report.

There has been a trend towards TPIM subjects having mental health issues.

The independent reviewer of terrorism legislation, Jonathan Hall KC, has noted in previous reports that the "Home Office recognises poor mental health as a dominant feature amongst recent TPIM subjects" and that "poor mental health and neurodivergence (autism)" as being in evidence amongst them.

A government spokesperson said TPIMs were "a last resort to manage the risk posed by terrorists who cannot be prosecuted or deported" and are "carefully considered and strictly focused" on stopping a person's "involvement in terrorist activity".

The government was dealing with a prison crisis it "inherited", the spokesperson added, and was improving training to help staff "manage risks of self-harm and suicide".

This article contains details some readers may have found upsetting. If you, or someone you know, are struggling with the issues raised in this article, support and information is available at BBC Action Line.

News.title: British Museum boss 'sorry' for Bayeux Tapestry visitor issues
News.content:
The head of the British Museum has apologised for the experience some visitors have had at its blockbuster Bayeux Tapestry exhibition.

The London institution has announced changes to how visitors see the historic work over concerns of overcrowding.

"Anyone that doesn't have a good experience, we're really sorry about that and we want to put it right," Nicholas Cullinan told the BBC's culture and media editor Katie Razzall.

The new plans include longer opening hours, an audio guide, additional seating and clearer signage.

Some people reported waits of up to two hours. Last week, hundreds of ticket holders were reportedly turned away due to backlogs when the museum closed early for a private event.

"You don't want anyone that comes to see it to have a bad experience, so our focus is very much on getting it right and learning lessons," Cullinan said.

"Obviously we want everyone that comes to have a fantastic experience. To put it into context, we're three weeks into the exhibition run. Next week, we'll hit our 100,000th visitor, which is a pretty extraordinary statistic. The vast number of visitors report having a very good experience."

Asked if the museum team had asked the embroidery's home museum in Bayeux for advice on queue management and timings, Cullinan said they had.

He also denied the museum had let too many people book tickets and said that the issues arose because visitors want to spend more time with the work than expected.

The problem "isn't just the interest, it's that people want to spend more time than anticipated. And that's a good thing. We want people to come and enjoy it, but it means we have to adjust accordingly and that's what we're doing," Cullinan said.

Some visitors have been spending longer than their allocated 40-minute slot viewing the tapestry, meaning others have to move through more quickly, he said.

News.title: Twelve arrests after protest over migrant boat arrival
News.content:
Twelve people have been arrested for offences including assaulting a police officer after a protest over migrant arrivals in a south coast town.

The Home Office said 149 migrants had been picked up in a mid-Channel rescue operation by the RNLI, alongside a French vessel, and were brought ashore at Gosport.

Flares were set off and there were scuffles with police during the stand-off at a marina in the Hampshire town, involving about 150 anti-migrant demonstrators on Sunday.

Eleven men and one woman were arrested on suspicion of offences including assaulting police officers, affray and racially aggravated public order. All remain in custody.

The migrants were taken by coach to a processing centre in Kent.

It is the second known landing of large numbers of migrants this far west along the south coast in recent years.

A police cordon was in place on Haslar Road in Gosport, where the atmosphere at the protest mostly remained peaceful.

Some protesters stopped police vans from advancing by standing in front of them and chanting "shame on you" and "deport the lot".

News.title: Man who killed dog walker should be deported, says judge
News.content:
The court was told that in the three days before the stabbings, Safi had attended an appointment at his GP, had a mental health assessment at Hillingdon Hospital and had sought help at Hayes police station.

After the stabbings, doctors concluded Safi was suffering from psychotic depression which had led to the violent offences.

Dr Elliott Carthy, who assessed Safi at Broadmoor, said he had "paranoid and persecutory beliefs", and voices in his head contributed to his actions that day.

He said a hospital order with restrictions was the best way to protect the public "going forward now and in anticipation of his release into the community".

He said Safi was likely to spend at least five years at Broadmoor before being considered for transfer to a medium security facility where he would stay for several more years, and if he is released into the community he would be under strict conditions and subject to lifelong monitoring.

Safi, who admitted manslaughter, was found guilty by a jury of attempting to murder Farrukh and pleaded guilty to causing actual bodily harm to the teenage boy, as well as possession of the knife.

Prosecutors dropped a charge of murder after the guilty plea to manslaughter was entered, and after receiving expert reports on Safi's mental health.

The judge told the court she would have sentenced Safi to life in prison with a minimum term of eight years if he had not been mentally unwell.

News.title: BBC appoints Rachel Jupp as new director of news
News.content:
Rachel Jupp has been appointed the new director of BBC News, nearly a year after the previous CEO resigned.

Deborah Turness announced last November that she would step down from the role following the fallout over how Panorama edited a speech by President Trump.

Jupp is a former deputy editor of BBC Two's Newsnight and has also served as Panorama's editor, but left several years before the controversial Trump episode aired.

In a statement, Jupp said she was "honoured to be asked to lead BBC News", while the corporation's director-general Matt Brittin described her as "an outstanding editorial leader".

The appointment comes as the BBC continues to make sweeping cuts to its news division. Around 550 job closures have been announced so far, with more expected to follow.

The BBC as a whole will cut between 1,800 and 2,000 jobs - almost one in 10 - in an attempt to save Â£500m over two years as it faces "significant financial pressures".

In a statement, Brittin said Jupp was "widely regarded for her news judgement, fairness and high standards".

"She brings a clarity of vision for the future, and the determined, collaborative approach needed to strengthen BBC News," he added.

News.title: Katie Price's ex urged girl not to tell, court told
News.content:
Katie Price's ex-husband, who is accused of raping a 13-year-old girl, told her to "not tell anyone" and said he might "get in trouble for this", a court has heard.

Kieran Hayler, 39, is on trial at Lewes Crown Court accused of three counts of rape and one count of sexual assault of the teenager in West Sussex in 2016, all of which he denies.

Earlier, jurors were told that on the first alleged occasion, Hayler told the 13-year-old he really liked her and began speaking to her about having sex.

He told her it was a "special thing" and they should do it, before he raped her, the court heard.

The court was played the complainant's police interview in which she said Hayler told her how special and "important" the first time was.

She said: "He started crying and saying, 'Maybe I shouldn't take it away from you, it's so important'."

The complainant said she did not have a "conversation" with Hayler afterwards, and recalled thinking "I was probably a bit young".

Hayler allegedly raped the girl again on two further occasions.

The second occasion, she said, was two or three weeks later.

On this occasion she said she remembered waking up to Hayler being there, and after, he acted like "like nothing had happened".

On the third alleged occasion, the court heard Hayler told her she should not tell anyone, and then sexually assaulted her.

She said he told her: "You can't talk about it, you can't tell anyone, I might get in trouble for this."

It is alleged he grabbed her hand and put it down his trousers.

Speaking after this alleged incident, the complainant told police: "I think by that point I knew it wasn't quite right, he kept telling me to 'shh', I had to be secretive and not tell anyone."

She told police: "I tried to forget it for so many years."

In 2021, the complainant contacted the NSPCC charity which referred her to the police, prompting the investigation.

Hayler was first interviewed by police in January 2022 and denied any of the allegations took place and that anything sexual occurred.

He was married to media personality Price at the time of the alleged incidents, before the couple's relationship broke down in 2018 and they divorced in 2021.

Hayler suggested his ex-wife had "launched a campaign" against him when their marriage ended, and the allegations form part of this, the court heard.

The alleged victim is not part of Hayler or Price's extended families.

Price is expected to be a witness in the trial which is expected to last about a week.

The trial continues.

Additional reporting by PA Media.

News.title: Jewish Greens chair says she could leave party over 'Zionism is racism' motion
News.content:
The chair of Jewish Greens Vivien Lichtenstein has told the BBC it is "quite possible" she will leave the party after Green members adopted a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism.

The motion, which has divided senior party figures, also backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

It has been condemned by some Jewish groups and Israel's foreign ministry.

Asked by BBC Radio 4's Today programme about her future, Lichtenstein said: "I haven't decided yet...It is quite possible that I will leave the party...I'm giving it a little time and to talk with colleagues."

Lichtenstein, who is a former chair of her local party, said she had opposed the motion from the first time she heard about it.

"I don't think it's helpful and it doesn't make any difference whatsoever to Palestinians in Gaza who have suffered devastation, orphans left behind, it doesn't make any difference to Palestinians in the West Bank who are currently suffering, are currently being attacked and killed."

Members of the Green Party of England and Wales endorsed the policy motion, which was put forward by a group of activists at the party's conference in Brighton, by 1,022 votes to 813.

There are 230,000 members of the Green party overall and not everyone attended the conference.

The party's leader Zack Polanski, who is himself Jewish, had called for the motion to be amended to add in protections for Jewish members and remove language referring to a "single democratic Palestinian State". Both of these amendments were defeated.

Polanski did not stay at conference to vote on either this or the substantive motion. He left early to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras, where he is standing in a by-election to be the MP. A full list of candidates in the contest can be found here.

The motion, among other statements, "supports the establishment of a single democratic Palestinian State in all of historic Palestine with Jerusalem as its capital, equal rights for all, and the right of return for Palestinians and their descendants".

It defines Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state".

The Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership Council, which criticised the motion, said "Zionism is anti-racism, creating a refuge for Jews in their ancient homeland after millennia of persecution outside it".

Lichtenstein said she defines herself as "both Zionist and anti-Zionist" depending on the definition, and said a problem with the motion is that there are many definitions.

She said she was not concerned about "people accusing me of supporting Israel's right to exist and therefore I'm a racist, which of course is not the case", but said the "very bad motion...crosses a line".

One way in which it did that, she said, was that the proposers said they had consulted some Jews, but did not consult the Jewish Greens, who would have made some amendments to improve the motion.

She said there was a "vast range" of opinions among Jewish Greens, some who supported the motion entirely, others who supported aspects, and others who were against it. Some Jewish Greens also support one state, she added.

She said that party policy was that "it's up to Israelis and Palestinians to choose their future - one state or two".

Last month, the UK and 11 allies reiterated their support for a two-state solution, which would recognise a Palestinian state alongside an Israeli one. Israel rejects a two-state solution.

Her concern with the motion was that the Green Party may accuse UK, Israeli, or Jewish organisations, including those that partner with Palestinians, of racism. She said she supports many of these groups working "against the occupation and even go out on the ground to assist Palestinians".

She said she knows of some non-Jews who are planning on not staying in the party because "they think the motion crosses a line" and also because of their work, if they might not be able to be associated with a party that has "Zionism is racism" as a policy.

Asked whether she believed there were antisemites inside the party, including at senior levels, she said "there are certainly some antisemites in the party, I don't know about at senior level, that is not my experience".

News.title: Southport Inquiry: Violent material left online for weeks
News.content:
This phase of the inquiry is examining how the risks posed by violence-fixated individuals can be managed, and the role the internet and social media play in influencing and enabling them.

Nicholas Moss KC, counsel to the inquiry, said: "The report outlines the result of a single eight-hour search across a selection of online platforms including X, TikTok, Reddit, Instagram and Discord.

"It is right to recognise that there was a spectrum of material of concern.

"It ranges from material with violent overtones, but which might be argued to be newsworthy, to material which can fairly be categorised as very violent or strong gore material."

Moss said 98.9% of the material was publicly accessible and 92.3% was not subject to any age restrictions.

All of the material was reported to the platforms, but a week later 87.9% of it remained live, the inquiry heard.

Moss said 14 days after it had been reported, 83.8% of the content was still available.

He said the platform providers would be asked about the report and "what appears to be, in some cases, arguable delay and failures to remove the material even when it had been reported to them".

Representatives of platforms, including TikTok, Reddit, X and Alphabet, the parent company of Google, are expected to give evidence to the inquiry in November.

News.title: Experts give update on whether polar vortex could hit the UK this autumn
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Freezing temperatures and unsettled conditions could sweep the UK as the El Niño weather phenomenon continues to wreak havoc on global weather.

Experts are predicting a wet and stormy autumn that could develop into an icy winter after the “super El Niño” smashed global benchmarks to become the strongest event in history.

The Met Office said the “unprecedented” phenomenon, which has already helped push temperatures to reach the hottest summer on record, will continue to have “far-reaching” implications for weather conditions across the world.

But while a peak in El Niño can weaken the stratospheric polar vortex, experts have warned it’s too soon to tell if this will send freezing arctic air further south this autumn and winter.

The forecaster said “it was too far away to give any forecast information” about whether a polar vortex could impact the UK and it remains “just one possible outcome dependent on many competing factors”.

El Niño is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon that develops in the tropical Pacific Ocean. It takes place when sea-surface temperatures across the central and eastern Pacific become significantly warmer than average, altering atmospheric circulation patterns and influencing weather around the globe.

open image in gallery The polar vortex is a high-altitude ring of swirling cold winds spinning above the Arctic ( NOAA )

While wetter weather is expected to move in, the UK just marked its fourth warmest September on record as the anomalous heat that hit the country this summer continues.

After three quarters of England was plunged into drought over the summer, Scotland has seen over a third more rain than its average for September, while southern England remained relatively dry compared to average – despite some recent rain.

Professor Adam Scaife, head of long-range predictions at the Met Office, said: “We have been signalling for months that the developing El Niño will be an unprecedented event. The fact that it has already exceeded previous records – with several weeks to go before it peaks later this year – shows the enormity of this El Niño.

“Scientists are still assessing whether the impacts will be in proportion to its magnitude, but we are already seeing expected effects worldwide.”

Forecasters warned the phenomenon could disrupt a large, high-altitude ring of swirling cold winds spinning above the Arctic known as the stratospheric polar vortex. These disruptions can weaken the jet stream, sending severe, freezing Arctic air plunging southward into North America and Europe.

open image in gallery Experts warned the weather event could bring a rainy and windy autumn ( AFP/Getty )

However, if this happens, it is more likely to trigger freezing temperatures later on in winter, meaning a polar vortex remains unlikely to sweep the UK this autumn.

The Met Office said that over the coming season, the phenomenon is likely to cause “wetter and stormier conditions” that could develop into “cold snaps” over the winter.

The early winter period could be “milder than normal”, the Met Office has said. But as El Niño peaks, the latter part of the season could see the stratospheric polar vortex weaken, leading to an increased chance of Sudden Stratospheric Warming, making cold weather more likely.

British Gas has issued advice in the likelihood of heavy snowfall, advising customers to improve their insulation, protect their pipes, remember where their stopcock is and stockpile at least three days’ worth of food and essentials in an easy-to-reach part of their home.

The forecaster warned that as significant as El Niño is, it can’t determine precise weather patterns and other outcomes are possible.

open image in gallery The science behind the polar vortex ( NOAA )

The agency’s long-range forecast predicts “changeable” conditions as Atlantic frontal systems bring spells of rain, showers and occasional strong winds. But they said temperatures are expected to be above average for the period as a whole.

For the second half of October, showers or longer spells of rain are expected with the wettest and windiest weather in the northwest, drier in the southeast.

There is a chance that a period of more widely dry conditions could develop for a time, but confidence in the details of this is low. Temperatures are expected to be above average overall.

Experts said every El Niño is different, so it is currently impossible to predict the impact of the weather system over the winter.

They added they will continue to monitor the El Niño “as it evolves” and warned that in the long term, it is likely to push up global temperatures in 2027 to new record levels.

Met Office scientist Dr Nick Dunstone explained: “During large El Niño events, significantly more heat is released from the ocean to the atmosphere leading to an increase in global average temperature, particularly in the calendar year following the winter peak of the El Niño.

“Hence, 2027 is very likely to replace 2024 as the warmest year on record and be yet another year to temporarily exceed +1.5 C above the pre-industrial period.”

News.title: Valtteri Bottas cycles from Sepang to Singapore ahead of the next F1 race
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Formula 1 driver Valtteri Bottas decided to cycle from Sepang to Singapore in the week between Grand Prix events.

The 37-year-old Cadillac driver set out for the next F1 stop in Singapore after failing to finish the Bahrain Grand Prix, being staged in Malaysia, last Sunday.

While other drivers and teams were preparing to fly from there to Singapore for this weekend's race, Bottas embarked on a ride of more than 320 kilometers (200 miles).

He posted on X to confirm the trip: “Yea I’m riding to Singapore... on the gravel roads less travelled.”

Bottas hasn't picked up a championship point in his Cadillac this season, with his best recorded finish being 13th at the Chinese GP in March.

He didn't finish last weekend — explaining he went off the track because of a gamble to use slick tiers in the damp conditions — his eighth DNF for the season.

Bottas has been driving in F1 since 2013 and has 10 victories and 67 podium finishes across his career.

Max Verstappen last week ended his long wait for another race win with victory at Sepang. The Bahrain-branded race was relocated because of the Iran war, becoming F1’s first event at the Sepang circuit in Malaysia since 2017.

News.title: Trump says journalists should be ‘arrested’ for reporting on empty seats at rally
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

President Donald Trump suggested on Monday that reporters from The New York Times and other media outlets should be “arrested” following their coverage of his weekend campaign event in Ohio.

The backlash followed a report by New York Times correspondent Katie Rogers, who noted that “several areas of an upper deck were empty” by the time Trump finished speaking on Saturday at Butler High School in Vandalia, Ohio. Rogers reported that the school’s student center, which hosted the event, has a capacity of 4,500 people.

Trump disputed those account details in a series of posts on Truth Social, claiming the venue was full and arguing that empty upper levels were merely the result of audience movement.

“The Fake News New York Times ‘reported’ on my Great, PACKED Rally in Ohio that, ‘the place was not full. Some upper sections were almost completely empty,’” Trump wrote. “In actuality, thousands of people were unable to get in. The Arena was totally MAXED OUT, including all upper sections.

“What does happen at all of my SOLD OUT Rallies, is that the people in the upper sections tend to migrate down to the Main Floor — The ‘migration’ process always happens!”

open image in gallery Reporting noted empty space at the 4,500-capacity high school gym in Ohio where President Donald Trump held a campaign event October 3, directly contradicting Trump’s claims that thousands were turned away ( Reuters )

In another post, Trump criticized media coverage of his crowd sizes relative to other political figures and called for legal action against journalists.

“The Ohio Arena was already full to the brim — And yet these people were still trying to get in,” Trump wrote. “The New York Times said, ‘There were empty seats’ when, in fact, there were none, and thousands of people had to be turned away. The New York Times, and many other Artificial Media Outlets, should be arrested for their dishonesty and disservice to our Country.”

He added: “When Bernie Sanders has 500 to 1,000 people, they make it sound like it’s the biggest event that ever took place. When PRESIDENT DONALD J. TRUMP has 50,000 people, they make it sound like nobody showed up!”

open image in gallery Truth Social posts accuse media outlets of double standards, alleging smaller crowds for US Senator Bernie Sanders receive far more favorable coverage ( AFP/Getty )

Trump also claimed that he uses video recordings to counter media reports about his events.

“I have cinematographers shooting the various Arenas where I speak, in that some of the Fake News likes to dishonestly report lies and untruths,” he wrote.

He insisted that his events remain “HOTTER than ever” and described them as “happenings” that “will never be duplicated again.”

During the rally itself, which was held to support Republican candidate Jon Husted in his Senate race against former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown, Trump addressed the crowd size directly from the stage.

“There are thousands of people outside [who] can’t get in,” he said. “If you’d like to give up your seat, please, we can work it out, get out of here.”

News.title: Trump spends campaign rally complaining about how he is treated by media amid record-low approval ratings
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

President Donald Trump went to Nebraska to drum up support for Republican candidates in the midterm elections. Instead, he spent the rally complaining about how he is treated by the media as he struggles with record-low approval ratings.

During his latest campaign stop in a red state as Republicans compete in tight races that they would normally easily win, Trump railed against outlets such as MS NOW.

“We need a fair media. We have some great people in the media, but we have some really terrible ones too,” Trump told his supporters on the Nebraska State Fairgrounds in Grand Island Monday night. “They've tried to smear us, to slander us, to persecute us, and demoralize us.”

Trump has intensified his attacks against the mainstream media during his second term, lashing out at female reporters who ask him questions about the Epstein files and the Iran war and trying to ban outlets from the White House for unfavorable coverage.

Last month, Trump announced that CNN, MS NOW and Politico would be barred from covering his daily activities at the White House, calling them “fake news.”

open image in gallery President Donald Trump has spent his Nebraska rally complaining about how he is treated by the media as he struggles with record-low approval ratings ( Getty Images )

The outlets sued to regain access to the White House, arguing the ban violated their First Amendment rights, and a federal judge subsequently ordered the Trump administration to temporarily reinstate the outlets’ press badges.

But these outlets are still reporting issues with gaining access to the president. Most recently, the White House blocked Politico from traveling with the president on Air Force One Monday.

The White House told The Independent that traveling on Air Force One is a “privilege not a right” and defended Trump as “the most accessible President in American history” who “will continue to grant an unprecedented level of access to the press.”

“Our nation is doing better now than it's ever done before…But the fake news media refuses to talk about our record-setting numbers,” the president said at his rally, specifically mentioning that Americans’ median household income hit the highest level ever recorded last year.

But the new Census Bureau data comes as the cost of living rises.

The cost of food rose 2.7 percent in August from the year before and energy costs rose 16.3 percent, which was largely driven by Trump’s war in Iran, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Consumer Price Index.

open image in gallery ‘They've tried to smear us, to slander us, to persecute us, and demoralize us,’ Trump said about the media while visiting the Nebraska State Fairgrounds in Grand Island Monday night ( Getty Images )

Trump’s approval rating slipped to a record low as his administration is dogged by a costly and unpopular war and scrutinized over an immigration crackdown that a significant number of Americans find too aggressive.

Just 32 percent of Americans approved of the job Trump was doing, while a whopping 65 percent disapproved, according to a new Reuters/Ipsos poll.

Later on in his rally speech, Trump coined a different insult for mainstream news, calling them “artificial media.”

Trump, who insists on the U.S. embracing artificial intelligence to beat China in a race to produce the most advanced technology, mentioned that he recently changed the name of artificial intelligence to “super intelligence.”

“I said, ‘The word ' artificial ' is an ugly word.’ I said, ‘Wait a minute, it pertains to the media. Artificial media.’ So now we have two names: fake news and artificial media,” Trump told the crowd.

Trump used his new insult in a rant about The New York Times, in which he called for journalists with the publication to be “arrested” after it released a report about several areas of empty seats at his recent rallies.

open image in gallery Trump has intensified his attacks against the mainstream media during his second term, lashing out at female reporters and trying to ban whole outlets from the White House for unfavorable coverage ( Getty Images )

“The New York Times said, ‘There were empty seats’ when, in fact, there were none, and thousands of people had to be turned away. The New York Times, and many other Artificial Media Outlets, should be arrested for their dishonesty and disservice to our Country,” Trump raged on Truth Social earlier Monday.

Trump repeated a familiar plea at his Nebraska rally: “Pretend I’m on the ballot.” While the president’s endorsements might’ve helped his fellow Republicans in the past, GOP candidates are struggling to outpace Democrats in states they typically win in.

Democrat James Talarico is leading Republican Ken Paxton 51 to 45 percent in Texas, according to New York Times/Siena University polls released Monday.

Democrat Mary Peltola is beating Republican Dan Sullivan 50 to 43 percent in Alaska and Democrat Sherrod Brown is beating Republican Jon Husted in Ohio 49 to 46 percent, according to the polls.

Republican Ashley Hinson is leading Josh Turek 48 to 47 percent in Iowa, and Democrat Adam Hamilton and Roger Marshall are tied at 45 percent in Kansas, the polls show.

“The fake news media is trying to demoralize Republican voters with rigged polls, but as you can see here tonight, our movement is the strongest it's ever been in the history of our country,” Trump said at his rally Monday night.

News.title: The gap between Americans identifying as Democrats over Republicans hasn’t been this wide since 2009
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

As both parties gear up for the midterm elections, the gap between Americans identifying as Democrats and Republicans has widened by more than 10 percentage points.

Fifty percent of Americans identified as Democrats or Democratic leaners, according to a new Gallup poll. This is 11 points higher than the 39 percent of Americans who identified as Republicans or Republican leaners in the third quarter of 2026.

The 11-point lead is the largest quarterly margin Democrats have recorded since the first quarter of 2009, poll aggregator Interactive Polls wrote on X Monday. At the time, former Democratic President Barack Obama had taken office after winning his first election, flipping nine states.

While the party in power typically loses congressional seats during the midterm elections, new polling shows just how much Democrats are gaining ground in Senate races in five red states just weeks before voters cast their ballots. This means Republicans will have to fight harder to keep seats that would normally be easy to win.

open image in gallery As both parties gear up for the midterm elections, the gap between Americans identifying as Democrats over Republicans has widened by more than 10 percentage points ( AFP via Getty Images )

Democrat James Talarico is leading Republican Ken Paxton 51 to 45 percent in Texas, according to New York Times/Siena University polls released Monday.

Democrat Mary Peltola is beating Republican Dan Sullivan 50 to 43 percent in Alaska and Democrat Sherrod Brown is beating Republican Jon Husted in Ohio 49 to 46 percent, according to the polls.

Iowa and Kansas are also seeing tight races. Republican Ashley Hinson is leading Josh Turek 48 to 47 percent in Iowa, and Democrat Adam Hamilton and Roger Marshall are tied at 45 percent in Kansas, the polls show.

The new polling favoring Democrats is a significant shift in public sentiment from when President Donald Trump won the 2024 election.

After he defeated then-Vice President Kamala Harris, Trump boasted about the “unprecedented and powerful” mandate the American people gave him as the Democratic Party was left to figure out what went wrong.

open image in gallery The new polling favoring Democrats is a significant shift in public sentiment from when President Donald Trump won the 2024 election ( Getty Images )

Trump had polled higher than Harris on major issues such as immigration and the economy.

But nearly two years into his second term as president, Trump faces a record-low approval rating amid a costly and unpopular war in Iran and scrutiny over how aggressive federal agents have been in carrying out his massive deportation of illegal immigrants.

The president has gone as far as to offer Americans a $5,000 “Trump Dividend” if voters help Republicans keep control of Congress, which he first announced during an usual two-day convention in Dallas that he headlined to drum up support for GOP candidates. Critics have accused Trump’s promise of $5,000 checks of amounting to bribery.

On Sunday, Trump wrote on Truth Social, “The Polls have ALWAYS underestimated MAGA.”
