Sports.title: Macklin: Does Whittaker have the toughness to win a world title?
Sports.content:
Ben Whittaker's recent scare against Conor Wallace has raised questions about whether he has the attributes needed to win a world title, says Sky Sports expert Matthew Macklin.

After controlling the fight from the start, Whittaker was troubled by a left hand from Wallace in the 10th round and then looked ragged in the 12th as he repeatedly slipped to the canvas before clinging on to claim a points win on Saturday in Birmingham.

Whittaker's victory lined up a shot at the IBF light-heavyweight belt which is held by unified champion Dmitry Bivol, but Macklin believes the Olympic silver medallist is not yet ready to challenge the Russian.

Macklin told Sky Sports: "Ben has been on a run of pretty spectacular performances, hasn't he? That said, if we're honest about the calibre of opposition, we know it's pretty low for him and where he is aiming towards being.

"All of a sudden, they stepped it up again with Conor Wallace. He boxed really well for most of the fight, but nonetheless, at the end of the fight, he struggled.

Image: Ben Whittaker fought through some adversity late on to beat Conor Wallace on Saturday

"He got caught and then struggled to shake off the effects of that shot. He recovered momentarily, but not properly. He got his head together a little bit, but was still hurt because you could see he didn't really regain control of the fight.

"I think he needs more than one [fight before Bivol], probably a few.

"While Conor Wallace is a nice boxer, you wouldn't put him in the category of your Bivols and your Callum Smiths.

"Look at the fight between Callum Smith and Joshua Buatsi, and what those two went through in that fight, and then you see how Whittaker unravelled on Saturday night, there's no way you'd say he beats those two guys.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player You won't see a better round of boxing! Watch the phenomenal sixth between Joshua Buatsi and Callum Smith which had both fighters in big trouble.

"He has the skill, the sleekness, the speed and the savvy to mix it with those guys, but has he got the toughness, the chin, the stamina, the power, the hardness to mix it with those guys over 12 hard rounds? He hasn't shown that so far.

"That's not to say that Ben isn't tough or hard. But we can only judge him on what we've seen, and we've seen him unravel a couple of times.

"In the first Liam Cameron fight, he was unravelling and then obviously they both fell out the ring. Fair play to him, in the rematch, he came out and looked brilliant, but against Conor Wallace, he was boxing well, controlling it, but then gets nailed a couple of times and, all of a sudden, he starts to unravel.

"Fair play again, he got through it. But against a Bivol or a Callum Smith, or a Buatsi or William Hutchinson, would he have got through it against those guys? Probably not.

Image: Is Ben Whittaker ready to fight IBF light-heavyweight title holder Dmitry Bivol?

"I think [his trainer] Andy Lee has done a great job with him, but I also think that there's only so much you can do in the gym. You've still got to get the experience on the night, under the lights, in a real fight against real high calibre opposition.

"What's happened with Ben in his career, is he hasn't fought enough high level opposition. If you look at who he has boxed, outside of Cameron and Conor Wallace, he's boxed absolutely nobody.

"For someone who was a top-class amateur, to be a professional as long as he has and to have fought the level of opposition he has, he's missed years of learning - and that could be a problem at the top level.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of Ben Whittaker's US fighting debut against Richard Rivera earlier this year. Courtesy of DAZN.

"It's great getting the highlight-reel knockouts - it's great for your ego, for the perception of you and from a promotional point of view, to create the star quality and the hype. That's important when you're trying to build a star, but you also need to build the fighter.

"You can't just build a star without building a fighter, because at some point he's going to be in a battle against another real fighter, who is of a high level, who wants it as much as he does, and can take a shot and give a shot.

"If you're not getting seasoned, if you're not putting the stuff that you're learning in the gym into practice, on the night and when you need it, it won't be there because you haven't developed it.

"By the way, I like him a lot and I want him to do well, but he hasn't been managed well in his career in terms of the opponents he's fought. He needs some proper fights."

Sports.title: How did some City fans become aggressive defenders of a nation state’s regime? | Sean Ingle
Sports.content:
A video of Liam Gallagher playing in a 1996 charity football match resurfaced on social media recently. Dressed in Manchester City blue and a bucket hat, in truth he appears to be in a fug of cigarettes and alcohol. But then, out of nowhere, he hits a shot into the top corner. Since last week, though, the Oasis singer has preferred to defend the honour of his club with his studs up.

As the fallout from the biggest scandal in British football history headed into a second week, Gallagher was asked what he made of rival fans wanting City to lose all their trophies after being found guilty of all the serious charges against them. “There all NEUROTIC little GIMPS,” came the reply on social media. It was one of dozens of sweary, punchy, and often amusing responses, all built on a solitary article of faith: that City will somehow find a way to wriggle free.

But Gallagher is hardly standing alone. Over at Bluemoon, the biggest City forum, the tone has been just as defiant – albeit with a sprinkle of gallows humour. “Have we been blamed for the Titanic hitting the iceberg yet?” asked one user. “Manchester City shot JFK,” wrote another. “This isn’t just a fight between the PL & City. It’s a fight for the heart, soul & future of football,” reckoned a third.

Staggeringly, the forum now has over 192,000 posts since the initial charges against City, dating back to 2023. Naturally the Premier League, jealous rivals and the media all come under heavy fire. Yet there remains a curious reluctance among fans to accept wrongdoing – or to criticise the club’s owners.

How might we explain that? I am not sure it is down to pure tribalism, or a determination among City fans to wait for the club’s appeal to play out. It’s more complicated, and more interesting, than that.

Let us try to get into the head of the most vociferous City fan since last Tuesday. For decades they were in United’s shadow, then everything changed. Their city did too, given how much Abu Dhabi United Group pumped into it. You can forgive them, then, for not wanting to believe that it was all built on sand during the legal process.

But now? Now there is no excuse. So what might explain the reluctance to accept what the independent commission report lays out in great detail? According to the Irish academic Colm Kearns, one reason is because the United Arab Emirates has not only brought unprecedented success and forged emotional bonds with City fans “but have also co-opted elements of the club’s fanbase as aggressive defenders of their regime”.

In 2023 Kearns and his colleagues analysed huge numbers of posts from City fans, going back years, and found that some of them would not only “overlook ethical violations by the Group, but decry and – in some cases – attack the Group’s critics.”

In other words the club’s owners had successfully leveraged the tribal loyalty of City fans into being Manchurian Candidates – or, rather, Manchesterism Candidates.

Kearns tells me that some sports journalists had even self-censored because of the impact of online abuse from City fans. “We had people talking about how fans would go online and try to find their troll through their personal social feeds, and it sent that on to their editor to get them in trouble,” he says.

There is another massive factor here: social media, and the way we now consume sport and communicate with other fans. Thirty years ago, most City fans would live near Manchester and see fans from other clubs at work and in the pub. Nowadays, they can dwell in an online space made up entirely of people who support their own club.

View image in fullscreen Social media has created tribal online spaces for sports fans. Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/Reuters

“I think it makes fans perhaps more tribally myopic than they would have been before and less likely to look outside of their own club’s perspective,” says Kearns.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Academics also talk of “sports fandom circles”, in which supporters across the globe increasingly mobilise and fiercely defend athletes or their teams. That phenomenon, which came out of east Asia with popular culture and music, leads supporters to be laser-focused on their own tribe. But it hardly encourages lighthearted banter, common ground, or compromise.

In City’s case, Kearns suspects that some fans are putting the club above the wider game, citing a Reddit post that said: “I am a City fan first and a football fan second.” Although, as he concedes, it is impossible to know how many online posters do not live in Manchester, or go to games, and therefore feel the need to prove their bona fide credentials by sticking up for the club at all costs.

Either way, where we could go next is interesting. If you were a far-right tech billionaire, why wouldn’t you want to buy a successful sports team – especially if you knew there was an army of potential defenders of your reputation among your new fanbase?

Over the weekend I went through the fan forums of other clubs to see what their supporters made of the guilty verdict against City. The overwhelming majority welcomed it, of course, even if some questioned whether City would really get properly punished for their crimes, given the relationship with Abu Dhabi and the British government.

“Once you lose faith that the rules apply equally, football becomes something else,” one wrote. “Every title, every match, carries a question mark. I feel cheated. I’m one of the victims. And for that, I hate Manchester City.”

Some will agree with that sentiment. Others will raise their eyebrows. I do wonder, though, would that poster feel the same way if the boot was on the other foot, and their club was in the line of fire?

Sports.title: Nations League roundup: Olise leads late charge as France bowl over Belgium
Sports.content:
Michael Olise came off the bench to inspire France to a 4-1 win over Belgium in the Nations League, handing Zinedine Zidane his first home victory since taking charge.

Dodi Lukébakio put Belgium on course for their first competitive win over Les Bleus in 45 years when he fired the visitors in front in the first half at the Stade de France. But the hosts turned the match on its head in a blistering finish, scoring four times in 14 minutes to preserve Zidane’s unbeaten start and move closer to the quarter-finals.

Désiré Doué hauled France level in the 77th minute with a low drive from the edge of the area before Olise teed up Rayan Cherki to fire them ahead four minutes later. Olise then put the result beyond doubt with a third goal before adding another in stoppage time to cap a stunning French comeback.

France, who also beat Belgium 1-0 in Brussels last week thanks to a late goal from Olise, moved three points clear of Italy at the top of Group A1, with Belgium another point back. Italy beat Turkey 3-1 in Bologna to condemn their opponents to a fourth straight loss, goals from Gianluca Scamacca, Riccardo Calafiori and Pio Esposito doing the business.

Zidane heavily rotated his team for the last match of this three-week long international window, with only Ousmane Dembélé keeping his place among the 10 changes. The Manchester United defender Leny Yoro and the Toulouse goalkeeper Guillaume Restes made their debuts, with Dembélé again captaining the side in the absence of the injured Kylian Mbappé.

Belgium were without the suspended duo of Kevin De Bruyne and Youri Tielemans but caught France cold when Roméo Lavia’s superb ball split open the home defence, allowing Lukebakio to race clear and produce a clinical finish. Maarten Vandevoordt, making his debut in goal for Belgium, kept out efforts from Esteban Lepaul and Cherki as France pressed for an equaliser, but the dam eventually burst.

Doué gathered the ball and shot on the turn, beyond the reach of Vandevoordt, to haul France level. Cherki then turned home a cutback from Olise to give the hosts the lead as the Bayern Munich winger stole the show late on.

Olise scrambled in a third in the 88th minute and rolled in a fourth after skilful work from Doué to complete a remarkable turnaround.

“That’s football, that’s what we love. There were ⁠difficulties, but that’s part of the game, part of the kinds of matches you can have,” Zidane told TF1.

“It’s good to put things right, and ​that’s what we did with an extraordinary second half. We were ‌just missing that final few metres in ‌the first half, but then we turned the match around, it was good.”

In Group B2, Mark Csinger’s late goal earned second-placed Hungary a 2-1 win against Ukraine in Trnava.

Viktor Gyökeres scored in his seventh consecutive Nations League game as Sweden earned a 1-0 win against Romania in Group B4, while Ivan Basic’s late penalty gave Bosnia and Herzegovina a 1-0 victory over Poland. The Burnley striker Marcus Edwards scored a stoppage-time winner as Cyprus hit back from behind to beat Latvia 2-1 in Group C2.

Sports.title: Mamardashvili saves penalty as Georgia hold Northern Ireland in Nations League
Sports.content:
This game concluded with mutual irritation and a touch of chaos. It is an indicator of Northern Ireland’s progress that scoreless parity led to wincing from players, management and fans alike. Isaac Price’s 84th-minute missed opportunity from the penalty spot added to the sense of annoyance.

Michael O’Neill’s team are atop B2 after a window which, going by the players’s physical condition in the dying stages, has been exhausting. Northern Ireland and their youthful setup are a fascinating international story. They are a team on an upward curve, with standards elevated accordingly. O’Neill bemoaned “immaturity” in the second half, saying: “The disappointing thing is we have eight points instead of 10.”

Georgia were reduced to fury with seconds of the five minutes of stoppage time remaining. The visitors were adamant they should have been awarded a spot-kick of their own as Saba Sazonov toppled under a challenge from Callum Marshall. Ramaz Svanadze, the Georgia coach, diplomatically said he would have to view the incident again.

The difficulty for Northern Ireland related to a rising expectation. The superb performance during Friday’s 3-0 win over Ukraine backed up victory away to Georgia and a draw with Hungary. O’Neill’s men were yet to concede a goal in this section. A team quietly tipped to peak around qualification for Euro 2028 was blossoming earlier than anticipated, and this without the long-term absentee Conor Bradley. Northern Ireland’s oldest starter for Georgia’s visit was the 28-year-old Ciaron Brown.

Georgia are a curious case, outside the top 70 in the world yet containing one of its finest players. Clearly Khvicha Kvaratskhelia cannot carry a nation on his own. Indeed, the superstar’s first act was to pass the ball straight to Ethan Galbraith in the Northern Ireland midfield. During the nondescript early exchanges, Kvaratskhelia also gifted possession to Jamie Donley.

What football existed in the first half came from the hosts. Ruairi McConville came closest to opening the scoring with a header from Justin Devenny’s cross, Giorgi Mamardashvili not at all convincing in denying him. Georgia responded, an excellent save from Pierce Charles necessary to deny Zuriko Davitashvili. The let-off triggered a sweeping Northern Ireland move which culminated in Devenny overhitting a low cross.

View image in fullscreen Khvicha Kvaratskhelia was kept relatively quiet, but even so came close to scoring a fantastic goal. Photograph: Cathal McNaughton/Reuters

Northern Ireland were frustrated by the wasting of umpteen set plays during that first period. That Davitashvili moment aside, Georgia offered nothing in an attacking sense. Northern Ireland should have edged ahead four minutes before the interval, Patrick Kelly instead fluffing his lines having evaded the Georgia defence from Trai Hume’s through ball. Kelly appeared in two minds over whether to shoot or play in a teammate, with the visitors seizing upon his indecision. The half ended with Price curling a free-kick into the wrong side of the side-netting.

Price, born in Yorkshire, exemplifies Northern Ireland’s diligence in sourcing players through bloodline eligibility. The Manchester-born Charles brothers – Shea, the captain, was once again classy in midfield as Pierce kept goal – do likewise. This is, however, no team pulled together from afar; Galbraith was a boy wonder in Belfast before being coaxed to Manchester United as a teenager. His imaginative playmaking will surely one day be worthy of a grander stage than Stoke and the Championship

This big-picture stuff was irrelevant as Georgia stood firm. This was a game of intrigue, where Northern Ireland were superior while lacking a ruthless touch. Georgia’s threat was understated but real.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Galbraith limped off with 25 minutes to play, in what constituted a blow to O’Neill. The game by now was tense and scrappy. While against better opponents that may have suited Northern Ireland, that was patently not the case this time. Georgia were managing to sap energy from the home support.

With fatigue apparent across the pitch, O’Neill turned to a 36-year-old who plies his club trade at Stevenage to beef up the attack. Josh Magennis edges ever close to 100 caps, this was No 93.

Kvaratskhelia had been strangely subdued for 79 minutes, but striding forward from midfield, the Paris Saint-Germain forward cracked a 20-yard drive just over the bar. What an outstanding goal it would have been.

Magennis was handed a golden chance but Mamardashvili saved. A melee from the subsequent corner led to the crossbar being struck but, more significantly, the video assistant referee’s attention drawn towards a kick in the face of McConville by Budu Zivzivadze. A spot-kick was correctly awarded. Up stepped Price, whose penalty was saved, low to his right, by the Liverpool goalkeeper. Northern Ireland had passed up their moment. Georgia believed they should have been given scope to rub salt into wounds.

Sports.title: Jude awakening: how a more fluid England are ‘unlocking’ Bellingham’s full potential
Sports.content:
Anthony Barry knows the hunt is on. The England assistant coach has been through the debriefs. He has mulled over the minutiae with Thomas Tuchel to such an extent he is allowed to make a joke at the boss’s expense. “He’s doing my head in,” Barry says with a smile. What is the missing piece of the puzzle? After all the emotion of England’s semi-final finish at the World Cup, how can they take the decisive step to glory?

It is early days in the Nations League campaign, which everybody at the Football Association wants to use as a slingshot into Euro 2028 when England will co-host, but Barry can see the genesis of an answer. It comes down to liberation, enabling England’s top players to fully express themselves, and there is a reason why he finds himself talking about Jude Bellingham.

The Real Madrid player was sensational in Saturday’s 7-0 win over Croatia in Rijeka, just as he was in the 3-2 defeat against Spain at Wembley on the Saturday before that. Playing in the No 10 role but with greater licence to drift, to overload on either side, there were times when Bellingham seemed to be playing with his own ball.

The story about why he wore the No 22 shirt at his first club, Birmingham, is well told. Because he was a No 4, a No 8 and a No 10 rolled into one. Tuchel appears to have reached a conclusion, the basis of which was formed at the World Cup when Bellingham excelled: when a talent like him can play in so many positions, perhaps it is better not to give him one at all.

“The structure [now in the Nations League] allows Jude to play more from his intuition,” Barry says, “and less from being locked down or caged in a certain position. It allows him to roam and operate in spaces in which he thinks he can be dangerous and so far it’s brought out the best in him.

“It is a challenge because Jude can play in any of those positions comfortably and on a high level. So the challenge is to give him a space where he can do it all at once inside of one game. Right now, in a short sample, it seems like we found a solution to unlock all of the potential that Jude has. But we have to continue.”

The point is that it is not just about Bellingham, even if he has drawn the eye almost inexorably so far this season. The blueprint was there for all to see against Croatia and it is one in which plenty of players were encouraged to push into new zones away from those traditionally dictated by their positions. Hence Tuchel had the full-backs extremely high, the wingers making zipping runs off the sides.

It is about the combinations, the slicker the better, but also about players dropping into unusual areas to provide cover and using their footballing intelligence to ensure the overall structure retains its shape. Hence there was the sight of Harry Kane dropping into defensive spaces out of possession, the kind where most No 9s would never tread.

View image in fullscreen Jude Bellingham takes on Luka Modric during England’s thrashing of Croatia. Photograph: Raddad Jebarah/Shutterstock

It was impossible to ignore the ferocity of England’s counterpress; how if one player lost the ball, he and his teammates sought to regain it within two or three seconds. Croatia were overwhelmed, especially in the first half, which ended with England four goals up. The intensity has to endure. But it is the proactive add-ons that the management hope will drive the new tournament cycle, continuing against Czechia in the Nations League at Wembley on Tuesday night. It is no longer a positional style. The idea is that it is freer. Is it a reaction to the inhibitions England came to feel in the World Cup semi-final defeat against Argentina?

“We have moved to a more principle-driven approach, which allows for more flexibility and fluidity,” Barry says. “But fluidity only looks good if it’s anchored by real principles. There is always a danger in international football with such a lack of time to prepare that if you go for this fluid model it can look quite messy. With the IQ of the players we have, it’s been quite natural for them to work together, operate in different spaces.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“It’s not about starting new, it’s about continuation and adding stuff on top. It’s less prescribed, less fixed in the idea of: ‘You play here, you play there.’ It’s more interchanges of position. We feel it suits this group of players and is the best way to break down opposing blocks.

“When you have players like Harry and Jude on the frontline that are really better at moving, that have this deep intuition and IQ for the game … [it is] to trust them, open up spaces for them to operate. It’s also part of the model that we’re moving forward with. We have elite penetration on the last line, whether that comes from our wingers or our full-backs. And we have fluid midfielders with Elliot [Anderson], Alex [Scott] and Declan [Rice], who are happy to move for miles.”

Kane is primed to win his 125th cap on Tuesday night and equal Peter Shilton’s England men’s record. It is a time for tributes and Barry was effusive in his praise of Kane’s professionalism and leadership, his selflessness, his lack of ego; how he is happy to “track back and do the dirty work”.

Barry had a better line. “He’s the best ball-striker I have ever worked with,” he said. It is worth noting Barry worked with Cristiano Ronaldo during his time with Portugal as the assistant manager to Roberto Martínez. It is one key reason for Barry’s sense of optimism. There are many others.

Sports.title: Police occupy Djibouti FA headquarters amid attempt to oust Fifa council member
Sports.content:
Attempts to oust Souleiman Waberi as the president of the Djibouti football federation (FDF) reached a dramatic climax on Monday as police occupied the federation’s headquarters after a group of club presidents called an extraordinary general assembly aimed at removing the Fifa council member and his executive committee.

The FDF said police first occupied its national technical centre at about 5.30pm on Sunday, without presenting an administrative document or court order. According to the federation, on Monday a much larger police contingent ordered Waberi, members of the executive committee, staff and other federation members to leave the premises.

The FDF said 16 club presidents then entered the building under police escort and proceeded to hold what it described as a “purported” EGM. The federation rejected the meeting as illegitimate, saying it had not been properly convened and that the notice periods and procedures required under its statutes and electoral code had not been respected. It declared any decisions taken “null and void”. But sources in Djibouti have insisted the number of delegates required by the statutes was present. They unanimously voted to remove Waberi and the executive committee before establishing an interim committee to oversee the federation.

Quick Guide How do I 

The confrontation follows weeks of mounting opposition to Waberi, a member of the Confederation of African Football (Caf) executive committee as well as Fifa’s council and a close ally of Gianni Infantino. At the start of September, a coalition of 27 clubs announced its intention to vote on the removal of the executive committee and insisted it had secured the two-thirds support required under the federation’s statutes.

The FDF disputed that calculation, saying it has 67 members and that 45 – not 27 – would be required to trigger an extraordinary assembly. The dispute escalated as additional clubs and delegates joined the campaign against the executive committee. The government then intervened, with the secretary of state for sport, Fatouma Ali Abdallah, ordering the FDF to convene an extraordinary general assembly within 72 hours.

The FDF has appealed to Fifa and Caf, arguing that the use of state security forces to remove elected officials could constitute interference in the affairs of a national football association. It warned that the consequences could include suspension, exclusion of Djiboutian clubs and national teams from international competitions, and a freeze on development programmes and funding. The Guardian has requested a comment from Fifa.

It is understood Waberi and several other officials could be facing charges this week after a police investigation of the FDF related to suspected embezzlement and money laundering was completed. They were arrested in September 2024 after a government inspection of the FDF identified financial and administrative irregularities, including weaknesses in procurement, cash management and financial controls. The government’s investigation also raised concerns about anomalies in payments to third parties, failure to pay tax on salaries and wages and “misuse of cash payments” totalling almost £500,000. The police then carried out its investigation.

Waberi has denied wrongdoing. He said in August after the FDF was accused by a club official of misusing funds that Fifa’s “monitoring mechanisms have revealed no indication of wrongdoing regarding the funds it disbursed”.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Sport in Focus Our picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown in Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Fifa, which along with Caf contributes more than $1m (£760,000) a year to the FDF through its forward development programme, has financed football infrastructure and youth-development programmes in Djibouti, including the Douda academy and artificial-pitch projects in Arta and Dikhil. But it is understood that various tenders are under investigation because they did not comply with standard procedures.

Several foreign workers who were not in compliance with immigration regulations were sent back to their home countries, meaning construction was halted. According to several Caf and Fifa employees and contractors, the projects in Djibouti are “a complete farce”. “We pass on the information but nothing happens,” said one contractor. “The money has gone missing, the projects are never finished – or if they are, it’s just a bare-bones version – and nobody says a word. It breaks my heart for the young people who just want to play football.”

Sports.title: Ronaldo’s break with Portugal is sad, fitting, and long overdue | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
If this is to be the end for Cristiano Ronaldo at international level, at least it can be said that he left the stage as he bestrode it: with monumental self-regard. Ronaldo has always been a preening, self-absorbed player, but for a time, when he was one of the best in the world, it could be tolerated. For the past four years, though, he has actively and obviously held Portugal back. There is a great generation of technical talent here weighed down by the monstrous albatross of his ego.

To recap the basic details of the past couple of weeks. Ronaldo played 67 minutes of Portugal’s scratchy 1-0 win over Wales. Portugal coach Jorge Jesus, who replaced Roberto Martínez after the World Cup, said he had a verbal agreement with Ronaldo that he would not start the following game against Norway but would perhaps come off the bench. Early in the second half, Ronaldo went to warm up – although whether that was on his own initiative or because Jesus had told him to is unclear. The game was tight, Portugal ultimately winning 2-1, and Jesus did not bring Ronaldo on.

To Ronaldo and his army of apologists, Jesus was guilty of an unacceptable provocation. Jesus’s view was that winning the game took priority over the extremely delicate feelings of a 41-year-old forward. Ronaldo walked out on the squad, and perhaps on his international career, although only three days later, seemingly after Jesus had refused to pay penance for his blasphemy. Which is sad, although perhaps not quite in the way Ronaldo thinks it is.

It’s possible Jesus, who also coached Ronaldo at Al Nassr, could have handled the situation differently. He is not, it’s fair to say, a diplomat. After Martínez’s soft-pedalling, that is, though, perhaps exactly what was needed. Jesus is 72. His vision of management is old-school, which is to say that he is a dictator and he takes orders only from the club president, and then only if he feels like it. His career has been characterized by rifts with players who have resisted him. In a sense the only surprise is that his falling out with Ronaldo took until the second game of his reign.

View image in fullscreen Cristiano Ronaldo was left on the sidelines against Norway. Photograph: Grzegorz Wajda/SOPA Images/Shutterstock

Others might have been cowed in the face of Ronaldo’s sulk, the online backlash and criticism from some of the Portuguese press, certain elements of which Ronaldo owns, but not Jesus. He is a man of great eloquence and is always quotable but, even by his standards, his response to the furore has been remarkable as he has insisted on the primacy of the team over any individual. “I can say to any player that you’re starting on the bench: if I need you for 30 minutes you’re going to play, if I don’t need you, you’re not going to play,” he said. “The way I was reading the game he didn’t come on. Because it’s not Cristiano, just like it will never be any player that will change my ideas as the coach. Never! Not him, not anyone in football. Not him, not anyone, not any president. Never! Zero!”

His hardline approach might have backfired had Portugal then lost to Denmark, but they won 4-2, playing superbly. Gonçalo Ramos, who might have thought he had already settled this argument by replacing Ronaldo at the 2022 World Cup for the last-16 game against Switzerland and scoring a hat-trick in a 6-1 win, set up the first and scored another against the Danes, having already scored the winner against Norway. “The new manager is a great help,” Ramos said. “We have clearer ideas; we know exactly where each teammate is, both in defense and attack. We’re improving day by day, and it’s all part of a process. We’re very happy with the win, once again against a good team.” Ramos was on target Sunday as Portugal came from behind to beat Norway at home, making it four wins out of four in this window.

The tendency until now has been for the other Portugal players to back Ronaldo, to insist he was an icon and that they didn’t mind his superannuated lumbering. Bruno Fernandes has been notably diplomatic, but others are starting to break cover. Ramos’s former Paris Saint-Germain teammate Vitinha, for instance, who has seen at club level how beneficial a purge of egos can be, observed that Portugal’s improvement has been “the work of the coach … I think beyond the win, the content of our game was great.”

Jesus has offered Ronaldo another meeting to try to resolve the situation, but the Portuguese football federation seems already to have accepted how the affair will end, beginning plans for a farewell game for the country’s record scorer. Both Jesus and Ronaldo have indicated they will say more this week.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

But the truth is that this is a break that should have happened long ago. For three tournaments, Ronaldo has undermined an extremely talented Portugal. This is a sad story. It is sad Ronaldo’s career should have ended this way. But the saddest element is that a great player could be so deluded about his own fading ability that a national team’s hopes and dreams should have been sacrificed to his quest to break goalscoring records.

Sports.title: WSL talking points: heat cranks up on Arsenal and Putellas and Diani shine
Sports.content:
1 Fans stay connected to Slegers

Travelling Arsenal fans showed no animosity towards the head coach, Renée Slegers, despite their side’s run of one win in six games in all competitions and slipping 10 points behind Manchester City. Slegers walked over to applaud the 2,000 away fans after the 4-2 defeat at Etihad Stadium, on Sunday and they applauded her back. Slegers said: “I mostly went there to thank them, connect with them and show them I care for them and appreciate them coming to Manchester. And also to show them that I feel – not sorry for them because I’m a big part of it and things are within my control – but they’re coming here and they’re not getting the rewards, just like the team. I wanted to connect with them instead of walking away and hiding.” Tom Garry

View image in fullscreen Lauren Hemp celebrates scoring Manchester City’s third goal. Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA

2 Forward-thinking Walsh lifts Chelsea

Chelsea’s midfield came to the fore again in their 3-0 win over West Ham. Keira Walsh was the heartbeat of the team, collecting her third straight player of the match award with the 29-year-old enjoying a more attacking role this season. With the introduction of Lexi Potter at half-time, Walsh was able to push forward fruitfully again. She scored her second WSL goal of 2026-27 – the same as she managed last season – and took more shots (five) and completed more dribbles (three) than anyone else. “It helps us a lot in terms of creating opportunities,” said her coach, Sonia Bompastor. “We know how good she is at the edge of the box … It’s good to have a player who is confident and brings us the solution to scoring goals.” Sophie Downey

3 Lionesses flex their muscles

London City showed their Champions League qualification credentials with a 6-1 rout of Tottenham to move above them into third. They were at their fluid and clinical best against a team many believe will rival them as challengers to the traditional top three, with 47.6% of shots on target compared with Tottenham’s 11%. Superstar signings Alexia Putellas and Kadidiatou Diani both scored twice, but most impressive was the muscle the squad showed. They looked more robust and hungrier than Tottenham, their physical presence combined with an aggressive press making the home team look pedestrian and lightweight despite an unbeaten start to the season. With lots of summer changes it can take time for players to gel and that physical presence can make a difference when things aren’t clicking. When things are clicking, though, it appears anything is possible. Suzanne Wrack

4 Pointless Charlton neglect basics

The Charlton manager, Karen Hills, did not mince her words after her side conceded five despite taking the lead at Brighton. “It’s unacceptable if we can’t deal with one v ones,” she said. “The game is about one v one duels, about tackling, doing the basics and doing them really well. Unfortunately, we didn’t do that today. We found ourselves on the end of the scoreline which isn’t very flattering for us. We need to be more accountable for some individual stuff, but at the same time I take full responsibility because that’s my team out there.” The international break comes at a critical time for the team, who are yet to pick up a point. Even with some time to work on their unacceptable handling of the basics, it is hard to where Charlton’s first point is coming from. SW

5 Liverpool unsuccessfully copy United

Gareth Taylor admitted surprise at Manchester United’s directness after his Liverpool team succumbed to a 1-0 defeat at Leigh Sports Village. Possession was split almost evenly, with 51% for Liverpool, and the hosts created more goalmouth opportunities, but could not convert them. Taylor told the BBC: “We ended up becoming what they are, very direct. We have got to be braver – and do what we do.” TG

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Julia Zigiotti Olme of Manchester United (left) celebrates after her goal settled the match against Liverpool. Photograph: Craig Brough/Action Images/Reuters

6 Familiar problems for Sørensen at Villa

Brian Sørensen’s first WSL game as Aston Villa’s interim manager ended in a 1-1 draw with Crystal Palace. The Dane took over on Tuesday after Natalia Arroyo’s dismissal, with Villa having won two points from their opening four league matches. Villa took the lead through Noelle Maritz in the 55th minute, but Abbie Larkin’s equaliser 19 minutes later ensured Villa remain without a league win. Villa were fortunate not to concede again as Palace’s confidence grew and created several chances late on, and the draw leaves them 12th. Villa and Sørensen have work to do, whether his appointment remains temporary or becomes permanent. Réshma Rao

7 Mace ends Everton’s goal wait

It was quite a feat for Everton to be in the top five without registering anything other than an own goal and their luck continues. They finally scored goals of their own in a 2-1 victory against Birmingham. It was all thanks to Ruby Mace, who scored them both. Her most recent WSL goal came playing for the visitors in 2021. The first was a stunning left-foot strike into the far corner; the second a deflected shot from the edge of the area. “I’m really happy. I have [been working on my shooting], putting in the extra work, and luckily today I managed to score,” she said. Renuka Odedra

Sports.title: The man staking his reputation - and £100m - on taking down Man City: Richard Masters has faced down mutiny, a pandemic and the Premier League owners club. Now insiders reveal how he'll fight the biggest scandal in British sport
Sports.content:
A couple of days after Manchester City were found guilty of cheating, the former chairman of a Premier League club attempted to describe the challenge of imposing law and order on British football.

He had a little think and then offered this soundbite to Daily Mail Sport: 'It can be a bit like managing a creche.'

That view was then relayed to an executive at one of the current 20 clubs comprising our top-flight. He made a slight update to the assessment: 'It's more like a difficult high school now - the kids have grown up and in some cases become delinquent.'

They were both joking around a serious point, but played to the common sentiment that few jobs in sport exist with the same complications as those faced by Richard Masters.

Since his appointment as CEO of the Premier League in December 2019, Masters has been confronted with a global pandemic, the Project Big Picture manoeuvrings from Manchester United and Liverpool, the mutinous intentions behind a Super League, an acceleration in foreign and state ownership and, of course, the era-defining trial of Manchester City.

To cite one of Masters' former colleagues and a close friend: 'Taking those areas as a whole, it's a f****** tough hand to be dealt.'

Premier League chief executive Richard Masters' reign will be defined by the eventual outcome to their legal case against Manchester City

Masters would strongly reject any notion of a crusade against Man City, highlighting that guilt was reached by an independent commission and that his job is to administer rules set by clubs

Daily Mail Sport has consulted a dozen sources who know Masters and have worked around him to better understand the highest-ranking individual on the side of the establishment.

Most are quick to agree on three details. One: Masters is nothing like his long-time predecessor, the charismatic Richard Scudamore, an arch-politician who found it easier to charm or coerce the room during a reign of constant financial growth. Two: The landscapes in which they worked have changed dramatically. Three: Masters would strongly reject any notion of a crusade against Manchester City, highlighting that guilt was reached by an independent commission and that his job, in the most reductionist terms, is to administer rules the clubs themselves had voted to play by.

But, on the latter, there is an observation worth making – the appetite to commit an estimated £100million in legal resources to the City battle has challenged the perennial accusation of judicial bias in favour of the big clubs. British football has never known a confrontation of such stakes.

Irrespective of whether Masters finds the personalisation of this fight inaccurate, his reign will be defined by its eventual outcome, as will a somewhat bigger issue – the integrity of the past two decades of the Premier League.

It is a far cry from Masters' arrival in the role, which occurred in highly unusual circumstances, because he was only fourth choice to replace Scudamore. A shambolic recruitment process that stretched 18 months had seen Susanna Dinnage named as successor, but she declined after her appointment had been announced and the current BBC director general Tim Davie also turned it down. Completing a chaotic hat-trick, David Pemsel was given the job but resigned before starting because of allegations about his private life. All of which opened a sliding door to Masters.

As a sales and marketing man, with long stints at the England and Wales Cricket Board, the EFL and the Premier League, his perception as an accidental candidate didn't help in the hornet's nest of football politics.

'Richard wouldn't have been human if there wasn't a little bit of imposter syndrome in the initial months in the job,' said one former colleague well acquainted with the machinations of a Premier League stakeholder meeting. Another source adds that there were individuals in those meetings, typically attended by two representatives per club and a further dozen Premier League staff, who felt Scudamore's replacement wasn't up to it.

Much of that derives from comparisons between very different men. One Premier League executive describes Scudamore as routinely making phone calls beyond midnight to corral the 20 clubs on big issues across his 20-year reign. 'A chief whip in another life', said the source.

Masters is viewed as being nothing like his predecessor Richard Scudamore, an arch-politician who found it easier to charm or coerce the room during a reign of constant financial growth

Masters is more corporate in style and less charismatic in nature, but his approach has slowly been viewed as a strength as football landscape has required a different kind of diplomacy

The depiction is of a CEO in Scudamore who never knowingly entered a vote without being reasonably sure of the outcome. 'Didactic' and 'controlling' were words used with some affection by a former staffer, with Scudamore's sharpest achievement rated as his ability to 'keep the peace' between 20 separate entities with conflicting agendas. By consensus, that was a more impressive feat than overseeing the consistent rise in television revenues.

Masters, an Aston Villa fan who turned 60 in June, is more corporate in style, more process-driven, far less charismatic in nature. For a time, that was interpreted as worse. But within Premier League circles it has slowly been viewed as a strength after a seven-year period in which the football landscape has required a different kind of diplomacy.

'There are still one or two in the room that are not convinced by him,' said a prominent source at a Premier League club.

There is no denying that Masters has had questionable moments – his reference to Everton and Nottingham Forest as 'small clubs' during their Profitability and Sustainability Rules skirmishes in 2024 was easy fodder for some of those who have detected two-tier justice in how the Premier League apply its rules.

A bigger matter was the takeover of Newcastle United by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund. The Premier League claimed they have 'legally binding assurances' that the Saudi state would not control Newcastle, which has long struggled with the smell test for one fact above others – the Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman is also the chair of the Public Investment Fund.

Some will see such decisions as flawed and acts of willing delusion; another would say that football's world has changed beyond recognition and there are not enough tiny violins to play notes of sympathy for those trying to control it. Masters' record within it is not without blemishes, especially in the balancing between financial regulation and the stifling of ambition. But there is an acknowledgement that he has overseen a uniquely challenging time, starting with Covid just months after taking office and extending to the City debacle.

'There was a perception that the Masters regime was worse than the Scudamore regime but that has softened quite a bit,' said an executive at a Premier League club.

'Scudamore had great abilities to do certain things. He was a master politician and a superb negotiator. He was a brilliant anticipator of problems and would get ahead of them. If Richard Masters could do anything better, it might be for him and Alison (Brittain, the Premier League chair) to get ahead of the problems quicker. They aren't as skilled politically, don't have the same nous, but he is very strong at working through a problem.

The takeover of Newcastle United by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund has been among the key challenges faced by Masters during his time as Premier League chief executive

'The stuff Masters has had to contend with is more extreme than his predecessors. He has done a very decent job of it in very, very choppy water. Covid was a huge thing to deal with – almost overnight, the revenue streams were being stopped and he was the man on a Zoom call having to answer 40 faces on a screen about when football could resume.'

A different source cites the threat of a Super League as the biggest crisis and City merely the messiest. 'It helps that he is a very calm guy,' said a club source. 'Whatever people think of how the Premier League works under him, he is a decent man with decent values and he is mostly applying the rules we as clubs have voted for.

'I have never seen him lose his temper in the meetings and there have been times when the criticism has been personal.

'He can be blamed for anything and everything. If there is a bad refereeing decision, he will get a call. If the economy in Singapore affects revenue, he will get blame. But again, he is very calm in the way he works through the role, very good at compartmentalising an issue, and I think he has done a solid job on balance.'

In a room of Premier League clubs, 'solid' and 'decent' can pass for a compliment.

Those meetings, of which there are around five per year, can be feisty. Some can spend hours arguing about the seemingly trivial. According to a source, one recent debate saw multiple changes to the draft of a rule about which side of the dugouts should be used for substitutes warming up mid-match.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, the meetings around the Covid protocols or the Super League breakaway are understood to have been the most heated. Discussions around Manchester City have not reached those levels. Presumably, too much popcorn was being consumed in the creche to kick up a fuss.

Sports.title: The 'mess' that Harlequins can't escape: Too many yes men, fears Marcus Smith could leave, pressure mounting on Jason Gilmore and Robbie Deans, recruitment errors and Quins legends' anguish at 'turning from a rugby club to a brand'
Sports.content:
The vacant look on George Furbank’s face after Gloucester scored their fifth try of eight on Saturday said absolutely everything about Harlequins’ horror start to the season. Perhaps he was debating whether he could tear up his new contract and run back to Franklin’s Gardens.

After winning two of the last three PREM Rugby titles with Northampton, Furbank’s summer move to London was supposed to herald a fresh start for his new team, who have gradually slid down the league since winning the league themselves in 2021.

It hasn’t happened. A home defeat by Bath and a 48-0 humiliation at Kingsholm have seen Harlequins’ poor form from last term – where they finished second bottom – continue.

That’s not what Furbank has been used to. You had to feel for him as Harlequins capitulated to what was their worst league defeat in 26 years and their third biggest of all time.

With nothing to show in terms of points from their opening two matches, Harlequins already look in real trouble, even if it is still early days. It is tough to see how they can turn the corner with a trip to a resurgent Sale to come in round three.

‘I didn’t expect last year to be as bad as it was, but I did expect it to get worse before it was going to improve,’ former Harlequins and England scrum-half Danny Care told Daily Mail Sport, before this season began. ‘They've got to be harder to beat. It can literally only get better.’

George Furbank (centre) was Harlequins' marquee signing this summer. He may already be wondering whether he made the right decision

Gloucester showed Harlequins exactly where they've gone wrong - they only finished a point above them last season but thumped them 48-0 on Saturday

Harlequins won six of 18 league games last season and the decision to hand head coach Jason Gilmore a contract extension raised plenty of questions.

There are issues everywhere you look at Harlequins. The club’s recruitment – led by Ed Spokes – has been questionable at best. Furbank is a fine player and he should still be England’s first-choice full-back when fit. But on a salary of more than £300,000-a-year, it is impossible to get away from the fact Harlequins' priority should have been investing in fresh grunt in the forward pack.

Gloucester, who finished just a point and a place above Quins last season, have evidently done a better job of recruitment - to the tune of a 48-0 thumping between the two teams last weekend.

With Quins slowly slipping down the PREM table ever since their 2021 title, finishing third, sixth, sixth, seventh and ninth since then, big questions are rightly being asked of Laurie Dalrymple, who has been chief executive since 2019.

One former Harlequins player, who asked not to be named, described Dalrymple as a ‘massive problem.’ He added: ‘There needs to be accountability for an underperforming rugby department. Harlequins have turned from a rugby club into a brand.’

The club’s problems were laid out in plain terms at Gloucester last weekend. Over the summer the Cherry and Whites added significant heft, bringing in Wales co-captains Dewi Lake and Jac Morgan and South Africa World Cup winner Jean Kleyn for a harder edge.

It has clearly worked, Gloucester badly exposing Harlequins’ shortcomings in that area. It was insult to injury for the capital club that two of Gloucester’s best players were former Harlequins Will Joseph and Will Trenholm.

Quins do hope to have their star No10 Marcus Smith and his fellow England international Fin Baxter back on the field in the coming weeks. Both have been on the sidelines so far with finger and foot injuries respectively and their team’s struggles must be analysed within the context of their absence. However, it is clear the problems at Harlequins run far deeper than just playing personnel.

Harlequins won six of 18 league games last season and the decision to hand head coach Jason Gilmore a contract extension raised plenty of questions

With Quins slowly slipping down the PREM table ever since their 2021 title, big questions are rightly being asked of chief executive Laurie Dalrymple

Daily Mail Sport understands there is concern among the club’s leading sponsors at the on-field struggles and that several leading ex-players now have nothing to do with their former employer, despite the expertise they could offer in a time of need.

‘No one has a relationship. It’s really bizarre,’ one said. ‘There’s a lot of Harlequins connections and rugby intellect there. I’m not saying that would fix everything on the field, but it would make the club a better-connected place. I really believe the club is in a mess.’

The facts facing Gilmore and his fellow Australian Robbie Deans, who is performance director, is that Harlequins have to improve and quickly. Another campaign of disappointment will surely not be tolerated by owners Duncan Saville and Charles Jillings. Saville joined the Harlequins board earlier this year to keep a closer eye on proceedings, and he can’t be happy at what he’s seen.

Sources have indicated there are too many ‘yes men’ at Harlequins. Decorated former Test guru Deans’ employment as performance director involves him spending ‘extended periods in the UK at critical points throughout the season’, though he also spends time abroad.

One gets the feeling that if he wasn’t already, Deans must be heading for the team’s Guildford training base as a matter of urgency given the way the first two games have gone. Things already look critical.

At Gloucester, Harlequins conceded a mammoth 21 penalties. It was one of a number of shameful statistics, after moments of promise against Bath. Last weekend, Gilmore’s men made just three entries into their opposition’s 22 and produced only four clean line breaks.

Perhaps most embarrassingly of all, given they are a team historically known for free-flowing attacking, and the number of tries being scored in PREM Rugby is as high as it’s ever been, Harlequins couldn’t even get on the board.

Care, who made a record 395 Harlequins appearances and now works for PREM broadcaster TNT Sports, said: ‘There have to be signs of improvement. There has to be a clearer playing style.

At Gloucester, Harlequins conceded a mammoth 21 penalties. It was one of a number of shameful statistics, after moments of promise against Bath

‘There have to be signs of improvement. There has to be a clearer playing style,' says Quins' record appearance-maker Danny Care

'They’ve got to get their best players on the pitch as much as they can because the turnover of injuries, with whatever was going on, isn’t good enough. I'd like them to give Marcus a platform to be able to show what he can do. Because if he gets that, then he can be the most dangerous player in the league.’

As a 10-team competition, the PREM is now played in short bursts around other competitions and international windows, meaning it can be difficult to re-establish momentum quickly, especially when you're rock bottom.

Another problem for them is that Newcastle, traditionally the league’s whipping boys, look much improved after another summer of investment from owners Red Bull.

‘I don’t know how they fix it or what they can hang their hat on,’ a source said. ‘Scoring zero points in a league where every team is finding it easy to score is not a good sign for a team whose USP is supposed to be their attacking game. There are better teams in the PREM than them at that now.’

Their base, in a well-heeled area just a stone’s throw from Twickenham, has meant Harlequins have always been able to charge high prices for tickets. While many are affordable, the top seats can cost more than £80.

For how much longer will loyal supporters be willing to spend such sums to watch a team that is badly underperforming?

The club’s decision to allow Ellie Kildunne to leave their women’s team was also unpopular with fans. England ace Kildunne is the most high-profile figure in the female game, but the World Cup winner has now joined Bristol Bears.

It has meant Harlequins have not only lost a hugely talented player, but one of rugby’s most marketable from either sex.

The club’s decision to allow Ellie Kildunne to leave their women’s team was also unpopular with fans - not only have Quins lost a hugely talented player, but one of rugby’s most marketable

As for Marcus Smith, Care fears he may look elsewhere soon if results don't improve

Smith, who has played more rugby for England at full-back than at No 10 in the past two years, is contracted at Harlequins until 2028. But his former half-back partner Care is concerned his club’s underperformance – alongside him being a bit-part player internationally – could cause him to look elsewhere.

Smith has previously been a target for big-spending French clubs and held talks with Paris-based Racing 92. ‘He's still got a couple of years, so I think that's great for the club,’ Care said of Smith.

‘But they're probably going to have to get better in the next couple of years to give him what he needs because I know how high his aspirations are. He wants to be winning games and winning trophies.’

Right now at Quins, that looks a long way off.

Sports.title: Grinning Cristiano Ronaldo returns to Al-Nassr training after walking out of Portugal camp - as Piers Morgan brands boss the 'Ten Hag of international football' by trying to 'belittle' star
Sports.content:
A smiling Cristiano Ronaldo has returned to Al-Nassr training after stunningly walking out on the Portugal squad during the international break following a rift with head coach Jorge Jesus. Al-Nassr warmly welcomed back the star, whose walkout dominated headlines around the Portugal camp during the international break. 'The GOAT in the heart of Najd, at Al Nassr', the Saudi Arabian club shared on social media, as Ronaldo arrived at the club's training centre. While Ronaldo's focus has turned back to his club, his international future remains unclear after his clash with Jesus. The star, 41, left Portugal's camp after Jesus's press conference last Wednesday, as the head coach appeared to confirm the forward would not start against Denmark in the Nations League. It came after Ronaldo had been left on the bench for the entirety of the 2-1 win over Norway last weekend. Cristiano Ronaldo returned to training with Al-Nassr after walking out of the Portugal squad during the international break Ronaldo left the camp following a dispute with Portugal's head coach Jorge Jesus Broadcaster Piers Morgan has claimed the dispute between Ronaldo and Jesus centres around broken promises by the Portugal boss, who he branded as the '[Erik] Ten Hag of international football'. Ronaldo had previously spoken to Morgan in an explosive interview back in 2022, which effectively ended his Man United career, as he stated he did not respect then Red Devils boss Ten Hag. Morgan, speaking on Sports Uncensored, has claimed Jesus tried to 'belittle and embarrass Ronaldo' and went back on his word over the star's playing time. 'What this goes down to is nothing about money or fame or any of these things,' Morgan said. 'He was given absolute guarantees about how he would be used, it was one of the reasons he decided to continue his international career. 'The new guy Jorge Jesus, who knows him from Saudi Arabia, said to him with the Nations League, they agreed he would play the first two games and would be rested for the next two. 'The first game he was told “you get 90 minutes” and he gets yanked after 67 minutes so he’s a bit p***ed off and afterwards the coach apologised to him and that he would go out and explain this shouldn’t have happened. 'He goes out and does the opposite, he pulls a Ten Hag, where he goes out and tries to belittle and embarrass Ronaldo and put him back in his box and say “all the players are as important to me”, which also p***es off Ronaldo. Piers Morgan has claimed Jesus broke promises made to Ronaldo, leading to the star walking out of the camp Morgan compared Jesus to former Man United boss Erik ten Hag, stating he had tried to 'belittle and humilate' Ronaldo 'Then he goes to Ronaldo and says “I know we said you would be rested for the second two games, but I want you for 30 minutes against Norway”. 'He went “okay, if that is what you want, I’ll do it”. He sits there and gets warmed up for 25 minutes and never gets on the pitch. So again he is p***ed off at the lack of respect. 'For him it is a question of respect, being promised one thing then the opposite happening, being warmed up and not used. Eventually he went f*** you and got on a plane and left. 'Does it sit well with you guys that Ronaldo might not get a farewell game for Portugal because a coach has decided he wants to be the big dog and humiliate him.' Jesus has insisted Ronaldo could return in the next international break in November, saying: 'As far as I'm concerned, everything is open. 'It's up to Cris to decide his own life. In the next call-up, if Cris is playing and wants to be in the national team, why not? 'Resentment? Nothing, it was a misunderstanding. In my opinion, it's easy to resolve. When will I resolve it? I don't know. The game is over, and only afterwards will we know how things will turn out. 'It's not up to me. To reach an agreement with two people, both people need to talk and agree. That's not up to me. Ronaldo's Portugal manager and team-mates insist he is welcome back should he choose Jesus has insisted the situation is a 'misunderstanding' and is easy to resolve 'Just because it was him, and perhaps rightly so because he's a symbol, this whole problem of him coming on, warming up, not coming on. How many players warmed up today and didn't come on? Will there be a problem? No. 'With Cris it's different, he's a symbol. But is it a problem? For me it wasn't a problem. If Cris wants to and is playing for Al-Nassr, he'll be in the next squad. We talked before this squad and we can talk before the next one. It's Cris who will decide.' The feud started when Ronaldo was left on the bench for Portugal's win over Norway – the first time in 18 years he had missed the full 90 minutes for the national side barring injuries and suspensions. Ronaldo said: 'After the national team coach's press conference, and following a conversation with the President of the Portuguese Football Federation, I have decided to leave the national team training camp. 'In due time, I will tell all Portuguese people the truth about the reasons that led to my departure from the national team, to which I have always dedicated myself. 'Now is the time to wish good luck to Portugal and to all my teammates.' The tension seems to have boiled over following Jesus' press conference. The manager said: 'There was no incident whatsoever. 'Any player - and I was a player myself - when you spend 20 or 30 minutes warming up and then don't get on, no-one is happy about that. After leaving camp, Ronaldo said: 'I will tell the truth to all Portuguese people about the reasons that motivated my departure' A sign has been placed outside the Estadio da Luz in Lisbon, backing Ronaldo over Jesus 'Afterwards, as coach, I decided not to bring him on. It's nothing to make a fuss about. 'It's not difficult for me to focus,' he added. 'You know what's difficult for me? It's not understanding what's going on inside. It's not knowing how to train my players. That's what's difficult for me. The rest... zero. 'What's important is what we have to do. The things that happen don't separate the group, they haven't separated us and they won't separate us.' Despite Ronaldo's walkout and controversy over his departure from the camp, Jesus's side won all four of the Nations League matches during the international break. Ronaldo's former Man United team-mate Rio Ferdinand has insisted Jesus needs to apologise to the star and claims the Portuguese Football Association have been 'panicking' after the rift. ‘The coach needs to come out and apologise,' Ferdinand said on Rio Presents. ‘Trust me, I think he has to come out and say “listen I have judged this situation wrong”. ‘I am telling you, something has gone on, I am sure something has happened when you look between the lines. Rio Ferdinand has claimed Jesus should 'come out and apologise' to Ronaldo ‘The president has come out and they’ve done the “Cristiano is the best, he’s the greatest, he’s this and that and the other". ‘They are trying to settle the situation, they are panicking behind the scenes now. 'This situation doesn’t play out the way it has if there are good communication skills. 'I think there has been terrible communication skills. 'I said this during the World Cup with Roberto Martinez and I think the same with this manager now, you have to sit with Cristiano Ronaldo and tell him this is what I want to do. And if you don’t want to be a part of it, then just tell me, but this is how I want it to work. 'That conversation I don’t believe has been had, because I don’t think you would be here with Cristiano going mid camp walking out like that.' The international break had remarkably begun with Jesus and Ronaldo sat side-by-side at a press conference, where the former had labelled the star as a 'symbol of Portugal'. Ronaldo had revealed he had considered retiring from international football in the summer before deciding to continue, but would walk away if the national team told him he was no longer required. 'Whenever they say they don't want me in the national team, I will be the first one to go,' Ronaldo said. 'When I think I am not adding anything to the team, or that I create an atmosphere, I will be the first to go. I will take my suitcase and leave. 'The Portuguese count on me, that's why I'm still here, just look at the numbers, I'm sure you can make some calculations, I'm still doing well. 'The day they don't count on me, no problem, I will leave. I will always be the No 1 fan of this federation.'
