World.title: Liberia: Bong Filled Pelelei with Praise for Ex-Supt. Jackson, Dead at 74, Yet Never Gave Him the Senate Seat in Four Tries
World.content:
Jackson asked Bong County for a seat four times and did not get it. On Saturday, in the town where he was born, Bong gave him something that no election could: a crowd of people, speaking one after another, telling him that he had mattered. He was 74. He could not hear it. The county, at last, said it anyway

PELELEI, Zota District, Bong County – The women came first, and they came together. Members of the Bong County Women Organization filed into the funeral grounds in Pelelei on Saturday carrying a gratitude that had been years in the making. Behind them came former players, former students, elders, businessmen and young people from Gbarnga, all gathered to bury a man who had asked Bong County for something four times and never received it.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

Dr. Ranney Banama Jackson Sr. was 74 when he died. He served as Superintendent of Bong County from 2006 until January 28, 2011, a stretch of years when the county was still finding its feet after the long civil war. He then sought the county’s Senate seat in 2005, 2011, 2014 and 2023, and each time the voters sent someone else to Monrovia. On Saturday, in the town where he was born, the same county that had turned him away filled the program with the words it had held back.



The hall that keeps giving

Madam Olivia Weetol, the former head of the Bong County Women Organization, stood before the mourners and spoke about a building. Jackson, she said, built the county’s first Women Center, a place where the women of Bong gather to hold meetings in the interest of the county.

Then she told them what the hall is doing now. Jackson is no longer around, she said, but the women still rent out the center, and the money they collect goes to needy women of the county who are desperately in need. Somewhere in Bong tonight, a woman who never met him may be eating because of a hall he raised. It was one of the quietest moments of the day, and for many people listening it was the hardest to bear. A man was being lowered into the ground, and something he built was still reaching for the hands of strangers.

The night he slept in the camp

Lincoln Gbaindeh did not come to talk about buildings. He came to talk about a night in 2008. Gbaindeh was a player on the Bong County team that reached the final of the National County Meet that year. He told mourners that Jackson did not stay in Gbarnga waiting for news. According to Gbeinteh, the superintendent literally slept in their camp, sitting among the young men and urging them to fight for the county and win it. That moment, Gbaindeh said, inspired them.

Bong won its first National County Meet soccer trophy that year. People who follow the county’s football say no superintendent has led Bong to that feat since. A county that rarely had anything to celebrate suddenly had a trophy, and a young man who had been afraid of the final had a superintendent beside him. Gbaindeh spoke for a few minutes, but he spoke like someone who had carried the memory for fifteen years, waiting for a place to put it down.

Tributes from every corner of Bong

One by one, others came to the podium, and every voice added something new. A Gbarnga resident, Gormah Flomo, said Jackson understood that the office of superintendent was not about sitting in Gbarnga and waiting for instructions from Monrovia. He believed the superintendent had a duty to bring development closer to the people. Flomo remembered improvements to public facilities, the work around the David Kuyon Sports Stadium and the efforts that helped improve electricity in Gbarnga. Those things may sound ordinary today, the resident said, but at the time they represented meaningful change for Bong County.

A resident of Suakoko District, Clyde Saul, spoke about young people. Jackson invested in them, the resident said, supporting education and scholarships so that many young Bongese could keep studying. More than 600 students reportedly benefited from a county scholarship initiative tied to his leadership, according to a biography from the AREPT organization. For families who could not afford school fees, the resident said, that help meant more than politics. It meant hope for their children.

A former student, Foster Peabody, stood up and made it personal. Some public officials are remembered because they held powerful positions, the former student said, and others because something they did touched ordinary people. When a child gets support to stay in school, that child can grow into a professional who contributes to society. That, Forkpah said, is why Jackson’s education work must remain part of Bong’s history.

A young resident, Jonathan McGill, of Gbarnga said Jackson showed that someone from Bong could rise through public service and still stay connected to home. His scholarship efforts, his development work and his later national service proved that his interest in public affairs went beyond one office. The young man hoped today’s leaders would take the lesson and invest more in education and opportunity for the next generation.

Remembering the ruins he inherited

Several speakers asked the crowd to remember the time Jackson served in. A Gbarnga businessman said Jackson arrived when Bong was trying to recover from the destruction and stagnation of the war years. He understood that development needed government facilities, investment and basic services, the businessman said. Whether people backed his politics or not, it is hard to talk about that chapter of Bong’s history without mentioning what happened under his watch.

The former Chiarman of the Bong Legislative Caucus, Attorney George Mulbah, said Liberia was coming out of a devastating civil war and Bong had enormous challenges. Jackson inherited a county that needed rebuilding, the resident said, and worked to restore public confidence and basic government functions. His contribution was not that everything was perfect, the resident said. His contribution was that he became part of the rebuilding.

Published accounts credit his administration with helping bring electricity to parts of Gbarnga and with renovating the presidential compound and rehabilitating the superintendent’s compound there. They also credit him with work at the David Kuyon Sports Stadium, though accounts differ on whether that was fencing or construction. Jackson himself once told a local radio audience in Gbarnga how he got it done. He clashed with members of the then Bong Legislative Caucus, some of whom opposed the idea, and he fenced the stadium anyway. Before that, residents had cut palm branches to ring the field on match days and big occasions.

A 2026 account says Jackson negotiated two multimillion-dollar rubber-processing plants for Gbarnga in 2008 and helped formalize the Sister States relationship linking Maryland in the United States with Liberia’s Bong and Maryland counties.

Those claims rest on that account and have not been independently verified, but they fit the portrait mourners painted of a man who looked beyond the county line.

The wound he carried

The people who loved him did not pretend he had never been hurt. In 2008, President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf suspended Jackson after an audit by the General Auditing Commission examined the management of county funds. Reports said he was accused of irregularities, including the use of US$10,000 of county money for a trip to the United States. He later repaid the money.

People who follow the county’s football say no superintendent has led Bong to that feat since. A county that rarely had anything to celebrate suddenly had a trophy, and a young man who had been afraid of the final had a superintendent beside him. Gbaindeh spoke for a few minutes, but he spoke like someone who had carried the memory for fifteen years, waiting for a place to put it down

Those close to the story say the journey had a purpose. Jackson and then Caucus Chair George Mulbah traveled with money from the Bong Social Development Fund to negotiate the sister-state relationship with Maryland, and one result was a dump truck from the State of Maryland that Bong County kept using. His political rivals, his supporters say, used the trip against him with the president. Sirleaf later explained, at a public forum in Gbarnga reported by FrontPage Africa, that she suspended him because he acted unilaterally, not simply because the money was spent.

A Bong County elder, William Kollie, spoke gently about all of this. Jackson was not perfect, the elder said, and like every public official his administration had controversies. But those controversies, the elder said, should not erase the things he did for the county. He carried Bong with him wherever he went.

Four times he asked

Behind the warmth of Saturday sits a record that is hard to read. In 2005, Jackson ran on the COTOL ticket and received 13,931 votes, or 7.8 percent, finishing fourth. In 2011, running for the Unity Party, he received 29,023 votes, or 25.56 percent, and finished second to Henry Willie Yallah, who received 29,804. The final margin from the National Elections Commission was 781 votes.

Seven hundred and eighty-one. It is a number small enough to fit in a single crowded church. It is the distance between the Senate and a long goodbye.

After that near miss, the support slipped away. In 2014, again as a Unity Party candidate, Jackson received 4,038 votes, or 10.4 percent, and finished third behind Jewel Howard-Taylor, who won with 13,672. In 2023, under the Rainbow Alliance, he received 6,552 votes, or 3.70 percent, and finished fifth in a race won by Johnny K. Kpehe with 78,122 votes. For a man who had once come within a whisper of the Senate, it must have been a lonely thing to watch the numbers shrink.

Bong has always been a difficult county to read. Sirleaf herself once said the people of Bong had been deceitful to her, after the 2011 returns. She received 48,374 votes there in the first round, or 42.9 percent, against 37,787 for Winston Tubman of the Congress for Democratic Change. In the November runoff her support climbed to 52,949 votes, or 83.45 percent, after the CDC declared it would not participate. With 467,561 people according to the 2022 census, Bong is Liberia’s third most populous county, and its voters have never been predictable.

Why gratitude does not always become a vote

Many people at the funeral wondered quietly why the love of Saturday had not appeared on election day. Nobody had a single answer. Elections turn on political alliances, party loyalty, personalities, changing priorities and the arrival of new faces. A politician can oversee projects that serve thousands and still fail to turn that record into votes years later.

But a funeral asks a different question. A ballot asks who should lead next. A funeral asks what a person meant. The woman who sits in the hall Jackson built, the player he encouraged, the student who stayed in school were not choosing between candidates on Saturday. They were answering for a life, and the answers came easily.

What love asks of the living

A community leader said the thing many in Pelelei were thinking. History will eventually judge every public official, the leader said, but Jackson deserves to be remembered for the development work done during his time as superintendent. He helped advance projects that touched public infrastructure, education and basic services. The best way to honor him,

the leader said, is not merely to praise him at his funeral, but to preserve the lessons of his service and keep building a better Bong County.

It is a heavy request, and a fair one. Love that comes late is still love, and the people of Bong showed on Saturday that theirs was real. But a hall that feeds the needy needs hands to keep it open. A scholarship needs someone to remember it. A stadium that no longer needs palm branches needs someone to remember why.

Jackson asked Bong County for a seat four times and did not get it. On Saturday, in the town where he was born, Bong gave him something that no election could: a crowd of people, speaking one after another, telling him that he had mattered. He was 74. He could not hear it. The county, at last, said it anyway.

World.title: Three Liberians Face U.S. Prison, Deportation Over Votes
World.content:
Three Liberians living in Minnesota are among ten immigrants indicted by a U.S. federal grand jury for allegedly voting or registering to vote while not citizens. Prosecutors say most of the votes were cast in the November 2024 presidential election. They face up to five years in prison, and U.S. officials warn deportation could follow.

Monrovia – She is 61. He is 48. The youngest is 43. Somewhere in Minnesota, three Liberians who built lives far from home now face the possibility of losing them, over a ballot.

By Rodney D. Sieh



A federal grand jury in Minneapolis on September 24 indicted Bhator Konah Bryant, Alan Barbu Kargbo and Chis Adam Pettiquoi, along with seven other immigrants, on charges of voting or registering to vote in American elections when they were not American citizens.

Of the ten people charged, from eight different countries, Liberia had the most.

What they are accused of

Prosecutors say Bryant falsely claimed to be a U.S. citizen when she registered to vote on October 18, 2024. They do not allege she cast a ballot.

Kargbo and Pettiquoi are each accused of going further. Prosecutors say both falsely claimed citizenship and voted in Minnesota on November 5, 2024, the day Americans chose their president.

All three have already appeared before a federal judge. None has been convicted.

More than prison at stake

On paper, the penalties are heavy: up to five years in prison and a fine of up to US$250,000 for falsely claiming citizenship to vote, and up to one year and US$100,000 for voting as a non-citizen.

But for an immigrant, the harder blow may be the one not written in the charge sheet. U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin made sure no one missed it.

“Our message to aliens who vote in American elections is clear: we will find you, arrest you, and you will face the consequences, including criminal charges and deportation,” he said.

For a 61-year-old woman, that could mean being sent back to a country she may have left decades ago, away from children, grandchildren and everything she has built since.

A community that fought for its place

The charges hit close to home for Minnesota’s Liberian community, one of the largest in the United States, centered in Brooklyn Park and the suburbs around Minneapolis.

Many came running from the civil wars of the 1990s. For years they lived on temporary permission to stay, renewed one deadline at a time, never sure whether the next announcement would send them home. It was not until the Liberian Refugee Immigration Fairness Act of 2019 that many finally got a path to green cards and, eventually, the right to vote.

For people who waited that long for a ballot, the idea that some Liberians may have cast one without the right to do so is painful. And at a time when the Trump administration is pushing hard against immigrants, many in the diaspora will worry that three names on a federal indictment could cast a shadow over thousands who did everything by the book.

Presumed innocent

The case was investigated by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Homeland Security Investigations, with help from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

U.S. prosecutors were careful to note that an indictment is only an accusation. Bryant, Kargbo and Pettiquoi are presumed innocent unless proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt.

World.title: Liberia: Sinoe Labour Commissioner Faces Harassment Claims as County Attorney Dispute Deepens
World.content:
GREENVILLE, Sinoe County — New video and photographic evidence obtained by FrontPage Africa has raised questions about the conduct of officials associated with the Sinoe County Labour Commissioner’s Office, amid competing accounts over the handcuffing of a Chinese national and a separate confrontation involving the County Attorney and county officials.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

The controversy comes as questions continue to surround an incident involving Sinoe County Attorney Cllr. Mmonbeydo Nadine Joah, who became involved in a dispute with Labour Commissioner Cleophas Nyantee Mah and County Superintendent Alexander Nah Slewion.



Mah, however, strongly denies allegations that he or members of his team have harassed, intimidated or extorted business operators.

He told FrontPage Africa that neither he nor members of his team have demanded unauthorized payments from investors or subjected them to harassment.

What the Footage Shows

Video obtained by FrontPage Africa appears to show a Chinese businessman seated on a green plastic chair with his hands handcuffed.

A man in plain clothes, holding what appears to be documents and a mobile phone, is seen speaking to the businessman and pointing in his direction.

The incident appears to have occurred inside a container-like office at what sources identified as a mining operation.

Mah acknowledged that the incident occurred but disputed accounts portraying him as responsible for the arrest and handcuffing of the Chinese national.

According to Mah, the incident occurred several months ago and was unrelated to the more recent confrontation involving the County Attorney and Superintendent.

He said he went to the location in his capacity as Labour Commissioner and that the Chinese national was arrested and handcuffed by members of the Liberia National Police who were investigating an incident.

Mah said his office subsequently imposed a fine on the company, but that the County Attorney later revoked the fine.

He also said the County Attorney subsequently accused him of abuse of office and took legal action against him.

Mah maintained that the matter was eventually dismissed by the Magisterial Court.

The County Attorney did not respond to FrontPage Africa’s request for comment on the matter.

Competing Accounts of the Mining-Site Incident

Darius Shajay Nagbeh Sr., Superintendent of Kpanyan Statutory District, disputed Mah’s account of what happened.

Nagbeh told FrontPage Africa that the incident occurred within his district at the Glorious Mining Company operation site following an incident involving the death of a miner.

According to Nagbeh, the County Attorney had established a team, led by him, to investigate the circumstances surrounding the death.

He alleged that Mah arrived at the site accompanied by a Community Police officer and participated in the arrest and handcuffing of the Chinese national.

Nagbeh also disputed the amount of the fine, saying the Labour Commissioner imposed a hefty fine on the company. Mah’s account also referenced a fine, but the parties differ over the circumstances surrounding its imposition and subsequent revocation.

Nagbeh said the County Attorney later revoked the fine and initiated legal proceedings against Mah, accusing him of abuse of office.

Mah maintains that the arrest itself was carried out by the Liberia National Police and that his role was limited to labour enforcement.

Allegations of Extortion

Separate allegations have emerged concerning the treatment of business operators in Greenville.

Sources familiar with the situation allege that members of the Labour Commissioner’s team have visited businesses operated by members of the Fula community and demanded payments allegedly outside Liberia’s established labour and work-permit procedures.

The allegations have not been independently verified.

Mah categorically denied the claims, saying neither he nor his team has engaged in extortion or intimidation.

He said his office recently dispatched the Deputy Labour Commissioner to collect information from businesses as part of its reporting responsibilities.

According to Mah, the dispute escalated after the County Attorney allegedly ordered the Deputy Labour Commissioner arrested while he was carrying out his official duties.

Mah said he resisted the arrest of his deputy after being informed of it and was subsequently accused by the County Attorney of obstructing justice.

Dispute Over County Attorney’s Intervention

The competing accounts have now become intertwined with a separate confrontation involving the County Attorney, the Labour Commissioner and Superintendent Slewion.

Mah said the County Attorney later went to his office with police officers to arrest him and his deputy.

He said they resisted the attempted arrests and that a confrontation followed.

According to Mah, the Superintendent became involved after being called to intervene, and the situation subsequently escalated.

Slewion offered a different account.

He told FrontPage Africa that Mah complained to him that the County Attorney had gone to his office to arrest him and asked for his intervention.

The Superintendent said he invited Joah to his office because the dispute involved officials from different government institutions and he wanted to mediate.

According to Slewion, Cllr. Joah declined to participate in the proposed intervention.

He said that when he later went to the Labour Commissioner’s office, he asked Cllr. Joah to stop recording and sit down for dialogue.

Slewion said Cllr. Joah refused and accused him of obstructing justice.

He further alleged that he was assaulted during the ensuing confrontation and had to be taken away from the scene.

The Superintendent denied knowledge of claims that Cllr. Joah’s phone was seized or that she was assaulted.

He said he has sought the intervention of Senator Augustine Chea, the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General over continued misunderstanding between him and the County Attorney but that the dispute remains unresolved.

County Attorney’s Hospitalization

Sources told FrontPage Africa that Joah was later taken to F.J. Grant Hospital following the confrontation.

There are also allegations that a man identified as Cornelius, reportedly associated with the Superintendent, struck the County Attorney during the confrontation.

Those allegations have not been independently established.

Cllr. Joah did not respond to FrontPage Africa’s requests for comment.

FrontPage Africa has gathered that the Ministry of Justice is reviewing aspects of the dispute.

Questions Over Official Conduct

The competing accounts raise broader questions about how labour and other regulatory authorities are exercising enforcement powers in Sinoe County.

Labour inspections, work-permit enforcement and related administrative actions are expected to be carried out under established laws and procedures.

The dispute also raises questions about the boundaries between the Labour Commissioner’s Office, the County Administration, the County Attorney’s Office and law-enforcement authorities when government agencies become involved in the same matter.

The growing controversy has prompted calls for an impartial investigation into the competing allegations.

World.title: Social Media Influencer Prophet Key And US-based Liberian Become Latest Victim of Relationship ‘Deception’
World.content:
Varney and Zoey

MONROVIA – The room was ready. Relatives had contributed money, the food was cooked, and a DJ was waiting for his cue. Uncle Alfred had opened his home. By every outward sign, a Liberian family was about to celebrate an engagement.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

Then the groom-to-be, a US-based Liberian known publicly only as Varney, picked up the microphone. He began the way such speeches usually begin, with thanks to the host, the contributors, the cooks and the DJ. Within minutes, the evening belonged to something else entirely.



Scene Two: A Man, a Phone, a Border

Two days later, on the late afternoon of Saturday, October 3, 2026, a different kind of broadcast began. Social media influencer Justin Nayapougma Oldpa Yeazeahn, widely known as “Prophet Key,” went live on Facebook. He was crying, and he did not hide it.

He said he had returned from a business trip to his home county, Nimba, to find a nearly empty house. His fiancée, an Ivorian woman by his description, was gone. So was his only daughter. So, he claimed, was US$33,000.

Together, the two videos made one of the most talked-about weeks on Liberian social media in recent memory.

The Groom’s Long Preamble

Varney’s speech did not start with an accusation. It started with a relationship history, and it was a candid one. He said he had known his girlfriend, Zoey Darblo, since 2021. The four years since, in his telling, had been a cycle of quarrels and silences. She would stop speaking to him for two days, three days, even a week, then return and ask why he had called. He would apologize. He admitted he can be sarcastic.

Plans to formalize the relationship were repeatedly delayed. He said he had been due to travel in July and postponed. He postponed again to August. At that point, he said, she told him it was over. It took Uncle Alfred stepping in as intermediary to bring the two back to the table.

Those details matter because they frame what came next. Varney was not presenting himself as a man blindsided from nowhere. He was describing a couple already on thin ice, who had decided, with family help, to try again.

The Unlocked Phone

The turning point, as Varney described it, came the day before the event. He said he had earlier asked Zoey to open her WhatsApp and that she had not. Then, he claimed, he found it unlocked.

What he said he found was, in his words, a woman in conversation with four different men, two of them actively. He singled out one who he said works at the National Social Security and Welfare Corporation (NASSCORP) and another he described as married with a child. He told the room she had once insisted she never got involved with married men.

He read portions of the alleged messages aloud. Guests who had come to celebrate heard the contents of a private phone read over a party-hall microphone. The engagement did not go ahead.

Clips of the moment spread fast, and the early response was largely comic. Memes and jokes filled timelines. The laughter was, for a while, the main story.

“Immigration, Don’t Let Her Pass”

There was no comedy in the Prophet’s broadcast, even if some viewers reacted with disbelief. He cried openly and repeated the same sentence like a refrain: she ran away with my daughter.

His appeal was precise and urgent. He believed two Ivorian buses were approaching the border and that his fiancée was aboard one. He addressed Liberian and Ivorian immigration officers directly, asking them to stop the vehicles. The buses, he stressed, had not yet crossed. The window was closing.

Prophet Key and family

He named the woman on air, acknowledging he might have misspelled her name. He also announced a US$1,500 reward for credible information leading to her and the child. With no message left behind, he said he could only presume she had gone to Côte d’Ivoire, a conviction rather than a confirmed fact.

Everything described here comes from his own account. No response from the woman has been published, and no authority has publicly confirmed any investigation, stop or arrest.

A Name Already Known

Prophet Key arrived at this moment with a long public record, and Liberian audiences know it well.

He returned to Liberia after years abroad, a homecoming linked to the government of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai and the Unity Party. Controversy followed. In 2024, the National Elections Commission blocked him from the Nimba County Senatorial By-election, alleging that he had submitted a fraudulent Biometric Voter Registration card.

He rejected the allegation, saying he had registered on April 27, 2023 and obtained his card legitimately. Fact-checkers countered that the BVR number he presented was invalid, absent from the NEC system and missing from the 2023 Final Registration Roll.

In February 2026, the Supreme Court of Liberia jailed him for contempt over remarks about members of the judiciary. He spent six months in the Monrovia Central Prison and was released after completing the term and meeting the Court’s conditions.

None of that bears on whether his fiancée left with his daughter and his money. But it explains why his latest video found such a ready audience: people were already watching him.

What the Two Men Had in Common

Set side by side, the incidents differ sharply in scale. One involves a missing child and a large sum of cash. The other involves wounded pride and a ruined party. Yet the parallels run deeper than timing.

Both chose the crowd over the closed door. Neither went first to a counselor, or, as far as is publicly known, to a formal process. Facebook was the first stop, whether as a rescue tool or a stage.

Both told their side first. The women in both stories have been described, discussed and judged by thousands of strangers without a published word in reply. That imbalance shapes everything readers think they know.

Both stories hit people who are not on camera. A young girl is at the center of one. Several men, one of them said to be married, were named in the other. Relatives who gave their time and money watched an intimate dispute unfold in front of them.

The Law Is Slower Than the Feed

The Prophet’s appeal highlights a basic mismatch. A live video can reach thousands in seconds. A police report, a custody claim or a cross-border request moves at the speed of paperwork. A parent who believes a child has been taken abroad usually has to go through police, immigration and, where relevant, courts and international channels. Whether any of that has begun in this case is unknown.

Public pleas can occasionally speed things up, but they carry risks. A named woman accused of theft and taking a child can face hostility before any facts are established. If the claims prove incomplete, the damage cannot be undone.

The Cost of the Clip

Varney’s case raises a different problem. The messages he described were private, and the guests who heard them were never asked whether they wanted to. Accusations of infidelity, even if true, are not usually settled in front of a DJ and a room of relatives. And once such a moment is filmed and shared, it follows everyone involved: the woman accused, the men named, the host who offered his home.

It is easy to read the viral moment as a punchline. It is harder to remember that the central figures will still be living with it long after the jokes stop.

When the Scroll Moves On

Public heartbreak is nothing new, but social media has changed its shape. A confession that once lived in gossip now lives in a link. A plea that once went to a village elder now goes to a worldwide audience, with all the sympathy and cruelty that implies.

By next week, other stories will fill the timeline. But a father in Nimba will still be waiting for news, a family in a party hall will still be sorting through what happened, and two women who have yet to be heard will still be at the center of narratives they did not write.

World.title: Liberia: National Traditional Liaison Officer Says CDC Could Win Bong Again as Unity Party Battles Internal Divisions
World.content:
Mr. Kollie further claimed that the Unity Party faces serious internal divisions in Bong, which he believes could open political space for the CDC. He attributed part of the division to disagreements among party actors over political influence and access to county leadership

GBARNGA, Bong County – A senior Liberian government official from Bong County says the opposition Coalition for Democratic Change (CDC) has a realistic chance of winning the county in the next presidential election, arguing that divisions inside the governing Unity Party (UP) could prevent it from consolidating support.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

William B. S. Kollie, Liberia’s National Traditional Liaison Officer and a native of Bong, said the CDC cannot be written off in the county,



particularly if it keeps its own house in order and strengthens ties with local political actors. “The CDC still has the potential to win Bong because the party has settled some of the differences that affected its performance. If the Unity Party remains divided, the CDC can take advantage of that situation,” Mr. Kollie said.

A county that changes allegiance

Mr. Kollie’s argument rests on Bong’s voting history over the past two decades, in which the county has moved from being a stronghold of former President Ellen Johnson-Sirleaf and the Unity Party to being an important base for former President George Weah and the CDC.

In 2005, Mrs. Johnson-Sirleaf defeated Mr. Weah decisively in Bong in the runoff, despite finishing third in the county in the first round. In 2011, she won 83.45 percent of the county’s runoff vote. In 2017, the pattern reversed, with Mr. Weah taking about 64.2 percent against Joseph Boakai’s 35.8 percent.

In 2023, Mr. Weah carried Bong again, but by a much smaller margin. He received 72,159 votes (52.92 percent) to Mr. Boakai’s 64,194 (47.08 percent), a lead of 7,965 votes, or 5.84 percentage points.

Mr. Kollie said the 2023 result should not be read as the CDC losing relevance in Bong. In his view, it shows the party retains a substantial base that could prove decisive if the Unity Party fails to resolve its differences.

“Bong politics is not permanently owned by any political party. We have seen this county move from the Unity Party to the CDC, and the party that organizes its people and builds stronger local relationships will have an advantage,” he said.

Mr. Kollie said the CDC has addressed some of the internal differences that, in his assessment, contributed to its underperformance in parts of Bong during the 2023 election period.

He pointed to the political importance of former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor, a Bong native, saying that having a major county figure on the CDC ticket had given the party an important link to voters there. He argued that the party’s ability to settle differences among its actors could make it more competitive going forward.

Funeral turnout as a political signal

Mr. Kollie also cited the funeral of Philip Taylor, son of Mrs. Howard-Taylor, as evidence of continuing ties between the CDC, the National Patriotic Party (NPP) and parts of the Bong population.

He said the ceremony in Gbarnga drew significant public attention even though Mr. Taylor was not a prominent political figure in the county. According to Mr. Kollie, residents, particularly CDC and NPP supporters, turned out along the route from the Old Iron Gate to the Gbarnga Administration Building to pay their respects. He said this showed that structures associated with both parties remain active in Bong.

He contrasted this with the reception for the remains of former Bong Superintendent Dr. Ranney Banama Jackson, which arrived in Gbarnga on Friday ahead of funeral ceremonies. Mr. Kollie described the turnout as relatively poor, given Dr. Jackson’s long association with the county and his former role as superintendent.

He cautioned against reading the difference purely as a measure of the two men’s importance. It could also reflect changing political networks, he said, and the ability of political organizations to mobilize supporters around particular events. He suggested political actors in Bong should reflect on

shifting loyalties and the relationship between leaders and ordinary citizens.

Claims of Unity Party divisions

Mr. Kollie further claimed that the Unity Party faces serious internal divisions in Bong, which he believes could open political space for the CDC. He attributed part of the division to disagreements among party actors over political influence and access to county leadership.

He also pointed to allegations involving Bong County Superintendent Lorleyah Hawa Norris. According to Mr. Kollie, some political actors allege that Superintendent Norris has been empowering or giving political space to individuals associated with the opposition CDC.

Those allegations are contested. They are Mr. Kollie’s account of claims circulating among political actors and could not be independently verified. No response from Superintendent Norris or Unity Party leadership was available at the time of writing.

Mr. Kollie said the controversy could deepen disagreements within the UP if members believe individuals or institutions linked to the government are creating opportunities for opposition actors. He argued that a governing party needs a cohesive county-level structure to defend its support, particularly where presidential elections have produced large swings.

Why he sees an opening for the CDC

Mr. Kollie said the CDC could benefit from what he described as uncertainty within the Unity Party’s Bong structure, because the county’s electorate has shown it will change allegiance when it perceives weakness in a dominant organization.

He said the UP cannot assume its 2023 national victory automatically gives it a lasting advantage in the county. The CDC’s task, he said, is to consolidate its existing support, repair remaining internal differences and maintain relationships with influential communities and political actors across Bong.

Political organizations, he stressed, must do more than rely on national popularity. Clan relationships, personalities, local development records and grassroots organization can all determine how voters behave.

World.title: Electronic voting: Africa should take a leaf from Brazil
World.content:
Africa counts its votes in days. Brazil counts 158 million in hours, and our governments should pay attention

Brazil counted the votes of more than 158 million people in less time than it takes a Lusaka minibus to crawl from town to Chilenje on a Friday evening. Zambia, with fewer than nine million registered voters, needed five days.

Zambia’s electoral process can benefit significantly from the implementation of electronic voting.

Money alone does not explain that gap. Design does. African governments should study it closely before the next disputed count, the next standoff outside a totalling centre and the next petition pushes another country to the edge.

A bigger country that finishes first

The figures are stark. Brazil registered 158,745,463 voters for its October presidential election, while the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) certified 8,786,300 for our August general elections.

Brazil’s electorate is nearly 18 times larger than ours. Yet Brazilians usually know their winner within two to three hours of the polls closing, while Zambians waited until 18 August, five days after polling day, before President Hakainde Hichilema was declared winner. Every electoral commission on this continent should be asking how the bigger country manages to finish first.

How Brazil counts 158 million votes

The answer begins with a fully electronic voting system. Roughly 560,000 secure electronic voting machines, the urnas eletrônicas, are spread across a country that stretches from the Amazon to the southern plains.

A voter walks in, punches in the candidate’s number, confirms and leaves. There is no ballot paper to fold, no box to stuff and no pile of papers to sort by candidate under a weak light at two in the morning.

Voting closes at 5pm local time, and each machine then calculates its own totals and prints a physical results sheet, the boletim de urna. That sheet is the heart of the system. It is the polling station’s result, printed on paper, at the place where the votes were cast, the moment voting ends.

From there, the encrypted results travel over secure, isolated networks to the Superior Electoral Court (TSE) in Brasília. The machines are not connected to the internet while people vote, and transmission begins only once the count is locked.

Because the figures arrive already counted, the central computers in Brasília simply add them up. That is why Brazil regularly processes more than 95 per cent of the national vote, and projects a winner, before most families have finished their evening meal.

The dangerous gap after the polls close

Set that against the African experience. On our continent, the most dangerous stretch of any election is not the campaign. It is the gap between the last voter leaving the queue and the commission chairperson reading out the final figure.

Rumours thrive in that gap. WhatsApp voice notes announce winners nobody has declared, party agents circulate their own tallies and crowds gather outside totalling centres. Every hour of delay looks to someone like an hour of manipulation, whether or not anything is wrong.

Kenya learned this the hard way in 2017, when the Supreme Court of Kenya annulled a presidential election over irregularities in the transmission of results. The ballots were not the problem. The journey of the numbers from the polling station to the national tally was.

Brazil’s model works because it closes that gap almost completely. When a machine prints its result at the polling station door, every party agent can photograph it, and every candidate can then compare those photographs with what the national electoral court publishes. A doctored figure at headquarters would stand out against thousands of printed sheets already sitting in the phones of rival camps.

Speed alone does not calm a nation, but speed combined with verification does. A fast count that anyone can check leaves very little room for the suspicion that so often turns into violence.

Namibia’s warning

Namibia offers the warning every African reformer should read before buying a single machine. In 2014, it became the first African country to use electronic voting machines in a national election, and it used them again in 2019. The machines carried one fatal flaw: they produced no voter-verified paper trail.

After the 2019 presidential vote, independent candidate Dr Panduleni Itula went to court. In February 2020, the Supreme Court of Namibia ruled that using the machines without a verifiable paper trail was unconstitutional. The court left the result standing, but the electronic experiment was over.

By the 2024 elections, Namibia had returned to paper ballots, and the return brought its own pain. Ballot shortages, long queues and an extension of voting followed, and the opposition Independent Patriots for Change refused to accept the outcome.

Namibia did not fail because technology fails. It failed because trust was never built into the machine, and a voter pressed a button and had to take it on faith that the button did what it promised. The lesson for Lusaka, Lilongwe, Harare and Kinshasa is therefore not to avoid electronic voting, but to never adopt it without paper.

Three locks on one door

An African version of the Brazilian model should go one step further than Brazil itself. Every vote cast on a machine should print a small slip the voter can see before it drops into a sealed box, and every machine should print its station result at closing. Both should be auditable against the digital count.

That places three locks on one door: the digital record, the voter’s paper slip and the printed station result. Anyone wanting to rig the outcome would have to defeat all three, in public, in front of agents from every party.

Starlink and the end of the connectivity excuse

For years, connectivity has been the standard excuse. How do you send results from a school in Shang’ombo, an island polling station on Lake Bangweulu or a village in the Luangwa Valley where a phone signal is little more than a rumour?

Satellite internet has removed that excuse. Low-earth-orbit services such as Starlink, now licensed to operate in Zambia, can connect a polling station anywhere a terminal can see the sky. A dish on a classroom roof, powered by a solar panel, can deliver an encrypted station result to Lusaka as quickly as a fibre line in Rhodes Park.

No electoral commission, however, should rest a nation’s democracy on a single foreign private provider. The sensible design is layered, with satellite as the main route, local mobile networks as backup and the physical memory card and printed result sheet carried by road as the final fallback. If every electronic channel fails, the paper still exists and the count can be rebuilt.

How it would work in Zambia

The first step is to start small. The ECZ could pilot machines at by-elections, where the stakes are lower and mistakes are cheaper, and every registered party should have access to independent audits of the machine software before a single vote is cast.

The second is to change the law. The Electoral Process Act would need to provide for the paper slip, the printed station result, the posting of that result at the polling station door and the right of every agent to photograph it.

The third is to publish everything. A public ECZ portal should display the result of every polling station, stream by stream, the moment it arrives, alongside a scanned copy of the printed sheet. A citizen in Kasama should be able to check her own polling station’s figure on her phone before she goes to bed.

None of this happens in one electoral cycle. Brazil introduced its machines in 1996 and spent years expanding them before the whole country voted electronically, and trust took decades to build. Africa need not wait that long, because it can learn from both Brazil’s success and Namibia’s stumble.

The cost of doing nothing

Some will say the money would be better spent elsewhere. They should count the cost of the alternative: tense nights, security deployments around totalling centres, months of court petitions and governments beginning their terms under a cloud of doubt. A fast, verifiable count is not a luxury for a young democracy. It is a guarantee of peace.

Zambia’s next general election is five years away, which is enough time to pilot, legislate, audit and train. The machines, the satellites and the model already exist, and what is missing is a decision.

Brazil showed this month that a nation of 158 million can know its president before dinner goes cold. Zambia, with fewer than nine million voters, has no reason to keep waiting five days.

World.title: Kasempa electoral officer calls for peace during nominations
World.content:
Kasempa District Electoral Officer Beston Kajoba has urged residents of Maako Ward to maintain peace during the upcoming nomination process, following violence that disrupted the filing in of nominations in the August elections.

Mr Kajoba appealed to Maako residents to remain peaceful during the nominations for the Maako Ward by-election which are scheduled for Thursday, 8 October 2026.

He said this during a briefing for aspiring candidates, election agents, the media, monitors and observers in Kasempa today.

“Our appeal this time around is to the people of Maako let us not experience what we experienced last time. So our appeal is, please, let us not go through that,” He added.

Mr Kajoba said Maako Ward by-election is among several that the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) will conduct on the same date nationwide, including in Mbala and Lumezi.

He said the by-elections had been caused by candidate deaths, uncontested seats in the recent general election, and nullified results by the Local Government Elections Tribunal.

Mr Kajoba said the ECZ expects candidates, political parties, supporters and other stakeholders to conduct themselves peacefully before, during and after the nominations, given what happened previously.

He urged political parties and candidates to adhere to the Electoral Code of Conduct, and election agents, monitors and observers to exercise professionalism and integrity.

Mr Kajoba said the Commission had lined up voter education, conflict management and staff training ahead of the by-election, and would also engage youths and women in preparation.

Mr Kajoba commended ECZ staff for passing on training from the general election, saying this ensured no candidate was turned away for failing to meet requirements.

“We never experienced a situation where a candidate was turned away or disqualified because they were missing this and that,” he said.

World.title: President Hichilema highlights Lobito corridor’s role in accelerating AfCFTA
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has emphasised the importance of the Lobito Corridor, as one of the responses to accelerating the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).

President Hichilema says the Lobito Corridor should be seen as a building block for connecting Africa, calling on Angola, Democratic Republic of Congo and Zambia, to work together, in collaboration with cooperating partners, to ensure the successful implementation of the Corridor.

Speaking when he officially opened the Second Lobito Corridor Coordination meeting in Lusaka, President Hichilema said that the corridor will in turn drive the desire to accelerate economic growth and benefits that come with such developments, including creation of jobs for the young people.

The President observed that Africa is vulnerable because of fragmentations and that the Lobito Corridor remains integral to the realisation of AfCFTA.

And President Hichilema noted that the ecosystem and peace, security, and stability of countries are largely anchored on actions, opportunities created for the young people across the three countries and beyond.

“There is a youthful population on our continent, we must provide opportunities for that youthful population, starting with education, skills, and also opportunities, formal jobs, informal jobs, self-employment, extremely important,” he stated.

Meanwhile, President Hichilema wants to see deliberate joint ventures amongst investors, businesses, partners from Congo, Angola, Zambia, the SADC region and Europe.

The Head of State underscored the importance of individual countries and responsibility to support their populations.

“When the region is connected, who picks a weapon against another? Because you don’t want to destroy your own business, whose operations are in Angola, in Congo, DRC, in Zambia, eventually Tanzania and elsewhere,” he said.

President Hichilema suggested that the engine room meeting pays particular attention to ensure that smooth flow of business activities is enhanced in the three countries and the SADC region at large.

He added that initiatives like the Lobito corridor also support the Grow Zambia Agenda in various sectors including tourism, mining, energy, trade and investment.

Representing the President of Angola, Joao Manuel Lourenco, Angola’s Minister of Transport Ricardo D’Abreu stated that the Lobito Corridor is a national priority for his country.

Dr D’Abreu explained that, it is in Angolan territory that Port of Lobito and 1300 kilometers of the Benguela Railway are located, the most direct link between the mining heartland of Africa and the Atlantic.

He said that the corridor serves more than eight million Angolans in transporting both minerals and other products.

“The guidance of President Lourenço is clear, to transform a transport corridor into an effective economic development corridor. Copper and other minerals are already being transported to Lobito, while sulphur and food products are reabsorbed inland, together with domestic Angolan Cargo using the same railways,” he noted.

Dr D’Abreu stressed the need to deal with border challenges, noting that the greatest immediate gains on the railway can be reflected with the time it spends on the border.

“To keep the Atlantic platform viable and open to cargo and minerals, Angola will work with both Zambia and DRC to transform the Angola Luau border crossing so that it operates as a one stop border in order to make our single window for foreign trade interoperable,” he said.

Leading the delegation from the Democratic Republic of Congo, Minister of Planning and Coordination of Development Aid Guylain Mbwizya stated that, the rehabilitation and modernisation of the railway network must form part of a coherent logistics chain, supported by connecting roads, efficient logistics platforms, and appropriate energy and digital infrastructure.

Dr Mbwizya charged that the vision requires a multisectoral approach linking railway and road infrastructure, logistics, energy, digital infrastructure, trade facilitation, vocational training and the development of the territories along the corridor.

He made emphasis on ensuring consistency between corridor investments and national development priorities, within the framework of balanced spatial development.

“The ambition is to move beyond corridors that are simply transit and resource-evacuation routes towards an integrated economic corridor capable of stimulating productive investment, supporting industrialisation, unlocking agricultural potential, developing small and medium-sized enterprises and creating sustainable jobs for our populations.

He added that the real impact will ultimately be measured by their capacity to open up previously isolated territories, strengthen regional trade, promote the local processing of resources and concretely improve the living conditions of the people.

And he reaffirmed DRC’s commitment to strengthening cooperation with Angola and Zambia, as well as with all partners, in order to accelerate the implementation of the initiative.

He said that the Democratic Republic of Congo attaches particular importance to the preparation of bankable projects, the mobilisation of financing, and the establishment of governance and monitoring mechanisms capable of translating our shared vision into concrete results.

World.title: Musokotwane reiterates significance of Lobito Corridor in fostering productivity
World.content:
Minister of Finance and National Planning Situmbeko Musokotwane has said Zambia is positioning the Lobito Corridor as a key instrument for driving an export-led economy, attracting Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), creating jobs and increasing productivity.

Dr Musokotwane charged that the corridor must go beyond facilitating the movement of goods and become an economic corridor that stimulates industrialisation, business opportunities and production across Zambia.

He said Zambia’s vision is to use the corridor to competitively and efficiently export commodities, while developing local capacity so that Zambians actively participate in economic activities generated by increased investment.

Dr Musokotwane was speaking in Lusaka today during the official opening of the Second Lobito Corridor Coordination Meeting, which has brought together Angola, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Zambia and cooperating partners.

“The three governments established the Lobito Corridor Coordinating Framework, popularly known as the “Engine Room,” after recognising that numerous meetings and pronouncements were not translating into sufficient action on the ground.

Dr Musokotwane explained that the framework, established with support from the World Bank, provides a platform for the three governments and their partners to regularly review progress, make collective decisions and ensure that agreed actions are implemented.

He explained that the Engine Room also facilitates coordination on cross-border transit and investment issues while ensuring technical follow-through among ministries, agencies and development partners.

Dr Musokotwane disclosed that Zambia had made progress towards improving road connectivity along the Lobito Corridor, with the financial package already secured through partnerships involving the African Development Bank (AfDB), the Millennium Challenge Corporation and the Zambian government.

He said the focus was now on expediting procurement and commencing construction.

“The railway will form a critical part of Zambia’s export-led economic strategy by enabling commodities to reach international markets more cheaply, quickly and competitively,” he added.

Dr Musokotwane said Zambia’s economic vision also includes attracting significant FDI, building the capacity of citizens to participate meaningfully in investment activities and creating a conducive business environment.

He further said the government will ensure that Zambians were not merely spectators as foreign investment comes into the country, but will instead acquire the skills and capacity required to participate in the resulting economic activities.

Dr Musokotwane said the Lobito Corridor will also support the implementation of the Grow Zambia Agenda by providing a platform for increasing production and exports.

Speaking at the same event, Head of the Presidential Delivery Unit (PDU), Kusobile Kamwambi, said the Meeting provides an opportunity for the three countries and development partners to review progress, address emerging challenges and strengthen coordination mechanisms for the full operationalisation of the corridor.

She said the corridor is strategically important for facilitating the movement of commodities from Zambia and the DRC westward to the Port of Lobito in Angola, as well as the movement of cargo eastward into Zambia and the DRC.

She said the Lobito Corridor coordinating mechanism, referred to as the “engine room,” was established to enhance coordination and scale up infrastructure, trade and investment activities across the region.

And World Bank Group Managing Director for Operations Anna Bjerde called for faster implementation of projects under the Lobito Corridor, saying political commitment and financing are no longer the main obstacles to the initiative.

Ms Bjerde said the focus should now be on operationalising the corridor with greater momentum and speed, while ensuring that infrastructure investments are matched by investments in energy, skills, agribusiness, water, land and secondary cities.

She pointed out that this is critical to transforming the Lobito Corridor from a transport route into a fully integrated economic corridor capable of creating jobs and generating broad-based economic benefits.

She charged that Zambia, Angola and DRC possess significant but largely untapped economic assets, including agricultural potential, industrial capacity, energy resources and strategic trade linkages.

“Zambia and the DRC together account for more than 17 percent of global copper supply and more than 70 percent of cobalt production, while Angola provides an important Atlantic gateway to international markets,” added Ms Bjerde.

She said the economic value of these resources depends largely on how efficiently they can reach markets and how effectively they contribute to local economic development.

Ms Bjerde noted that the corridor also has the potential to transform the lives of an estimated 23 million people living along its route.

“An additional eight to 10 million people are expected to enter working age across Angola, the DRC and Zambia by 2030, making job creation an important measure of the corridor’s success,” added Ms Bjerde.

She also announced the launch of Locomotive, a corridor monitoring tool that tracks projects under implementation and their status.

Ms Bjerde also disclosed that the International Finance Corporation (IFC) has identified 118 anchor investment opportunities worth more than US$28 billion across sectors including mining, energy, agribusiness, logistics and auxiliary investments.

She said the World Bank and other development partners were ready to provide the necessary support, but urged the three countries to maintain strong coordination and accelerate implementation.

And Lobito Corridor Transit Transport Facilitation Agency (LCTTFA) Executive Director Amadeu Nunes has called for stronger coordination and faster implementation of agreed measures to ensure the corridor delivers tangible economic benefits to Angola, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Zambia.

Mr Nunes said the Lobito Corridor Engine Room should evolve from being a platform for discussions into a mechanism that accelerates implementation, resolves bottlenecks and delivers measurable results.

He, however, said while significant progress has been made on initiatives such as the Joint Trade Facilitation Roadmap, Locomotive Tracker and Corridor Observatory, there is need to better connect the various work streams and accelerate execution.

Meanwhile, AfDB Director for Infrastructure and Urban Development Mike Salawou is happy with the enhancement of coordination among Zambia, Angola and the DRC, further pledging more support toward the implementation of the Lobito Corridor.

“We are with you on this Corridor and we will not leave you, until this Corridor is transformed,” said Mr Salawou.

World.title: ZUPED commends Government for free education policy
World.content:
The Zambia Union of Professional Educators (ZUPED) has commended Government for introducing the free education policy which has enabled more than 2.6 million learners to return to school.

ZUPED Director for Administration Sharon Mutukwa, says the Government has recorded notable development in the education sector.

Speaking during the Teachers’ Day commemoration in Chilanga today, Ms Mutukwa cited the recruitment of more than 42,000 teachers since 2022, the construction of over 2,800 classroom blocks, new secondary schools, the provision of approximately 1.5 million desks among others.

“These interventions have contributed to learner retention and improved the education sector,” she observed.

Meanwhile, Chilanga Acting District Commissioner, Maureen Chilende urged teachers to support learners facing challenges such as teenage pregnancy, absenteeism and school dropouts.

Officiating at the commemoration, Ms Chilende noted that the implementation of the Re-entry Policy gives teenage mothers an opportunity to return to school and continue their education.

She also commended schools participating in the Presidential Irrigation Initiative Programme, saying it equips learners with practical agricultural skills and contributes to the school feeding programme.

She further urged parents and communities to work closely with teachers to foster quality education.

“Education is a shared responsibility and our children’s success requires all of us to play our part,” Ms Chilende said.

Chilanga South Member of Parliament, Ngenda Situmbeko said the government prioritises education and is working to provide teachers with a conducive working environment.

“The government is doing everything possible to ensure that teachers have a conducive working environment because we need skilled manpower to grow the economy,” Mr Situmbeko said.

And Chilanga District Education Board Secretary, Lenny Longwe, in a poetic speech, praised teachers for their impact on society, describing them as multitaskers who contribute greatly to shaping the future of children.

World.title: Climate expert calls for groundwater management education
World.content:
Climate-Smart Agriculture and Climate Resilience Expert Oliver Bulaya says the rapid expansion of solar-powered irrigation could create a new water crisis if farmers and communities gain access to pumping technology without adequate education on groundwater conservation and sustainable water use.

Dr Bulaya explained that groundwater is part of a wider hydrological system influenced by rainfall, soils, vegetation, forests, wetlands and the ability of landscapes to absorb and retain water.

He said excessive groundwater abstraction, particularly in areas where ecosystems have been degraded, can place increasing pressure on aquifers and undermine long-term water security.

Dr Bulaya said Zambia must guard against the unintended consequences of replacing expensive hydro- or fuel-powered irrigation with solar energy while leaving the management and conservation of the underlying water resource largely unaddressed.

He therefore called for water-use education to become a core component of solar irrigation programmes, rather than treating the installation of solar pumps as an end in itself.

“Farmers and communities should be supported to adopt efficient irrigation methods, schedule irrigation according to crop water requirements, improve soil health, use mulching and rainwater harvesting, and protect forests, wetlands and groundwater recharge areas,” suggested Dr Bulaya.

He said agriculture cannot be called ‘climate-smart’ simply because the pump is powered by the sun because climate-smart agriculture must also protect the natural resources on which future agricultural production depends.

Dr Bulaya stressed that trees, forests, wetlands and healthy soils should be regarded as part of Zambia’s natural water infrastructure.

He noted that when vegetation is removed and soils are degraded, surface runoff can increase while water infiltration may decline, potentially reducing groundwater recharge.

Dr Bulaya also called on the Government, farmers, traditional leaders, development partners, financial institutions, technology providers and civil society organisations to integrate groundwater management and water-conservation education into the expansion of solar-powered irrigation.

World.title: Nkulukusa stresses proper utilisation of public funds
World.content:
Secretary to the Treasury Felix Nkulukusu has stressed the need for proper management of public funds, with focus on the limited resources available for programmes that make the biggest difference in people’s lives.

Speaking when he officially opened the 2027/2029 Medium Term Budget Plan and the 2027 Budget Hearing at Mulungushi International Conference Centre in Lusaka, Mr Nkulukusu disclosed that the 2027 National Budget is being prepared at an important time for the country, with a focus on maintaining economic stability, supporting inclusive growth and delivering the Grow Zambia Agenda.

Mr Nkulukusa also highlighted that rising salaries, increased funding requirements arising from the expansion of constituencies, payment of maize marketing arrears and the possible impact of the 2026/2027 El Niño are putting pressure on the national budget.

Meanwhile, Ministry of Finance and National Planning Permanent Secretary for Budget and Resource Mobilisation Mwaka Mukubesa disclosed that total resources for 2027 are projected at K271.9 billion, representing an increase of K18.8 billion, or 7.4 percent, from the 2026 approved budget.

Ms Mukubesa said that the domestic revenues are projected to increase to K290.1 billion by 2029 from K206.5 billion in 2026, while concessional borrowing is expected to reduce to K33 billion by 2029 from K44.9 billion 2027.

She further highlighted that the discretionary budget will increase from K67.8 billion in 2026 to K86.8 billion in 2027, with the additional resources supporting key programmes including the Constituency Development Funds (CDF), Free Education Policy, School Feeding Programme, Social Cash Transfer and Farmer Input Support Programme (FISP).

World.title: Chama farmer dies after Insecticide ingestion
World.content:
A 54-year-old peasant farmer of Chisani Village in Chama District has died after allegedly drinking poisonous insecticide following a domestic dispute.

The dispute is alleged to have stemmed from an argument over money that was said to have gone missing.

The deceased, identified as Zenga Zimba, reportedly took the poisonous substance, locally used for spraying cotton plants, after suspecting his son of stealing K700 from his house.

“The child had the habit of stealing money and other small items from his father. So when he discovered money was missing, he asked his son if he was the one who had stolen it but the response from the son did not please him,” Eastern Province Police Commanding Officer Robertson Mweemba confirmed the incident.

He said it occurred on Sunday, 4th October, 2026, between 01:00 hours and 13:00 hours.

“The now deceased was rushed to Chikwa Rural Health Post, where he was admitted and received medical attention but later died around 13:00 hours,” he said.

Mr Mweemba said the matter was reported to Chama Police Station around 15:00 hours by a 36-year-old Community Crime Prevention Unit member from the area.

Police have since opened an inquiry into the matter.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 5, 2026
World.content:
press review

Tigray Rebels Withdraw From Mekelle as Fighting Intensifies

Rebel forces in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region have temporarily withdrawn from the regional capital, Mekelle, as fighting with government forces moves closer to the city. The Tigray People's Liberation Front said it relocated its fighters to reduce risks to civilians. The residents said that pro-government forces now control Mekelle and mobile phone services have resumed in parts of the city. The renewed fighting has spread across Tigray, Afar and Amhara, raising fears of a wider conflict in the Horn of Africa. The TPLF recently joined six other armed groups in an alliance seeking to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government. The development comes amid worsening relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea, as well as tensions with Egypt and Sudan, with Ethiopia accusing its neighbours of supporting the rebels. The United Nations has warned that the deteriorating security situation is disrupting humanitarian operations. The latest violence threatens the fragile 2022 peace agreement that ended a devastating two-year civil war in Tigray, which an African Union mediator estimated killed about 600,000 people.

France Steps Up Support for Ebola Fight in DR Congo

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

France said that it will increase support for efforts to contain a major Ebola outbreak in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, where more than 4,000 people have died. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot announced the additional support during a visit to Bunia in Ituri province, one of the areas hardest hit by the outbreak. According to the DR Congo Health Ministry, 4,042 people have died among 8,376 recorded cases since the outbreak was declared on 15 May. France has already allocated €13.4 million towards the response. Barrot said he would seek additional humanitarian funding during discussions on France’s budget. Although the number of new cases has declined in some areas, health officials warn the outbreak remains severe, with insecurity and difficulties accessing communities complicating the response. Doctors Without Borders says the situation has worsened in North Kivu, which has accounted for 40% of new confirmed cases since late August. DR Congo Health Minister Roger Kamba said that the epidemic has peaked. France is urging continued vigilance to prevent further spread.

Rwanda Genocide Justice Campaigner Dafroza Gauthier Dies

Dafroza Gauthier, a Rwandan genocide survivor who spent decades helping track down people accused of participating in the 1994 genocide and living in France, has died of cancer at the age of 72. Alongside her French husband, Alain Gauthier, she founded the Collective of Civil Plaintiffs for Rwanda, which filed civil cases against dozens of genocide suspects in France. Their efforts helped bring several suspects to trial under universal jurisdiction, with seven ultimately receiving final convictions and prison sentences ranging from 14 years to life. Gauthier, who was born into a Tutsi family in southern Rwanda, witnessed ethnic violence from a young age and lost much of her family during the genocide, including her mother, who was killed in a church in Kigali. After attending a genocide trial in Belgium in 2001, the couple began systematically investigating suspects living in France. Their work contributed to the 2014 conviction of former Rwandan intelligence chief Pascal Simbikangwa, who received a 25-year sentence for genocide and crimes against humanity. Gauthier maintained that her goal was justice rather than revenge and continued the work until her death.

Somaliland Rejects Somalia Claims Over Israel and Berbera

Somaliland has rejected comments by Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud about its relationship with Israel and the strategic port of Berbera, saying Somalia has no authority over Somaliland’s foreign relations. Somaliland's Foreign Ministry described the president's remarks as misleading and reaffirmed its claim to sovereignty, saying its diplomatic ties with Israel are sovereign decisions intended to promote cooperation, development and regional stability. It also rejected claims that Berbera could be used as a platform for aggression against other countries. Somaliland defended its support for negotiated arrangements allowing landlocked Ethiopia access to the sea and criticised Somalia’s opposition to the 2024 Ethiopia-Somaliland memorandum of understanding. Somaliland and Israel established diplomatic relations after Israel formally recognised Somaliland in December 2025. The Somaliland government accused Somalia of interference and threats of force and called for restraint. It said that it would continue pursuing peaceful diplomacy and partnerships across the Horn of Africa and Red Sea region.

Close 

Chivayo and Wife to Be Buried Despite Missing Remains

The bodies of Zimbabwean businessman Wicknell Chivayo and his wife, Lucy Muteke, will be buried at Glen Forest Cemetery in Harare on Thursday, despite some remains, including their heads, still missing after their helicopter crash. The couple died when their Bell 430 helicopter crashed at Kudenga Farm in Marondera while they were travelling from their rural home in Gandami, Chikomba East. Three other people also died in the crash, which left the bodies severely fragmented and some remains destroyed by fire. A family spokesperson dismissed social media claims that several skulls had been recovered, saying the last identifiable personal items found were Chivayo's wristwatch and his wife’s watch. Because the remains are incomplete, there will be no body viewing before the burial. The couple will be buried side-by-side in separate graves. The family has also rejected claims that the funeral will be private, saying anyone wishing to mourn Chivayo is welcome to attend. Chivayo was declared a provincial hero.

World.title: South Africa: Fochville Crash Accused Due in Court - South African News Briefs - October 5, 2026
World.content:
press review

Fochville Crash Accused Due in Court

The man accused of causing the deaths of 11 learners and their scholar transport driver in Fochville is expected back in court, reports EWN. Gert van Emmenis faces 12 counts of culpable homicide and a charge of reckless and negligent driving over the July 2024 crash, in which a Ford Ranger collided with a taxi carrying the children. The taxi overturned and caught fire, killing the 11 children, all under 14, and their driver. The case has been postponed several times for further investigations. The court is expected to consider representations before the matter can move forward. Van Emmenis was granted R20,000 bail after the State did not oppose his application.

Thembisa Women Demand Safer Community



Women living in the Vusimuzi informal settlement in Thembisa, Ekurhuleni have said that they fear for their safety and want the area declared a danger zone following the discovery of 12 women's bodies across Ekurhuleni in the past two months, reports SABC News. Residents said that criminals operate with little police visibility, with women reporting robberies, attacks and incidents of criminals entering homes at night. Their concerns come after 23-year-old Boitumelo Mashita was shot and killed in Thembisa on 28 September, allegedly by her estranged husband. Mashita was laid to rest.

AKA and Tibz Murder Trial Begins

The long-awaited murder trial of rapper Kiernan "AKA" Forbes and celebrity chef Tebello "Tibz" Motsoane is set to begin at the Durban High Court, nearly three years after the pair were gunned down outside a restaurant on Florida Road, reports EWN. Seven men are expected to stand trial for the two murders. The case has faced delays, including the extradition of brothers Siyabonga and Malusi Ndimande from Eswatini after they allegedly fled there following the February 2023 killings. They were returned to South Africa last year and charged with the murders. The trial is expected to run until 6 November, with a break on 4 November for the elections.
