World.title: How the shooting death of a Houston father is igniting Latino politics in Texas
World.content:
Pushing back

Lorenzo Salgado Araujo woke before dawn on a hot Houston morning on July 7, as he did most days. He had lived in the U.S. for decades without legal status but was in the process of getting a work permit. He had no criminal record.

He picked up workers in his white van and was driving to a jobsite when he was pursued by immigration agents in unmarked vehicles. An officer shot him, according to authorities, after they say he used his vehicle to ram them. It’s a story contradicted by witnesses in the van, but it’s one immigration authorities have told before in explaining how a traffic pursuit turned deadly.

This time, though, the family wasn’t having it. Salgado Araujo’s eldest son stood before cameras and delivered an emotional testimonial to his father that went viral.

“He was a hardworking family man who never wanted his name to be known by anyone outside of his family,” Ronaldo Salgado said at a news conference days after his father’s shooting, as his brother held up a photo of their father.

Ronaldo Salgado stressed that the story of his dad ramming government vehicles could not be true. Their father had always taught his kids that if law enforcement attempted to pull them over, they were to pull off the road, hand over their license and registration and act respectfully.

In the end, authorities admitted Salgado Araujo was not the intended target of the operation.

In an interview with NBC News, Ronaldo Salgado said as immigration arrests became more prevalent in 2025, they talked to their father about the procedure if he had an encounter, including calling his family, and that they’d contact their attorneys.

“Just remember, don’t sign anything. Call us,” Ronaldo Salgado said he told his father.

Sitting at Las Perras Cafe in Houston, where a makeshift altar to his father sits in the corner, Ronaldo Salgado recited the names of those who had been killed by immigration officers, including Renee Good, Alex Pretti and Ruben Ray Martinez, saying the country is not now safe because of their deaths.

“These are lives that are lost, and they need to be investigated, just like any other life lost. It needs to be investigated with the full cooperation of the agents involved and the agencies involved,” the son said.

Ronaldo Salgado at a makeshift altar to his father, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, at Las Perras Cafe in Houston. Natasha Korecki / NBC News

“All of this isn’t making us any safer. How is going after my dad going to work making the city safer?” Ronaldo Salgado said. “Criminals don’t wake up at 5 in the morning to pick up their crew and go to do a day of backbreaking labor. You don’t.”

In an unusual move, federal officials made public an FBI search warrant to get inside Salgado Araujo’s van after his death. Then, federal officials released a stinging detail: The bureau sought entry to look at baggies with crystals that they said resembled meth.

When he heard that, Ronaldo Salgado said he couldn’t help but break into a little smile: “Ohhh, they messed up.”

He knew what it was. And it would only make things worse for federal authorities. It was a homemade electrolyte mixture, mainly of salt, that his father later mixed into Gatorade for himself and workers to combat the triple-digit Houston summer heat outside.

The U.S. attorney’s office later confirmed that the mix was in fact not methamphetamine, surprising few who knew Salgado Araujo.

Ronaldo Salgado felt it was an effort to sully his father’s reputation and dampen public outrage.

The implication just added to community anger, viewed as a thinly veiled attempt at smearing the man immigration authorities killed.

“It really shook the community,” said Jasmine Khadem González, an immigrant rights organizer with the Houston Democratic Socialists of America. “A lot of us who are Latino, we have somebody in our family: If it’s not our father then it’s our uncle who has a very similar job. … To see somebody like that be targeted for just being on his way to work or for the color of his skin or for the kind of truck that he’s driving — because it’s associated with Latino men — to see somebody like that be targeted for doing a very everyday thing. For just existing.”

In the NBC News/Telemundo poll, 31% of Latino voters say they or someone close to them started carrying identification over concerns about ICE enforcement, while 27% say they know someone who has been deported or detained by ICE in the last two years.

Amy Zachmeyer, the executive director of New Economy for Working Houston, a group that helped organize community vigils and demanded accountability and transparency in the probe, said the Salgado family’s high-profile pushback kept authorities in check.

“They’ve shown incredible strength to be able to really defend their father,” she said.

Zachmeyer grew emotional as she spoke about the sons. “They never let a narrative set in that he was anything but a loving father, a Houstonian, a Texan, a hard worker.”

Anger reshapes local politics

Adrian Garcia, a Harris County commissioner, said Latinos are “feeling a lot of attack and disrespect.” Over the last year, he’s worked to reach out to those who don’t vote often. From his view, people now are willing to walk across broken glass to send a message to the Trump administration.

“The low-propensity voters that I’ve been speaking to absolutely have a great intensity to vote in this election, and they specifically speak to ICE enforcement. A lot of young kids: ‘I’m voting for my mom. I’m voting for my dad.’ I hear that a lot,” Garcia said.

More Latino registered voters than ever — 72% — rated their interest in the upcoming election as 10 out of 10 in the NBC News/Telemundo poll.

Garcia described the greater impact that fear of immigration enforcement has had across the Texas economy.

“This is not what our community deserves, and it is also what is impacting the things that we care about the most, the business, the economy. They’re hurting the industry,” he said. “They’re hurting those who work hard and play by the rules.”

Jareli Barrera, who works as a server at the popular Cielito Cafe in Houston, said she has never been so tuned into an election. Today, she said she’s helping others, including co-workers, to register to vote.

She cannot stand seeing the level of fear in her community, including among those who are citizens but fear being separated from family or an aggressive encounter.

“Republicans are probably going to lose. It’s not going to be the greatest thing for them at the end of the day,” Barrera said. “Most of these immigrants are the ones that are making the U.S. successful. They’re doing the hard work. … If everyone’s deported, who’s gonna do the hard labor? Who’s gonna construct? Who’s going to do all this cleaning that they don’t want to do?”

Since 2025, local activist groups have tried to work with the city of Houston to better protect Latinos as they watched intense enforcement operations in cities like Minneapolis, Los Angeles and Chicago upend life for residents and lead to encounters with immigration authorities that turned violent or deadly.

Jennefer Canales-Pelaez, a Houston-based senior policy attorney and strategist with the Immigrant Legal Resource Center, said Salgado Araujo’s death was a “culmination of years of Texas entrenching itself, entangling itself with ICE” and “illustrated to them the fear, the levels of persecution of justice that immigrant communities have been living with in Texas for a very long time.”

Before Salgado Araujo’s death, Canales-Pelaez was among those who worked to deter cooperation between Houston police and federal police agencies and pushed for greater transparency into immigration operations. Abbott, the three-term governor and a staunch Trump ally who is up for re-election in November, threatened to block $200 million in grants to Houston and other major cities if they didn’t change local rules that directed police forces not to hold individuals they encounter for longer time periods to assist ICE. The cities, including Houston, reworded their ordinances.

Houston Mayor John Whitmire, a centrist Democrat, told The New York Times last October that he kept his head down as other city and state leaders in the country grew combative with the White House over immigration operations. Whitmire said his city had avoided “turmoil” that others faced.

Whitmire initially declared his hands were tied after the shooting; the Houston Police Department had no jurisdiction to conduct an independent investigation. After community uproar, the city changed course. Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare has now launched a probe, with the county government approving the $2.5 million request to fund it.

“It ignited this flame and really showed other people that aren’t necessarily living this experience or working in this line of work, ‘Oh, this got to us,’” Canales-Pelaez said. “When the mayor told us that we weren’t going to be another Minneapolis, we weren’t going to be a Los Angeles, well, now we are. Someone’s dead. That really has sparked this rage, this collective, righteous anger.”

World.title: Alleged Chinese agent makes federal court appearance
World.content:
A suspected Chinese agent appeared in a Los Angeles federal court Monday after she allegedly surveilled the Taiwanese president's son near Seattle last year.

Orange County, California, realtor Wanying "Heather" Zhang, 34, appeared calm, dressed in a tailored, white zip-up jacket, sweatpants and white sneakers, with shackles on her wrists and ankles. CBS News was first to report that the FBI arrested Zhang on Sunday at Los Angeles International Airport before she boarded a flight to Shanghai, China.

In court, she spoke only to confirm her name and that she understood the charge against her of working as an unregistered agent of the Chinese government.

Wanying "Heather" Zhang. FBI

Zhang was represented by a public defender at the hearing.

Judge Steve Kim rescheduled her detention hearing to Wednesday to give Zhang more time to hire a private criminal defense attorney.

Zhang was remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals until her Wednesday hearing.

The public defender, Chad Pennington, told the judge he believed Zhang intended to hire private counsel.

Her husband, Edric Ding, watched the proceedings, flanked by his sister, attorney Elaine Lori.

Standing at the podium, Zhang looked back at her husband briefly, but showed no emotion.

Lori and Ding declined to comment inside the courthouse and remained silent as they were questioned by reporters as they walked to their car after the hearing. When reached by phone on Sunday, Ding told CBS News, "I don't know anything yet," and declined to comment further.

Three prosecutors represented the Justice Department: Scott Lara of the National Security Division's Counterintelligence and Export Control Section, and Assistant U.S. Attorneys Amanda Elbogen and Colin Scott. They said they were not authorized to comment.

FBI agents arrested Wanying "Heather" Zhang at Los Angeles International Airport on Oct. 4, 2026. U.S. Department of Justice

U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli posted a video on X of Zhang being frogmarched through the airport by federal law enforcement on Sunday, wearing the same outfit she wore in court on Monday.

A criminal complaint, filed in federal court by a member of the FBI's counterintelligence squad in L.A., accused Zhang and an accomplice of allegedly traveling to Seattle in September 2025 and taking pictures at the suburban home of a top Taiwanese official's family.

Law enforcement sources told CBS News that the target was Ting-Yu Lai, the son of Taiwanese President Ching-Te Lai.

Ting-Yu, an engineer in his 30s, attended college in America and has a young U.S.-born son with his wife, Hsiao Chen, according to Taiwanese media reports. He now works for the Dutch multinational electronics firm Philips.

The FBI agent's affidavit claimed the government obtained text messages between Zhang and Chinese government officials evidencing the alleged surveillance.

In one exchange, Zhang allegedly texted her supposed Chinese government handler on the day of her alleged Seattle trip, "Saw him. Young male. It's that young one," and "I am videorecording," while footage from Ting-Yu's neighbor's security camera showed her "appearing to film" the president's son, his wife and their child as they arrived home that evening, according to the affidavit.

As well as arresting Zhang on Sunday, FBI agents also searched her home in an upscale suburb of Irvine, California.

A resident of the neighborhood said she saw about 10 FBI agents searching Zhang's home on Sunday morning.

"Several of them were sitting at a table inside the garage," said the neighbor, who asked to remain anonymous due to safety concerns. "Even the ones standing guard were wearing gloves. They told us there was a search going on."

Zhang appears to have been renting the home, after selling her 6,030-square-foot, six-bed house a mile away for $6 million in June, according to property records.

A former neighbor told CBS News he was surprised that the young realtor couple could afford such an expensive property.

"She introduced herself as Heather," said the neighbor, who also asked to remain anonymous due to safety concerns. "She was super friendly.

"Usually, the people here, they're a little bit older, because the price of the homes is from $3 million to $10 million. But they were very young," the neighbor continued. "They did a lot of upgrades. Even though the house was almost brand new, they started changing so many things."

"Two years later, they only sold it for a little bit higher than what they purchased. It didn't make sense why would they want to lose money after spending all of that money," the neighbor added.

The Justice Department claims Zhang was working as an unregistered agent of the Chinese government from June 2025 to September 2025, and plotted her surveillance mission with Beijing officials during a trip to China in June 2025.

"The complaint in this case lays bare a brazen plot directed by the Chinese government to conduct a covert surveillance mission on U.S. soil targeting close relatives of a Taiwanese government official," Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI's Counterintelligence and Espionage Division said in a statement released Monday.

"Wanying Zhang's arrest for allegedly acting as an unregistered agent of the Chinese government makes clear how far China's authoritarian regime will go to advance its goals. However, this case also demonstrates the FBI's unwavering commitment to defending the sovereignty of our democratic allies and combating all attempts by the Chinese government - and any foreign adversary - to conduct transnational repression within our borders," Rozhavsky said.

The Chinese and Taiwanese governments have not responded to requests for comment.

World.title: FBI arrests woman at LAX accused of being Chinese agent
World.content:
The FBI arrested a suspected Chinese agent at Los Angeles International Airport after she allegedly surveilled the Taiwanese president's U.S.-based son, law enforcement sources told CBS News.

Wanying "Heather" Zhang, an Irvine, California, realtor, was cuffed by federal law enforcement on Sunday before she boarded a flight to Shanghai, China, from LAX, on a charge of acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government.

Zhang's husband Edric Ding, a realtor at the same firm, told CBS News when reached by phone Sunday: "I don't know anything yet," and declined to comment further.

It was not immediately clear if Zhang has an attorney.

Wanying "Heather" Zhang. FBI

A criminal complaint, filed in federal court by a member of the FBI's counterintelligence squad in L.A., accused Zhang and an accomplice of traveling to Seattle, Washington, in September 2025 and taking pictures at the suburban home of a top Taiwanese official's family.

Law enforcement sources told CBS News that the target was Ting-Yu Lai, the son of Taiwanese President Ching-Te Lai.

Ting-Yu, an engineer in his 30s, attended college in America and has a young U.S.-born son with his wife, Hsiao Chen, according to Taiwanese media reports. He now works for the Dutch multinational electronics firm Philips.

"If the PRC [People's Republic of China] wish to obtain leverage over the President of Taiwan during any potential conflict, the location and pictures of the close relatives of a high-ranking Taiwanese government official, including pictures of their homes and cars, could be useful to the PRC," wrote FBI Special Agent Kevin Holt in the Oct. 3, 2026, criminal complaint.

Taiwan has been the focus of high geopolitical tensions for decades. It asserts its independence, while the Chinese government claims it is part of China. The island is in a key position astride major shipping lanes, and is where many of the world's most advanced semiconductor chips are manufactured.

CBS News reached out to the Taiwanese consulate for comment.

The complaint said Zhang, 34, and a man named only as "Individual 1" flew from Las Vegas to Seattle on Sept. 1, 2025, rented a black Nissan Rogue and drove to their target's home.

Images from a neighbor's security camera included in the complaint allegedly show the two "appearing to film" Ting-Yu, his wife and their child as they arrived home that evening.

CBS News matched the images to an address near Seattle owned by Ting-Yu.

Zhang allegedly texted her Chinese government handler: "Saw him. Young male. It's that young one," and "I am videorecording," followed by two license plate numbers, according to the complaint.

The FBI agent wrote that the texts from the Chinese messaging app WeChat were obtained from a search warrant on Zhang's iCloud account.

"Zhang was in contact with at least two people whom she appeared to acknowledge worked for the PRC government," the agent wrote.

FBI agents arrested Wanying "Heather" Zhang at Los Angeles International Airport on Oct. 4, 2026. U.S. Department of Justice

The complaint claims Zhang was introduced in June 2025 to one of the Chinese government officials by a classmate from her alma mater, Beijing's University of International Relations, which Holt said has close ties to the Ministry of State Security.

Holt's affidavit claims Zhang booked a private room in Changsha, China, during a June 2025 trip, where she allegedly met the government official and received her surveillance mission.

She later texted the official, "I can take care of this thing," according to the complaint.

On Aug. 26, 2025, Zhang wrote: "I will be busy with work in L.A. this week. I will probably go to Seattle next week," and the official replied: "Ok. Thank you for your hard work," the complaint said.

Zhang is a licensed California realtor with JC Pacific Capital Inc. Her Zillow profile says she has 130 sales and listings around Los Angeles and neighboring counties.

Ting-Yu received his bachelor's in electrical engineering from Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, Ohio, in 2012; a master's in Bioengineering Innovation and Design from Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, the following year; then a PhD from the Department of Bioengineering at the University of Washington, according to a profile from one of his academic publications.

Taiwan TV news station SETN reported that he met his Taiwanese wife while studying for his doctorate. They married in 2018 and had a child in the U.S. in 2020, according to CNA, Taiwan's national news agency.

Chinese government agents have previously been caught spying on and harassing Chinese dissidents and pro-democracy activists in the U.S.

Federal prosecutors said Shujun Wang, 75, infiltrated and informed on a Chinese pro-democracy group in Queens, New York, for the Chinese Ministry of State Security for 17 years. He was convicted in 2024 of acting as a foreign agent.

Two people were arrested in April 2023 for their involvement in an unofficial Chinese police station in Manhattan set up to monitor Chinese dissidents.

The Justice Department has warned of a plan by the Chinese security services called Operation Fox Hunt aimed at repatriating wanted Chinese nationals around the world, which targets enemies of the regime.

New York-based Quanzhong An, who prosecutors say is a leader of the U.S. wing of Operation Fox Hunt, was sentenced in March 2025 after harassing a Chinese dissident in an attempt to bring them back to China.

In California, former Arcadia Mayor Eileen Wang was charged with acting as a Chinese agent in May. She admitted to being paid to spread pro-Chinese government propaganda in the U.S., including an essay on her blog denying "forced labor" in China.

World.title: Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan to be executed by firing squad, Pentagon says
World.content:
The Trump administration has approved a plan to execute former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan — who killed 13 people in a 2009 shooting at Fort Hood — by firing squad, chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said late Monday.

Parnell said on social media the plan to use an Army firing squad was recommended by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and approved by President Trump.

"The Secretary of the Army will set the time and place of the execution. Judgement day for Hasan has finally come," Parnell wrote.

CBS News has reached out to Hasan's attorney for comment.

A former Army psychiatrist, Hasan was convicted of murdering 13 people and injuring more than 30 in a 2013 court-martial. Hasan acknowledged at trial that he was responsible for the shooting, claiming he opened fire on fellow members of the Army in an attempt to protect Islamic insurgents from U.S. military forces. He was sentenced to death.

Hasan's case could mark the military's first execution of an American service member since 1961, when a soldier was hanged for raping and attempting to murder an 11-year-old girl.

It would also mark a rare use of a firing squad. The method was used in South Carolina three times last year, marking the first firing squad executions since 2010.

The federal government typically uses lethal injection for civilian death penalty cases. Earlier this year, the Justice Department said federal officials should consider other methods, including firing squads, electrocution and lethal gas.

The decision by Hegseth comes after a lengthy appeals process for Hasan. He chose to represent himself at trial, and in an unusual course of events, he clashed with his own court-appointed standby attorneys, who worried that Hasan was intentionally seeking the death penalty.

Hasan asked the Supreme Court to review his case in 2024, arguing the judge violated his right to a public trial by clearing the public from the courtroom before discussing some of his issues with the attorneys. The high court declined to take up the issue last year.

World.title: The iconic Arthur Read made his TV debut 30 years ago
World.content:
The iconic Arthur Read made his TV debut 30 years ago

toggle caption i WGBH Educational Foundation, WildBrain and Marc Brown Studios

This is part of a special series in which NPR looks back at its coverage of major news stories from the past.

Which long-running cartoon features this protagonist: he's got round ears, an iconic yellow sweater, and a snarky little sister?

If you immediately pictured an animated, 8-year-old aardvark, you've likely heard of Arthur Read, a character who made his TV debut 30 years ago on Oct. 7, 1996.

But before the bespectacled third-grader made his way onto our screens and into our hearts, Arthur's first home was in the world of books.

Here's a look at the beginnings of Arthur.

Sponsor Message

A Bedtime Story

The author of the Arthur books is Marc Brown, a writer and illustrator who was raised in Erie, Pa.

Although Brown was interested in art from a young age, after graduating from the Cleveland Institute of Art in 1968, he pursued a string of different jobs working as everything from truck driver to to short-order cook to assistant professor.

Brown says he got the inspiration for Arthur when his son Tolon asked for a bedtime story about a "weird" animal. The first weird animal that came to mind? An aardvark. From there, Brown wrote and illustrated his first picture book depicting an aardvark named Arthur. This animal, with its long anteater snout and small ears, starred in Arthur's Nose, published in 1976.

While working on the next book, Brown made a pivotal change to the character's design. The second book titled, Arthur's Eyes, featured Arthur getting a new pair of glasses. As Brown drew the glasses, he realized there was a problem.

Speaking to NPR's Linda Wertheimer in 1997, Brown said, "I was drawing Arthur, and I wanted him to face the viewer in the book. And I could not show his mouth because his — his nose was so long. And so I shortened it a little bit. And I thought to myself, gee, if there are two books about Arthur, well there might be a third book. Now how do you really want this character to look?"

Sponsor Message

So Brown spent more time redesigning Arthur's visage, making his face "a little rounder" and "a little more lovable looking." The result, Brown said, made Arthur "more human-like." As Brown published and sold more Arthur books, he was able to make a living writing books. Though they were not an immediate commercial success, Brown's picture books resonated with families, including Carol Greenwald's.

Like Brown, Greenwald was no stranger to bedtime story pleas from her two children. When her son was 3 years old, their neighbor gave them an Arthur picture book. After reading it a few times, Greenwald realized it was unique.

"After reading it for the seventh time," Greenwald told NPR in 1997, "I realized I wasn't tearing my hair out … There are so many books you read to your kids that they love to read, and you read them over and over again, and it makes you feel like you want to scream. But this particular book was not making me feel that way."

Greenwald also said she liked the way Arthur dealt with problems involving school, personal relationships and activities like reading. As a TV producer at the Boston-based public media station GBH, Greenwald raised the idea with her colleagues in the early '90s.

"We have a lot of research that tells us that a kid who watches a TV show based on a book is more likely to want to read that book, is more likely to want to read other books, and is even more likely to go to the library."

toggle caption i WGBH Educational Foundation, WildBrain and Marc Brown Studios

From books to television

Although Greenwald believed Arthur was ready to make his public television debut, Brown was less sure. Brown said he was hesitant to allow Arthur to make the multimedia leap, stating that he wanted to keep "control of the character."

But GBH's offer and the subsequent jump in book sales made Brown reconsider.

Sponsor Message

“I went from, you know, maybe selling two million books over a period of several years to selling two million books in a month,” Brown said. “And to me, that happening is just unimaginable…”





He worked closely with the show's writers and artists to preserve the essential little kid that is Arthur.

Produced by GBH and the Montreal-based animation studio Cinar, the first episode of the series premiered on PBS Kids on Oct. 7, 1996. Its storyline draws directly from the second picture book, "Arthur's Eyes," as Arthur "re-tells" the story of wearing glasses to school for the first time.

The premiere also brought the rest of the Elwood City animal community to life with sound and emotion. Every character is an animal, from Arthur's aardvark parents and sister D.W. (short for Dora Winifred) to the students in Mr. Ratburn's Lakewood Elementary class, including an athletic chimpanzee named Francine and Arthur's best friend, a bunny named Buster. One of the show's underlying themes of getting along with others in your community is present even in its joyful, reggae theme song, "Believe In Yourself" by Ziggy Marley and the Melody Makers as Arthur bops around Elwood City, interacting with family, friends, and trusted neighbors.

Shortly after the series premiere, Brown was asked whether Arthur would remain in third grade or be allowed the opportunity to grow.



“I don't think of Arthur as ever leaving third grade," Brown said. "I sort of think of Arthur as having this portrait in the attic that's aging. (laughs) But Arthur will stay forever in third grade.”





The legacy of a wonderful kind of day

True to his word, Arthur and his friends remained third-graders throughout the entire series' 25 seasons. As reported by the Los Angeles Times in 2022, Arthur aired over 250 episodes and seven television specials. The critically acclaimed series also won four Daytime Emmy Awards for outstanding children's animated program and one Peabody Award.

Sponsor Message

Although Arthur began as the star, the series evolved to focus on a diverse cast of other characters and their lives as they navigated relatable milestones for 8-year-olds such as developing asthma, learning with dyslexia, and living with diabetes. The principles of believing in yourself, valuing family and friendship, and loving reading carried from season to season.

But not all the characters' stories were celebrated. In 2019, Alabama Public Television refused to air an episode featuring a same-sex wedding between Arthur's teacher, Mr. Ratburn, and his partner, Patrick. As reported by the New York Times in 2006, when an episode of the spinoff "Postcards from Buster" featured a Vermont family with two moms, then-Secretary of Education Margaret Spellings wrote a letter to the then-president and CEO of PBS, Pat Mitchell, reminding her that the show received funding from the Department of Education. She added, "Many parents would not want their young children exposed to the life-styles portrayed in this episode."

When speaking to NPR in 2022, Brown said, "We, as adults, owe children the truth. They're trying to make a foundation on which they can build their lives, and if there isn't truth in that foundation, things get pretty shaky."

For 26 years, Arthur helped families build a foundation of truth and belonging with the animated, animal residents of Elwood City. The series finale titled, "All Grown Up," aired on Feb. 21, 2022. The characters were no longer children, but adults, each aged up 20 years and settled into their respective careers. And of course, Arthur became an author of graphic novels.

World.title: Dennis Hastert, longtime Republican House speaker who went to prison, dies at age 84
World.content:
Dennis Hastert, longtime Republican House speaker who went to prison, dies at age 84

toggle caption i Christian K. Lee/AP

Dennis Hastert, whose political legacy as Congress' longest-serving Republican House speaker was later fouled by allegations that he had molested high school athletes during his prior career as a teacher and wrestling coach, has died, a coroner said Monday. He was 84.

Hastert, who was speaker from 1999 until 2007, died Saturday of natural causes at his home while receiving hospice care, according to Kendall County Coroner Jacquie Purcell.

When he was sentenced in 2016 to more than a year behind bars, the former history teacher became one of the highest-ranking American politicians ever ordered to prison.

In the late 1990s, Hastert was a little-known Illinois lawmaker with a reputation for congeniality that had helped him ascend the ranks of congressional leaders. When Newt Gingrich lost support because of ethics violations and the GOP's poor showing in an election, Republicans elected Hastert to succeed him. In his first weeks on the job, he presided over the House while the Senate conducted then-President Bill Clinton's impeachment trial.

Sponsor Message

After the GOP reclaimed the White House, Hastert helped pass then-President George W. Bush's legislative agenda, including massive tax cuts and a measure that amounted to a huge expansion of prescription drug benefits — the biggest change in Medicare in decades.

His legacy was suddenly thrown into doubt in 2015, when he was accused of evading banking regulations as part of a plan to pay hush money to conceal unspecified "prior misconduct." Nearly a year later, prosecutors filed papers that described what media reports had suggested for months: Hastert's alleged misconduct involved the sexual abuse of teenage boys on his wrestling team in the small town of Yorkville, west of Chicago.

During a 16-year coaching career, he led his team to a state championship and was named national coach of the year in 1976. But behind the accolades, prosecutors said, Hastert sexually abused at least four team members from 1965 to 1981.

The person Hastert was paying, identified in court papers only as Individual A, said the abuse occurred in a motel room when he was 14 on the way home from wrestling camp. Hastert allegedly touched other wrestlers in a locker room after saying he would give them massages. Two wrestlers said Hastert performed sexual acts on them.

Sponsor Message

Prosecutors also described a recliner where Hastert often sat in the locker room with a direct view of the stalls where the boys showered.

Hastert agreed to plead guilty to evading banking laws. In all, he paid more than $1.7 million out of $3.5 million that he had promised to Individual A, sometimes in lump sums of $100,000 cash.

At the sentencing hearing where he received 15 months behind bars, the visibly angry judge called Hastert a "serial child molester." A former wrestler struggled with his emotions as he told the court about his "dark secret" from adolescence.

In his own statement, Hastert said he was "deeply ashamed" and admitted that he "mistreated" some of his athletes. But he never referred directly to sexual abuse.

The public knew nothing about Hastert's past when Republicans lost seats in the 1998 midterm elections.

Hastert's path to the speaker's office was cleared when Louisiana Rep. Bob Livingston, who was considered a lock to replace Gingrich as speaker, resigned after acknowledging several extramarital affairs.

Hastert was aware of the personal pitfalls of holding the powerful position.

"You know, in this business, especially in a job like this, you can get your head someplace where it shouldn't be," Hastert said in a 1999 interview with The Associated Press. "But you come back home, and you're home. You're back where you've always been, and your feet are back on the ground."

Hastert said he lacked the appetite for higher office.

As the recount of the 2000 presidential election dragged on, Hastert's aides briefed him on the possibility that he might become acting president in the event of an Electoral College deadlock.

"I really didn't want to be president, temporary or otherwise," he wrote in his book. But he decided that he would not pass the office to the constitutional officer next in line if an Electoral College deadlock extended beyond Inauguration Day. In the end, the Supreme Court's 5-4 ruling ended the recount, and Bush moved into the White House.

Sponsor Message

Hastert's journey to Congress from his boyhood farm appeared to be the result of fate and luck.

In 1980, he finished third in an Illinois House primary. But the incumbent became fatally ill, and GOP leaders chose Hastert to take his place on the November ballot, where he won in a traditional GOP stronghold.

Hastert became a congressional candidate in 1986 and beat the Democrat with 52% of the vote, his smallest margin of victory in a congressional race.

In Washington, Hastert served quietly in House leadership, working closely with Gingrich and then-House Majority Whip Tom DeLay after Republicans took control in 1995.

Hastert became wealthy largely through a complex web of transactions that coincided with one of his own highway earmarks increasing the value of land he had purchased in his district.

He was forced to step down as speaker in 2007, when Democrats gained control of the House, and he resigned his seat later that year.

Born in Aurora, Illinois, Hastert earned a bachelor's degree in economics from Wheaton College in 1964 and a master's in education from Northern Illinois University in 1967.

In 2007, Wheaton named its newly created public policy center the J. Dennis Hastert Center for Economics, Government and Public Policy. After Hastert's indictment, the school removed his name in 2015. Other organizations abandoned associations with Hastert, and his portrait was removed from a hallway outside the House chamber.

Hastert lived his entire life in Chicago's suburbs, primarily in the Yorkville area. While growing up, he helped his father with the family feed business.

Survivors include his wife, Jean, and two adult sons.

World.title: Drones buzz overhead, troops hunker underground in Ukraine's hellish kill zone
World.content:
Drones buzz overhead, troops hunker underground in Ukraine's hellish kill zone

toggle caption i Andriy Andriyenko/Ukrainian 65th Mechanized brigade/Ukrainian military via AP

KYIV, Ukraine — The front line in the Russia-Ukraine war stretches the entire length of this country, from north to south. It has barely budged in four years and is sometimes compared to the static, deadlocked, trench warfare of World War I.

Yet straddling this front line is the kill zone, dominated by constantly evolving drone technology that's defining this conflict — and the future of warfare.

"This kill zone is a belt of territory which is full of Russian drones, Russian mines and also artillery. It's nonstop reconnaissance and surveillance," said Ukraine's Sr. Lt. Taras Myshak, the spokesman for Ukraine's 59th Separate Assault Brigade. He spoke with NPR on Zoom, just a few miles from the front line in eastern Ukraine.

Sponsor Message

Ukraine has a similar arsenal threatening the Russian forces that are dug in on the other side of the line.

The most important thing to know about the kill zone is that any sign of movement — just sticking your head out of a foxhole for fresh air — can get you noticed, and attacked, by the drones constantly buzzing overhead.

Myshak says even routine movements, like rotating troops in and out of this zone, is a nightmare.

"Not far from where we are talking today, we have a group that moved through the kill zone, and they will walk four hours just to go 1 kilometer," he said. "Because all the time they hear the drone, and they have to hide and wait. Then the drone passes, and they can move."

Nightfall doesn't make it any safer to move because the drones have thermal cameras that detect body heat and make it even harder to hide.

"In the night, it's even more dangerous," he said.

toggle caption i Iryna Rybakova/Ukrainian 93rd Mechanized Brigade/Ukrainian military via AP

A front line that barely budges

When Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, it advanced rapidly in conventional fashion with large columns of troops in armored vehicles. Later that fall, Ukraine's counteroffensive drove the Russians back in some places.

Sponsor Message

Since then, the two armies have settled in, and the front line has moved only incrementally, mostly with limited gains by Russia. This line now stretches more than 700 miles. On either side of the line, the kill zone is a band roughly 10 to 20 miles wide and dominated by drones.

"The kill zone is basically a product of drone warfare," said Rob Lee, a U.S. Marine veteran who now lives in Ukraine and monitors the war for the Foreign Policy Research Institute of Philadelphia.

Because Ukraine has far fewer troops and relies heavily on drones, it has a remarkably small presence on the front line.

Lee said that in many places, Ukraine has fewer than 10 soldiers per mile, in small groups, spaced out hundreds of yards apart.

"Those infantrymen are maybe two positions where it's two to four people," said Lee. "They're underground for the most part. They're trying to remain hidden."

These troops are not really trying to hold back advancing Russian soldiers, he added. They act more as spotters, relaying Russian movements to Ukrainian drone operators behind the front lines, who then track down the Russian intruders from the air.

Lee says the front line is so saturated with drones that it's virtually impossible for either side to pull together a large ground force without being detected and drawing fire.

Military vehicles like tanks and armored personnel carriers are even easier to spot and attack.

"Because of such a high density of drones, it became very difficult to bring vehicles near the front line at all," he said.

toggle caption i Genya Savilov/AFP via Getty Images

Neither army planned to fight this way.

Ukraine had no real drone industry at the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says the country will make 10 million this year.

Russia has ramped up its own drone production. It's expected to make more than 7 million this year, including jet-powered aircraft that are often evading Ukraine's defenses.

Sponsor Message

Starting from scratch

When Dima Putiata joined Ukraine's military four years ago, he knew nothing about drones and didn't think this was a manly way to wage war.

"When I saw that we have drones, I was not smart enough. I said, 'No, we don't need to have it. Let's fight like men.' I was a little bit maybe romantic in this way," said Putiata.

In addition to skeptics like Putiata, few Ukrainian troops were trained to use these new weapons.

"No one had drone operators," he recalled. "It's just, 'Oh, you're a driver? You can use it.' Or, 'Oh, can I use a drone? You can try.'"

By the time he left the military in May, Putiata, a sergeant, was commanding 26 drone crews in and around the kill zone in northeastern Ukraine.

Both sides have rapidly embraced the technology even if they don't know where it's headed next, he said.

"They understand how to use it here and right now, maybe not really understanding how to use it in the future," he noted. "My point is, you just need to keep going and adapting."

toggle caption i Iryna Rybakova/Ukrainian 93rd Mechanized Brigade via AP

Recognizing the role of drones

Two years ago, Ukraine became the first country to establish drones as an independent branch of its military.

This innovation now includes the widespread use of ground drones, which look like trollies and perform a wide range of tasks that have become too dangerous for troops.

The robots deliver food, medicine and ammunition to the front line. The robots can be loaded with machine guns that now carry out regular attacks.

The ground robots are also being used to evacuate wounded soldiers from the kill zone. But drone operators and combat medics have separate skills, and it turns out you need both.

"The drone operator doesn't know how to properly evacuate a wounded soldier, and the medic doesn't know how to operate a ground robot," said Lyuba Shipovich, a Ukrainian American who heads a private group, Dignitas, that trains troops on drones.

Sponsor Message

"So now we're trying to create combined program that will train both the medic and the robot operator," she said.

Media coverage tends to focus on long-range airstrikes that Russia and Ukraine are inflicting deep inside each other's territory.

But the vast majority of the fighting is in the kill zone, with drones now responsible for 80% of all casualties, according to Rob Lee and other military analysts.

Dima Putiata, the former Ukrainian soldier, says what started in this war has already spread to other conflicts.

"With drones, this is the cheapest flying munition that can be massively produced. You can destroy a lot of stuff," he said. "It's much cheaper than it used to be to have a war, unfortunately."

A kind of war, he predicts, that the world will see more often.

NPR's Hanna Palamarenko contributed to this story.

World.title: FBI arrests a woman accused of spying on Taiwan leader's family for China
World.content:
FBI arrests a woman accused of spying on Taiwan leader's family for China

BANGKOK — The FBI arrested a woman at Los Angeles International Airport as she was leaving the country and accused her of spying on the Taiwan president's family for China.

Wanying Zhang, also know as Heather, surveilled the Taiwanese president's son and his family for the Chinese government while in the United States, according to the FBI.

Zhang, 34, was arrested on charges for working for China as an unregistered agent, Assistant U.S. State Attorney Bill Essayli announced on social media. Zhang took photos and videos of her targets and sent license plate information to Chinese officials, he said.

Zhang was arrested as she was departing for a flight to China. Her nationality was not clear, and an attorney who represents her could not be determined. She was due to appear Monday in federal court in Los Angeles.

Taiwan's Presidential Office confirmed President Lai Ching-te's relatives were the targets, without specifying if it was the president's son, saying that "this is a classic case of transnational repression."

"Taiwan condemns in the strongest terms such barbaric acts — which disregard human rights and national sovereignty and aim to suppress, threaten, or even harm individuals advocating for freedom and democracy or their families — as such behavior should not be tolerated in the civilized world," spokesperson Karen Kuo said in a statement.

Sponsor Message

The Chinese Embassy in the U.S. did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday and the Foreign Ministry in Beijing was closed for holidays.

Taiwan and China split after a civil war in 1949, but Beijing claims the island as part of its own territory. Lai, who was voted into office in 2024, has said that Taiwan and Beijing do not belong to each other and that the "People's Republic of China has no right to represent Taiwan."

China considers him a separatist and has called him a "destroyer of peace."

While in office, Lai has stepped up spending on defense for Taiwan, notably pledging to increase defense spending from 3% to 5% of the GDP, and pushing through a special budget for the construction of a T-Dome air defense system.

World.title: Imran Khan supporters march in Pakistan to demand his release after talks failed
World.content:
Imran Khan supporters march in Pakistan to demand his release after talks failed

toggle caption i Maaz Awan/AP

ISLAMABAD — More than 5,000 supporters of imprisoned former Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan began a dayslong march toward Islamabad on Sunday to demand his release, after talks between the government and the opposition fell through.

The looming showdown threatens to deepen Pakistan's political uncertainty at a time when the country is also grappling with a surge in militant attacks.

Khan is current Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's main political rival and has been imprisoned since 2023 on corruption and other charges that he and his party say are politically motivated. Despite his imprisonment, he retains a substantial and passionate support base, keeping him at the center of Pakistan's turbulent political landscape.

Sponsor Message

The demonstrators, traveling in a convoy of trucks, buses and cars, departed from Lakki Marwat district in the northwestern province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where Khan's party holds power. Organizers have planned overnight stops along the route as the caravan makes its way toward the capital. Sohail Afridi, the province's chief minister, and a staunch Khan supporter is leading the march.

Speaking from a specially designed container truck emblazoned with a large portrait of Khan, he expressed confidence in the movement's ability to press its demands and bring the political standoff into the heart of the capital.

Authorities have erected roadblocks, using containers, at the entrance to Islamabad and inside the city.

Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party, or PTI, and the federal government were in talks to postpone the march but failed to reach a resolution. Gohar Khan, the party's chairman, said negotiations remained deadlocked after two rounds.

Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi blamed Afridi for the failure of the talks, warning that he would be held responsible for any loss of life during the planned march.

Sharif's government urged postponement of the march, citing a surge in militant attacks by the Pakistani Taliban in the northwest. His government has accused PTI of sympathizing with the Pakistani Taliban, also known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan.

Sponsor Message

The organizers now vow to reach the capital after rallying with hundreds of thousands of Khan supporters.

Besides Khan's release, protesters are demanding his transfer to a hospital and permission for his family to visit him. Officials say he is in good health and receives regular family visits but maintain that meetings with the imprisoned former leader cannot be used for political purposes.

The march was originally scheduled for Sept. 27 but was postponed after party leaders said authorities blocked key approaches to Islamabad, including Attock Bridge, a major crossing for convoys from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

Previous protests by Khan's supporters have turned violent, including one in 2024 in which security personnel and civilians were killed.

Khan, a former cricket star, was ousted in a parliamentary no-confidence vote in April 2022. Sharif returned to office after the February 2024 election, which Khan's party says was rigged to deny it victory. The government denies the allegation.

World.title: SCOTUS hears major climate change case. And, Brazil's presidential race goes to runoff
World.content:
SCOTUS hears major climate change case. And, Brazil's presidential race goes to runoff

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

Investigators have found that the co-pilot who attempted to take control of a flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv last week aimed to crash it into Israel's Ben Gurion airport, according to a person familiar with the matter but not authorized to speak publicly. Authorities in the United Arab Emirates who are leading the investigation say the incident has been classified as a terrorist attack. They have not identified a clear motive, and the investigation is ongoing.

toggle caption i Erik Marmor/Getty Images

🎧 The co-pilot likely acted alone, according to the source. He carried out the attack with a crash axe, which is an emergency tool meant for breaking through panels or doors in the event of a crash. Israeli officials report that the co-pilot is from Oman. NPR's Kat Lonsdorf tells Up First that the co-pilot's origins have raised concerns about how he was allowed to fly in Israel, as the country prohibits pilots from nations with which it doesn't have diplomatic relations to fly in its airspace. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says Israel checks the backgrounds of pilots flying into the country, and this pilot must have gotten through a "loophole." While people in Israel are praising the passengers and the captain as heroes for averting disaster, a broader debate is emerging over government failures that allowed something like this to happen, Lonsdorf says.

Sponsor Message

A new Supreme Court term starts today with arguments in a significant climate change case. Boulder, Colo., is suing Suncor and Exxon Mobil, arguing that the companies misled the public about the harms of fossil fuels and caused costly disasters that cost the city time and money. This case could impact other states seeking to hold companies accountable for allegedly harming local communities.



🎧 The energy companies argue that this case should not be in state court, saying climate change is a global issue best addressed by the federal government, according to NPR's Carrie Johnson. Only eight justices will hear the case after Justice Sam Alito's surprising recusal last week, Johnson says. Alito has no stock in the two companies involved, but he has investments in other energy companies that could be impacted by the court's ruling. His recusal raises the risk of a tie, which would uphold the Colorado Supreme Court's ruling allowing the case to continue in state court.

Brazil's presidential race will go to a runoff later this month between left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro. In the tight first round, Bolsonaro, the son of Brazil's former far-right president, led with about 47% of the vote, while Lula followed closely with 45%.



Sponsor Message

🎧 Lula must close the runoff gap by attracting new voters, particularly among the millions who sat out yesterday's election, NPR's Carrie Kahn says. Winning over the 8% who supported other candidates will be challenging, as the people they backed are right and far-right candidates who will align with Bolsonaro. Disillusioned with politics, many Brazilians wanted new, younger candidates. Yasmin Soares, a Lula supporter, told Kahn that Bolsonaro's strong performance is scary and that the right brings hatred. Kahn says she heard similar sentiments from many Lula voters who fear a Bolsonaro conservative back in power.

Life advice

Penguin Random House/Lindsay Owens/NPR

Tech companies are "reinventing the rip-off," according to Lindsay Owens, head of the consumer advocacy group Groundwork Collaborative. She says corporations try to hide pricing schemes, such as using browsing data or a customer's geo-location to determine the cost of goods and services. In her book Gouged: The End of a Fair Price — And What That Means for Your Wallet, she uncovers these schemes and offers advice on how to protect yourself from being overcharged. In an interview with Life Kit, Owens explained steps you can take to get the best possible deal.

💸 Avoid shopping through retailer apps. When signed in, they might experiment with your data, potentially manipulating prices against you.

💸 Comparison shop by checking the product's price across multiple devices while logged in, logged out and with and without incognito mode.

💸 Regularly clear your browsing data and cookies to protect your information. Consider using a VPN to conceal your location, which may help avoid higher charges.

💸 Try shopping the old-fashioned way in person, but keep in mind that big-box retailers and grocery stores are increasingly using electronic shelf labels to change prices at any time.

For more advice on how to avoid being ripped off, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.

Sponsor Message

Behind the story

by Andrew Limbong , Society & Culture Reporter

Harper

In a town not far from Barbara Kingsolver's house in southwestern Virginia is a historic marker noting Marion, Va., as "the birthplace of modern Mountain Dew." I came across it on the drive down I-81 to interview the Pulitzer-Prize winning author. It took me by surprise — I didn't expect such a momentous event here, in Appalachia. After all, isn't this the middle of nowhere?

There's some quibbling — the drink's roots trace back to Knoxville, Tennessee, which is why the word "modern" is in the designation. But it's here, in Marion, where the Dew truly realized both its potential and its propensity for change.

When I first encountered Kingsolver's work (The Poisonwood Bible, in high school AP English class), I was more partial to Mountain Dew Code Red — the version most associated with hardcore gamers. That didn't end up being my life, though.

Contested memories, an overlooked and condescended-to town, expectations of the future that go awry, how things change (but do they, really?) — we get into all of that in my interview with Kingsolver about her new novel, Partita. It's about a young classical pianist from Appalachia who has the chops to really make it, until her life gets upended. Kingsolver grew up loving classical music, and even went to college on a music scholarship. But that didn't end up being her life, either.

Give the full interview a listen in NPR's Book of the Day podcast feed.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i Akilah Townsend for NPR

Contemporary art world titan Theaster Gates is taking his career in a new direction by acquiring Pickard China, the last remaining manufacturer of fine china in the United States. Philadelphia's historic Academy of Natural Sciences closed just short of its 200th birthday last week amid an intense effort by local residents, politicians and scientists to save it. The U.S. Coast Guard says searchers have found debris off Nantucket, Mass., from a Canadian air ambulance that disappeared Saturday while carrying six people from Bermuda to Boston.

Sponsor Message

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen. Majd Al-Waheidi contributed.

World.title: FlyDubai attacker intended to crash plane into Tel Aviv airport, investigation finds
World.content:
FlyDubai attacker intended to crash plane into Tel Aviv airport, investigation finds

toggle caption i Jack Guez/AFP via Getty Images

TEL AVIV, Israel — An ongoing investigation into last week's midair attack on a FlyDubai plane has found that the co-pilot who tried to take control of the flight intended to crash it into Israel's Ben Gurion International Airport, a person familiar with the matter but not authorized to speak publicly told NPR.

The plane was flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv and was intending to land at Ben Gurion midmorning on a busy weekday. The co-pilot attacked the plane's captain midflight with an axe and attempted to take control of the plane.

Sponsor Message

It is believed that the co-pilot likely acted alone, the source said.

Authorities in the United Arab Emirates — which is leading the main investigation into the incident, with help from Israeli officials — and in Israel have deemed the attack an attempted terrorist attack, although the motive is still being investigated.

The commercial flight had 172 people on board, according to the airline, the majority of whom were Israeli. All passengers and crew were safe and accounted for after the plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. They were flown to Tel Aviv late Wednesday.

Investigators said that the co-pilot carried out the attack with what's called a crash axe — a lightweight emergency tool stored in the cockpit to break through panels or jammed doors in the event of a crash.

The aviation tracking site Flightradar24 said data shows at one point the plane descended more than 14,000 feet, or nearly 3 miles, in under 30 seconds — way faster than normal.

The pilot was able to open the cockpit door during the attack, and passengers rushed in and subdued the attacker, while another pilot who happened to be on board helped land the plane, according to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who spoke to the injured pilot as he was recovering in the hospital.

Sponsor Message

Both the pilot and the co-pilot are alive and have been transferred to the UAE for questioning.

Attacker is an Omani national

The co-pilot is from Oman, according to Israeli officials. Omani and Emirati officials have not confirmed that publicly.

The detail of his nationality is raising questions in Israel about how he was allowed to fly a plane heading to Ben Gurion, as Israel does not allow pilots from countries it doesn't have diplomatic relations with to fly in its airspace. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Fox & Friends that Israel checks the background of pilots flying routes into the country, and that the attacker must have gotten through a "loophole."

Officials from Israel's Ministry of Transportation and security services have traded accusations over the lack of oversight and vetting of the pilot. Meanwhile, several of Netanyahu's political opponents have said the security breach is a failure on the prime minister's part and have called for a larger investigation.

Netanyahu announced late Sunday that there will be a formal examination into the security situation around "foreign civil aviation into Israel," but did not provide further details.

A politically tense time in Israel

National elections in Israel — which will determine whether or not Netanyahu will remain prime minister — are just weeks away. It's the first such national election since the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, which sparked the war in Gaza.

Polls in Israel show that the race is tight, and analysts say the FlyDubai attack would likely not change Israelis' attitudes on how they will vote.

Netanyahu has been campaigning largely on the idea that he alone can protect Israelis from the external threats that Israel faces, while his opponents have pointed to what they see as major security failures under his leadership — including the Oct. 7 attack.

World.title: Nobel medicine prize goes to 3 scientists for research into brain activity
World.content:
Nobel medicine prize goes to 3 scientists for research into brain activity

toggle caption i Pontus Lundahl/TT News Agency via AP

STOCKHOLM — The Nobel Prize in medicine was awarded Monday to three scientists working on the mechanisms the brain uses to switch on, or off, the activity of individual nerve cells.

Karl Deisseroth, 54, Peter Hegemann, 71, and Georg Nagel, 73, have carried out research into light-gated ion channels and optogenetics. They are based at universities in Germany and the United States.

toggle caption i Eugene Hoshiko/AP

The Nobel committee lauded their work, writing on X that the method "is now being used in laboratories around the world to reveal the brain's mysteries."

The Nobel Assembly said Deisseroth is based at Stanford University in California, while Hegemann is at Humboldt University in Berlin and Nagel at the University of Würzburg in Germany.

Sponsor Message

Thomas Perlmann, the secretary of the medicine committee, said he was able to reach all three winners by phone Monday.

The prize was announced at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, kicking off Nobels week.

The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million).

Last year, the prize went to three scientists researching the immune system.

Monday's medicine prize is followed by the physics prize on Tuesday, chemistry on Wednesday and literature on Thursday.

After Friday's peace prize is awarded, the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced on Oct. 12.

The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organization.
