World.title: Going to Iron Maiden at Estadio Nacional? What to Know Before Thursday
World.content:
If you have tickets for Iron Maiden at Estadio Nacional this Thursday, leave the umbrella at home. It’s on the list of items you won’t be allowed to bring in, even though afternoon storms are common in San José this time of year. Gates open at 4 p.m. British band The Raven Age opens at 6 p.m., and Iron Maiden is scheduled to take the stage at 7:30 p.m. The show is part of the band’s Run For Your Lives anniversary tour.

Your entrance depends on your ticket, so check it before you head to La Sabana. The Trooper ticket holders go in through the northeast access. Gradería Norte enters on the north side of the stadium, diagonally across from the Hilton hotel. If you’re in Sombra, Platea or Balcón, use the east side. General Standing goes in through the southwest access, across from the Teletica studios, and Gradería Sur enters on the south side.

Organizers recommend downloading your NFC ticket and saving it to your phone’s digital wallet before you leave home. That way you’re not trying to load a ticket on an overloaded mobile network while you wait in line. Pack light, because the banned list is long. You can’t bring weapons or sharp objects, vapes, lighters, umbrellas, food or drinks, professional or semi-professional cameras, selfie sticks, insulated tumblers, wallet chains, drones, drugs or seats of any kind.

Bags can’t be larger than 30 centimeters (about 12 inches), and flags or signs can’t be larger than 1 meter (about 3.3 feet). A packable rain jacket or poncho isn’t among the banned items organizers announced, which makes it your best bet if the weather turns. If you don’t have tickets yet, two sections were still on sale as of Monday. The Trooper costs 71,600 colones (about $155) and General Standing costs 41,800 colones (about $90). Both zones are restricted to adults 18 and over, so don’t plan on bringing a teenager into either one.

Expect heavy traffic around La Sabana, Rohrmoser and Paseo Colón as crowds arrive in the late afternoon, right as the evening rush hour builds. If you can, take a taxi or rideshare and agree on a pickup point a few blocks from the stadium. If you’re staying nearby, note that water service is scheduled to be cut in Mata Redonda, Hatillo and Pavas from 10 p.m. Thursday to 4 a.m. Friday for system work, according to the national water utility AyA. Fill a few containers before you leave for the show.

After San José, the tour continues through Latin America, with a stop in Bogotá, Colombia, on Sunday.

World.title: Canadian arrivals in Costa Rica jump 24% as travelers skip the US
World.content:
Canadians who have turned away from vacations in the United States are showing up in Costa Rica in record numbers, and they are staying long enough to change the math of our tourism economy. Figures from the Costa Rican Tourism Institute (ICT) show 232,949 Canadians arrived in the first eight months of 2026, up from 187,781 in the same period last year. That is a 24.1% increase and the fastest growth of any major market.

Canada’s share of all visitors climbed from 9% to 10.6%. Arrivals from the United States, which still supplies well over half of all tourists, rose just 2.7% over the same months. What’s driving it is no mystery as Canadian travel to the United States has fallen sharply since early 2025 amid trade disputes and political tension between the two countries, and the winter travelers who once filled Florida condos have been looking elsewhere.

Connie Salazar, executive director of the tourism promotion group Proimagen has said Canadians who favored the Florida coast no longer want to go there and that Costa Rica has proven a natural fit with its beaches, nature and wellness offerings. Costa Rica moved quickly to catch that demand. The ICT’s air connectivity team spotted the opening as Canadian traffic to the United States and parts of the Caribbean dropped, then traveled to Canada with airport authorities to pitch the airlines directly.

Carriers responded with more frequencies and new routes. Air Canada, WestJet, Air Transat and Porter now all fly here and Air Transat and Porter have converted seasonal flights into year-round service. In December Air Canada will launch a Vancouver-Liberia route, Air Transat will connect Quebec City with San José and Porter will add four weekly flights between Toronto and Juan Santamaría International Airport. By high season travelers will be able to fly nonstop from seven Canadian cities.

What makes this market so valuable is not only how many Canadians come but how long they stay. ICT data show the average Canadian visitor spends 14.9 nights in the country and about $203 (₡93,000) per day. That works out to roughly $3,000 (₡1.4 million) per person per trip. Applied to the 45,000 additional Canadians who arrived through August, the growth alone represents something on the order of $135 million (₡62 billion) in new spending. It is a rough estimate, but it shows the scale.

A visitor who stays two weeks or more behaves differently from one on a five-day resort package. Long-stay travelers rent houses and condos, shop at local supermarkets and ferias, hire guides, eat at neighborhood sodas and move around the country. Their money reaches small businesses and communities that rarely see the short-stay crowd. Many are retirees and remote workers escaping the northern winter, and the rules favor them, since Canadians can remain in Costa Rica for up to 180 days as tourists.

Some of those who return year after year go on to rent long term, buy property or apply for residency, which carries the benefit well beyond hotels and tours. The gains so far are concentrated in Guanacaste. Daniel Oduber Quirós International Airport in Liberia received 71% of all Canadian air arrivals in the first four months of the year, a 32% jump over 2025, and Canadians now account for roughly 26% of tourist arrivals there.

Hotels, vacation rentals, restaurants and tour operators along the northern Pacific coast are the most direct beneficiaries. The challenge for the rest of Costa rica is to draw those long stays south and inland. There is also a strategic benefit since with Americans making up close to six of every 10 visitors, Costa Rica’s tourism business has long been exposed to a downturn in a single market. A growing Canadian base, along with steady gains from Europe, spreads that risk.

Canadian demand remains weighted toward the winter months, though the move to year-round flights by two carriers suggests that is starting to change. Tourism officials are not yet declaring victory as air arrivals slowed in June, which the ICT attributed to geopolitical tension and higher jet fuel costs and the institute has said it is watching the second half of the year with caution.

The strong colón, trading near ₡460 to the dollar, makes Costa Rica a more expensive destination than it was a few years ago, a cost that weighs on visitors who earn Canadian dollars. And part of the current surge depends on a political mood in Canada that could shift. For now the trend favors Costa Rica with airlines are adding seats rather than cutting them and the ICT has stepped up promotion in Toronto, Montreal and other cities.

First time visitors to Costa Rica during a winter away from Florida may keep coming back even if relations with Washington improve. If they do, those who arrived because of a boycott could become one of the steadiest sources of Costa Rican tourism.

World.title: Costa Rica Landfill Plan in Mora Faces New Land-Use Challenge
World.content:
A decades-long fight over a proposed waste project in Picagres has flared again after the Mora municipal administration issued a new land-use certificate for Parque Industrial Jateo, prompting residents, local officials and lawmakers to question whether the project should be allowed to move forward.

Residents and members of the Mora Municipal Council toured the area Saturday, Oct. 3, with lawmakers and legislative advisers. The visit focused on the roads that would be used by garbage trucks and the environmental conditions around the proposed site in Cordel, a community in the district of Picagres.

Among those joining the visit were Álvaro Ramírez Bogantes, leader of the opposition National Liberation Party in the Legislative Assembly, and Frente Amplio lawmaker Vianey Mora Vega, who represents San José province. Ramírez questioned whether the existing roads could handle the volume and weight of truck traffic associated with the project, while Mora raised concerns about water sources and nearby ecosystems.

The controversy was revived after it became known that the municipality had issued a land-use certificate for Parque Industrial Jateo. That certificate does not by itself authorize construction or allow the waste facility to begin operating, but opponents say the decision is significant because the lack of a valid municipal land-use document has been one of the major obstacles facing the project for years.

The Mora Municipal Council has called an extraordinary meeting for Monday, Oct. 5, at 6 p.m. to review the file and hear from Mayor Rodrigo Alfonso Jiménez Cascante and municipal staff involved in the process. Council members are expected to examine the technical and legal basis used to issue the certificate.

Parque Industrial Jateo is planned for a property of roughly 237 hectares, or about 586 acres, in Picagres. Court records describe the proposal as a complex intended for the treatment and recovery of waste generated in the Greater Metropolitan Area. The project has been debated in Mora since the 1990s and has repeatedly faced opposition over access roads, water, forests and the suitability of the location.

The project does have an important approval already in place. Costa Rica’s National Environmental Technical Secretariat, known as SETENA, granted environmental viability in May 2013. Appeals against that decision were rejected by the Environment Ministry in 2015. However, the developer later asked SETENA to suspend the deadline for beginning construction while it worked through municipal and Health Ministry requirements.

SETENA subsequently tied that suspension to the resolution of disputes involving municipal land-use authorization. That history makes the newly issued Mora certificate particularly important, although it remains unclear whether the document will be enough to clear other administrative or legal hurdles facing the project.

Environmental concerns remain at the center of the opposition. Documents cited by community groups and municipal representatives say the National System of Conservation Areas identified forest cover on the property in 2024. A separate 2025 review by the Water Directorate of the Environment Ministry identified six water sources on the property, including four permanent springs connected with the Mesas and Pacayal streams.

The property also sits next to the El Rodeo Protected Zone and within the Garcimuñoz Biological Corridor, according to records cited by opponents. They have also questioned whether an environmental study prepared years ago adequately reflects current conditions on the property.

Water has been a recurring issue around the site. An official notice published in La Gaceta in 2023 showed Parque Industrial Jateo seeking water concessions from the Pacayal, Las Mesas and Cacho streams on the Picagres property. The developer has publicly presented Jateo as more than a traditional landfill, describing the concept around waste management, recovery, research and innovation. Court records similarly describe it as an industrial complex for treating and recovering value from waste produced in the Greater Metropolitan Area.

The dispute comes as Costa Rica continues looking for additional ways to handle solid waste from the metropolitan region. Health Ministry planning documents have previously listed Jateo among possible projects intended to serve municipalities in the Greater Metropolitan Area.

For now, the new land-use certificate has not ended the debate. Instead, it has reopened one of Mora’s longest-running environmental disputes and shifted attention to Monday night’s Municipal Council meeting, where residents are looking for an explanation of why the project received a document it had struggled for years to obtain.

World.title: Jamie Young murder trial delayed after attorney falls ill
World.content:
Jamie Young murder trial delayed after attorney falls ill

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The murder trial of Jamie Caesar Young, accused of killing 30-year-old Damion Dominique Baptist during a deadly highway pursuit in 2024, has been postponed after Young’s attorney fell ill.

Young appeared before Justice Candace Nanton in the High Court on Monday, when his trial had been scheduled to begin. However, the matter could not proceed because his attorney, Dr. Lynden Jones, was unable to attend due to illness.

The case was consequently adjourned to October 13, 2026.

Young is accused of murdering Baptist, a former Belize Defence Force soldier and bus driver from Burrell Boom Village, on March 16, 2024.

According to police allegations, Baptist was driving a red Ford Fusion along the Philip Goldson Highway with Laneedrah Dawson when they were allegedly pursued by Young, Dawson’s former boyfriend.

Police say the confrontation began near the HRCU housing area, where Young allegedly attempted to collide with Baptist’s vehicle before pointing a firearm in their direction.

Investigators allege that Young then followed the pair in a grey Wingle pickup and fired at their vehicle near Tubal Training School, shattering a passenger-side window.

The chase allegedly continued toward Ladyville, where police say Young again pulled alongside the Ford Fusion near Our Lady of the Way RC School between Miles 8 and 9 and fired into the vehicle.

Baptist was struck in the head, lost control of the car and crashed into a lamp post. He was transported to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where he was pronounced dead.

Young later surrendered to police and was formally charged with Baptist’s murder as well as aggravated assault upon Dawson.

The case has since moved through the High Court’s pre-trial process. In May, BBN reported that prosecutors intend to rely on surveillance footage, photographs and material allegedly extracted from a phone, while Young’s defence indicated that it intends to call an alibi witness. Trial dates had been scheduled for October 5 through October 13.

Young remains accused and has not been convicted of the offences.

World.title: Sandhill woman remanded after being granted bail and never showing up again; may face attempted arson charge
World.content:
Sandhill woman remanded after being granted bail and never showing up again; may face attempted arson charge

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Sandhill Village woman is back behind bars after the Chief Magistrate revoked her bail for repeatedly failing to appear in court, while police are also reportedly considering an additional attempted arson charge against her.

Thirty-year-old Francine Milligan appeared in Court #1 on Monday after being picked up last Friday on a bench warrant issued for her non-appearance in an ongoing damage-to-property case.

Milligan was unable to provide the court with a satisfactory explanation for why she had failed to return for her case after being granted bail, and the Chief Magistrate subsequently revoked that bail and remanded her to the Belize Central Prison.

She is due back in court on Thursday, October 8, when she is expected to receive disclosure in the damage-to-property matter.

During Monday’s appearance, Milligan was also informed that police may bring an additional charge of attempted arson in connection with an alleged incident involving her neighbour’s property. If that charge is ready by Thursday, she could be arraigned during her next court appearance.

The original case dates back to September 2025 and involves Milligan’s neighbour and relative.

According to police allegations, on September 1, 2025, Milligan went onto the woman’s property at Mile 19 on the Philip Goldson Highway in Sandhill Village and became involved in a confrontation with the woman and her husband.

The complainant alleged that Milligan told them to move out of the house, insulted them and, before leaving the property, broke a palm tree valued at $60.

Police said the woman also reported previous disputes and alleged threats involving Milligan.

Milligan was later detained on September 13 and arraigned on September 18, 2025, for damage to property.

Public reporting from the time confirms that Milligan was initially granted bail but was subsequently sent to prison following an outburst during her court appearance.

She was later released on bail again, subject to conditions that included staying away from the complainant and her property. The court was told Monday that further complaints have since been made against Milligan, raising concerns that she may also have breached those bail conditions.

The Chief Magistrate told Milligan that her failure to attend court and the alleged breaches left the court with no option but to revoke her bail.

World.title: ‘MOVE B***H’: IT technician remanded over allegedly hitting 2 people with vehicle in Magistrate’s Court parking lot
World.content:
‘MOVE B***H’: IT technician remanded over allegedly hitting 2 people with vehicle in Magistrate’s Court parking lot

By Breaking Belize News Staff: He wasn’t repairing a computer but a 27-year-old Belize City IT technician has been remanded to the Belize Central Prison after allegedly trying to fix two people’s business and being charged in connection with an alleged vehicle attack in the parking lot of the Belize City Magistrate’s Court that reportedly left two people injured.

Jahshield Tyrique Myles, of a Tibruce Street address, appeared before a Magistrate in Court #5 on Monday in the presence of his attorney, Leeroy Banner.

The charges stem from an incident on September 28, 2026, in the Magistrate’s Court parking lot on Coney Drive.

Police allege that Myles used a motor vehicle as a dangerous instrument with the intent to cause harm to another man. He was charged with use of deadly means of harm in relation to that man.

Myles was additionally charged with grievous harm and wounding upon a woman. Court reporting also indicated he faces a harm charge in connection with the incident.

The police prosecutor strongly objected to bail, citing the seriousness of the allegations and the fact that the incident allegedly occurred immediately outside the court building.

Banner argued that the charges remain allegations and that his client is presumed innocent until proven guilty. He told the court that Myles is the father and sole provider of one child, and argued that remanding him could cost him his job, customers and livelihood.

The attorney further submitted that Myles is not a flight risk and argued that prosecutors would ultimately have to prove that his client intentionally used the vehicle to cause the alleged injuries.

After standing the matter down briefly, the Magistrate denied bail at approximately 11:16 a.m. and remanded Myles to the Belize Central Prison.

A bail plea was taken on the charge of use of deadly means of harm, while Myles pleaded not guilty to the other charges read to him.

World.title: Taiwan condemns “transnational repression” after US arrest
World.content:
Taiwan condemns “transnational repression” after US arrest

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Taiwan is speaking out after US authorities arrested a woman accused of spying on President Lai Ching-te’s family for China.

Taiwan’s Presidential Office confirmed that the President’s relatives were the targets, calling it “a classic case of transnational repression.” The office strongly condemned the alleged acts, saying they violate human rights and national sovereignty and are meant to intimidate those who stand for freedom and democracy.

The FBI arrested Wanying Zhang, a 34 year old real estate agent from Irvine, California, at LAX on Sunday. She is accused of conducting surveillance on the President’s son in Seattle and passing photos, video and vehicle details to Chinese officials.

FBI Director Kash Patel warned that America is not a playground for foreign adversaries.

The case is part of a wider US crackdown on alleged Chinese agents. The Justice Department says Beijing has worked to track and harass pro democracy activists in the US and to influence American politics. In May, the mayor of Arcadia, California, agreed to plead guilty to acting as an illegal agent for China and resigned.

China, which split from Taiwan after a civil war in 1949, claims the island as its territory and views President Lai as a separatist. The Chinese Embassy in Washington did not immediately comment.

For Belize, the case involves one of its closest partners. Belize has recognized the Republic of China (Taiwan) since 1989 and remains one of only a handful of countries with formal diplomatic ties to Taipei.

Just last week, Taiwan’s Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung visited Belize, meeting Prime Minister John Briceño and signing agreements to establish the Taiwan Caribbean Academy at the University of Belize and to train Belizean diplomats.

Zhang has not yet entered a plea.

World.title: Construction begins on new cattle export corral in Chan Chen, Corozal
World.content:
Construction begins on new cattle export corral in Chan Chen, Corozal

By Zoila Palma: Construction is officially underway on a new cattle export corral in Chan Chen Village, Corozal District, as the Government of Belize moves to strengthen infrastructure supporting the country’s livestock sector.

The project is being implemented through the Climate Resilient and Sustainable Agriculture Project (CRESAP), by the Belize Social Investment Fund (BSIF) and the Ministry of Agriculture, Food Security and New Growth Industries (MAFSNGI), in collaboration with the Ministry of Economic Transformation (MET).

The new facility is expected to strengthen Belize’s livestock value chain by improving cattle handling and supporting greater export readiness. The investment is also intended to create increased opportunities for livestock producers by providing infrastructure to facilitate the movement and preparation of cattle for export markets.

The initiative is being undertaken in partnership with the Belize Livestock Producers’ Association (BLPA) and is being described as an important step toward building a more resilient, competitive and sustainable livestock sector.

World.title: $500,000 investment could earn foreigners residency in Belize
World.content:
$500,000 investment could earn foreigners residency in Belize

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Foreign investors could soon secure residency in Belize, but it will come with a price and conditions.

The Ministry of Immigration, Governance and Labour has outlined the main features of the proposed Investor Residence Program, which Minister Kareem Musa says is meant to bring in investment while keeping the immigration system secure.

Applicants will need to invest at least $500,000 and spend a combined 12 months in Belize within three years.

Those who lie on their applications or fail to keep up with the requirements risk having their investor status taken away.

The program was approved by Cabinet in December 2025. The US State Department’s 2026 Investment Climate Statement noted the plan, while pointing out that the enabling legislation was still pending.

Several Caribbean countries already operate similar programs, and Government says they have helped stimulate economic activity.

For Belize, the hope is that the program will bring new capital, create jobs and support growth in priority sectors.

Further updates are expected from the Ministry as the program moves forward.

World.title: Police investigate Coastal Road collision that killed Ramzi Asaad
World.content:
Police investigate Coastal Road collision that killed Ramzi Asaad

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating a fatal collision on the Coastal Road that claimed the life of Belize City resident Ramzi Asaad.

According to police, officers responded on Friday to a road traffic accident involving a trailer truck and a car.

Investigators say Hector Morales was driving the trailer truck and was making a turn when the car collided with the trailer.

The car subsequently caught fire and was extensively damaged.

The driver of the car was identified as Ramzi Asaad of Belize City.

Public reporting following the crash indicated that Asaad, a father, had been travelling from Belize City toward Dangriga when the collision occurred.

Police say Morales was served with a notice of intended prosecution and a sample was obtained from him as part of the investigation.

Investigators will determine whether any charges should be brought once the relevant evidence has been reviewed.

The investigation remains ongoing.

World.title: Police say alcohol involved in crash that killed Chad Borland near Belmopan
World.content:
Police say alcohol involved in crash that killed Chad Borland near Belmopan

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police say alcohol is believed to have been involved in the fatal road traffic accident that claimed the life of 28-year-old Chad Anton Borland near Belmopan.

Borland died after the Mazda he was travelling in left the Hummingbird Highway near La Cabana and crashed into bushes.

Police say Borland was driving when he lost control of the vehicle and was thrown from it.

Another passenger, identified in earlier reports as 28-year-old Jeffrey Perez, sustained minor injuries and is in stable condition.

During Monday’s police press briefing, investigators were asked whether alcohol may have played a role in the crash and confirmed that information received by police indicates that alcohol was involved.

Earlier reports say the crash occurred at around 4:00 p.m. on October 1. The Mazda reportedly travelled approximately 150 feet off the highway before coming to rest in thick bushes. Borland was found near the vehicle and later pronounced dead at the Western Regional Hospital.

Police investigations continue.

World.title: OUR calls for more coordinated water sector amid drought
World.content:
File Photo

KINGSTON, Jamaica — The Office of Utilities Regulation (OUR) is calling for better planning in the water sector amid ongoing drought conditions

During a recent public education webinar, the OUR called for stronger coordination, long-term planning and accountable investment across Jamaica’s water sector to improve service delivery and strengthen resilience in the face of increasing climate and operational challenges.

It comes as Jamaicans face water lockoffs and increasing food prices.

“Jamaica has established a sector governance framework, institutions and instruments, but service remains uneven. We need to connect planning and financing more closely to what customers experience at the tap and on their bills,” said OUR Director of Regulation, Policy, Monitoring and Enforcement, Duane Rowe.

He maintained that Jamaica must strengthen the links between planning, financing and customer outcomes to achieve meaningful improvements in water service delivery. He said while adjustment measures are in place to address the current situation in the short term, there is also a need to establish the long-term arrangements required for effective operation of the sector.

Rowe also underscored the need for greater coordination across the sector through a strengthened legislative framework.

“Stronger water sector coordination would benefit from an umbrella legislation. Such legislation could clarify stakeholders’ responsibility, address gaps in the current framework and require coordination, including information sharing and joint planning,” said Rowe.

The webinar also included representatives from the National Water Commission (NWC) and the Water Resources Authority (WRA) examining issues affecting the sector, including infrastructure investment, drought response, non-revenue water (NRW) reduction, water security, climate variability and regulatory reform.

NRW is water produced and supplied by the NWC that does not generate income because it is lost to leaks, illegal connections, theft, or other unbilled uses.

Rowe noted that despite a NRW level decline from 75.1 per cent in 2021 to 73.4 per cent in 2025, significant losses continue to affect operational efficiency, financial sustainability and service reliability.

According to Rowe, addressing these challenges will require a sustained focus on long-term water planning, reducing non-revenue water, improving service reliability and tackling the energy and financing constraints that continue to affect the sector.

NWC’s Acting Vice President of Operations, Dr Phillipa Campbell-Francis, said the utility continues to advance major projects, including the Rio Cobre Water Treatment Plant, the Western Water Resilience Improvement Project and the Greater Mandeville Water Supply Project.

“The NWC is serious about ensuring that our customers are served during this time and also to ensure that we are building resilience for the future, as demonstrated in the projects that we are now doing to improve reliability,” said Campbell-Francis.

She also outlined the NWC’s islandwide NRW programme, which aims to reduce losses from approximately 70 per cent to 30 per cent through auditing, infrastructure upgrades and sustained maintenance.

Meanwhile, hydrogeologist at the Water Resources Authority, Maurice Wallace, who presented worrying data on reduced water levels in some of the major freshwater systems, said Jamaica’s water sector should build on greater investment in science, research and monitoring, while strengthening collaboration among key agencies to support evidence-based policymaking and sustainable water resource management.

World.title: GET SLAVERY HISTORY RIGHT
World.content:
Warmington

THE Global Afrikan Congress (GAC) has pointedly told Government Member of Parliament Everald Warmington that he has a “misinformed understanding” of history in relation to the transatlantic slave trade and has urged him to apologise for his recent comments on the issue in the legislature.

Additionally, the organisation recommended that he undertake a process of what it calls “historical self-repair” and directed him to the works of historians, scholars and writers who have examined the history of Africa, the Caribbean, European expansion, slavery, colonialism, and resistance.

In an open letter to the St Catherine South Western Member of Parliament, the GAC, described as an international umbrella organisation created by and for Africans and people of African descent, challenged Warmington’s comments relating to Jamaica’s petition to King Charles III and the King’s referral of the appeal to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.

The petition asks the Privy Council to make determinations on Britain’s seizure, transportation, chattelisation, and enslavement of Jamaica’s ancestors from the mid-17th century to 1834. On September 22, after Culture Minister Olivia Grange — who led a delegation that delivered the petition to Buckingham Palace on September 7 — informed Parliament that King Charles has referred the petition to the Privy Council, Warmington said he found the delegation’s visit to London embarrassing.

“I’m embarrassed at the spectacle of the photo ops in London. We went there and [it] remind me of this nursery rhyme: Pussycat, Pussycat where have you been? I’ve been to London to see the king.

Pussycat, Pussycat what did you do there? I left a petition on the empty chair,” Warmington declared in the House.

“We keep on speaking of the buyers of the slaves, but nobody speaks of the sellers of the slave. The white man didn’t go to Africa and pick up enslaved people and take them across here.

They were caught by black people who sold them to the white man to come here,” he added. In response, the GAC said Warmington displayed a “subjective and derisive formulation of history”.

“We respect your right to your own interpretation of history, though it is a colonial formulation and historically falsified to justify their crimes.

However, we vigorously assert that you don’t have the right to rewrite history based on your obviously misinformed understanding of it,” the organisation said in the letter signed by its Ambassador General Cikiah Thomas.

“The problem is not that you have raised the question of African involvement in the history of the slave trade.

The problem is that you have presented an extraordinarily complex historical system of European invasion, military coercion, commercial expansion, warfare, forced transportation, plantation enslavement, colonial law, and racial ideology as though a simple distinction between African sellers and European buyers can adequately explain it,” the GAC said.

The group argued that there was no market for buying and selling free Africans. “On the contrary, there was coercion at bayonet point by Europeans to forcibly coerce Africans to round up other Africans, not for sale but for European appeasement; and forcible capture for the enslaved person awaiting ships.

Hence, your depiction of a market in Africans is not only based on misinformation, but it is also an example of how many of us have internationalised racism.”

The GAC insisted that the history of the transatlantic slave trade cannot properly be understood by asking only who physically captured a particular African and who purchased that person.

Rather, much larger and more insightful questions needed to be asked, such as who created the enormous transatlantic demand for enslaved labour; who organised the Atlantic commercial system for African labour; who financed and insured the voyages of European ships and their cargoes; who controlled the ships and shipping networks; who established and protected the plantation economy; who developed colonial laws defining Africans and their descendants as property; who accumulated wealth from the system, and where is the wealth; who defended the enslavement of Africans through colonial governments and legislatures; and who maintained the system through military and imperial power?

“Unfortunately, contrary to your simplistic and infantile responses in our country’s Parliament, the cited questions cannot be answered by simply saying that Africans sold Africans,” the GAC told Warmington.

It said that the colonial miseducation and misconception that Warmington demonstrated as an MP requires clarification for him and “other black folks who may think, like you, that the existing African communities did not resist the massive European invasion and encroachment on those communities.

Thus, it must be underscored that African societies fought against the capture and enslavement of their peoples.”

The GAC said that had Warmington taken some time to inform himself about the vicious history of the European invasion of Africa he would have learned that Africans resisted that invasion and that limitless numbers of Africans were slaughtered.

In relation to Jamaica’s petition to King Charles, the GAC said it was unclear what Warmington found embarrassing about a legitimate action regarding reparation. “Are you embarrassed about asking legal questions and holding white power structures accountable? Are you embarrassed about asking questions that make white people uncomfortable?” the GAC asked the MP.

“Specifically, the legal questions raised in the petition concern whether the seizure, transportation, and enslavement of Africans in Jamaica under British rule were lawful under English law; whether those practices breached relevant international obligations; and whether the United Kingdom has a legal obligation to provide a reparatory remedy to Jamaica.

What is there to be embarrassed about these fundamental questions of justice regarding African humanity?” the GAC said. It noted that the petition has now become a legal matter, and told Warmington that the least he could and should do “is allow due process of the law and the historical evidence to be examined”.

World.title: Not true
World.content:
TULLOCH-NEIL…it may be useful to determine what should constitute a formal complaint on the issue

NEW YORK, United States — Diaspora leaders here have rubbished a claim by permanent secretary in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade Sheila Sealy Monteith that there are no complaints among Jamaicans abroad about unspent Hurricane Melissa donations.

“We have been hearing voices of concern about how the donations have been or is being spent,” Irwine Clare Sr, a leading Diaspora advocate told the Jamaica Observer.

“There are many who believe that there is a serious trust issue when it comes to how donations from the Diaspora are handled by Government. We are not seeking to cast blame, but we believe we have a vested interest in seeking accountability and transparency in this matter.

We had a vested interested in what is considered as the most massive mobilisation of donations to help those who were affected by the hurricane, and we will do it again, but we must have clarity,” Clare Sr said.

On Thursday, September 30, 2026, Sealy Monteith told Parliament’s Internal and External Affairs Committee that the foreign ministry “had many opportunities to receive feedback from the Diaspora” but had not received any indication of concern.

She was responding to a question from Opposition Member of Parliament for St Ann South Eastern Dr Kenneth Russell as to whether the ministry has received any feedback from members of the Diaspora and donors about the slow use of their contributions. Jamaicans abroad and at home, as well as other groups and individuals, had donated millions of dollars to help the country recover from the ravages of Hurricane Melissa, which hit sections of the island last October.

But questions have been raised about the slow pace of utilising the funds, after the auditor general found that only about 1.7 per cent of the donated funds had been used months after the contributions were made.

Last Thursday, Sealy Monteith said that the ministry had not seen evidence of a decline in confidence in Jamaica’s ability to handle international support.

“We have used the strength of our diplomacy to ensure that countries who wish to contribute are enabled to contribute, that we are able to record it. We are providing direction for them, and we pass them on to the relevant authorities. We have not received any indication to date that there has been a loss of confidence in our abilities to use it,” she told the committee.

However, there was unanimity among Diaspora leaders who spoke to the Observer that there is widespread concern about the handling of the millions of dollars in donations made by members of the Diaspora. Former Global Jamaica Diaspora Council (GJDC) representative for the Northeast United States Dr Karren Dunkley cautioned against “interpreting the absence of formal complaints as an absence of concern”.

She said that she has “personally heard from Diaspora leaders and members across the globe who are deeply concerned about the pace of recovery”.

“Most importantly, there are also concerns about Jamaicans who still need meaningful assistance.

The reported utilisation of only 1.7 per cent of the donated Hurricane Melissa funds, understandably, raises serious questions about urgency, transparency, accountability, and our collective capacity to translate generosity into tangible relief for those who need it most,” Dunkley said.

“The Jamaica Diaspora remains deeply committed to our homeland, but generosity must be matched by timely action and clear communication about what was received, what has been spent, where resources have gone, what barriers may be slowing development, and when those waiting can expect assistance,” Dunkley added.

Dr Allan Cunningham, a university lecturer and leading Diaspora advocate in Florida, also alluded to what he argued is a trust issue some people within the Diaspora have when it comes to donating money to be used for relief efforts in Jamaica.

While he was careful not to blame the Government, Cunningham related a matter in which he said he was instrumental in raising US$800,000 to assist with COVID-19 relief efforts in Jamaica but never got any response on how the funds were used.

He said he is not surprised by the present concerns about the Melissa relief funds. “While the permanent secretary is reporting that there have been no complaints from the Diaspora regarding the slow response of the recovery spending, it would have been useful if mechanisms were put in place to inform us, and the general public, about the recovery programme,” said Cunningham.

Current GJDC representative for the Northeast United States Michelle Tulloch-Neil, while acknowledging that there are concerns among several members of the Diaspora over the issue, believes that it may be useful to determine what should constitute a formal complaint on the issue.

She believes that with the matter now in the open it might be the right time for it to be dealt with by the Diaspora. Another Diaspora leader, Peter Gracey, said it is unfortunate that the ministry has not received any complaints about the slow pace of the recovery effort and how financial donations are being used.

World.title: Designing Resilience
World.content:
“WHO knew that within a few weeks of Design Week Ja 2025, held under the theme ‘Creative Resilience’, Jamaica would be confronted with the devastating impact of Hurricane Melissa?” asked Jamaica Observer Design Week Ja conceptualiser Novia McDonald- Whyte at Sunday’s launch event for the 2026 edition.

Back again with aplomb and renewed purpose — powered by Tile City & Home Centre and KOHLER — this year’s edition is aptly themed ‘Restoration & Resilience’.

The S Hotel Kingston-hosted launch featured presentations from industry players and partners all on board with fervour for the continued mission.

“We wanted a slate of presenters who understood the magnitude of Hurricane Melissa — people who had survived it, lived through it, and were now considering what they could contribute to the wider conversation around Restoration & Resilience,” shared McDonald-Whyte.

Here, pictured at the Sunday, October 4 kick-off are McDonald-Whyte (centre) with presenters and partners (from left) Marsha Parchment, Nastassia Morrison, Joelle Smith, Michelle Arroyave, Annaliesa Lindsay, and Dwayne Berbick.

Donnielle Robe, marketing manager, Tile City & Home Centre, who announced that as her team works on expanding offerings to build back Jamaica even better, they will soon open a signature showroom.

World.title: Sandals Island Challenge hits £100,000 fund-raising target
World.content:
Participants pose before competing in a 21km run through the town of Falmouth in Trelawny and into the hills of the Good Hope Eco Park, hosted by Chukka Caribbean Adventures, on Saturday as part of the Sandals Foundation Island Challenge.

FALMOUTH, Trelawny — The Sandals Foundation Island Challenge Jamaica has reached its £100,000 fund-raising target, paving the way for the purchase of critical equipment to help restore neonatal and paediatric services at Falmouth Public General Hospital nearly one year after Hurricane Melissa devastated the facility.

The milestone was reached on Sunday as participants took on day three of the four-day endurance challenge, completing a 21-kilometre half-marathon through Falmouth, with the route taking them past the hospital that has been at the heart of this year’s fund-raising effort.

The achievement represents a major boost for the hospital which suffered extensive damage when the record-breaking Hurricane Melissa struck sections of Jamaica as a Category 5 system on October 28, 2025. Falmouth Public General Hospital lost much of its roofing and, consequently, critical medical equipment, furniture and appliances.

Sunday’s half-marathon brought the purpose of the Island Challenge into sharp focus as participants made their way through the historic town. Workers from the hospital gathered outside the facility to cheer on the runners as they passed. Nurse/midwife Monique McKenzie-Matherson was among those who welcomed the initiative.

“I am super excited about this initiative. We are really in need — the babies at the hospital and the wider community. “Melissa came and she did a number on us, and we are grateful that somebody saw the need and is willing to assist,” she said. Psychiatric nursing aide Shawn Daley shared similar sentiments, stressing the importance of assistance as the hospital continues its recovery.

“It is something I think we should do early. The devastation was very bad so the help is very crucial for the staff, community and the parish,” Daley said.

For the hospital’s administration, the £100,000 will allow attention to be placed on replacing the equipment that was lost when the hurricane ripped through the facility. Falmouth Public General Hospital CEO Carlington McLennon said the extent of the losses went beyond the visible structural damage.

“While a lot of persons focus on the infrastructural impact we had, what they fail to realise is that the equipment, furniture and appliances were also destroyed as a result of us losing the roof,” McLennon said. “With Sandals Foundation we can now focus on the equipment and appliances.”

Head of the hospital’s paediatric department, Dr Kerri-Ann McKenzie, said the funding will help to replace several pieces of essential equipment while also allowing the department to acquire resources it did not have before the hurricane.

For McKenzie, the support represents a significant step towards restoring the hospital’s ability to adequately care for some of its most vulnerable patients. “Words cannot express how grateful I am. This is a significant contribution, and I just want to say thanks to Sandals Foundation and to the athletes,” she said.

The Sandals Foundation Island Challenge is being staged in Jamaica for the first time, bringing together approximately 30 participants from the United Kingdom — including athletes, travel industry figures and other supporters — for four days of physically demanding activities across the island.

The challenge began last Friday with participants completing a 10-kilometre run from Rio Nuevo Fishing Beach in St Mary to Sandals Ochi Beach Club in St Ann, followed by a five-kilometre kayak journey along the White River Fish Sanctuary.

On Saturday the group climbed the world-famous Dunn’s River Falls before heading to the Bogue Forest Reserve where participants completed a rainforest trek and joined a reforestation effort which saw 300 West Indian cedar trees being planted as part of continued recovery efforts following Hurricane Melissa.

Sunday’s 21-kilometre half-marathon through Falmouth marked the third and one of the most symbolic legs of the challenge, allowing participants to see first-hand the hospital and community that will benefit from the funds raised.

The challenge concludes on Monday in St Andrew, where participants are scheduled to face a military-style endurance challenge in Newcastle before embarking on a partial hike of the Blue Mountains, reaching approximately 4,500 feet above sea level. Jamaica is the fourth Caribbean country to host the Island Challenge, following Antigua and Barbuda in 2023, St Vincent and the Grenadines in 2024, and Saint Lucia in 2025.

Previous stagings collectively raised more than £300,000 and benefited approximately 1,800 babies across the region.

World.title: Wet Music Festival paints waterfront
World.content:
Soca artise Lyrikal takes control of the Wet crowd.

DOWNTOWN Kingston’s waterfront became a playground of paint, foam, and water as hundreds of revellers welcomed daylight in a spectacularly colourful fashion at the Xodus Wet Music Festival on Saturday.

Staged at Port Spectrum, the cooler-friendly event brought rum, food, and infectious Caribbean rhythms together for a morning in which where drenched was part of the pleasure and leaving spotless was practically impossible. The venue was already full by 4:00 am, with patrons ready to surrender to the music.

As dawn gave way to daylight, the party revealed its full palette — paint-covered bodies, foam-flecked hair, and smiling faces that wore the evidence of a thoroughly good time.

Some revellers were so completely coated in blue that they could have passed for a delegation from the Smurfs’ village; although this crew had swapped mushroom houses for coolers and came armed with considerably more waistline action. DJs Zess, Rico the DJ, Nocturnal, Fatalic, Banka, and Tonio kept the waterfront moving, supplying the soundtrack for hours of dancing as water, paint, and foam added fresh excitement to the festivities.

A mini dance-off between two women, one Jamaican and the other Trinidadian, brought a playful dose of island rivalry to the celebration. Their friendly showdown added to the vibes, capturing the Caribbean camaraderie running through the event. “Between the music, the paint, and the water, I had the best time.

I came to enjoy myself, and Xodus gave me every reason to stay until the very end,” one female patron told the Jamaica Observer. There was plenty to keep appetites satisfied, too. Foska, Elle & Vire, KFC, and Pizza Hut provided complimentary food, while Janga’s sold meals of jerk, allowing patrons to refuel before returning to the revelry.

“The vibes were strong from early, and they never dropped. Good music, food, and everybody enjoying themselves. That is what made the morning for me,” a male patron added. At exactly 10:21 am, soca artiste Lyrikal stepped onstage, joining a party that was already in full swing.

His arrival gave fans another reason to keep the energy flowing. His performance included favourites Look Back, Judgmental, Happy Place, and Dip and Roll, bringing a live dimension to the morning’s musical offerings. Amid the celebration, Lyrikal also paid tribute to late soca star Ricardo Drue, performing selections from his catalogue, including Professional.

The tribute made room for remembrance while keeping Drue’s music woven into the Carnival spirit he helped shape. Even the advertised 11:00 am finish could not quite contain the festivities.

The party continued for approximately another halfhour, with Fatalic keeping the momentum going and ensuring female patrons had ample opportunity to enjoy themselves during the closing stretch.

The event came just days after Xodus launched its 2027 costumes under the theme Reign, carrying that excitement from the costume unveiling into a waterfront celebration bursting with colour and Caribbean flavour. The morning ended perfectly with a downpour, giving the paint-splashed revellers one final soaking, and the event a cooling finish.

World.title: Bartlett moves to plug tourism import leak
World.content:
Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett (right) making a point, last Friday, to Damine Sinanan, chief executive officer of the Caribbean Export Development Agency, following the plenary session on ‘Practical Building Blocks for Export Expansion’. It was held during the final day of the six-day Caribbean Week of Agriculture 2026 at Ocean Coral Spring Hotel in Trelawny. (Photo: Horace Hines)

CORAL SPRING, Trelawny — Warning that the region is losing billions of dollars in potential earnings by failing to adequately connect its farmers and agro-processors with the tourism industry, portfolio minister Edmund Bartlett is calling for a major overhaul with the establishment of a Caribbean Tourism Agricultural Logistics Centre among a raft of proposed initiatives.

He made the call last Friday, the final for the six-day Caribbean Week of Agriculture 2026 held at Ocean Coral Spring Hotel in Trelawny.

His comments came during the plenary session on ‘Practical Building Blocks for Export Expansion’.

The proposed Caribbean Tourism Agricultural Logistics Centre, Bartlett said, should go beyond conventional storage.

“It’s not a warehouse we’re looking for here, but what we’re seeking is a repository of all the supplies from within the Caribbean area, [for example] what Barbados provides, what Guyana provides, what Jamaica provides,” he said.

The facility, he explained, would accommodate fresh agricultural commodities as well as processed products — including juices, nectars, jams, and jellies — and facilitate their distribution throughout the region.

Other measures he proposed include establishing a dedicated tourism agricultural loan programme for small farmers, and harmonising food and agricultural standards across the Caribbean.

Bartlett also wants Jamaica’s Agri- Linkages Exchange (ALEX) platform, which links farmers with tourism buyers, expanded into a Caribbeanwide system. “We know the example we’ve had in four years — over $2 billion of trade between small farmers and hoteliers,” he said of ALEX.

Under the proposed regional platform, farmers in one Caribbean country could access buyers in another, with information on prices, quantities, availability, and delivery schedules made accessible to facilitate transactions.

Meanwhile, Bartlett said the tourism agricultural loan programme would be specifically designed to help small farmers achieve the consistency, quantity and quality required by hotels, while continuing to produce distinctive crops that can enhance the visitor experience.

He pointed to Jamaica’s experience, saying the Government placed $1 billion in EXIM Bank to support a lending programme, offering up to $25 million to smalland medium-size businesses at a 4.5 per cent interest rate, repayable over five years.

Bartlett said 443 small entities had benefited, with about $3 billion already re-lent through the revolving scheme and another $750 million available.

Agriculture and Fisheries Minister Floyd Green welcomed the tourism minister’s proposals. “I support a regional ALEX,” Green said, while calling for hotels to provide real-time information on their requirements so farmers can better match production with demand.

He also backed adapting Jamaica’s tourism lending experience to agriculture. “The experience of having pioneered the loan scheme that focuses on tourism enterprises clearly can be remodelled for our small farmers,” Green said.

Bartlett further called for the harmonisation of food safety and agricultural standards across the Caribbean, arguing that common protocols would remove barriers to regional trade and make it easier for major hotel brands to source from Caribbean producers.

His proposals, he said, are aimed at creating a Caribbean tourism economy in which a greater share of the money generated by visitors remains within the region — turning the relationship between the Caribbean’s “oil” and “soil” into a stronger engine of economic growth.

Bartlett argued that tourism, the Caribbean’s major economic driver, must be deliberately used to create a larger and more reliable market for regional agriculture.

“Tourism is our oil in the Caribbean…thanks to Guyana. Yes, and agriculture is our soil. The effort, therefore, is to bring our oil in consonance with our soil, and to create a Caribbean outcome that feeds the Caribbean, and then invite the world to come and taste it, and pay for it,” the tourism minister argued.

He said the region needs a comprehensive policy framework linking production, financing, infrastructure, marketing, and distribution, while eliminating leakages from the tourism economy.

Noting that agriculture accounts for about 42 per cent of visitor consumption requirements, he questioned how much of that demand is being met by Caribbean producers. “Where does the food come from?

Whose food are they consuming? Is it the Caribbean food, or is it imported food?” he asked. The minister argued that the scale of imports represents a major opportunity for local producers, insisting that the region must move away from an overly extractive tourism model.

“We have been concerned because, for us, tourism is the driving economic force of the region but it has been a very extractive industry — and that requires a paradigm shift,” Bartlett said.

World.title: HOT SEAT!
World.content:
El Salvador’s Marcelo Diaz (right) tackles Jamaica’s Bailey Cadamarteri during the Concacaf Nations League Cup football match at Cuscatlan Stadium in San Salvador on October 2, 2026. (Photo: AFP)

ALTHOUGH Jamaica’s Reggae Boyz are in pole position to qualify for the Concacaf Nations League knockout stage, interim Head Coach Rudolph Speid says they will take nothing for granted ahead of tonight’s rematch against host Honduras at Chelato Uclés National Stadium in Tegucigalpa.

Kick-off is at 9:00. The national senior men’s team currently sit second in Group B on six points, a point behind leaders Suriname, with a game remaining. The top two teams will advance to the knockout stage and the Jamaicans can guarantee their spot with a win.

However, their lone defeat of the competition was a 0-1 loss to Honduras at the National Stadium recently, which ended Jamaica’s 13-year unbeaten streak against the Central American team.

A win for the Hondurans, who sit fourth on three points, could also see them overtake the Boyz in the standings, if they win by two goals. Speid says he’s expecting another tough contest from the hosts, with a spot in the next round on the line.

“They are a good team, a dangerous team, and that is something that the Jamaican contingent will have to contend with in these games,” he said. “They are very skillful, fastpaced, resolute, tenacious.

Even when they went down to 10 men, they were able to hold us off and get a famous victory, so we are mindful and aware of their strengths.” Striker Javon East, who scored Jamaica’s two goals in their win over El Salvador on Friday, also spoke of the difficulty ahead for the Boyz.

“We know they have good qualities, technical players, so we expect a difficult match with many fans supporting them and on a complicated pitch,” he said.

“We can’t rule out the Honduran team because they’re a good team and have a good coach, so we expect a great battle. We just have to go there and follow the coach’s instructions.” A win for the Boyz is the safest option as three teams, including Honduras, can overtake them if they drop points.

A Jamaica defeat would see Guatemala advance with a win over Suriname. If Guatemala fail to win, Martinique could still move ahead of Jamaica by beating El Salvador by two or three goals.

Speid says his main focus is getting all three points against Honduras. “We could still lose and continue the competition but we know that the safest way is to get a victory and another way is to probably get a draw, so we are aware of all the permutations,” he said.

“We understand and we see that Honduras are really a good team.

I know what has been happening — all the teams in our zone have been able to defeat each other at some point or not so I think all the teams are even, and that’s where we have to start.”

Winger Kaheim Dixon believes a win for Jamaica could help to soften the blow of missing out on last summer’s FIFA World Cup. “For the whole country it would mean everything.

We missed out on a chance in the World Cup qualifiers but now we have a chance to make it right,” he said. “It’s not just about me, but for the whole country at this point.”

After losing Renaldo Cephas, Rumarn Burrell, Isaac Hayden, Kasey Palmer and Tayvon Gray following the Honduras loss, Speid will now also be without defender Joel Latibeaudiere (injury) and striker Bailey Cadamarteri (suspended), who both started in the 2-0 win over El Salvador.

Goalkeepers — Andre Blake, Amal Knight, Shaquan Davis

Defenders — Damion Lowe, Richard King, Ronaldo Webster, Kyle Ming, Christopher Ainsworth, Miguel Freckleton

Midfielders — Dwayne Atkinson, Karoy Anderson, Brandon Cover, Courtney Clarke, Ramone Howell

Forwards — Kaheim Dixon, Tyreece Campbell, Javon East, Jahmarie Nolan, Jamone Lyle, Tajay Grant

World.title: Spanish election threatens to blow up Brussels’ political balance
World.content:
“There might be a temptation to look more critically at Council positions if there is no [longer] a Socialist prime minister of a large country,” said René Repasi, head of Germany’s SPD delegation in Parliament.

A second senior S&D lawmaker said Sánchez helped “balance” decisions at the leaders’ table and that his absence would unsettle the informal alliance of the S&D, liberals and the center-right European People’s Party that Commission President Ursula von der Leyen relies on to pass legislation.

“If what comes out of the leaders’ table, and the guidelines it gives the Commission, becomes more conservative, it will be less appealing for progressives to feel part of that governing majority,” said the lawmaker, who was granted anonymity to speak about sensitive group matters.

The S&D has lost ground elsewhere in Brussels. Since the 2024 European election shifted Parliament to the right, the EPP has passed some legislation with far-right groups. The Socialists have less representation in national governments and fewer commissioners of their own, fueling repeated tensions and attempts to repair the alliance. With Sánchez gone, the last center-left leaders would be Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen and Malta’s Robert Abela — with Magdalena Andersson working to form a government in Sweden.

Spain’s election will sound the starting gun a year of consequential votes across major EU countries, including Italy, Poland and France, where the far-right National Rally is leading the polls ahead of the 2027 presidential election. Far-right forces in Brussels are pressing the EPP to drop its ban on cooperating with them and break with its traditional ties to the S&D.

Fewer incentives for compromise

The S&D, Parliament’s second-largest group, has repeatedly threatened over the past two years to withdraw support for von der Leyen, with some lawmakers urging a more forceful stance on EU policy.

World.title: Tories want to duck Burnham’s social care fight
World.content:
There’s a wide political consensus that England’s status quo on adult social care is awful. Care, which includes support for people in the final years of their lives, can be inadequate and costly, and family homes are sold off to fund essential help.

But political controversy has long greeted attempts at reform — leaving the issue unresolved.

Burnham used his first conference speech as Labour leader in Liverpool last week to touch three live wires in British politics: EU membership, electoral reform and changing state pensions protections to help fund a social care overhaul.

A second member of the shadow Cabinet admitted the country is “completely f–ked” unless the cost of dying is rectified — but downplayed the likelihood of the Tories offering real reform.

“We will have things to say about all these things,” they added. “I don’t think they will be the centerpiece of our offer at the election.”

Even trying to play it safe would open up a major ideological divide in British politics, teeing up a battle over how far the state should intervene to tackle an issue Burnham has vowed to stake his premiership on.

World.title: France’s debt troubles stir memories of the euro crisis
World.content:
Sumitomo Mitsui DS Asset Management, one of Japan’s largest asset managers, said at the weekend it had sold all its French debt. In case of accelerated sales — or even worse, forced sales — the risk of contagion to other eurozone member countries rises further.

Who ya gonna call? Spread-busters!

The widening so-called spreads between national sovereign bond yields have raised questions about whether and how the European Central Bank might stop the rot. The ECB’s Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI) allows it to buy government bonds in the secondary market to counter “unwarranted, disorderly” market dynamics — but only under certain conditions. Before the ECB can use it, the Bank has to determine that a country is pursuing sound and sustainable fiscal and economic policies. For France, that would require big adjustment measures that will be nigh-impossible to pull off ahead of the 2027 elections.

“Help would likely require real commitment to stability, through fiscal discipline, reforms or both. Getting that support won’t be easy politically,” said Allianz Global Investors. Chief Economist Christian Schulz.

Stop (in the name of love for the euro)?

The ECB could also, in theory, intervene by using its balance sheet. For the last couple of years, it has allowed the bonds that it bought during years of “quantitative easing” to “run off” its balance sheet at the end of their lifetimes. That has forced governments to refinance the maturing debt in the markets instead. That increases the net supply of bonds to the market and adds to the upward pressure on yields.

Carsten Brzeski, ING’s global head of macro research, argued that the ECB could “pause quantitative tightening temporarily and reinvest maturing bonds in its portfolio ‘flexibly,’ sending a positive signal to bond markets.”

That possibility was also floated on Monday in an op-ed by Lorenzo Bini Smaghi, an Italian former member of the ECB’s board. It’s also at the heart of an appeal by Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the far-left’s presidential candidate in France, for the ECB to put a chunk of government debt “in the freezer.”

World.title: France’s Mélenchon doubles down on student protests despite violent clashes
World.content:
The blockades have taken place at 400 to 500 high schools, Geffray added, about 10% of the total in France.

The protests began last month when students and teachers blockaded schools, calling for more funding and better working conditions. They have since become a nationwide movement and a political issue as the campaign for next year’s presidential election heats up.

“In the field of education, as in all other public services, policies of penny-pinching and budget cuts have led to the near-collapse of the system,” Mélenchon said.

Students block the entrance to Saint Charles De Foucauld High School, holding signs denouncing the lack of resources in public education, in Paris on October 5, 2026. | Djoudi Hamani/AFP via Getty Images



Mélenchon’s opponents — including France’s historically unpopular government — accuse him of using fiery rhetoric to fuel a febrile political environment that incites violence.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu’s office said the government and intelligence agencies “shared the assessment” that France Unbowed and its ideological allies helped foment the student protests.

The 75-year-old has denied encouraging violence — he called the allegation “absurd” in his video and blames the police for brutally dispersing protests — but he’s not backing down from a rhetorical fight. In a blog post over the weekend, Mélenchon made it clear he sees the moment as an opportunity to seize the political narrative, as he did with French debt last month, and push his already strong advantage with the youth vote.

World.title: Diplomat is Romania’s fourth prime ministerial candidate in five months
World.content:
His task is formidable: Amid bitter divisions between the parties, lawmakers rejected two of Dan’s previous nominees, and a third didn’t even make that far. Dan made his announcement after holding talks with the parties at Cotroceni Palace on Monday afternoon.

After three previous candidates failed, the president is already facing calls to dissolve parliament for an unprecedented snap election. But he is reluctant to do so, fearing it would bring a far-right euroskeptic opposition party closer to power.

“My proposal for the position of prime minister is Luca Niculescu, a man who, as a diplomat, knows how to harmonize different positions,” Dan said on Monday evening. “It is necessary for Romania to have a government as soon as possible, because there are institutions that need rectification, and there is a need for a budget for next year. Prolonging the uncertainty will have effects on the lives of Romanians.”

One politician who refused to take part in talks with Dan on Monday was George Simion, leader of the hard-right Alliance for the Union of Romanians party, which currently leads opinion polls. Simion — who challenged Dan for the presidency last year — reiterated his demand for an election to end the chaos.

The president confirmed that the new government would have no place for parties that are anti-Western — which is his code for far-right groups, especially AUR. “I have the guarantee that a government with Luca Niculescu will maintain Romania’s pro-Western direction and will respect the financial targets and all the commitments that Romania has undertaken,” he said.

Dan said the uncertainty was affecting exchange rates, interest rates and investments in Romania. Over the past four years, Niculescu has led Romania’s accession process to the OECD, a major milestone in the country’s development. Dan said his candidate would have the freedom to decide whether the government was “political or technocratic.”

Accepting the nomination, Niculescu said Romania was grappling with a “long” period of uncertainty at a difficult time. “The first mission will be to build a parliamentary majority that will vote for a government that will be deeply anchored in Romania’s European and Euro-Atlantic direction,” he said. “I will have discussions with the parliamentary parties to build this majority and to agree on a realistic governing program.”

World.title: America’s bomber withdrawal points to wider UK-US friction
World.content:
Something deeper is wrong

London has yet to outline a path to meet the NATO standard of spending 3.5% of GDP on defense by 2035 — up from its current level of around 2.7%. It has also been shut out of a subgroup within the alliance convened by Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby. The group is slated to meet again in Poland some time later this month.

Late last month, Colby hinted at that frustration with London, saying the countries' long history will continue to bind them, but the British government needs to make the case to its people for spending more on defense.

“There's this incredible legacy, and that's what we want to rekindle,” Colby said. “Exactly how you convince the British people [to spend more on defense] I would not presume to say, but … there's probably sort of a degree of reconciliation between what the U.K. wants to be doing, what it spends, and what it spends on, because you know a modern military is not cheap.”

The U.S. is also conducting a sweeping review of its posture in European NATO countries — including the U.K. — which will determine the number of American troops and military assets on the continent.

Sophia Gaston, a senior national security researcher at King’s College London, said: “The Trump administration is undeniably sensitive to the costs of the Iran conflict as they head into the midterms next month, so their caution is understandable.

An armored vehicle is seen at RAF Fairford on Sept. 28, 2026. | Ben Stansall/AFP via Getty Images

“It’s also hard not to, at some level, perceive a degree of uncertainty about the capacity of the British services to currently prevent such an attack. That partly reflects the innate challenge drones and other aspects of modern warfare pose to the sitting ducks of expensive kit.

World.title: Sam Altman à Decoded : “Le monde devrait accepter que certaines choses négatives se produisent” face aux bénéfices de l’IA
World.content:
Sam Altman a approuvé l’appel lancé le mois dernier par Dario Amodei à ralentir le développement des modèles d’IA les plus avancés. Son entreprise a même emboîté le pas à Anthropic en soutenant de nouvelles lois d’Etats fédérés américains qui imposent des exigences de sécurité plus strictes que celles qu’OpenAI avait précédemment défendues — ce qui marque un léger revirement par rapport à sa stratégie antérieure en la matière. Par ailleurs, ses lobbyistes ont récemment apporté leur soutien à une proposition bipartisane de la Chambre des représentants qui obligerait les principales entreprises du secteur à accueillir des auditeurs indépendants chargés d’évaluer la sécurité de leurs modèles.

Malgré cette convergence, Sam Altman a tenté de distinguer la position de son entreprise en matière de réglementation de celle de Dario Amodei, rappelant les accusations de capture réglementaires contre Anthropic, formulées par des conseillers tech du président Donald Trump.

“Je ne suis pas d’accord, mais je comprends le point de vue de ceux qui se disent : ‘Cette technologie va devenir tellement puissante, et elle est tellement dangereuse, qu’un seul laboratoire à San Francisco devrait en disposer et veiller à ce qu’il n’arrive rien de grave, tout en trouvant le moyen d’en répartir les bénéfices’”, a exposé Sam Altman. Pour lui, c’est un “compromis totalement inacceptable” qui va à l’encontre de la “position plus souple en matière réglementaire” défendue par OpenAI.

“Je ne ferai pas le compromis de dire : ‘Nous veillerons à ce qu’il n’y ait pas de piratages majeurs, pas d’utilisation abusive de cette technologie, zéro escroquerie [ou] toute autre chose négative qui pourrait se produire’”, a poursuivi le patron de l’éditeur de ChatGPT. “Car je pense que les gens feront énormément plus — d’un ordre de grandeur supérieur — de bonnes choses que de mauvaises.”

Le PDG d’OpenAI a ajouté ne pas croire aux “risques véritablement catastrophiques”, notamment à la possibilité d’“une grave perte de contrôle face à l’IA”.

Interrogé à ce sujet, un porte-parole d’Anthropic a répondu que les “propositions réglementaires [de l’entreprise] ne s’appliquent qu’aux modèles de pointe”. La société a également fait référence à un échange sur les réseaux sociaux en août entre Dario Amodei et un gestionnaire d’investissements, dans lequel il répondait aux critiques concernant la captation réglementaire et les répercussions sur les petites entreprises.

World.title: From the rent crisis to Trump: 5 things that will shape Spain’s snap election
World.content:
Here are five things to watch.

Kingmakers on the extremes

Spain’s two largest parties — Sánchez’s center-left Socialist Party and Alberto Núñez Feijóo’s center-right People’s Party — are expected to get roughly the same results as they did when voters went to the polls in 2023, with both falling short of a governing majority. That means the next government will be led by whoever can cobble together the largest parliamentary alliance.

Polls put the People’s Party at around 34 percent, ahead of Sánchez’s Socialists, who are backed by 26% of voters. PP leader Feijóo says he is comfortable governing with the far-right Vox party, which is polling at around 18 percent, according to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls. The PP already governs alongside Vox in several regions.

Sánchez’s hopes of reelection hinge on pulling off the same unlikely feat he achieved three years ago, when he managed to form a parliamentary majority with far-left, regional and separatist forces.

This time around, that option appears to be out of reach as a result of the collapse of the country’s left-wing political forces. Sumar — the junior partner in Sánchez’s coalition government — has plummeted in the polls and is currently leaderless.

Health Minister Mónica García is among the frontrunners to head the new alliance, which plans to present itself as the “Broad Front” later this month. It will be up to its eventual leader to try to forge a viable left-wing electoral alliance with bitter rivals Podemos, as well as big personalities like housing activist and former Barcelona Mayor Ada Colau.

World.title: Measles cases are spreading in the US this year, with over 1,000 infections reported in Pennsylvania
World.content:
A measles outbreak in Pennsylvania has topped 1,000 cases, with neighboring New York declaring a disaster emergency and mobilizing measures to fight the spread.

Over 1,000 cases of measles have been recorded so far this year in Pennsylvania alone, health officials in the northeastern US state said on Monday, the largest outbreak in a US state since the early 1990s.

The US Center for Disease Control (CDC) has put the number of cases recorded nationwide so far this year at 3,869, in what is seen as the worst year for measles since 1991.

What do we know about the latest measles outbreak?

The current outbreak started west of Philadelphia in April, health officials said. Nearly 200 people have been hospitalized and five have died. Nearly all of the cases involved people who were not vaccinated, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health.

In neighboring New York on Monday, Governor Kathy Hochul declared a month-long state disaster emergency to "strengthen ongoing efforts to confront" measles.

Over 100 cases have been recorded this year in New York State outside of New York City, with 92 of those reported in "under-immunized" rural areas since July 15.

The executive order suspends regulations on administering vaccines, expanding permission to paramedics and midwives, while allowing nurses to order testing and lowering permission barriers.

"No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease," Hochul said.

US vaccine coverage dips

Since last year, measles has broken out in several US states, including Texas, Utah and South Carolina, which has reported just under 1,000 cases.

Measles includes symptoms like high fever, cough, and rash. It can cause serious complications, especially in young children. It is highly contagious but can be prevented with vaccines.

However, skepticism toward vaccines in the US has risen in recent years, with more parents waiving routine vaccinations amid disinformation about vaccine safety.

Is the US experiencing a vaccine crisis? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In 2000, the US had eliminated the domestic spread of measles with high vaccination rates, but coverage has recently dipped below the 95% necessary to prevent outbreaks.

US Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr, who has expressed views skeptical of vaccines that are not backed by science, has characterized vaccinations as a "personal choice."

Although Kennedy maintains that the measles vaccine is the best defense against the highly contagious and potentially fatal infection, he has also advocated unproven "alternative treatments" like taking vitamins.
