World.title: Combatir la agenda neoliberal desde la izquierda: así son las recetas de los mejores economistas progresistas del mundo
World.content:
Entre el calentamiento global, la desigualdad rampante cuyo máximo exponente es la crisis inmobiliaria y la inteligencia artificial (IA) buena parte del mundo vive con una espada de Damocles sobre sus cabezas. No es para menos. La época que nos ha tocado vivir está aliñada de incendios que hacen creer en el infierno climático hasta al más obcecado, profesionales que temen su pronto reemplazo por granjas de servidores que ni enferman ni protestan, jóvenes que regresan con sus padres porque no pueden pagarse su propia casa, multimillonarios que hablan de mandarnos a Marte y un sur global de 3.500 millones de pobres que cada vez tienen menos que perder.

Frente a tanto susto, crece la ultraderecha en las urnas y en las encuestas. ¿Por qué? ¿Acaso desde la izquierda no hay propuestas para semejantes desafíos? EL PAÍS se ha puesto en contacto con algunos de los principales economistas progresistas del planeta para conocer sus recetas. ¿Alcanza con un impuesto del 2% a las fortunas que superen los 100 millones de dólares, como propone el economista francés Gabriel Zucman? ¿O la desigualdad no se puede abordar sin incluir en el paquete la lucha para que el planeta siga siendo habitable, como defendió en junio el también francés y economista Thomas Piketty durante la presentación del informe Global Justice Project (proyecto de justicia global)?

“Sin ese enfoque dual, los gobiernos se arriesgan a repetir los errores que desencadenaron las protestas de los chalecos amarillos en Francia contra un impuesto al carbono que habría afectado a la clase media y trabajadora más que a los ricos”, dijo Piketty durante la presentación del informe, donde es coautor junto a otros 44 académicos, que muestra el camino para llegar a 2100 manteniendo el calentamiento por debajo de los dos grados y multiplicando los ingresos para una gran mayoría del planeta.

Si la reacción ultraconservadora se alimenta del miedo a retroceder, las luchas que mejoran la vida de las mayorías siempre necesitaron la ilusión por avanzar, aunque a muchos les sonase a utopía inalcanzable lo de la semana de cinco días o lo del mes de vacaciones pagadas. En ese terreno se mueve el Global Justice Project, que aspira a terminar el siglo dividiendo por dos el número de horas trabajadas, llevando el gasto en educación y sanidad del 13% al 38% del PIB global, y multiplicando los ingresos del 89% de la población mundial hasta llevarlos a 5.000 euros al mes por persona.

Limitar el calentamiento a 1,8 grados es técnicamente posible, escriben los autores del informe, si reformamos la arquitectura financiera global, reducimos el consumo de carne, y gravamos a los más ricos con impuestos de hasta un 20% para dotar un fondo soberano que compense la injusticia del actual reparto mundial invirtiendo en transición energética y reorientando hacia educación y sanidad, de menor impacto material, una parte significativa de los flujos de capitales que hoy van a actividades industriales y mineras.

En un apartado que parece escrito para adelantarse a los escépticos, el informe incluye la posibilidad de aranceles correctivos de hasta el 180% para los países que no se adhieran a la gran coalición internacional que requiere (por infligir daños ecológicos al resto) y recuerda la historia de la revolución socialdemócrata del siglo XX, cuando el gasto público pasó de representar un 10% a prácticamente la mitad del PIB, y se crearon los sistemas universales de educación y salud. “Una era habitable y equitativa en el siglo XXI es materialmente posible”, concluye el informe. “Lo que se interpone no es una imposibilidad técnica, sino una elección política y el difícil pero crucial trabajo de construir la coalición para llegar a ella”.

Branko Milanovic "El Global Justice Project sirve de esquema para el pensamiento futuro"

“La aproximación de Piketty es muy ingeniosa porque por primera vez intenta incluir en un solo paquete todos estos problemas existenciales y ponerles números”, explica a EL PAÍS en conversación telefónica Branko Milanovic, economista del Centro de Postgrado de CUNY (Nueva York). “Sería incorrecto tomar por separado los números del informe para desestimarlo argumentando que son totalmente irrealistas, como el que afirma que toda la población del mundo tendrá en 2100 el mismo ingreso mensual de 5.000 euros”. En opinión de Milanovic, especialista en desigualdad económica, la principal contribución del informe es mostrar la interrelación que hay entre todos los problemas: la tributación a ingresos y patrimonios elevados, la dotación de un fondo de reparaciones, la reducción de las desigualdades dentro de los países y, entre ellos, la reducción de las emisiones y el desplazamiento de la producción del PIB hacia los sectores de salud y educación.

“Si la situación actual del mundo mejora y los grandes países realmente acuerdan una reforma de las organizaciones multilaterales, algo muy relevante que también destaca el informe de Piketty, hará falta un marco conceptual, una idea de qué hacer, y el informe es una muy buena primera aproximación para integrar los diferentes aspectos del problema”, explica Milanovic. “Antes que detenerse a juzgar si los números son o no factibles y alcanzables, la grandísima utilidad del informe es servir de esquema para el pensamiento futuro”.

De cualquier modo, para dar pasos más decisivos contra el calentamiento global no hace falta esperar a la gran coalición de naciones a la que aspira el Global Justice Project de Piketty. Según Abhijit Banerjee, cofundador del Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab y ganador del Nobel de Economía junto a su esposa Esther Duflo, la Unión Europea tiene ya un tamaño más que suficiente como para exigir impuestos al carbono a las potencias que no los incorporan en el grado necesario. “La Unión Europea es un mercado gigantesco para los productos y servicios tecnológicos estadounidenses, eso le da un poder de negociación que ahora mismo no está usando para que EE UU incorpore en el precio de su producción las emisiones de carbono por el coste medioambiental que imponen sobre todo el planeta”, plantea Banerjee durante una conversación por Zoom.

El actual enfoque europeo es muy extraño, añade este economista, porque penaliza a los productores europeos con elevados impuestos al carbono sin exigir lo mismo de sus principales socios comerciales. En su opinión, aumentar esa exigencia es políticamente viable dentro de Europa si se articula como una preocupación nacionalista, además de medioambiental, que incluya así las sensibilidades de los gobiernos de derecha. “El mensaje sería ‘no queremos que Estados Unidos haga lo que le dé la gana con nosotros”, explica. “Ahora mismo estamos en el peor de los mundos, permitiendo que EE UU niegue los valores que nuestros gobiernos europeos se han comprometido a respetar”, añade Banerjee.

Mariana Mazzucato "Los gobiernos no han de limitarse a poner tiritas donde el mercado produce daños"

No solo la Unión Europea tiene que ponerse en su lugar. Según la economista ítalo-estadounidense Mariana Mazzucato, tomar conciencia del propio poder es también la asignatura pendiente para muchos gobiernos nacionales que, tras décadas de pensamiento neoliberal, han ido reduciendo su papel hasta convertirse en meros facilitadores de la actividad privada. Dejar atrás la era de grandes consultoras privadas fijándole el rumbo a las administraciones, o de ministros aislados con sus pequeños proyectos personales en el mejor de los casos, para pasar a un enfoque coherente donde el Gobierno nacional fija las misiones que alinean a todos los ministerios y ordenan la actividad del sector privado.

El ejemplo clásico de Mazzucato, que en Londres dirige el Institute for Innovation and Public Purpose de la UCL, es la carrera espacial de los años sesenta, cuando la NASA definió claramente lo que necesitaba para poner a un hombre en la Luna y las empresas del sector aeronáutico trabajaron para conseguir el contrato. O el más reciente del Gobierno de Brasil, subraya Mazzucato por teléfono, “cuando puso la transición ecológica en el centro, haciendo que hasta el ministro de Finanzas, Fernando Haddad, tuviera que recalibrar las funciones de los bancos públicos para ayudar a lograrla”.

“En vez de la actual pasividad donde se limitan a poner tiritas allí donde los mercados provocan daños, los gobiernos deben crear valor desde el principio y poner las condiciones”, señala Mazzucato, que acaba de publicar la versión en español del libro Bien común: una nueva economía que funcione para todos (Taurus). “Hay que pensarlo como una recompensa, ¿quieres trabajar con el Gobierno en una transición ecológica sostenible? Adelante, aquí está este préstamo para tu producción de acero, pero siempre y cuando bajes el contenido material del proceso”, explica como ejemplo.

Según Mazzucato, ese acuerdo no funciona cuando los gobiernos no tienen nada bueno que ofrecer a cambio y se limitan a poner reglas. “Un Gobierno que no ha invertido en investigación pública, que no ha invertido en un buen sistema educativo y sanitario ni en buenas infraestructuras, no puede exigir condiciones a las empresas porque no tiene nada que ofrecer”, explicó. “El enfoque de la misión sirve también para que los gobiernos se den cuenta de que tienen que olvidar todas esas reglas fiscales absurdas que no tienen en cuenta el valor que genera la inversión pública en el crecimiento de largo plazo”, agrega.

Dani Rodrik "Los mejores resultados para reducir las emisiones vienen de las políticas verdes de China"

En cierta medida, la política industrial que el economista Dani Rodrik defiende en su libro Shared Prosperity in a Fractured World (publicado por Princeton University Press en 2025) también es una historia de gobiernos asumiendo su poder transformador. Un país oficialmente comunista como China es para Rodrik ejemplo de innovación empresarial para enfrentar el desafío ecológico. “Los economistas llevan tiempo defendiendo los impuestos al carbono, y sistemas equivalentes como el mercado de carbono, como los mecanismos más eficientes para reducir las emisiones, pero los avances más espectaculares y reales que ha habido en este campo han venido por la política industrial verde de China”, escribía en octubre Rodrik, profesor de Política Económica Internacional en la John F. Kennedy School of Government de Harvard. “Orientada en torno a metas nacionales, pero implementada a nivel local por las autoridades municipales, esta política ha reducido el coste de la energía solar, de la eólica y de las baterías hasta niveles que han hecho a las renovables más baratas que los combustibles fósiles”.

Según Rodrik, las tan publicitadas subvenciones que China otorga a sus empresas son solo una pata de una política industrial más amplia donde también son relevantes los contratos de aprovisionamiento del sector público y el apoyo de empresas públicas de capital riesgo. Además de mucha experimentación, donde una parte importante de los proyectos se queda por el camino. ¿Es el enfoque de la prueba y error más viable en una autocracia como China, donde la opinión pública no ejerce tanta presión cuando se producen esos errores?

“Todo depende de cómo lo presentes”, dice Rodrik a este periódico por correo electrónico. “En EE UU la gente acepta que no todas las tecnologías y empresas apoyadas por el DARPA [Agencia de Proyectos de Investigación Avanzada de Defensa] tienen que funcionar, la filosofía del capital riesgo está implícita en el funcionamiento de esa agencia [del Gobierno estadounidense, encargada de desarrollar tecnologías de uso militar]”, explica. “Eso es lo que hay que lograr con las iniciativas de política industrial, presentándolas como un paquete que funciona de manera global, aunque algunas de sus partes fallen, y evitando el error que cometió la Administración de Obama cuando singularizó su apoyo a Solyndra, la empresa de paneles fotovoltaicos que luego fracasó y se convirtió en un problema de imagen”.

Luchar contra el cambio climático es otro de los poderes que algunos atribuyen a la inteligencia artificial (IA), por su potencial para mejorar la gestión de residuos, optimizar el uso de la energía y afinar las predicciones meteorológicas, entre otros avances. El Nobel de Economía y profesor del MIT Daron Acemoglu no figura entre los que así lo creen. “Por ahora, lo único que sabemos de los modelos de IA es que están afectando negativamente a la lucha contra el cambio climático porque tienen demandas energéticas muy grandes, incluso si mejoramos la eficiencia; lo que necesitamos son avances en baterías y en energía solar y eólica, y todo eso es posible con más inversiones”, explica durante una entrevista por Zoom.

Para Acemoglu, la IA también puede generar consecuencias indeseadas en el mundo empresarial, y no solo por una posible pérdida de empleos sino de competitividad. Su tesis es que la IA sigue teniendo peor desempeño que las personas en una gran mayoría de trabajos, y un reemplazo demasiado rápido de humanos por máquinas puede provocar lo que él llama una “automatización mediocre”. Para evitarlo, su propuesta es cambiar las leyes impositivas que en EE UU y otros países desincentivan la contratación de personal fomentando un exceso de automatización. En 2020, Acemoglu publicó un estudio junto a Andrea Manera y Pascual Restrepo demostrando que el tipo impositivo efectivo promedio que las empresas estadounidenses pagaban por los empleados era de 25%, frente al del 5% que pagaban por el capital. “Si terminamos con ese sesgo en los impuestos, no necesitaremos discernir algo que ahora mismo es muy difícil de saber: cuál es la IA que mejora la productividad y cuál es la que provoca una automatización mediocre”, explica.

Daron Acemoglu "No se debe descartar que los Estados entren en el capital de las empresas de IA"



¿Y si incluso así somos reemplazados por robots que sí mejoran la productividad? ¿De dónde sacarán los gobiernos el dinero para financiar la transición hacia los nuevos trabajos del futuro? Según Acemoglu, antes que imponer un impuesto específico a la IA que puede provocar efectos secundarios por su poder distorsionador, lo mejor es aumentar los impuestos a los ingresos o al patrimonio. “La opción de hacer que los gobiernos entren en el capital de las empresas de IA no se puede descartar de entrada, teniendo en cuenta el potencial absolutamente transformador que puede tener la tecnología, pero debe ser considerada teniendo en cuenta sus costes”, dice el premio Nobel.

Entre esos costes figuran las protestas con que las empresas de IA se resistirían de manera legítima a la medida, por considerarla un cambio en las reglas del juego. También, los efectos que la entrada de los gobiernos en el capital tendrían sobre el sistema de libre competencia. “No podrías esperar imparcialidad de un Gobierno con intereses en una empresa de IA, lo normal sería que cuando tenga que buscar un proveedor de IA termine favoreciendo a sus propios modelos”, según Acemoglu. “Podríamos terminar favoreciendo el desarrollo de una IA con medidas de seguridad mucho peores, por ejemplo, solo porque es la que pertenece al Gobierno”.

Para Acemoglu, otro avance necesario es el desarrollo de una IA competitiva en la UE, aunque en la actualidad esté completamente fuera de la carrera que libran EE UU y China en este sector. En su opinión, Europa cuenta con los recursos humanos que hacen falta para lograrlo (“en su mayoría, trabajando en las empresas americanas”), y mejores instintos democráticos que Pekín y que Washington para ponerla al servicio de los trabajadores, y no contra ellos. “Requeriría la creación de centros neurálgicos para el desarrollo de la IA, no puedes tener una empresa en cada una de las capitales europeas, y una estructura financiera que permita canalizar fondos para que las empresas de tamaño mediano puedan escalar”, dice a este periódico. “En Europa hay mucha riqueza privada, y los patrimonios privados son los que han financiado una parte importante de la inversión mundial en IA”, añade. “Un modelo viable para Europa sería desarrollar su propia versión de la industria de capital riesgo estadounidense, menos obsesionado con la escala y la expansión”.

Pero no ha hecho falta esperar a la IA para ver cómo los incrementos en productividad derivados de las nuevas tecnologías se implementaban sin mejorar la vida de los trabajadores. Según Rodrik, eso es exactamente lo que ha ocurrido en una parte importante del sector servicios durante los últimos años. “Solo hay que pensar en el efecto que las nuevas tecnologías introducidas por empresas como Uber o Amazon ha tenido en sectores tan tradicionales como el del comercio y los taxis, por no hablar de los beneficios que los restaurantes han registrado gracias a los pedidos online y a los servicios de entrega a domicilio”, explica. “El problema es que los trabajadores, por el momento, no han podido apropiarse de esas mejoras”.

Y es que subir los impuestos o entrar en el capital de las empresas de las nuevas tecnologías no son las únicas formas de hacer que las mejoras en productividad beneficien a los trabajadores. En opinión de Rodrik, también son especialmente importantes las políticas que aumentan el poder negociador de esos trabajadores, “permitiendo los convenios colectivos y sectoriales y comprometiendo a las empresas en una relación quid pro quo que da preferencia en sus tratos con el Estado a las que se comprometen con mejoras en la forma en que tratan a sus empleados”.

Abhijit Banerjee "Parte del malestar es por la idea equivocada de que la inmigración cuesta mucho dinero"

Según Banerjee, la IA va a representar un gran desafío incluso en los mejores futuros posibles. Como, por ejemplo, el escenario en el que la IA solo mejora la productividad de los trabajadores, asistiéndolos en vez de reemplazándolos. “La elasticidad en la demanda de muchos servicios donde mejorará la productividad no es infinita: la gente no va de repente a comprar 20 veces lo que antes compraba una vez, por más que ahora sea más fácil de producir”, dijo. “Las personas que antes solo necesitaban un contable y ahora pueden resolver ese trabajo en 10 minutos con la IA no van a contratar a más contables”.

En su opinión, tenemos que empezar ya a preguntarnos qué hacer si algo así ocurre. No solo por la forma de derivar hacia los ciudadanos los beneficios obtenidos por las empresas gracias a la IA, sino por lo que puede significar “un mundo donde la gente tenga mucho tiempo libre y nada que hacer”. Los principales experimentos de poblaciones con una especie de renta básica y nada que hacer, dice este economista, están en las reservas indias de EE UU. “No está claro que haya conducido a una gran felicidad”, explica. “No hemos pensado mucho en este tema porque el mundo está escorándose hacia la derecha y no parece que haya mucho espacio para hablar de redistribuir la riqueza generada por la IA, pero imaginemos que sí lo queremos y podemos hacer, ¿cómo lo haríamos?”, se pregunta.

Para Banerjee, una posible respuesta sería formar y certificar a los ciudadanos en los nuevos sectores de desarrollo. “Los gobiernos podrían apostar por expandir el sector social, por ejemplo, con más asistencia a los ancianos, mejor cuidado para los niños, y otros servicios donde la gente suele preferir que sea una persona y no una máquina quien se ocupe de los abuelos y los niños”, sugiere. “La gente también va a exigir que esas personas que cuidan de sus familiares estén capacitadas, por eso creo que es importante entender que los gobiernos no van a tener que limitarse a redistribuir dinero, también tendrán que invertir en ese rediseño de la sociedad”.

Posible abandono

En el Global Justice Project de Piketty, solucionar la desigualdad es solucionar mucho. Y no solo por los fondos globales que canalizarían hacia los países pobres parte de lo recaudado subiéndole los impuestos a los millonarios. También ayudaría a las zonas de los países ricos con las peores tasas de desempleo, como el norte de Francia o el este de Alemania, donde el malestar por la sensación de abandono se ha traducido más claramente en políticas de rechazo a la inmigración.

Claro que no hace falta esperar a que se ponga en práctica el proyecto. Según Banerjee, “es posible crear ya un mecanismo, dirigido especialmente a los jóvenes de esas zonas, para ayudarles a mudarse y a que consigan trabajo en otros lados”. “Es verdad que si por ahora no lo hemos logrado, se debe en parte a la escasez de las arcas públicas y a la resistencia que presentan los millonarios cada vez que se habla de subirles los impuestos”, subraya.

La percepción de los fenómenos migratorios en los países de acogida también puede cambiar si mejora la información. Como dijo Banerjee, “gran parte del malestar tiene que ver con la idea equivocada de que los inmigrantes cuestan un montón de dinero al erario, cuando lo cierto es que suelen ser gente joven, en edad de trabajar, que aportan más de lo que reciben”. En sus estudios, Banerjee ha demostrado que la llegada de cantidades importantes de trabajadores nuevos de poca cualificación no baja los salarios locales. “A la gente le cuesta creerlo, pero esa es la evidencia y se debe a que estos trabajadores también aumentan la demanda general, son personas que no viven del aire, además entre ellos hay muchos emprendedores que crean empleos”, enfatiza. “De hecho, los que sí bajan los salarios locales son los inmigrantes de alta cualificación, que paradójicamente son los que todos los países quieren tener”.

Con una tasa de natalidad que en 2024 llegó al mínimo de 1,34 hijos por mujer para la UE (y de 1,1 para España), la llegada de inmigrantes es imprescindible para el sostenimiento de la economía y el sistema de pensiones. Según Banerjee, planificar bien su llegada es una de las claves para su gestión. “En Alemania lograron una integración notable de los sirios simplemente porque se ocuparon de crear un mecanismo que los distribuía por diferentes lugares del país, evitando la creación de asentamientos aislados del resto”, dice. “Pero el tema de la inmigración se ha vuelto tan incómodo que no lo reconocemos como existente y no adoptamos una política para abordarlo, lo mismo que pasa con muchas actividades delictivas”.

Ha-Joon Chang "Las pujas de los millonarios por las mansiones elevan el precio del resto de pisos"

Según el economista Ha-Joon Chang, profesor en la SOAS University of London, las dificultades para acceder a la vivienda que enfrentan los ciudadanos en muchos países del mundo también se aliviarían con una reducción de la desigualdad. Y es que, según sus análisis, “las pujas al alza de los multimillonarios para acceder a las propiedades inmobiliarias más exclusivas terminan elevando el nivel general de precios para el resto de propiedades”.

Aunque el problema no tenga una solución rápida, Chang es partidario de aprender de lugares que lo han gestionado mejor, como Singapur. “El Gobierno de Singapur maneja el 85% del mercado de la vivienda, desde los pequeños hogares en alquiler para los jóvenes hasta los apartamentos de lujo, y eso hace que en el 15% restante, a cargo de desarrolladores enteramente privados, no puedan excederse con los precios si no quieren que los clientes se vayan a la oferta oficial”, dice en una videoconferencia.

“De Singapur hay dos lecciones: una es que los estándares de las casas son bastante buenos, no puedes limitarte a hacer bloques de edificios sin jardines, parques, o buenas instalaciones públicas porque en cuanto la gente mejora un poco su nivel adquisitivo se va de allí y la zona termina degradándose”, dice. “La otra, que el Gobierno pasó de controlar el 50% del suelo en 1965, cuando el país comenzó su independencia, hasta el 90% de hoy, unas adquisiciones que ha ido ejecutando poco a poco y que ahora le permiten proveer a su población de viviendas asequibles”.

World.title: Cabinet wants phones out of schools from January
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The cabinet is calling on all primary and secondary schools to ban mobile phone use starting from January.

In a new proposal from digital economy minister Willemijn Aerdts, children would not be allowed to use their phones on school grounds, rules about children appearing in family vlogs would be tightened and the time children spend scrolling would be limited.

“Online, on social media or in video games, children quickly become exposed and face unacceptable risks,” Aerdts said in the proposal, called ‘Strategy Letter on Children’s Rights’.

Since 2024, there have been national agreements prohibiting the use of phones in the classroom.

The government does not have the authority to order schools to implement the policy and the education ministry will work with schools to come up with an agreement.

Aerdts is also keen to limit how children are used in online content, like family-style YouTube.

The cabinet also intends on commissioning research into sites like Netflix, YouTube, Roblox, Fortnite, ChatGPT, Instagram, Snapchat, and TikTok and their impact on children.

Earlier this year, the government has backed an EU-wide minimum age for social media. D66, VVD and CDA agreed in their coalition agreement to push for an enforceable European minimum age of 15.

World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Nine Dutch restaurants have won Michelin stars for the first time in the 2026 edition of the guide, and two of them went straight in with two stars.

Azurite in Delft, run by chef Mario Ridder, and Suis in Schin op Geul, near Valkenburg, both entered the guide at two-star level, broadcaster NOS reported.

Suis only opened at the end of April, after chef Ralf Berendsen left La Butte aux Bois to start his own restaurant.

The 7 new one-star restaurants are spread across the country: Nassau in Groningen, Le Epifaan in Veeningen in Drenthe, Wild Atelier at the De Echoput hotel in Hoog Soeren, Bij Sidney in Loenen aan de Vecht, De Cuijt in Mierlo near Eindhoven, Rozewied in Kortgene in Zeeland, and Ambrozijn in Valkenburg.

Le Epifaan is run by Jarno Eggen, who previously cooked at two-star De Groene Lantaarn in Staphorst before it closed. Rozewied’s chefs, Noëmie Haentjens and Ferdy van Rijswijk, also won Michelin’s Young Chef Award.

Matthijs Vrancken and Nouri Haj Romdhane of Brut172 in Reijmerstok won the sommelier award. Château Neercanne in Maastricht won the award for service.

De Librije in Zwolle remains the only three-star restaurant in the Netherlands, a rating it has held since 2004. Nelson Tanate now leads the kitchen following the death of co-owner and chef Jonnie Boer in April 2025.

No Amsterdam restaurant won a new star this year, and Daalder and De Juwelier lost theirs, AT5 reported.

In total, the Netherlands has 119 starred restaurants, the same number as last year.

World.title: Is it hard to make friends with the Dutch or is it you?
World.content:
Our regular columnist wants to know whether the Dutch are really so hard to make friends with – or is the problem you?

“It’s just so hard to make friends with the Dutch,” the woman seated next to me bemoans. I’m at a dinner party made up mostly, but not entirely, of internationals.

In fact, a Dutch woman seated across from us agreed. She’d recently moved to The Hague after living in Groningen for the past few years and was apparently also struggling to meet people.

It’s an oft-heard complaint in international circles.

Pretty much every organisation catering to internationals in the Netherlands has some advice for how to achieve this virtually impossible feat.

“Many locals have their own social groups that they have maintained since childhood,” the Leiden International Center patiently explains.

The city of Amsterdam sets the bar low. “A neighbour doesn’t have to become a friend (although they might!) – even just being on nodding terms with the people living around you can help you feel at home,” it advises.

There are dozens of threads on Reddit from the recently relocated who are struggling to find connections amongst the Dutch.

True to form, one Dutch poster replies: “We don’t know you, you might just be unlikable for all we know.”

While this may be harsh – sorry, direct – it’s also probably the truth.

You might not be unlikeable in an existential sense. You’re probably a nice person who has friends and loved ones that just happen to live elsewhere. But to the average Tina, Henk and Luca, you just don’t bring much to the table.

First, let’s start with the idea that Dutch people establish their social roster before evacuating the womb.

It is true, in my experience, that Dutch people maintain the friendships they made in childhood and university. This is also true of literally everyone. I concede that the country is small, which makes it easier to keep up with those friendships.

But really, most of us make our friends prior to our early 20s. You just choose to leave yours behind for clogs and tulips. Now your lineup is empty and you’re clawing for a position on a team with few openings.

Which leads me to my second point: there is a reason most of us make friends early in life. It is significantly easy to make friends prior to reaching adulthood. The foundations of primary school friendships are “The other child was randomly selected to sit next to me” and “Who wants to play the same game at recess.” You go to school all day, you see these people all the time and you haven’t yet been downtrodden by the stresses of life.

Now you need to find more of a connection than “I like playing in the sandbox with you” and you need to find the time to make that connection, somewhere between working, exercising, raising your children, spending time with your partner and remembering to order a shower curtain. (If my husband is reading this, I am sorry – I forgot again.)

Even the aforementioned Dutchie at my dinner party was struggling. It’s not simply because you’re a foreigner, it’s just hard to make friends post-graduation.

It is, however, also because you are a foreigner. Dutch people do speak English but that doesn’t mean they want to speak their second language all the time. The language barrier also makes it harder for you to mesh into a group. If you make a Dutch friend and they invite you to their birthday party, you’re now forcing everyone in the circle to switch to English.

Plus, you don’t share the same cultural references, the same jokes, the same base understanding of the world. None of this is insurmountable but it all makes it more difficult to form a bond.

If you came here looking for advice on how to make friendships with the Dutch, you’re in the wrong place. This isn’t an advice column. Making friends as an adult is challenging and you’re playing that game on hard mode by trying to do it across cultural and language differences.

In the meantime, you can try just nodding at people. Maybe eventually one of has them just moved from Groningen and is also desperately trying to convince others that they are likable.

World.title: International train connection from Groningen to Leer returns
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

After almost 11 years, people can again travel by train from Groningen to the German city of Leer.

Services were suspended in 2015 after a cargo ship crashed into the Friesenbrücke, the rail bridge over the Ems on the German side of the border.

At Groningen central station, travelers lined up at 5:30am to catch the first train in over a decade.

The rebuilt Friesenbrücke is 335 metres long and is Europe’s largest lift-swing rail bridge. Its 145-metre central section lifts and turns to let ships pass.

The new bridge was opened in 2024, but needed additional testing before rail service could resume.

Regional Director Gerrit de Groot of Arriva, which maintains the rail service, told RTV Noord he was “delighted” with the reopening. “It is fantastic that, as a regional carrier, we are making international transport possible in this way. It is a wonderful moment,” he said.

The journey takes around 90 minutes. Arriva expects that they will see peaks of travel during the holiday season when people want to visit the Christmas markets across the border.

World.title: Minister seeks inquiry into benefit fines for non-Dutch surnames
World.content:
People with non-Dutch surnames get fined more often and more harshly by the benefits agency UWV’s fraud unit, according to an internal analysis the agency’s board has had since December, AD and current affairs programme EenVandaag reported on Monday.

Social affairs minister Hans Vijlbrief said he wants the claims thoroughly investigated and the UWV to take appropriate measures. “Your surname or background must play no role at all in whether you get a fine or how high that fine is,” he told AD.

The two outlets based their joint investigation on confidential documents and interviews with more than 10 current and former staff, including managers, at the fraud unit, which employs around 600 people.

The analysis divided 1,682 case files into Dutch and non-Dutch surnames. In the region covering Alkmaar, Amsterdam and Utrecht, 44% of the people in the files had a non-Dutch surname, but they received 74% of the fines.

In the southern district, which includes Heerlen and Eindhoven, the figures were 36% and 71%. Because their fines were also higher, that group paid 98% of the total there, although fewer files were examined in that district.

The authors recommended further research, but this was never carried out, according to EenVandaag.

Country of origin

A 2015 work instruction for detecting fake employment contracts also listed the applicant’s “country of origin” as a possible risk characteristic. When a court asked about the document, the UWV denied in an official letter that it used risk characteristics at all, AD said.

After 2020, a thin line was drawn through the criterion, but it remained legible until at least mid-2026. “I have never seen such clear evidence that it happens as in this document,” lawyer Ayhan Kara, who obtained the uncensored version, told AD. He is considering filing a criminal complaint with the public prosecution service.

The UWV says the criterion was never used, was officially removed in 2020 and has now been taken out of all documents.

Current and former staff also described racist remarks in the fraud unit. Managers born outside the Netherlands were referred to as the “Arab League”, and during a case meeting someone said the solution was “to kick all Moroccans out of the country”.

Political reaction

MPs from both coalition and opposition parties reacted angrily. Stephan Neijenhuis of the centrist D66 told AD there was possibly “institutional racism” at the agency.

Mariëtte Patijn of the opposition party Pro said the revelations reminded her of the childcare benefits scandal, in which thousands of parents were wrongly labelled fraudsters by the tax office. “It is not systems selecting wrongly by accident, it is the UWV’s own people,” she told AD.

Dogukan Ergin of the left-wing, multicultural party Denk said it fitted a pattern. “First it was the tax office, then [student finance agency] DUO, now the UWV again: if you have a migration background, you are distrusted and dealt with more harshly,” he said.

According to AD, the minister was only informed of the analysis after the paper put questions to the ministry. The UWV told broadcaster NOS it had informed the ministry in January.

Apologies issued

Abdeluheb Choho, who became the UWV’s chairman on September 1, said in a statement that it was reprehensible that some staff still made discriminatory remarks to one another. “We apologise to everyone who feels discriminated against or has been treated in a racist way,” he said.

However, the agency said in a statement that the analysis was not scientific research, and that its data and method were not suitable for drawing conclusions about structural unequal treatment. A separate external study into equal treatment is due later this year.

The UWV has asked anyone who has experienced discrimination by or within the agency to report it to integriteit@uwv.nl.

In 2024, a reader who took part in a DutchNews survey on discrimination said UWV staff had told them to go back to their own country when they applied for unemployment benefits.

World.title: Polymarket goes to court to overturn Dutch gambling ban
World.content:
US prediction platform Polymarket has gone to court in The Hague to overturn a Dutch ban on its services, arguing that it sells financial products, rather than bets.

The company confirmed the case to the Financieele Dagblad. The judges will reportedly be asked to decide whether betting on real-world events counts as gambling, which the Dutch gambling regulator Ksa says that it is.

Polymarket argues that it is more like trading in derivatives, which should be supervised by financial markets regulator AFM.

Polymarket users buy contracts that pay out in USDC, a type of cryptocurrency whose value is equal to the US dollar, if a particular event does or does not happen. The company says this is comparable to futures contracts traded on financial markets.

Fines and bans

The Ksa ordered Polymarket to stop serving Dutch users in an order dated January 20 and made public on February 17. It said the platform was offering games of chance without a licence and threatened a penalty of €420,000 a week, up to a maximum of €840,000.

Polymarket stopped Dutch users from placing bets later in February, but the regulator ruled it had acted too late and in May demanded €420,000, and rejected the company’s objection in June.

The platform drew widespread attention in the Netherlands after users staked millions of dollars on the outcome of the October 2025 general election.

Only sport

According to the Ksa, Dutch law only allows betting on sport, so a licence would not be an option for Polymarket either.

“Prediction markets are on the rise, in the Netherlands too,” Ksa director Ella Seijsener said in a statement in February. “These types of companies offer bets which are not allowed on our market under any circumstances, not even by licence holders.”

Last week, MPs voted down a motion from the far-right Forum for Democracy (FvD) asking the government to look into regulating prediction markets as a separate category within gambling law.

Gambling lawyer Micha Schimmel told the FD he gives Polymarket’s case little chance. He pointed to a 2015 ruling which found that a service can be a financial product and still count as gambling. Polymarket is also banned in France and Germany.

World.title: School textbooks overpriced and poor quality, watchdog warns
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Consumer watchdog ACM has criticised educational publishers for pricey and poor-quality textbooks, calling on the industry to change its practices.

The ACM says that for the past seven years, prices for educational materials have been rising faster than those of other products and schools say the publications are not meeting their needs.

In a statement, the watchdog said it “calls on educational publishers to stop mandatory tied selling of licences and textbooks, and to better align product supply with demand.”

One major problem the organisation highlighted is that textbooks and the licences for e-materials are bundled together, which drives up costs. The ACM wants them to be sold separately.

The organisation also calls on schools to do more research into the textbooks they purchase.

“Pressure on publishers starts with schools’ willingness to switch to other learning materials,” board member Martijn Snoep said in a statement.

Secondary schools buy around €280 million worth of learning materials every year.

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The Netherlands men’s football team beat Serbia 2-1 in the Nations League in Eindhoven on Sunday, marking Xavi Hernández’s second win in four games as head coach.

Substitute Joshua Zirkzee scored the winning goal in the 71st minute in a game that also marked captain Virgil van Dijk’s 100th cap, public broadcaster NOS reported.

Teun Koopmeiners put the home side ahead in the first half with a free kick. Serbia equalised soon afterwards by a goal from 19-year-old Anderlecht striker Mihajlo Cvetkovic.

Zirkzee tapped in the winner from close range after Crysencio Summerville’s cross was laid back by Tijjani Reijnders. The Dutch finished with 10 men after Micky van de Ven went off with a hand injury, as Xavi had already used all his substitutes.

Xavi, who was appointed in August, has now won twice and drawn twice in his first four games. Germany and Greece drew 0-0 on Sunday, which leaves the Netherlands joint top of their group.

The next round of international matches is in November.

World.title: Reports claim Trump tried to change Poland’s government. What do we know?
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Media reports claim that US President Donald Trump, during a previously unreported meeting earlier this year with Poland’s defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, suggested that he leave Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition and form a new government with the right-wing opposition. Kosiniak-Kamysz has confirmed that the meeting took place, but has not commented on what was discussed. Meanwhile, Tusk himself has said that, while he wants to “maintain discretion”, the information he received from Kosiniak-Kamysz indicates that Trump was interested in discussing the “internal situation in Poland”. Foreign minister Radosław Sikorski has even more bluntly suggested that the meeting may have served as “an attempt to involve a foreign state in our internal politics”. Below, we outline how the controversy unfolded, what we know so far, and how senior political figures have commented on the issue. The context Poland’s government is a broad coalition that ranges from left to centre right. Although Tusk’s centrist Civic Platform (KO) dominates, it would not have the parliamentary majority necessary to rule if it lost any of its junior coalition partners. One of those partners is the Polish People’s Party (PSL), which is the most conservative element of the coalition. It has clashed with its partners over issues such as abortion and LGBT+ rights. PSL is led by Kosiniak-Kamysz, who serves as both deputy prime minister and defence minister. Some elements of the right-wing opposition have suggested that PSL could break with Tusk to form an alternative government, perhaps even with Kosiniak-Kamysz as prime minister. Last year, PSL controversially polled its members on whether they would want to do so. However, PSL and its leader have repeatedly insisted that they remain loyal to Tusk’s coalition. The Polish People's Party's parliamentary survival is on a knife edge, and could determine whether @donaldtusk's coalition remains in power after next year's elections.@AleksSzczerbiak looks at the challenges facing PSL and how it may respond to them https://t.co/MmswSLNWJE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 30, 2026 Meanwhile, the government is in constant conflict with President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the opposition. Nawrocki is also a close ally of Trump, who endorsed him during last year’s presidential election. By contrast, Tusk and his government have clashed with the Trump administration, though they also seek to maintain close relations with the US as Poland’s most important security partner. The meeting The news that Kosiniak-Kamysz had met with Trump in March this year came to light in a rather roundabout way. On 21 September, Poland’s defence ministry announced that a planned meeting at the Pentagon between Kosiniak-Kamysz and his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, planned for 23 September, had been cancelled “at the urgent request of the American side”. The official reason for the change of plans was Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the US at the same time. However, some commentators in Poland claimed that Hegseth had actually cancelled the meeting at the behest of figures close to Nawrocki. In an effort to debunk those claims, Adam Bielan, a senior PiS figure from the opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, claimed that he and Nikodem Rachoń, a presidential advisor, had helped to arrange a meeting earlier this year between Kosiniak-Kamysz and a US figure “much more important than Hegseth”. Rachoń later confirmed this, but said that the meeting had been secret and he was unable to reveal the identity of the US official. He urged Kosiniak-Kamysz to do so. The defence minister obliged, confirming that the meeting had been with Trump himself and had taken place at the White House on 2 March, alongside a ceremony at which a US army officer, Michael Ollis, was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honour for giving his own life to save that of a Polish officer, Karol Cierpica, in Afghanistan. “I had the opportunity to talk to President Trump for a moment, for which I am very grateful,” said Kosiniak-Kamysz, who noted the role of Nawrocki’s office in arranging the conversation. What did Trump say to Kosiniak-Kamysz? Neither Rachoń nor Kosiniak-Kamysz indicated what had been discussed at the meeting. However, last Friday, Dominika Wielowieyska, a leading Polish journalist, claimed that her conversations with various sources, who she did not name, had indicated that Trump used the meeting to encourage Kosiniak-Kamysz to split with Trump and form a new government with the right-wing opposition. “Trump suggested to Kosiniak-Kamysz that it would be best if he formed a coalition with the right, and that then they would have 100% support from the United States and the presidential administration, and the door would essentially be open to achieving great success for many Poles,” said Wielowieyska, who writes for Gazeta Wyborcza, a leading liberal daily that is hostile towards Nawrocki and sympathetic towards Tusk. She added that Kosiniak-Kamysz had immediately shared information about the meeting with the government but that Rachoń had failed to submit a note about it to the foreign ministry, despite that being normal practice and despite a request for a note from foreign minister Radosław Sikorski. Today, Republika, a right-wing broadcaster with close ties to Nawrocki and the opposition, likewise reported, based on unnamed sources, that, “during the conversation with Kosiniak-Kamysz, there were indications that the Americans were interested in a change of prime minister in Poland”. What has Poland’s government said? On Friday, Sikorski took to social media to respond to a claim by Bielan that the Trump-Kosiniak-Kamysz meeting was intended to “unblock” negotiations regarding Poland’s desire to host a new permanent US military base. “In the case of such an important conversation, the organiser [Rachoń] had an obligation to prepare a note,” wrote Sikorski, adding that such a document never reached the foreign ministry. “Could that be because the meeting also served as an attempt to involve a foreign state in our internal politics?” Z tak ważnej rozmowy organizator miał obowiązek sporządzić notatkę. Do @MSZ_RP ona nie dotarła. Czyżby dlatego, że spotkanie służyło też próbie zaangażowania obcego państwa w naszą wewnętrzną politykę? https://t.co/0wL0QZBxPv — Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) October 2, 2026 On Monday, Tusk himself told broadcaster TVN that Kosiniak-Kamysz had informed him about his meeting with Trump immediately after it took place. He added that the subject of the meeting “is too interesting to talk about publicly”, but that military “bases were not the topic of the conversation”. “The conversation was of a confidential nature, and therefore I feel obliged to maintain discretion. It was more about the internal situation in Poland, that’s how I would put it most delicately,” said Tusk. Kosiniak-Kamysz himself also confirmed on Monday that the question of a permanent US base in Poland had not been discussed at the meeting. He noted that, in March, that issue was not even seriously on the table, because it was only two months later that Trump announced he intended to send additional troops to Poland The defence minister did not give any further details about the content of the meeting, which he described as “informal”. World.title: Thousands of protesters trap Polish bishop in church amid anger over dismissal of local priest
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Thousands of protesters blockaded a bishop inside a church in a Polish village on Sunday – and some even physically attacked him – amid anger over the dismissal of a popular long-serving local Catholic priest. As a result, police were called in and, after efforts by negotiators to calm the crowd failed, officers escorted the bishop away from the premises after midnight. „Kościół w Grojcu otoczyło kilka tysięcy osób, parafian i uczęszczających do grojeckiej świątyni. #Aktualnie Okrzyki „jesteśmy z Tobą” dla księdza Józefa Zborka." Materiał od @FaktyOswiecim pic.twitter.com/3zaqlBCDF6 — Sebastian Kościelnik (@S_Koscielnik) October 4, 2026 The incident took place in the village of Grojec, near the city of Oświęcim in southern Poland. The municipality has an official population of around 3,200, but local media – including the Gazeta Krakowska newspaper and Fakty Oświęcim website – report that around 3,000 people gathered on Sunday evening to protest. They were angered by the decision to remove local priest Józef Zborek, who has served in the parish for almost 30 years, from his position. The diocese of Bielsko-Żywiec says the priest was found in church proceedings to have been guilty of “serious and proven irregularities in the performance of his duties”. However, the actual nature of his offences has not been publicly revealed, with the church noting that, under canon law, only Zborek himself can do so. The case against him was initially reported in 2024. The priest repeatedly appealed against the decision, taking the case to the Vatican. However, the decision to remove him was upheld, with Zborek removed from his position on Saturday. On Sunday, Roman Pindel, the bishop of Bielsko-Żywiec, visited Grojec to meet with the parish council and discuss the situation. Afterwards, he proceeded to the local church to attend the Eucharist. However, before his arrival, thousands of people had gathered around the church, holding signs saying “Don’t take away our parish priest”. Some burst inside and disrupted the ceremony. Asked about the reasons for Zborek’s popularity, one woman told Gazeta Krakowska that he had accepted children who had been turned away by other priests for first communion and had “no problem baptising illegitimate children”. News website Onet reports that one local theory is that the priest was removed from his position because he had not charged parishioners for sacraments. Churches in Poland generally expect people to make payments in return for sacraments such as baptism, confirmation and marriage. 🔴Sceny pod kościołem. Biskup w eskorcie policji. Jest nagranie Nocna interwencja policji przed kościołem w Grojcu w Małopolsce. Biskup bielsko-żywiecki Roman Pindel wraz z towarzyszącymi mu księżmi został wyprowadzony ze świątyni pod eskortą funkcjonariuszy. Wszystko po… pic.twitter.com/XEXU3LOMXm — Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) October 5, 2026 After the church service had been disrupted, Pindel and several other priests retreated to the sacristy. Social media videos show protesters shouting angrily at the bishop. Some even physically assailed him and had to be pulled away. Once inside, the bishop faced continued verbal aggression. Shortly afterwards, the police arrived, including specialist negotiators. Pindel spoke to the crowd, explaining that the decision to dismiss Zborek had been confirmed by the Vatican and was final. The bishop reiterated that only Zborek himself was authorised to disclose the reasons for his dismissal. But, with a large, angry crowd still gathered outside and blocking all exits, the bishop was evacuated under the protection of officers at around 1 a.m. Hundreds of people have protested in Kraków’s Kazimierz district against plans to evict residents and businesses – including some of the area's famous bars and galleries – from historic church-owned buildings that will be redeveloped into a luxury hotel https://t.co/Xo3SmkWc9g — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 24, 2026 Subsequently, the Bielsko-Żywiec diocese issued a statement saying that the “aggressive crowd” had “threatened the health and lives of the priests”. It also noted that Zborek had been dismissed after a full canon law process in which he had been able to defend himself and appeal. “We know that many people, especially his parishioners, are experiencing this pain,” they wrote. “However, we ask that you accept this decision in a spirit of faith and in unity with the church.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland updates nuclear strategy with delays to launch of first two plants
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The government has updated Poland’s nuclear strategy for the first time in six years, with the new document acknowledging that the country’s first-ever nuclear plant will go online in 2036, three years later than previously planned, and the second in 2040, one year behind schedule. The delays were widely anticipated, as Poland is already behind the schedule set out in the previous nuclear programme, adopted under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government in 2020. However, the current administration says the country is still on track for nuclear to become a major part of a more diversified energy mix, providing around 15-16% of electricity generation by 2040. “This is not just a plan to develop new capacity, but also to build a strong Polish nuclear industry,” energy minister Miłosz Motyka wrote on social media. “We are building a nuclear sector that will drive the Polish economy and serve our security for decades to come.” Rząd przyjął aktualizację Programu polskiej energetyki jądrowej 🇵🇱 To nie tylko plan rozwoju nowych mocy, ale także budowy silnego polskiego przemysłu jądrowego ⚡️ ✅ W sumie do 9 GWe nowych mocy jądrowych; ✅ coraz większy udział polskich firm – docelowo nawet 70 proc. przy… pic.twitter.com/8DorRLUWUj — Miłosz Motyka (@motykamilosz) September 29, 2026 Under the updated Polish Nuclear Power Programme (PPEJ), Poland plans to develop two nuclear power plants with a combined capacity of around 6 GW to 9 GW, using large-scale Generation III+ reactors. The first plant, which will have a total capacity of about 3.75 GW, is being built in partnership with an American consortium made up of Westinghouse and Bechtel in the municipality of Choczewo on the Baltic coast. Preparatory work at the site is already underway. The European Commission last year approved Polish state aid for the project, which is set to receive 60.2 billion zloty (€13.8 billion) in public support between 2025 and 2030 In March 2026, the investor submitted an application to the president of the National Atomic Energy Agency for a permit to construct the plant, with the pouring of the first nuclear concrete scheduled for 2028. The first reactor is now expected to enter commercial operation in 2036, three years later than previously planned. Construction of Poland’s first nuclear power plant is now set to begin after the @EU_Commission approved Warsaw’s request to allocate 60 billion zloty (€14.2 billion) in state aid for the project https://t.co/Z7BJpRRKnq — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 9, 2025 Plans are already underway for a second nuclear power plant, with construction scheduled to begin in 2032 and the first unit expected to come online around 2040, one year later than previously planned. Bełchatów and Konin in central Poland remain the preferred locations for that plant, with both areas offering existing energy infrastructure and extensive experience in electricity generation. Companies from the United States, France and Canada are currently competing to supply the technology and build it, with Poland to choose its partner next year. Alongside expanding nuclear capacity, the programme aims to increase the role of Polish companies in the sector. Domestic firms are expected to account for about 40% of the value of the first reactor project, according to the government. That share could rise to as much as 70% for subsequent units as Polish companies build up expertise, experience and the necessary certifications. The government also plans to develop the broader skills base needed to support the nuclear industry, involving universities, research institutes, technical schools and businesses. A group of prominent Polish businesspeople – including @RBrzoska of @InPostPL and @mati Staniszewski of @ElevenLabs – are investing in a project to develop small modular nuclear reactors being led by Poland's richest man, Michał Sołowow https://t.co/NFoCh9JmYz — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 1, 2026 The expansion of nuclear power is part of a broader effort to reduce Poland’s traditional reliance on coal, which currently generates around half of the country’s electricity. That is by far the highest figure in the EU. Poland has already been diversifying its energy mix. Coal has declined from supplying 87% of power a decade ago. Meanwhile, the share of renewables has risen from 9% to 29% over the same period. Under a national energy and climate plan approved in June, Poland aims by 2040 for coal to account for only 0-5% of the energy mix. Around 15-16% will come from nuclear, 7-8% from gas, with most of the rest from renewables: onshore wind (22-27%), offshore wind (18-21%) and solar (14-18%). Poland’s first offshore wind farm has begun to deliver electricity, with Prime Minister @donaldtusk celebrating the development as a "key element of our energy security and sovereignty". The government wants 20% of power to come from offshore wind by 2040 https://t.co/EodvInFmrn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 10, 2026 As well as traditional large-scale nuclear power plants, Poland is also pursuing small modular reactor (SMR) projects. SMRs, which are prefabricated in factories before being installed onsite, are much smaller than traditional reactors, and proponents say they provide a faster and more cost-effective way of adding nuclear capacity. World.title: Remains of 115 Polish WWII soldiers exhumed in Ukraine
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish and Ukrainian researchers have exhumed the remains of over 100 Polish soldiers who died in 1939 defending the city of Lviv – which is now in Ukraine but was then part of Poland and known as Lwów – during the invasions by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union at the start of World War Two. The work continues recent moves towards reconciliation over the issue of exhuming victims of the war, which has long been a point of contention between the two countries. ℹ Komunikat o zakończeniu prac ekshumacyjnych na terenie dawnego cmentarza w miejscowości Hołosko Wielkie ⚠️ Zakończyły się prace ekshumacyjne na terenie dawnego cmentarza w miejscowości Hołosko Wielkie, znajdującej się obecnie w granicach administracyjnych Lwowa. Działania… pic.twitter.com/w9rSHuLeua — Instytut Pamięci Narodowej (@ipngovpl) September 28, 2026 During the work on a 260-square-metre area at Holoskivske Cemetery in Lviv, which began in August, experts found 133 burials. They were identified as 115 soldiers from the Polish army and 18 from the German Wehrmacht. They died during the Battle of Lwów in September 1939, when Poland sought to defend the city from Nazi Germany, which had invaded from the west on 1 September, and the Soviet Union, which invaded from the east on 17 September. On 22 September, the Polish forces surrendered and the city came under Soviet control, as Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union had decided when secretly agreeing to divide up Poland in the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact earlier that year. Efforts are now focused on identifying the remains. Experts have taken bone samples for DNA testing, which will be compared with samples from possible relatives. Another part of the puzzle will be the roughly 2,900 objects – including identification tags, bayonets, helmets and religious items – discovered at the site alongside the remains. “For us, the identification of the remains is the most important stage of the work, because it is important to return these people their names,” said Dominika Siemińska, a researcher from Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), in a statement published by Lviv city council. “Currently we have a list of 76 [potential] names,” she added. However, because “so many years have passed, it will be difficult to find their relatives”. Siemińska also expressed her gratitude to the authorities in Lviv “for providing us with protection, support and the opportunity to work peacefully”. She said that “cooperation with the Ukrainian side is going very well”. The final stage of the work will be the burial of the recovered remains of Polish soldiers at the Polish cemetery in the Ukrainian city of Mostyska. The date of the ceremony has not yet been announced. The German remains are being handed over to the Volksbund organisation, which specialises in searching for and reburying German soldiers, said the IPN. The remains of 55 Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII have been reburied at a ceremony in Ukraine attended by political and religious figures from both countries. The victims, around half of them children, were exhumed this summer https://t.co/4q3giZhBAL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 31, 2026 Last year, Ukraine also granted permission for the exhumation of Polish soldiers in Lviv. Researchers subsequently found the remains of 31 people, as well as possible remains of dozens more that were difficult to identify due to them having been reburied and the manner of their death in artillery fire. They were also reburied in Mostyska, at a ceremony attended by prominent officials from both Poland and Ukraine. Previously, from 2017 to 2024, Ukraine had banned searches for Polish victims of World War Two on its territory in response to the dismantling in Poland of a monument to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a nationalist partisan formation that fought against the Soviets but also led the massacre of ethnic Poles. However, in a major diplomatic breakthrough last year, Ukraine allowed exhumations to resume, including both the Polish soldiers in Lviv as well as victims of the UPA-led massacres, tens of thousands of whom are believed to remain buried in unmarked mass graves. Poland has cautiously welcomed President @ZelenskyyUa's announcement of a five-point plan to alleviate the diplomatic crisis triggered by his earlier decision to name a military unit after a group that led massacres of Poles during WWII https://t.co/M3GXD9vtAr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2026 Researchers have subsequently uncovered the remains of dozens of victims of the massacres, who have also been reburied in ceremonies attended by both Polish and Ukrainian officials. However, such steps towards reconciliation have been hindered this year by a dispute sparked by President Volodymyr Zelensky’s decision to name a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That prompted his Polish counterpart, Karol Nawrocki, to strip Zelensky of Poland’s highest state honour. Since then, both sides have moved to calm tensions, with Zelensky setting out a five-point plan to resolve the dispute, including issuing “a substantial number of permits for search and exhumation work”. World.title: Polish coal mining giant JSW to shed 4,200 jobs – 21% of its workforce – this year
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish state-owned mining firm Jastrzębska Spółka Węglowa (JSW), which is the EU’s largest producer of coking coal and one of Poland’s biggest employers, has announced that it will cut over 4,000 jobs, 21% of its workforce, by the end of this year. The plans come as JSW seeks to turn around its finances after years of large losses, as well as a broader shift in Poland away from reliance on coal. Jastrzębska Spółka Węglowa do końca 2026 r. zwolni ponad 4,2 tys. osób. – Musimy kierować się interesem spółki – mówił na konferencji prasowej prezes JSW. Więcej: https://t.co/7Sxrhuuaja pic.twitter.com/evJoQal0c3 — Gazeta.pl (@gazetapl_news) October 1, 2026 On Wednesday, JSW’s management board announced that it expected the size of its workforce to decline by 4,248 by the end of this year, bringing it below 16,000, down from 20,135 at the end of March. “We anticipate that approximately 2,200 people will leave in the third quarter, and about 1,400 in the fourth quarter,” adding to those who have already left, said the firm’s CEO, Bogusław Oleksy, quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Last year, Poland introduced a new law making it easier for coal companies to close mines and reduce their workforce. It provides for large severance payments and other measures intended to soften the blow for those who lose their jobs. News service Strefa Inwestorów says that, on this basis, more than 3,000 JSW employees have the option to take so-called mining or mineral-processing leave while just under 1,200 can opt for one-off severance payments. President Nawrocki has signed into law a government bill that makes it easier to close down coal mines and provides severance pay of 170,000 zloty to miners. The measures are seen as a key part of Poland’s transition towards cleaner forms of energy https://t.co/vH6MU4nBsv — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 15, 2025 The workforce reduction is part of JSW’s recovery plan for 2026-2035, announced this week. Other key objectives include cutting costs and investment without decreasing production while increasing the share of coking coal in output. When asked how the workforce reduction would affect production, Oleksy said the company would optimise its operations to make more efficient use of employees and equipment. He noted that most of the losses would be administrative positions rather than staff directly involved in production. In February this year, the company reached an agreement with unions to reduce labour costs in order to help stabilise the company’s financial position. JSW employees almost unanimously supported the agreement, reported broadcaster TVN. The initial results of the cost-cutting measures are beginning to show. In the first half of 2026, the cost of extraction per tonne fell to 609 zloty (€139) from 778 zloty a year earlier. JSW’s long-term goal is to bring the cost down to around 560 zloty per tonne. The company is still posting heavy losses, though those have also fallen this year. JSW posted a net loss of just over 1.0 billion zloty in the first half of 2026, around half the 2.1 billion zloty figure from the same period a year earlier. For the full year 2025, the company recorded a loss of 6.3 billion zloty, which was down from a record figure of 7.3 billion zloty in 2024. Polish state-owned mining giant JSW, the EU's largest producer of coking coal, has reported a record annual loss of 7.3bn zloty. It attributed the results to falling coal prices, lower production volumes, and the impact of a one-off write-off https://t.co/vrSgRu630b — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 11, 2025 JSW’s announcement comes just as some officials and industry representatives are warning that the energy crisis caused by conflict in the Middle East could increase demand in Poland for coal, which is still used to generate around half of electricity and to heat almost a fifth of homes. Polish coal is among the most expensive in the world to extract, and the industry survives largely due to heavy public subsidies. In 2026, the state is expected to spend 5.5 billion zloty propping up the sector, after an outlay of 9 billion zloty last year. Successive governments have been seeking to move away from coal, which went from producing 87% of Poland’s electricity in 2015 to 52.2% in 2025. Meanwhile, between 2015 and 2024, the proportion of households using hard coal for heating fell from 40% to 17%, while those using natural gas doubled from 10% to 21%. However, the energy crisis prompted by US and Israeli attacks on Iran this year has resulted in natural gas prices soaring. As a result, Poland’s state assets minister, Wojciech Balczun, said last month that the geopolitical situation meant coal’s role this year would be “larger than we anticipated”. “We are currently increasing output at coal companies and are aware of the energy sector’s demand for coal as a stabilising factor,” he said, quoted by news service Money.pl. World.title: Polish president backs down and approves government’s windfall tax on fuel companies
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki has reversed course and signed into law a windfall tax on fuel companies’ excess profits that he had previously blocked. The government had been pushing the president to approve the measures amid soaring fuel prices. In announcing his decision on Thursday, Nawrocki, who is aligned with the opposition, insisted that he now expected the government to move to lower fuel prices for consumers. A few hours later, the government confirmed that it would do so, and on Friday morning it announced cuts in VAT and excise duty on fuels. Nie pozwolę rządowi dłużej odsuwać od siebie odpowiedzialności za tę trudną sytuację. Podpisałem ustawę dotyczącą nadmiarowych zysków koncernów paliwowych i zakończę proces ustawiania Polaków w roli politycznych zakładników. To rząd ponosi pełną odpowiedzialność za ceny paliw -… pic.twitter.com/7AX8v4a9Q0 — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) October 1, 2026 The windfall tax will levy a one-off charge of 60% of excess profits from liquid fuel sales, calculated as the amount that would have been generated using a company’s average 2025 fuel sales margin, increased by 20%. It is expected to raise around 4 billion zloty (€914 million). When announcing the plans, the finance ministry said the levy was justified by this year’s “exceptional economic and geopolitical conditions that have led to above-average financial results in a specific segment of the fuel sector, not resulting from improved operational efficiency…but from a supply shock”. The tax was intended to offset some of the roughly 4.7 billion zloty the government spent on keeping fuel prices lower for consumers amid the crisis in the Middle East by cutting VAT and excise duty and introducing a maximum daily price. Those measures were initially in place from March to June. However, in July, Nawrocki announced that he would not sign the windfall tax into law. He instead sent it to the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) for assessment. That process can take years, effectively killing off the bill. The president argued that the proposed measures “raised serious constitutional concerns”. In particular, he criticised the fact that the tax would be retroactive, applying to revenue earned from the beginning of March. Since then, he and the government have been locked in a dispute over the issue, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk arguing that measures to reduce fuel prices, which were briefly reintroduced in the last two weeks of August, can only be restored if Nawrocki signs the windfall tax. Nawrocki’s office, however, has argued that fuel companies would pass the costs of the tax onto consumers, therefore actually increasing prices. President @NawrockiKn has obstructed a planned windfall tax on fuel companies by sending it to the constitutional court, where it could stay for years The tax aimed to offset fuel price protection costs after the Iran war surgehttps://t.co/UojVuYhvdV — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 27, 2026 In September, the government’s majority in parliament passed the windfall tax bill a second time. And Nawrocki has now backed down, announcing in a recorded speech on Thursday evening that he would sign the bill into law. However, he has still asked the TK to assess its constitutionality. Nawrocki declared that he was seeking to call the government’s bluff. He claimed that they were actually hoping the windfall tax would fail so that the treasury could continue obtaining normal tax revenue from high fuel prices, as well as dividends from state oil giant Orlen. By signing the bill, the president said he was “ending the process of holding Poles hostage”. He now expected the government to “immediately” reintroduce measures to bring down prices at petrol stations, as well as the cost of fuel for farmers. To nie ja wygrałem. Wygrali Polacy, którzy już w weekend zapłacą mniej za paliwa. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) October 1, 2026 In response, government spokesman Adam Szłapka told broadcaster TVN that they were ready to make the necessary decisions to reduced prices on Friday and that the measures could be in force already by the weekend. “It’s good that the president has stopped blocking this,” he said. On Friday morning, the government announced that it would reduce VAT on fuels from 23% to 8% and cut excise duty – both measures it also used earlier this year. The new policies will be in place until 31 December. Energy minister Miłosz Motyka told Polskie Radio that maximum daily prices would also be reintroduced. Earlier, on Thursday evening, finance minister Andrzej Domański announced on social media that he estimated fuel costs would be reduced by 1.2-1.3 zloty per litre once the subsidies were reintroduced. According to price monitoring service ePetrol, diesel prices are currently averaging around 9.14 zloty per litre while PB95 petrol is at 8.19 zloty. Those are both record highs. Ustawa o podatku od nadmiarowych zysków koncernów paliwowych właśnie wpłynęła do RCL. Jeszcze dziś będzie ogłoszona. Oznacza to, że już w weekend ceny na stacjach paliwowych będą niższe. Szacunkowo o około 1,2-1,3 zł na litrze. I po co były te gierki, Panie Prezydencie? — Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) October 1, 2026 The dispute over financing fuel price cuts comes at a time of growing concern over Poland’s public finances, something Nawrocki referred to in his address on Thursday. Poland has been running one of the EU’s highest deficits, despite the government committing to bringing it down after being placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure. Public debt passed the EU’s limit of 60% of GDP for the first time this year. Last month, Moody’s, one of the big three global credit rating agencies, lowered Poland’s rating from A2 to A3, pointing to a “deteriorating” fiscal situation and the “limited willingness or ability” of the authorities to take necessary action. The last time the country was at A3 level was in 2002.
