World.title: Tomato soup tin explodes in man's face, slicing open his nose
World.content:
A tin of tomato soup may not seem like something to be afraid of.

But that is now the case for one northern Victoria farmer, who had a soup tin explode in his face, leaving him with a deep cut on his nose.

Dick Lanyon, from Boort, recounted to the ABC what happened in his kitchen last week.

"Last Wednesday night I heard an explosion in my kitchen — I went out to have a look and couldn't find anything and just assumed something must have fallen down," he said.

"The next morning I saw in my cupboard there was soup sprayed up the back of it and I saw a tin of soup where the lid had blown off."

The first soup tin explosion in Dick Lanyon's kitchen left a mess in his pantry. (Supplied: Dick Lanyon)

That was just the beginning of Mr Lanyon's soup ordeal.

The next day he discovered another tin of the same Heinz Big Red tomato soup — this one with the bottom badly distended.

Fearing another explosion was imminent, he attempted to dispose of the tin in his rubbish bin.

"I got to the bin, and the tin exploded in my face and the whole lid sliced up the side of my nose," Mr Lanyon said.

" It was tomato soup, so I was covered in tomato soup and blood as well. "

After a trip to the hospital, Mr Lanyon's nose was patched up, but he's been left with an enduring wariness of soup tins.

"I've thrown all my other soup tins in the bin," he said.

"No-one expects a tin of soup to explode in their face."

The tins of tomato soup expanded at their bases, before the lids blew off. (Supplied: Dick Lanyon )

Mr Lanyon said he had no idea why the cans exploded, although he had since read online about similar incidents caused by bacterial contamination.

"I can't find an expiry date on them, but they were probably three to five years old," he said.

"I've heard incidents of people trying to heat up cans in a campfire and having horrific injuries, but I certainly didn't expect this to explode for no reason at all.

" And it was very strange that two cans would explode within two days of each other. "

In a statement, Food Standards Australia and New Zealand said the shelf life of canned food depended on whether the tins were kept in a cool, dry place.

The why According to the FoodTrients website, tins can swell and potentially (though rarely) explode thanks to: hydrogen produced from the interaction of acids and the metals of the cans

bacteria that causes spoilage and creates gas build-up

packaging issues, altitude and food temperature at the time of packaging.

"Consumers should always check canned foods for signs of damage before use, including swelling, leakage, rust, dents or damaged seams.

"Food in swollen, leaking or otherwise damaged cans should not be consumed."

Despite his injuries, Mr Lanyon had a positive outlook on the incident, and said he didn't plan to lodge a complaint with Heinz.

"It could have been a lot worse — I was very happy it didn't hit me in the eye, because that would have done a lot of damage," he said.

"Because I'm not badly injured, I thought I'd probably just let it slide."

He did, however, urge others to check their pantries for bulging tins.

Heinz has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Severe cyclone likely to hit Qld this season, weather bureau warns
World.content:
Queensland is likely to see a severe cyclone this season, fed by warmer sea temperatures off the Coral Sea, the weather bureau has warned.

A severe cyclone is category 3 and above. One to two systems typically cross the coast each season in Queensland.

Last season saw two category five systems, ex-Tropical Cyclone Narelle and ex-Tropical Cyclone Maila, in the Coral Sea for the first time since records began in 1970.

Cyclones could also continue their move south, Bureau of Meteorology forecaster Laura Boekel said.

Tropical Cyclone Alfred caused damage right along the Queensland coast in 2025. (ABC News: Tobias Loftus)

"This season there is an increased chance of seeing a cyclone that is severe, with warmer sea surface temperatures forecast to develop over the coming months," she said.

"The warmer the sea temperatures are, the more energy that the cyclones have to become more severe."

The bureau is also predicting warmer than average temperatures across large parts of the state, as well as below average rainfall until December.

"This will increase the chance of heatwaves occurring, and will increase their severity as well," Ms Boekel said.

BOM forecasts unusually high temperatures for most of Australia from October to December. (Supplied: BOM)

Meanwhile, dry conditions have led to an "incredibly busy start" to the bush fire season, with activity up 20 per cent on this time last year, according to Queensland Fire Department Commissioner Steve Smith.

"Since the first of September we've had almost 2,000 responses to bushfires," Mr Smith said.

He said four years of good rainfall had led to an "incredible amount of fuel".

Conditions are expected to deteriorate until forecast heavy rains later in the year.

"We need people to understand that this season could be very significant, and to stay aware of the conditions around them," Commissioner Smith said.

World.title: Calls for Cornell president to resign during protests over gang rape allegation
World.content:
Hundreds of Cornell University students have protested the university's handling of gang rape allegations in what many hope will be a turning point in the oversight of sexual violence cases on campus.

The woman, identified only by the pseudonym Jane Doe, alleged she was gang raped at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024 after being pressured into drinking and taking drugs.

In September this year she sued the university, seven former students, the fraternity and others, prompting a new criminal investigation.

Hundreds of students, staff and members of the public gathered at the campus in Ithaca, New York, on Monday local time, calling for the president of the university to resign and for an overhaul to how allegations of sexual assault are handled.

They wore purple ribbons and held signs with messages including "support survivors, expel rapists" and "Justice 4 every Jane Doe".

Students attended the protest in support of Jane Doe. (AP: Adrian Kraus)

Suzie Barrows, a sophomore at Cornell University, attended the protest.

She said that the incident had been re-traumatising for her due to her own experience of sexual assault.

"Seeing how this case was handled really struck me to the core, and was deeply unsettling and upsetting to know that the university that I've come to love so much is capable of this and that this happened here on campus," she said.

"It's definitely brought up a lot of memories, a lot of painful memories."

Suzie Barrows is a sophomore at Cornell University. (ABC News: Phoebe Hosier)

Ms Barrows said rape culture was still prevalent.

"[It] has been allowed to thrive for so long and it needs to end," she said.

"But what truly shocked me was how Cornell was allowing it to continue in this way by not providing proper consequences to the perpetrators.

"It has the effect of taking away hope and faith in the system in total."

Demonstrators hold a demonstration on campus. (AP: Adrian Kraus)

She said she was hopeful the momentum from this incident will create change.

"I do feel like this is a turning point and that the world is waking up, in a sense," Ms Barrows said.

Protesters gather on campus

At the weekend, New York Governor Kathy Hochul said she was "deeply disturbed" by how police handled the allegation.

It follows a report from the New York Times that an assertion by Jane Doe that she was "100 per cent" confident she was raped was left out of an official police report sent to prosecutors, who dropped the case.

Students called for action at Monday's protest.

"Too often we are met with silence, we are met with statements, we are met with procedures, but not enough support," student Athena Holloway told the crowd.

"How much does it take for our university to stand with survivors?"

Student Athena Holloway addressed the crowd at the protest. (AP: Adrian Kraus)

Photos from earlier in the day showed that the administration building's glass doors had been damaged, and the walls beside them were marked with red-painted messages condemning patriarchy and the university's handling of sexual assaults.

Cornell spokesperson Kyle Kimball acknowledged students' "frustration and strong emotions" and said the university was investigating the damage.

Calls for resignation over handling

Speakers at the demonstration criticised fraternities and Cornell president Michael Kotlikoff, accusing him and his administration of prioritising protecting the university's reputation over students' safety.

Demonstrators made a series of demands, including changes to how the student code of conduct defines sexual consent. ( AP: Adrian Kraus)

"Kotlikoff, resign!" demonstrators chanted, as they marched to the damaged administration building to present a list of demands including changes to how the student code of conduct defines sexual consent.

They also called for expulsions or revoking the degrees of all students involved in the alleged 2024 assault.

The group's chants included "ban the frats!"

No criminal charges have been filed.

The Chi Phi chapter at Cornell has been shut down, and Cornell said it expelled some students and suspended others.

The Chi Phi fraternity house at Cornell University. (AP: Heather Ainsworth)

In a statement last week the administration bristled about the "false narrative that there were minimal consequences in this case".

Students, however, have demanded more accountability and transparency.

Ms Hochul has said Jane Doe was "failed by people and institutions" including the Cornell police and local District Attorney Matthew Van Houten.

The governor has ordered the state's attorney-general to take over the criminal investigation into the allegations and has called for an independent review of Cornell's handling of the matter.

AP/ABC

World.title: Trump approves firing squad execution for convicted US military base shooter
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has approved the execution by firing squad of a US Army psychiatrist who shot and killed 13 people at a military base in 2009.

The Pentagon said Nidal Hasan would be executed for the attack at Fort Hood in Texas, which also wounded more than two dozen people.

It will be the first execution carried out by the US military since 1961.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth "has recommended — and President Donald J. Trump has approved — death by U.S. Army firing squad for convicted terrorist Nidal Malik Hasan," Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a post on X.

"The Secretary of the Army will set the time and place of the execution. Judgement day for Hasan has finally come," Mr Parnell wrote.

Then US president Barack Obama spoke at the memorial for the 13 victims of the Fort Hood shooting. (Kevin Lamarque: Reuters)

Hasan was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013 for carrying out the Al-Qaeda inspired mass shooting at Fort Hood.

He chose to conduct his own defence during the trial but called no witnesses and gave no testimony, and made no attempt to deny the charges.

Court-appointed defence attorneys expressed concern that he was seeking execution.

Military base shootings rare in US

In November 2009, the US-born shooter, opened fire at a medical facility on the base.

The base served as a staging point for soldiers to deploy to combat zones in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Soldiers light candles during a vigil in 2009. (Reuters: Jessica Rinaldi)

Twelve of the dead and 30 of the wounded were soldiers.

Hasan was shot and partially paralysed by a police officer who responded to the attack.

The court that convicted Hasan was told he was opposed to the US military's occupations of Iraq and Afghanistan and he had spoken online with an alleged Al-Qaeda figure.

While mass shootings in the United States are common, they are rare at military facilities.

Soliders outside Fort Hood on the day of the shooting. (AFP: Ben Sklar)

History of base shootings

In 2025, a soldier opened fire at a US military base in the state of Georgia, wounding five fellow troops before he was tackled and apprehended.

In 2019, a US sailor fatally shot two people and wounded a third at a base in Hawaii, while a Saudi military student shot dead three people at a military facility in Florida the same year.

A Kuwaiti-born US citizen attacked two military installations in Tennessee in 2015, killing four marines and a sailor.

The FBI concluded the violence was inspired by a "foreign terrorist group".

Two years earlier, a man killed 12 people and wounded eight at the Washington Navy Yard in the US capital, before being shot dead by officers.

AFP

World.title: 'Heartless': Pro-Palestinian groups criticised for October 7 vigils
World.content:
Pro-Palestinian organisations have been criticised for planning vigils for the third anniversary of the Hamas attacks on Israel, in which more than 1,200 people were killed.

Jewish organisations across the country will hold commemorations on Wednesday for those lost in the terrorist attack.

Jews Against the Occupation 48 will also hold a vigil in Sydney and Wollongong Friends of Palestine will gather "to stop and remember the martyrs and all those who suffer and continue to resist".

The organisers of the Sydney vigil are using the slogan "Don't let Israel steal the date" and said October 7 was also three years since air strikes began on Gaza in response to the attack.

They said, according to the Israel Defense Force's timeline, its fighter jets conducted strikes in Gaza the same morning, shortly after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu declared that Israel was at war.

Chris Minns urged Labor MPs to not attend the gathering. (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

NSW Premier Chris Minns has condemned the pro-Palestine events being held on that day, labelling them "heartless" and "in poor taste".

He said he believed organisers chose the date to attract attention and feared the vigil would not prove be as peaceful as organisers may wish.

"There are some people suggesting it can be stopped, the constitution doesn't allow that," he said.

"They can certainly do that, it's not against the law but as a citizen I've got a right to make a judgement on it too."

Mr Minns added: "Police will do what they always do and that is keep the public safe."

He also asked his Labor colleagues not to attend.

"I can certainly speak for my cabinet and I can certainly speak for my senior colleagues but history has proven I can't speak for all of them," he said

"In all fairness, I don't know if anyone's [Labor MPs] going to go."

Executive Council of Australian Jewry co-CEO Alex Ryvchin said October 7 was a "solemn day" for Jewish and Israeli communities.

"I ask those people: Leave that day alone," he said.

"Choose any other day in the calendar and carry on your obnoxious protest and divide society as you do.

" You can't be stopped, and that's fine, but this day belongs to the victims and we will remember them on that day. "

Mr Ryvchin said he had been told there was concern from government such "anti-Israel" rallies like this would foster extremism and antisemitism.

He said especially in light of the Bondi Beach massacre in December last year, October 7 this year would also be remembered as an event that ushered in a new era of antisemitism.

'Pick any other date'

NSW Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane told 702 ABC Sydney she found "the whole thing entirely sickening and reprehensible".

"A lot of people are very distressed by what they're seeing in Gaza and should be able to protest," she said.

"But this undermines that very intent of peace by having it on a day where 1,200 innocent people were slaughtered in the most brutal and unimaginable way, at a time when there was no retaliation by Israel."

Ms Sloane says holding the events on the anniversary date is "sickening". (ABC News: Gavin Coote)

Ms Sloane said she wanted the premier to explain how the events would be managed.

"There have been so many rallies that have been declared to be peaceful that turn out to be anything but," she said.

"We need to make sure that if that happens that we use the laws to make sure that these people are held to account."

She acknowledged that events that organisers have described as a peaceful gathering could not be banned but urged protesters to "pick any other date of the year".

"364 other dates are possible ... if you believe in peace, then please choose them," she said.

She also demanded Mr Minns order Labor MPs to stay away from the planned events.

World.title: Being fetishised broke me. Now I'm taking back my power
World.content:
Do you love me, or the idea of me? As an Asian woman, this question haunts me every time I enter a romantic relationship.

Who could blame me? I've been burnt too many times. And it's all thanks to this thing called "yellow fever".

Yellow fever is a slang term for when people have a strong sexual attraction to those of East or South-East Asian descent.

In plain terms, from my experience: white guys with a fetish for Asian women.

As a self-professed recovered hopeless romantic, I would fall hard and fast, only to be left with a gnawing feeling that something was very wrong.

Things like a predilection for Asian pornography pointed to something deeper and darker than a preference.

For a long time, it is something I ignored.

I thought I was ugly

Kelly says she grew up not fitting into "Eurocentric beauty standards". (Supplied: Kelly Lim Harris)

I was born and raised in New Zealand to a Malaysian Chinese mother and New Zealand-European father. It was a time before K-pop and Wasian royalty — a time when bringing anything but a Vegemite sandwich to school was considered absurd.

I'm not white passing in the slightest. I was bullied. I didn't have a lot of friends. And the ones I did have weren't white.

A consummate over-achiever, people assumed I must have had a tiger mother, but quite the opposite was true. My parents gave me an overabundance of love and never pushed me in the slightest.

I pushed myself. If I couldn't be pretty or popular, at least I would be smart and talented.

It created a strange dissonance when I would visit family in Malaysia and Singapore with my mum.

Every day I would have strangers tell me I was beautiful and my mum would respond, "it's because she's mixed".

My beauty was contingent on my proximity to whiteness. And back in New Zealand, I didn't have that.

I've since been able to educate my mum on how harmful her mindset was and I'm lucky she is so willing to learn and grow.

Together I'm proud of how we're untangling the knots of colonialism. But it hasn't always been easy.

For much of my life I thought I was ugly because I didn't fit Eurocentric beauty standards.

And I wondered, who would want me?

An object of desire

Kelly says she has been able to confront past shame through her performance. (Supplied: Ven Tithing)

When men started showing interest I was flattered by the attention, yet an unease followed me. A pattern emerged.

They always seemed to have Asian ex-girlfriends, an interest in Asian culture, and a mindset that Asian women proved superior girlfriends, wives and mothers.

In isolation these could all mean nothing, but together they pointed to that term, yellow fever.

How strange that the very thing I once thought deemed me undesirable, now turned me into an object of desire.

Older men would ask me how much I was when I wore a cheongsam, a traditional Chinese dress.

Younger men would joke about me being "slanted" down below. I would be catcalled on the street that I looked like a geisha or told I looked like a little China doll.

One boyfriend declared he liked me because I was "exotic but not too exotic". Others said they "just had a preference" for Asian girls.

Why did I stay? Part of me desperately wanted to believe that this attraction could turn to real love.

I remember the night that changed.

A man I was in a relationship with asked me to put on an accent. I laughed it off, part horror, part shock. But it broke me.

I realised that to these men I would never be more than a prop.

It's about power, not love

I've been working as a performer for several years now, across opera, musicals, plays, and most recently cabaret.

Throughout my career, I have often been lumped into playing one of two tropes — the "lotus blossom", delicate and submissive, or the "dragon lady", manipulative and sexualised.

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

I feel this oriental fantasy has been fed to men over and over.

Perhaps it's a comforting illusion to think there are women out there that will worship them just because they're white.

And when men explicitly seek me out because I'm Asian, I don't think they are looking for love. I think they are looking for power.

In some ways I pity them. They want something that isn't real.

Date any Asian woman and you'll soon realise we are not a monolith. We are layered, unique, and ultimately human.

I deserve better

For Kelly, her art has become a powerful tool in countering harmful tropes. (Supplied: Lia Eden Shiloh)

Last year I wrote a show about my experiences. When I first workshopped it, people were shocked. They'd say: "Did those things really happen?"

What was horrifying to the outside world had become my normal.

I realised how much shame I carried and writing my show was an incredible way to bring clarity and closure to years of buried feelings about my race, love, and art.

One reviewer wrote I was "seeking revenge in the most tasteful way". I had to laugh. That was never my intention.

I wrote the show that I needed to see when I was teenager — to tell her she deserves better.

Kelly Lim Harris is an award-winning performer and multi-hyphenate creative based in Naarm/Melbourne.

World.title: Early morning car burglary ends in dramatic arrest on Melbourne freeway
World.content:
Police have arrested six people in a dramatic operation on the Monash Freeway in Melbourne's south-east.

More than a dozen police officers, some dressed in tactical gear, were seen detaining several males on the freeway near Chadstone at lunchtime.

Traffic was brought to a standstill as the outbound lanes were closed, but all lanes had reopened by about 1:15pm.

Traffic was backed up as the police operation continued in the outbound lane. (ABC News)

Police say the arrests followed the theft of two cars in an aggravated burglary in Brighton East just after 5:30am this morning.

One of the vehicles, a Nissan 4WD, was later seen being driven erratically on the Eastlink toll road before it was intercepted by police in Chadstone just after midday.

Unmarked police vehicles appeared to pin the grey 4WD, which sustained damage to its front.

More than a dozen police officers in tactical gear were involved in the operation. (ABC News)

Police said the six occupants were being interviewed after their arrest.

No-one was injured during the incident.

The second stolen vehicle, an Audi, was also recovered in Endeavour Hills following a collision earlier today.

Police were seen collecting items from the vehicle. (ABC News)

Vision from the scene showed traffic significantly backed up the freeway before the lanes were reopened.

Police investigators were also seen removing items from the 4WD and putting them in evidence bags.

World.title: Police Commissioner Grant Stevens appointed SA's next governor
World.content:
SA Police Commissioner Grant Stevens has been appointed South Australia's next governor and will succeed Frances Adamson, whose term expires today after five years.

SA Premier Peter Malinauskas made the announcement this morning, saying he had recommended Mr Stevens's appointment as the 37th governor of South Australia to King Charles III.

"It is the sovereign's appointment — [the governor] is the sovereign's representative in the state of South Australia," Mr Malinauskas said.

"I'm very grateful that His Majesty King Charles has decided to appoint Grant."

Mr Stevens will be sworn in on Wednesday, December 9.

The 62-year-old has served as police commissioner since 2015 and was the state coordinator during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Frances Adamson AC was appointed governor of South Australia in 2021. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

He will formally step down from the commissioner's role on October 23, with Deputy Commissioner Linda Williams to assume the role in an acting capacity.

Mr Stevens — who joined the force in 1982 — said he was "excited" and "deeply honoured" when he was first approached to take on the new appointment, succeeding Ms Adamson, who is a former head of the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade.

"I don't think I can express sufficiently just how honoured I am that I have been asked to step in as the replacement for Frances Adamson," he said.

"I am slightly daunted by the work ethic that [she] has demonstrated over her term."

Mr Stevens acknowledged the rumour had been circulating for "quite some time, so it wasn't something that we hadn't contemplated, [wife] Emma and I".

"Both Emma and I saw this as an opportunity to continue being part of the South Australian community in a way that positively influences how South Australians live, work and enjoy what we have here," he said.

'No clue, no concept'

He said he had one year and nine months left on his contract as police commissioner, and that he was approached to take on the new role some time in early to mid September.

"I don't specifically remember the date but I will admit that I walked away from that meeting quite blown away. I finally figured out the rumours were true," he said with a smile.

"I had no clue, no concept when I was a 17-year-old boy walking through the academy gates in 1982 that I would ever be the commissioner of police, let alone asked to step into the role of governor."

Deputy Commissioner Linda Williams will serve as acting commissioner when Mr Stevens formally relinquishes his current role. (ABC News: Ethan Rix)

Asked about his own successor as police commissioner, Mr Stevens said the selection process would be a matter for the government — but spoke highly of the deputy commissioner.

"Linda has been an amazing support to me — she has acted as commissioner and she has done so admirably,"

"Linda has demonstrated a capability in that regard, without any hesitation."

He said that given the significance of the new role, he would step down from his position on the board of the Adelaide Football Club and as chair of charity Operation Flinders Foundation.

World.title: Rogue pilots may be the most dangerous threat to passengers. They’re ‘just about impossible’ to stop
World.content:
Analysis BusinessCompaniesAviation Rogue pilots may be the most dangerous threat to passengers. They’re ‘just about impossible’ to stop Chris Zappone October 6, 2026 — 1:22pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The near-tragic incident with the Tel Aviv-bound flydubai jet has the industry scrambling to manage what could be best described as the ultimate nightmare for passengers and airlines – what do you do if the pilot goes rogue? The flydubai flight FZ1073 incident on September 30 is being described as an attempted terror attack by co-pilot Hamam al-Hammami. The alleged attack was thwarted because the other person in the cockpit - Captain Smit Machchhar - was able to unlock the door, allowing passengers to intervene. Omani pilot Hamam al-Hammami is accused of attacking his colleage on a flydubai flight to Israel. 9News It was the narrowest of escapes, owed to the actions of those onboard, but it exposes a number of weaknesses that the aviation sector will have to address. The first is the insider threat posed by a rogue pilot, which in the flydubai flight’s case was Al-Hammami’s attempt to plunge himself and all on board the jet into a fatal dive. It’s not without precedent in aviation history.





Dr Warren Harrex, a specialist in aerospace medicine said that while much progress had been made in reducing human factor errors in flight, it was “just about impossible to, with testing, identify people who might be at risk of acting adversely in the cockpit”. Loading “The best way really is to get to know people and to note if there’s any change in their behaviour or demeanour. Otherwise, there’s no real test you can do to prevent a pilot going rogue.” “These events are very rare, but they’re high-profile when they do occur, of course,” said Harrex. How rare? About 130,000 flights per day take off and land without incident, according to the International Air Transport Association.



Related Article Aviation Aviation industry needs to learn from Germanwings crash: French investigators “Yet if somebody’s really determined to behave badly, like we see with terrorist attacks, it’s very difficult to predict.” The globalised industry with large workforces has processes in place to continually assess capabilities of pilots. Central Queensland University associate professor Geoffrey Dell said if a pilot started to get radicalised, or had other mental health issues, one would expect the system would identify that in advance. “There is a fairly rigorous reporting.” Airlines continually check and recertify pilots on simulators, giving them opportunities to evaluate employees on the job. Pilots must also regularly fly with check and training captains who ensure “operational safety-critical personnel are proficient” in the skills required to keep the plane flying safely. These are in-person interactions in which a pilot’s performance is judged. Yet al-Hammami was hired by flydubai after losing his job at Oman Air.



There have been cases of flight-deck assaults that could lead to suicide, such as a 1994 FedEx flight departing Memphis, Tennessee, in which a disaffected employee sought to subdue pilots on a cargo plane and then crash it. Crisis24 global risk management aviation lead Dr Alejandra Gentil said the FedEx case highlighted “the importance of background checks on crew members, since the attacker was being fired by FedEx because he had presented false information upon employment related to his flight hours”. A significant section of the rudder was missing from flydubai flight FZ1073. Instagram The insider threat risk had been part of the international aviation security framework for many years, she said. The International Civil Aviation Organisation had developed tools to manage it but “it falls upon the appropriate authorities of the state to conduct a thorough background check”, Gentil said.



She said background checks in the UAE were a prerequisite for being given a residence permit. While details are still being uncovered, media outlets have reported al-Hammami had earlier lost a job with Oman Air because of an apparent interest in extremism. Gentil said yearly mental health checks are mandated by the UAE regulator as prescribed in the Civil Aviation Regulations, which gives them the authority and the responsibility for conducting them. The safety of aviation is built on redundancies, including in oversight of the plane. A former commercial pilot said the incident should dissuade the industry from moving towards allowing a single pilot to fly at cruising altitude. “There was a strong move towards it by the airlines a few years ago for economic reasons,” and “the manufacturers were designing for it.” Had planes moved to a single pilot cruise model, “then [al-Hammami] wouldn’t have had to stab the other pilot of the aircraft”. Incidents such as this reinforce why the European Union Aviation Safety Agency banned single-pilot operations, he said.



Related Article Opinion

Aviation I felt safer piloting planes after 9/11. But now terror can lock itself inside the cockpit David Evans Former Qantas captain The flydubai flight FZ1073 will also bring into focus the potential danger posed by a locked cockpit door. The measure was introduced after the September 11 attacks as a way to stop hijackers from taking control of a plane. Usually, the pilot holds the key and while other crew members have emergency access, in case there is a health emergency, who gets inside the cockpit is still largely in the hands of the pilot. The flydubai incident may need the aviation sector to rethink the need for further emergency countermeasures. Brisbane-based CW Aviation Security Consulting director Shannon Wandmaker said both the locks on doors, as well as the vetting of pilots before hiring would probably be reviewed as a result of the flydubai incident. A relaxation in the hardened/locked cockpit door requirements would seem unlikely, he said. “It’s always easier to implement a security measure than it is to remove one.”



“It may be the case that we see some governments move unilaterally to implement additional, or more stringent measures related to background checks, and this may happen quite quickly,” Wandmaker said. Airlines themselves try to be proactive on pilot mental health. Virgin Australia, for example, has a wellbeing strategy which is regularly reviewed by senior management. Qantas was approached for comment. The Department of Home Affairs, which has authority over access to flight deck in Australia, said: “there are strict requirements regarding cockpit security, including when the cockpit door must remain locked, and the persons authorised to be in the cockpit during flight”. The department regularly reviews aviation security settings. If you are troubled by this report or experiencing a personal crisis, you can call Lifeline on 131 114 or Beyond Blue on 1300 224 636. World.title: Teacher at prestige girls’ school charged with sex assault of student
World.content:
A teacher at Melbourne’s prestigious Methodist Ladies’ College has been charged with the sexual assault of a student.

In an email to parents, the school said police had notified it that Kam Kenny-Jones, a teacher at the school until just weeks ago, had been charged at the weekend with one count of sexual assault of a child under 17.

Methodist Ladies’ College in Kew. Paul Jeffers

MLC principal Julia O’Shea said the news was confronting and unsettling but she felt it important to update the school community in a clear and timely manner.

“In September, concerns about Mr Kenny-Jones were brought to the college’s attention, and we immediately stood him down from his duties that day while we investigated and reported the matter to the relevant authorities, including Victoria Police,” she wrote in the email sent on Monday.

Queensland Rail CEO Katarzyna Stapleton has told staff she will leave the job next year. Stapleton, known as Kat, will not seek to extend her appointment, which was due to finish in April 2027. Before joining Queensland Rail in 2019 as the chief financial officer, she held executive roles with NBN Co and was CFO for Bahrain Telecommunications company. Queensland Rail chief executive Kat Stapleton outside the Fair Work Commission offices on Eagle Street in May after a day’s negotiation with unions. Cameron Atfield She was appointed as Queensland Rail’s chief executive officer in April 2022 during the former Palaszczuk Labor government.

Queensland Rail Train services to be fully restored as QR finalises pay deals with unions The last of seven agreements was reached last month. World.title: Flagship puts bigger fence around Canadian copper giant
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Flagship puts bigger fence around Canadian copper giant Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward October 6, 2026 — 1:19pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Flagship Minerals looks to have picked its moment perfectly in Canada’s British Columbia, securing three new mineral claims that more than double its Whipsaw copper tenure, just as the province rolls out the red carpet for miners and copper prices hover near record highs. The company initially swooped on the massive copper play in June for a mere A$6.5 million. However, its latest ground grab has added a further 37.5 square kilometres to the project, swelling Flagship’s position by a hefty 132 per cent to about 66 square kilometres. The company says the new ground captures prospective strike extensions to its existing exploration target, which sits within a colossal porphyry mineral system stretching roughly 3.7km long and 1.2km wide. Flagship Minerals’ Whipsaw copper project sits just 17km west of Hudbay Minerals’ operating and expanding Copper Mountain mine in British Columbia. Whipsaw is already backed by 58 historical drill holes with standout hits, including 283.47 metres at 0.28 per cent copper equivalent from 70.1m, 193.7m at 0.30 per cent copper equivalent from 4.42m and 124.93m at 0.33 per cent copper equivalent from 26.3m. Notably, the project also features a sizeable JORC-compliant exploration target of between 510 million and 1.02 billion tonnes, grading between 0.2 and 0.4 per cent copper equivalent, hinting at the sort of scale that’s likely to get pulses quickening. The expansion comes as British Columbia puts its pro-mining “Look West Strategy” into overdrive, with the government actively looking to fast-track major project approvals. Recent examples include Skeena Resources’ Eskay Creek mine, which saw its application-to-decision timeline cut by 40 per cent alongside Centerra Gold’s Mount Milligan extension, which was approved 60 per cent faster than previous processes.



‘Our objective is straightforward: Advance Whipsaw in a capital-efficient manner for a spin-out to unlock value for Flagship shareholders.’ Flagship Minerals managing director Paul Lock Flagship says its own claims were granted in just over three months, a timeline that appears to back up the provincial government’s promise to revive its mining sector. That push already seems to be bearing fruit almost on Whipsaw’s doorstep, with Hudbay Minerals’ New Ingerbelle expansion at its Copper Mountain operation, just 17 kilometres away, securing key permits and breaking ground in recent months. New Ingerbelle is expected to deliver 750,000 tonnes of copper, 900,000 ounces of gold and 5.5 million ounces of silver over its mine life. The geological neighbourhood only adds to the intrigue in what can be fairly described as elephant country for copper. The ground separating Whipsaw from Copper Mountain is held by Collective Metals, whose exploration has already identified porphyry-style targets. Just 134 kilometres north, Teck’s giant Highland Valley operation underscores the region’s pedigree, containing a resource of over 2.2 billion tonnes grading 0.26 per cent copper. Flagship Minerals managing director Paul Lock said: “The additional tenure strengthens our position at Whipsaw and captures prospective extensions to what is already a very large mineralised system, with a very large drill supported JORC compliant Exploration Target. The approval process and timeline bodes well for the BC Government’s push for a mining revival, aiming to transform the province into a leading mining jurisdiction.” The market is also putting serious money behind emerging British Columbia copper stories. Amarc Resources, with a market value of C$228 million (A$229M), has Freeport-McMoRan funding its exploration. At the same time, the more advanced Northisle Copper and Gold, with a defined 1.2-billion-tonne resource, carries a market capitalisation of C$1.45 billion (A$1.46B).



Those numbers provide a good example of how the market can progressively revalue big copper systems as they are de-risked, which is pertinent given Flagship’s plans to spin Whipsaw out into a dedicated listed vehicle. Since Whipsaw currently has little to no value assigned to it in the company’s market cap, a spin-out could put the asset under a market spotlight of its own, allowing Flagship to maintain its focus on advancing its flagship 2.1-million-ounce Isidora gold project in Chile. With the new claims now locked in, the company plans to kick off low-cost LiDAR and drone magnetic surveys to help generate fresh drill targets. As it prepares to launch its new geophysical surveys over a much larger footprint, in a jurisdiction that is actively encouraging development, Flagship appears to be piecing together all the right ingredients for its Canadian copper aspirations. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au
