World.title: ‘Long story short, I’ve got breast cancer’: Comedian Judith Lucy reveals diagnosis
World.content:
Breaking CultureCelebrityBreast cancer ‘Long story short, I’ve got breast cancer’: Comedian Judith Lucy reveals diagnosis Kayla Olaya October 6, 2026 — 1:19pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Comedian Judith Lucy has revealed she has been diagnosed with breast cancer … in a way only she could. In a video uploaded to social media, Lucy matter-of-factly delivers the health update, sandwiched between quick quips about her newly released wellness book and recent faecal transplants. Judith Lucy reveals she has been diagnosed with breast cancer. Simon Schluter “Not so fun update from me,” Lucy says at the start of the Instagram video. “I got an email from BreastScreen Australia, telling me that my mammogram result was a bit weird. May I take this opportunity to say, ladies, for the love of God, keep up with your mammograms. “Long story short, I’ve got breast cancer.”



Lucy said three weeks ago she was going to “pick up yet two more syringes of yet another stranger’s turds” for her fecal transplants when she received the email. “I went on last Friday for a lumpectomy, and a doctor – I’m not making this up - called Doctor Fun found more cancer,” Lucy said. The cancer is “relatively non-aggressive”, Lucy shared, adding she is removing both her breasts by the end of this week via mastectomy – despite only one breast being cancerous. “Doctor Fun is amazing. I am in her debt, but we have gone from a lumpectomy to a mastectomy, which I am having Friday week,” she said.



“I said, while you’re there, let’s get rid of the other one because you know something. I have had 40 years of, if I do say so myself, large and spectacular breasts. You had your chance, fellas. “I think I’m quite fine with going bra-free for my last chapter, and my last chapter is going to be very long and healthy.” More to come

World.title: The real reason behind St Kilda’s steep asking price for Marshall
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLTrading and drafting The real reason behind St Kilda’s steep asking price for Marshall Michael Gleeson October 6, 2026 — 1:19pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

While he was lying on the couch watching Netflix or cleaning out his sock drawer, or indeed doing anything at all rather than going to his club’s best and fairest night, Rowan Marshall quietly finished 10th at the St Kilda awards function he was not at. Marshall avoided needing to pose for red carpet pics or speak disingenuously of his love and affection for a club he has felt neither from in the past year. (We’re not talking about his teammates, players always love their teammates.) Loading Marshall didn’t want to be at Moorabbin this year after the club brought Tom De Koning in over the top of him last October. We were told Marshall was fully on board with having a new stable partner. We now know he wasn’t. But then, as now, Marshall had a contract so he sucked it up and played the season. Played it well, too, to come tenth in the B&F. Interestingly, TDK was not in the top 10. This trade period Marshall is less inclined to suck it up. Monday night was a first statement.



Twelve months ago, St Kilda rejected Geelong’s overtures for Marshall and never stated what would persuade them to change their minds. This year they have at least put a price on a trade. They want Geelong’s first round pick and “a player”. Say what? OK, it’s an opening gambit, but sheesh, a first rounder and a player? It would be remarkable were that to be the eventual trade price. There is a logic to the ambit bid though, and it’s a logic that that ripples through deals involving Geelong, Carlton, Brisbane and GWS. St Kilda Saints ruckman Rowan Marshall. AFL Photos via Getty Images St Kilda needs to lose a Marshall to gain a Marshall. Rowan needs to leave so Sam can come in. The Saints want midfielder Sam Marshall, the Brisbane academy product who was taken at pick 25 in the 2024 draft. The Lions want a similar pick for him now and unfortunately the Saints don’t have one: their first pick is at eight (too much even for a club that gave up pick seven for Sam Flanders 12 months ago) and their next is 49.



Lions list boss Dom Ambrogio said on Monday: “[St Kilda] have got an awareness of what we are looking for, albeit it’s not in their hands at the moment in that they don’t hold the pick in the range we think is appropriate.” Whether “what we are looking for” and “what is appropriate” are the same thing in any trade is doubtful and normally depends on what colours you wear. In this case, what the Lions are looking for and thus what they hope is appropriate for Marshall is a pick in the 20s. So the Saints are trying to find a pick in that range. Losing one Marshall might buy them the draft capital to pass on for the other Marshall. Brisbane midfielder Sam Marshall. Getty The Cats are reluctant to part with their first pick (14) for a 30-year-old ruck, albeit a contracted one. Their next pick, the one they have offered for Rowan Marshall, is currently 34.



The problem is that the Cats’ pick 34 won’t satisfy Brisbane for Sam Marshall. Why not? It’s not far off the pick they want. Thirty-four seems fairly close for a player who played one game this year, is out of contract and has Essendon also keen on him – and thus able to take him for nothing in the pre-season if it came to it. But Brisbane want a pick in the 20s because they have a good academy player available (yes, another one. One out, one in). They need a pick to cover that bid. Academy player Caylen Murray is likely to be bid on somewhere in the mid-to-late-first round. Under new rules the two grand finalists have a 20 per cent loading on the points required to match a bid that comes in the first 18 in the draft for an academy player. And you can only use two picks to match any bid. Brisbane academy prospect Caylen Murray. via Getty Images So the Lions really need another pick in the 20s to be able to cover a bid on Murray. Pick 34 won’t cut it. So unless St Kilda can find another way of bringing in a pick in the 20s – another player going out? - the Saints will need more from Geelong for Rowan Marshall, to be able to pass it on to Brisbane. But Geelong don’t have one. Or do they?



Gryan Miers did a medical at West Coast on Friday before he flew overseas. It was a precaution in case the trade world moved while he was away. Given he partially tore his ACL this year and has not had surgery to repair it, the normal buyer beware caveat carries more heft. He’d rather stay at Geelong but is clearly open enough to West Coast’s interest to be doing a medical there. If the medical is clear enough and the Eagles want him, and Geelong is prepared to trade him (and that’s lot of ifs) what is Miers worth? A pick in the sweet spot with West Coast’s second round pick at 21? Bear in mind that when bids come for Dougie Cochrane and Cody Walker early in the draft, West Coast as one of the bottom five clubs will be compensated with an extra pick at the end of the first round. So they will have picks at what is now 21 and 24. Miers, anyone? Lachie Whitfield of the Giants could be on the move. Getty Carlton are in a similar pickle trying to satisfy GWS for Lachie Whitfield. The Blues have picks at 23 and 24 and have offered one for Whitfield, which seems about bang on market price for a 32-year-old being swept up in the Giants’ list renewal. But the Giants want more; they want a first round draft pick. They were also filthy not to get a first round or end-of-first-round pick as compensation for losing Toby Greene. They got pick 26 instead and really, that’s decent for a 33-year-old, albeit one on about $1 million a year. Unhelpfully for the Giants, pick 26 only further framed the idea that Carlton’s pick 23 is market rate for Whitfield.

World.title: ‘I never want to see it again – but I also want to book for tomorrow night’
World.content:
COMEDY

Creepy Boys | SLUGS

Meat Market, until October 17 This is Fringe at its purest – and this show comes with more content warnings than a film by Larry Clark. SLUGS was nominated for Best Comedy Show at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe last year, and rightly so. It’s delirious mayhem from Canadian artists S.E. Grummett and Sam Kruger. SLUGS is at Meat Market until October 17. Bokeh Media How often do you see the genitalia (some accompanied with googly eyes) of both performers, and see them threatening an audience member at gun-point, then offering another a very raunchy sex service that can’t be printed in these pages? Free candy is also extended to the crowd, so it’s not all R18+ (but it is 99 per cent of the time). There’s deliberately poorly performed puppetry (shout-out to a terribly voiced Joni Mitchell), and the two cosplaying as a horse. Essentially, it’s Play School on crack with a decent dollop of existential doom and dread woven in. If you’re a fan of comedic chaos with the capability of warping your mind, then I couldn’t recommend it more highly. If you prefer your comedy more middle of the road and TV friendly, then stay far, far away. SLUGS is a paradox of a show. It’s advertised as being about “nothing, nothing, nothing, nothing, nothing, nothing, nothing, nothing” but is somehow about everything. It’s breathtakingly stupid but ingeniously clever. I never want to see it again, but I also want to book again for tomorrow night.

★★★★★

Reviewed by Tyson Wray



CABARET

Mara Knezevic | Kauboj

The Motley Bauhaus – Cabaret Stage, until October 11 In the hands of a master storyteller such as singer-songwriter Mara Knezevic, a simple tale about a Croatian man’s life and ambition, becomes an enthralling and touching adventure. Two years after first staging Kauboj at Sydney Fringe Festival, the classically trained artist has brought her show to Melbourne. Kauboj is at The Motley Bauhaus until October 11. Benjamin Draisma We hear about a chef-slash-cowboy named Jakov, who lives in the fictional Dalmatian town of Božje Selo. It’s a migrant story of hope and disillusionment. Through spoken word and song, Jakov’s world – brimming with purpose, love, fear and failure – is deftly and vividly created. Electric guitarist Daniel Potaczala strums along. Nostalgia and hints of humour are seamlessly woven in. Knezevic’s soulful, evocative vocals tackle a mix of traditional folk, covers and originals. Tender original tunes Till I See You Again and Cecilia’s Lullaby enchant, while we’re asked to sing along to an upbeat Kauboj Café and Grill. Professionalism reigns as stage lights flicker and falter and the sound plays up for a few moments. It’s a delightful hour that passes quickly.

★★★★★

Reviewed by Donna Demaio



THEATRE

In Bed With My Brother | Philosophy of the World

Meat Market, until October 3 Affectionately known as the best worst band ever, The Shaggs were a trio of young sisters from Exeter, New Hampshire, whose astonishingly inept songs were later reappraised as genius by the likes of Kurt Cobain and Frank Zappa. Philosophy of the World. Rona Bar & Ofek Avshalom That’s the official story, at least. Here, another trio reviews the legacy forced on three women who never wanted their spot in the limelight, but who were made to perform and record by a domineering father. In other hands, this material would lend itself to satire and condescension, but UK outfit In Bed With My Brother treats The Shaggs with respect while simultaneously trashing most conventions of respectable theatre. If you like your performances truly unpredictable, this is your ticket. Bristling with barely containable energy and randomly erupting into violence, music or comedy, the work suggests that to truly redeem artists with no aesthetic merit requires us to rewrite the rules of art itself.

★★★★★

Reviewed by John Bailey



DANCE and PHYSICAL THEATRE

Emma J. Hawkins and Leisa Prowd | Exhibit

La Mama Courthouse, until October 4 Two short-statured women walk on stage, inviting the audience to stare. But how do we see them? Is it with the weight of the caricatures and tropes that come with bodies their size on a stage, or as they see themselves? Can they shed the limitations placed upon them by expectation, or are they restricted by our acceptance of what they can and cannot be? Exhibit is a compelling performance by Leisa Prowd and Emma J. Hawkins exploring the roles of viewer, audience, watcher and watched. Exhibit is at La Mama Courthouse until October 4. Darren Gill Hawkins and Proud are frequently controlled by other people’s narrow expectations – audiences, directors, casting agents – but in Exhibit claim the freedom to perform to their potential as leading ladies with complexity, emotional depth and charisma. Deeply funny, the comedy is not thrust upon them by infantalisation but found in the performers subverting expectation. Dance brings vitality and exuberance to the performance, conveying their tumultuous experiences with movement ranging from graceful interludes to urgent, rapidly repeated passages. As our invited gaze is subverted and audience becomes subject, an unsettling mood evolves and the performance moves from comedy to disquiet. It is not so easy to remain passive when we cannot dictate how and when we too are perceived.

★★★★

Reviewed by Lefa Singleton Norton



THEATRE

Jessie Ngaio | Dirt Church

Meat Market, until October 3 Dirt Church. Teague Leigh Imbuing cult theatre with a whole new meaning, this part-church sermon, part-variety act has just about everything you could want from a Fringe show: nudity, poetry, music, dance, glo-paint, eco-feminism, body positive queer manifestos, beautiful costumes forged from rubbish, exquisitely shot BDSM films, and … live worms. Also, thankfully, comedy – especially from the church’s first disciple, the delightfully filthy and golem-like “Spider Crotch”. Think ConFest meets end-of-school-camp play, but the camp is for adults only, and the writing is good. The many rituals in this religion centre around themes such as decomposition, rebirth and revelling in the miraculous beauty of nature, sex and art. We go from weird to earnest to hilarious and back again. A song about the future we’re leaving our children dampens the tone where most of the hour is otherwise playfully creative, constructive and hopeful. Highlights include a crass and absurd opening banger about birthing, and a contemplative descent into the earth inviting us to “consider the worms” – set to a vocal track reminiscent of Yello’s Oh Yeah. Fringe theatre at its best.

★★★★

Reviewed by Hannah Francis



COMEDY

Ruff as Gutz | Dune but Worse

Trades Hall, until October 24 You’re in for a memorable show when your usher hands you a knife on admission. New Zealand clown Sean Burnett Dugdale-Martin’s solo rendition of Frank Herbert’s epic Dune saga pulls off something unexpectedly grand in scale, including an interstellar battle featuring his entire audience. You’ll emerge unscathed but won’t forget the moment. Dune but Worse is at Trades Hall until October 24. Tyler Clarke I’m an Arrakis tourist at best, and if you don’t know your Atreides from your Harkonnens, this will be an experience as baffling as the famously difficult source material. Dune is hardcore SF, but Dugdale-Martin is equally well-read and irreverent. Their audience is in on the joke: All it takes is a mask of a grumpy Zendaya to prove that love and derision can occupy the same space in fandom. Watching a giant, blindfolded worm chase a random audience member around the room only drives home the ridiculousness of our devotions.

★★★★

Reviewed by John Bailey



CABARET

Briefs Factory | Briefs: The Works

Spiegel Haus Melbourne: Spiegeltent until October 18 On a small (cramped?), round stage, a troupe of saucy performers titillates through striptease, while showcasing impressive feats of physical prowess and core strength. Lovers of drag (replete with lip-syncing and banging tunes), circus acts and full-frontal nudity, this is a show for you. Briefs: The Works is at Spiegel Haus Melbourne: Spiegeltent until October 18. Aitor Santomé Select numbers are perfection. Glistening aerialist Dylan Rodriguez captivates and hula-hoop legend Jess Love is also a dazzling flying trapeze artist. Fez Faanana, who founded Briefs Factory in Brisbane 18 years ago, hosts the affair as alter-ego Shivannah. Biting quips, filthy lines and general silliness mostly work but frustratingly, occasional stumbles in delivery hinder both the message and flow. “Dirty laundry” confessions, extracted from the audience, are ribald, comedy nuggets. Prepare for the possibility of flung garments, including still-warm underwear, to strike you in the face. Or for a naked performer to plonk onto your lap. There’s plenty of celebration of self, with Shivannah wrapping up the show by urging those gathered to “look after each other”.

★★★★

Reviewed by Donna Demaio



COMEDY

Elliot Wood | Mrs Lovett’s Famous Meat Pies Grand Reopening Extravaganza

Trades Hall, until October 4 Fancy a bit of cannibalism with your comedy? Elliot Wood has you covered – and it’s no wonder why this show scored a Best Newcomer nomination at the Comedy Festival and has returned for an encore season. Mrs Lovett’s Famous Meat Pies Grand Reopening Extravaganza. Iz Zettl Two centuries on from the partnership with the demon barber Sweeney Todd in the penny dreadful series, Wood (literally) carves out an, ahem, deliciously camp and deranged version of Mrs Lovett. But didn’t she die? No, in Wood’s world she was cryogenically frozen rather than thrown into a furnace. She’s departed Fleet Street and comes to Melbourne to indulge in her favourite pastime: making meat pies filled with the human remains of Todd’s murder victims. Accompanied by a disturbingly muted assistant named Kitchenette, Lovett engages the crowd to help prepare her signature dishes. While audience participation is rife, Wood ensures that only the willing are brought to the stage (you’re offered a raffle ticket on arrival, and if your number is called and you’d prefer to stay in your seat, the show moves on seamlessly). The gags come rapid-fire and the wordplay is first-rate. One would be wise to not wear white, however: there is a splash zone. While the hour will give your stomach a workout, it’s a shame that the main cuisine on offer in the foyer of Trades Hall this year is almost all pies. You don’t quite leave with a craving for one.

★★★★

Reviewed by Tyson Wray



EXPERIMENTAL

Chamber Made | The Enormous Radio

The Substation, until October 10 A tiny audience is surrounded by a multitude of vintage radios, each tuning into spectral frequencies whose origin is never clear. Bird calls, cicada chirps and predatory growls dissolve into electronic chaos, while the mind strains to figure out whether these are field recordings put through digital filters, or human-made sounds expertly crafted to pass as the real thing. The Enormous Radio is at The Substation until October 10. Sarah Walker Roslyn Oades and Bob Scott’s aural installation is an uncanny meditation on the interconnectedness of the animal, the human and the technological. Most unsettling is when language enters the mix. At one point, I’d decided that the buzzing of a fly was definitely authentic – and then it began talking. Captions appear on screens to translate the half-comprehensible phrases, which range from menacing to comic (whales, it turns out, aren’t the amiable types you’d expect). It’s audio wizardry reminding us that humans and the things we create are all just another part of nature. There’s no agenda here, no narrative to follow, and it ends without fanfare. Just like life.

★★★★

Reviewed by John Bailey



THEATRE

Cat Finch and Rose Bishop, performed by Annie Lumsden | Ghostware

Festival Hub: Meat Market – Craft Room, until October 10 “Loose in the cloud” calls to mind something free-flowing and ethereal, but in the play, Ghostware, its connotations are far more sinister: Gertie (Annie Lumsden) is plagued by a version of her dead sister Bea’s consciousness that is permanently embedded in the digital ether. Thanks to a watertight contract, Bea is here to stay and what’s worse: she pays for herself by continually unfurling sponsored content on her grief-afflicted family. Ghostware is at Meat Market until October 10. Matthew Dunn Back after its debut at last year’s Fringe, Cat Finch and Rose Bishop’s tight one-hander masterfully conjures a time in which manufacturing has all but been outsourced and robotic essential workers are commonplace. That the world-building is so effective is due in large part to Lumsden, who expertly conveys Gertie’s interiority while inhabiting the flights and foibles of various characters – from her eccentric parents to the decrepit lawyer and young hacker she seeks in desperate attempts to rid herself of AI Bea. Amid a sea of baby-blue packing boxes, we watch as Gertie grapples with the spectres of loss, unfulfilled potential and acute unbelonging. Ghostware is a deeply felt, darkly humorous and strangely affecting play about the things we do to escape ourselves and others.

★★★★

Reviewed by Sonia Nair



THEATRE

Mary-Agnes O’Loughlin | Glimpses of Heaven

The Motley Bauhaus, until October 4 In Glimpses of Heaven, Mary-Agnes O’Loughlin draws inspiration (or should that be devastation?) from the battles with alcoholism, drug dependence and mental health issues of her own mother, comedic veteran Fiona O’Loughlin. Fiona’s struggles in the past are well-documented. She’s never been one to shy away from detailing her addiction and a 2013 suicide attempt (she credits Mary-Agnes for saving her life). Glimpses of Heaven. Ruby Healey A partly fictionalised story, the reality of Mary-Agnes’ truths about her upbringing are laid bare. She performs as Hannah, attending the apartment of her mother – an illustrious musician with chaotic habits (of whom Fiona herself provides the voiceovers) – to pack her belongings. All of the sentimental keepsakes elicit memories from a childhood with a mother constantly in the spotlight and turning a blind eye to the lowlights caused due to her compulsions. The show asks: is unconditional love possible when you’re watching a family member slowly killing themselves? Is any amount of fame and fortune amassed worth it if you seem destined to join the 27 Club, even if you may be a few years past the admission date? Under the directorial eye of another Australian comedy mainstay, Damian Callinan, there’s also humour to be found throughout the morbid storytelling intertwined with well-choreographed dance and music. Glimpses of Heaven is a tender, vulnerable exploration of the struggles with the concepts of familial love, intergenerational trauma and the catharsis found in forgiveness. While it must come recommended with the caveat of a strong trigger warning for anyone with a history of domestic distress, it’s a very impressive solo debut deserving of a main-stage season in future runs to come.

★★★★

Reviewed by Tyson Wray



THEATRE

Ryan Hamilton and Georgie Wolfe | F--- Your Funding

Festival Hub: Trades Hall - Solidarity Hall, until October 4 What if, over the course of a night, you could agitate for the arts to occupy a more central place in the political agenda and redress inequitable funding models? Such concerns reach an apotheosis at the 2026 Melba Awards, a fictional annual celebration of seriously high stakes in the play F--- Your Funding. Hosted by a venerated opera singer and opened by an imagined version of the Victorian arts minister, the night descends into chaos when two cultural terrorists hold them at gunpoint with a list of demands. F--- Your Funding. Jaimi Houston F--- Your Funding is at its most uproarious when it’s laying bare the arts sector’s greatest hypocrisies. A slide containing a list of morally vacuous donors? Tick. A politician lauding the cultural cachet of Melbourne while refusing to bolster the arts sector in any real, tangible way? Tick. As the play lurches wildly from farcical hijinks to sincere proselytising about the role of art in a whiplash-inducing manner, it simultaneously lampoons itself and us while paying homage to its intended audience. Leftists too busy preaching to the converted and fighting among one another to organise. Artists making work centred on their latest diagnoses. Clowns.

★★★★

Reviewed by Sonia Nair



DANCE

Caroline Meaden | Immacolata

Chunky Move Studios, until October 3 Immacolata. Caroline Meaden, Jeff Busby and William McBride This is a beautifully strange and melancholy solo dance vigil: a restless choreographic grisaille, delicate and disquieting. Caroline Meaden struts and frets, with crisp bird-like movements, then hesitates. Always there is hesitation in this work. Then an arm – or a hand or a leg – begins to wobble. It’s like a part of the body just turns to water. The dimly lit stage is furnished with only a clothes rack, some biscuit crumbs and a stool, but Meaden keeps mostly to its edges. She is pulled backwards or drawn into the corners, as if kept out of the empty centre by some unseen force. Immacolata tantalises with the mystery of its significance. What does it all mean? Is there a story behind its troubling silences? In fact, Meaden provides an accompanying essay, intended to be read after the performance, which does explain much of what we see – and gives the work’s air of sadness a touching specificity.

★★★★

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann



COMEDY

Holly Bohmer, Mario Hannah and Taylor Griffiths | Nosebleeds

The Improv Conspiracy, until October 18 Nosebleeds is at The Improv Conspiracy until October 18. Simon McCulloch and Mario Hannah The Nosebleeds, veterans of improv comedy, know it doesn’t take much to evoke the horror genre, even less to make fun of it. The trio, together for a decade, are back at Melbourne Fringe to take a proverbial (and literal) stab at the evergreen genre with an hour of uneven but charming sketches. Exorcisms become blind dates, séances turn into couples therapy, and haunted mansions turn nipples into weapons. Rather than looking to recent films, the self-described “comedian cinephiles” pull from an older vintage of horror. It’s Mel Brooks via Henry James. Holly Bohmer is the perfect wide-eyed governess with no fear of her homicidal employer, Mario Hannah is the ever-likeable himbo contacting the dead to learn more about the Titanic, and Taylor Griffiths, who delivers the night’s best punchlines, is uproarious as every manservant with a handlebar moustache or ghost child. But by the fourth Victorian-era conceit or ill-formed attempt at audience engagement, the show becomes static and its parodies rote. It’s a fun night out, but it’s not quite a scream.

★★★

Reviewed by Guy Webster



THEATRE

Gregory Nussen | QFWFQ

Trades Hall, until October 4 In this brave dissection of self, politics and art, Californian performer Gregory Nussen takes their cue (and title) from Italo Calvino’s metafictional work, If on a winter’s night a traveller. Centre stage is a writer’s desk piled with Calvino’s extended works, and we continue through a series of false starts as Nussen keeps attempting the play they’re “meant” to perform. QFWFQ. Sonya Katerina It’s a neat framing device for their autobiographical narrative, in which the preordained script of a rigid Jewish upbringing creates visceral and lasting internal conflict for a protagonist whose sexuality and gender identity don’t stick to the script. The most powerful moments draw an elegant through line between the cognitive dissonance of war and propaganda (both historical and current), and the terrifying and complex pursuit of self-actualisation and truth in a world where, too often, two plus two continues to equal five. There is plenty to like here, but the overall result is too many references and layers – some of them heavy-handed to begin with, then unnecessarily explained – which distract from its beating heart.

★★★

Reviewed by Hannah Francis



VISUAL ARTS and FILM

Youbi Lee | OBANG 오방

ArtPlay, until October 25 If you’re accustomed to picking up after a toddler, this interactive visual arts experience will make you feel right at home. OBANG 오방 combines the Korean term for five, O, with the word, BANG, referring to direction or room. The minimalist space is set up as a halmoni’s (grandmother’s) house, with individual stations representing the kitchen, bedroom, toilet and living room, alongside a partitioned area for the bathroom. OBANG 오방 is at ArtPlay until October 25. Darren Gill Familiar household elements ignite sensory play: a mini kitchenette, a bed, a clothing line and a blow-up bath. Tactile elements feed curiosity: plastic puddle decals, a dumpling steamer, silk manchester, a straw hanging and a wooden puzzle. The experience is low stimulation, with gentle traditional music and a wall projection adding an audiovisual dimension. The space is modest, which creates a safe and contained environment, but limits the number of families that can engage simultaneously, and the amount of time you can occupy an active toddler. As you leave, respect halmoni’s home by leaving the space as you found it, which is a good lesson for the young.

★★★

Reviewed by Vyshnavee Wijekumar



COMEDY

Blak Out: An Indigenous Comedy Showcase

Trades Hall, until October 4 Blak Out is an ideal comedy show to see early at Fringe. It offers a range of performers delivering a taste of what they offer, leaving the audience hungry to seek them out elsewhere at the festival. The featured comedians hail from all over the country, and with a mix of four performers each night there is a satisfying variety of styles. Blak Out: An Indigenous Comedy Showcase is at Trades Hall until October 4. When I attended, Wiradjuri/Kamilaroi performer Jacob Keed opened with a laconic storytelling style to ease the audience in, followed by Gamilaroi comic Ben Moodie. His material skewed darker with quick jabs that met their mark. Ngarrindjeri actor/producer/comedian Kimmie Lovegrove’s personal material offered a tempting preview of the material in her solo show, which will open later in Fringe. Kamilaroi performer Cameron Ribbons, the MC for the evening and the closing act, stole the show on this night by hitting a sweet spot of storytelling and punchy jokes. His re-enactment of crocodile spotting was the perfect crescendo.

★★★

Reviewed by Lefa Singleton Norton



DANCE

Weichen Cui | In Green, In White

Dancehouse, until October 3 The Chinese folk legend of Lady White Snake is forever shedding one skin for another. The most recent retellings shift the focus from White Snake’s mortal lover to her demonic servant, Green Snake, recasting the bond between mistress and maid in terms of enduring female friendship and homoerotic desire. In Green, In White is at Dancehouse until October 3. Georgia Moloney Choreographer Weichen Cui explores this queer transformation in a new duet with Jiawen Feng. At first, the performers are silhouetted behind separate screens, isolated, wearing costumes informed by tradition. As if reflecting the evolution of the story, the two figures are gradually brought together – culminating in a final serpentine tangle of limbs. There are interesting moments, such as the use of waacking to playfully disrupt a fan dance. But overall, the episodic structure feels slow and over-formal, arresting the flows of desire it seeks to release. It might also be a little long – compressed to half an hour, this duet could bring its strongest moments into more volatile contact.

★★★

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann



DANCE

Joyce Liu | INTERLINK_SYSTEM

Dancehouse, until October 3 Joyce Liu stands before us in the gloom, a tangle of red wires trailing from one arm, fingers twitching. Finally, we get it: she is actually controlling the soundscape, summoning jackhammer bursts and ominous bass drones from a body that barely seems to move. As the noise intensifies, four creatures wake inside a plastic greenhouse behind her. They claw at its walls, tearing them open. Free at last, the juddering young humanoids – all in their underwear – begin feverishly coupling in a sort of grotesque orgy-of-Doctor-Moreau. INTERLINK_SYSTEM is at Dancehouse, until October 3. Carlin Stephenson Liu – also director and choreographer – builds a convincingly creepy laboratory atmosphere, with smoke and wildly sweeping lights lending urgency to the action. There’s also some irony, even comedy, in the monstrous debauch – though it does go on and on. I do think, however, we could have stayed with that opening image of the human wired for sound a little longer, perhaps giving the idea of an interlinked system more room to unfold – before rushing into the bioengineered bacchanal.

★★★

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

CORRECTION An earlier version of the review of Dirt Church misstated the videographer as Bridie Noonan.

World.title: Rogue pilots may be the most dangerous threat to passengers. They’re ‘just about impossible’ to stop
World.content:
Analysis BusinessCompaniesAviation Rogue pilots may be the most dangerous threat to passengers. They’re ‘just about impossible’ to stop Chris Zappone October 6, 2026 — 1:22pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The near-tragic incident with the Tel Aviv-bound flydubai jet has the industry scrambling to manage what could be best described as the ultimate nightmare for passengers and airlines – what do you do if the pilot goes rogue? The flydubai flight FZ1073 incident on September 30 is being described as an attempted terror attack by co-pilot Hamam al-Hammami. The alleged attack was thwarted because the other person in the cockpit - Captain Smit Machchhar - was able to unlock the door, allowing passengers to intervene. Omani pilot Hamam al-Hammami is accused of attacking his colleage on a flydubai flight to Israel. 9News It was the narrowest of escapes, owed to the actions of those onboard, but it exposes a number of weaknesses that the aviation sector will have to address. The first is the insider threat posed by a rogue pilot, which in the flydubai flight’s case was Al-Hammami’s attempt to plunge himself and all on board the jet into a fatal dive. It’s not without precedent in aviation history.





Dr Warren Harrex, a specialist in aerospace medicine said that while much progress had been made in reducing human factor errors in flight, it was “just about impossible to, with testing, identify people who might be at risk of acting adversely in the cockpit”. Loading “The best way really is to get to know people and to note if there’s any change in their behaviour or demeanour. Otherwise, there’s no real test you can do to prevent a pilot going rogue.” “These events are very rare, but they’re high-profile when they do occur, of course,” said Harrex. How rare? About 130,000 flights per day take off and land without incident, according to the International Air Transport Association.



Related Article Aviation Aviation industry needs to learn from Germanwings crash: French investigators “Yet if somebody’s really determined to behave badly, like we see with terrorist attacks, it’s very difficult to predict.” The globalised industry with large workforces has processes in place to continually assess capabilities of pilots. Central Queensland University associate professor Geoffrey Dell said if a pilot started to get radicalised, or had other mental health issues, one would expect the system would identify that in advance. “There is a fairly rigorous reporting.” Airlines continually check and recertify pilots on simulators, giving them opportunities to evaluate employees on the job. Pilots must also regularly fly with check and training captains who ensure “operational safety-critical personnel are proficient” in the skills required to keep the plane flying safely. These are in-person interactions in which a pilot’s performance is judged. Yet al-Hammami was hired by flydubai after losing his job at Oman Air.



There have been cases of flight-deck assaults that could lead to suicide, such as a 1994 FedEx flight departing Memphis, Tennessee, in which a disaffected employee sought to subdue pilots on a cargo plane and then crash it. Crisis24 global risk management aviation lead Dr Alejandra Gentil said the FedEx case highlighted “the importance of background checks on crew members, since the attacker was being fired by FedEx because he had presented false information upon employment related to his flight hours”. A significant section of the rudder was missing from flydubai flight FZ1073. Instagram The insider threat risk had been part of the international aviation security framework for many years, she said. The International Civil Aviation Organisation had developed tools to manage it but “it falls upon the appropriate authorities of the state to conduct a thorough background check”, Gentil said.



She said background checks in the UAE were a prerequisite for being given a residence permit. While details are still being uncovered, media outlets have reported al-Hammami had earlier lost a job with Oman Air because of an apparent interest in extremism. Gentil said yearly mental health checks are mandated by the UAE regulator as prescribed in the Civil Aviation Regulations, which gives them the authority and the responsibility for conducting them. The safety of aviation is built on redundancies, including in oversight of the plane. A former commercial pilot said the incident should dissuade the industry from moving towards allowing a single pilot to fly at cruising altitude. “There was a strong move towards it by the airlines a few years ago for economic reasons,” and “the manufacturers were designing for it.” Had planes moved to a single pilot cruise model, “then [al-Hammami] wouldn’t have had to stab the other pilot of the aircraft”. Incidents such as this reinforce why the European Union Aviation Safety Agency banned single-pilot operations, he said.



Related Article Opinion

Aviation I felt safer piloting planes after 9/11. But now terror can lock itself inside the cockpit David Evans Former Qantas captain The flydubai flight FZ1073 will also bring into focus the potential danger posed by a locked cockpit door. The measure was introduced after the September 11 attacks as a way to stop hijackers from taking control of a plane. Usually, the pilot holds the key and while other crew members have emergency access, in case there is a health emergency, who gets inside the cockpit is still largely in the hands of the pilot. The flydubai incident may need the aviation sector to rethink the need for further emergency countermeasures. Brisbane-based CW Aviation Security Consulting director Shannon Wandmaker said both the locks on doors, as well as the vetting of pilots before hiring would probably be reviewed as a result of the flydubai incident. A relaxation in the hardened/locked cockpit door requirements would seem unlikely, he said. “It’s always easier to implement a security measure than it is to remove one.”



“It may be the case that we see some governments move unilaterally to implement additional, or more stringent measures related to background checks, and this may happen quite quickly,” Wandmaker said. Airlines themselves try to be proactive on pilot mental health. Virgin Australia, for example, has a wellbeing strategy which is regularly reviewed by senior management. Qantas was approached for comment. The Department of Home Affairs, which has authority over access to flight deck in Australia, said: “there are strict requirements regarding cockpit security, including when the cockpit door must remain locked, and the persons authorised to be in the cockpit during flight”. The department regularly reviews aviation security settings. If you are troubled by this report or experiencing a personal crisis, you can call Lifeline on 131 114 or Beyond Blue on 1300 224 636. World.title: Teacher at prestige girls’ school charged with sex assault of student
World.content:
A teacher at Melbourne’s prestigious Methodist Ladies’ College has been charged with the sexual assault of a student.

In an email to parents, the school said police had notified it that Kam Kenny-Jones, a teacher at the school until just weeks ago, had been charged at the weekend with one count of sexual assault of a child under 17.

Methodist Ladies’ College in Kew. Paul Jeffers

MLC principal Julia O’Shea said the news was confronting and unsettling but she felt it important to update the school community in a clear and timely manner.

“In September, concerns about Mr Kenny-Jones were brought to the college’s attention, and we immediately stood him down from his duties that day while we investigated and reported the matter to the relevant authorities, including Victoria Police,” she wrote in the email sent on Monday.

Queensland Rail chief executive Kat Stapleton outside the Fair Work Commission offices on Eagle Street in May after a day’s negotiation with unions. World.title: Flagship puts bigger fence around Canadian copper giant
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Flagship puts bigger fence around Canadian copper giant Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward October 6, 2026 — 1:19pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Flagship Minerals looks to have picked its moment perfectly in Canada’s British Columbia, securing three new mineral claims that more than double its Whipsaw copper tenure, just as the province rolls out the red carpet for miners and copper prices hover near record highs. The company initially swooped on the massive copper play in June for a mere A$6.5 million. However, its latest ground grab has added a further 37.5 square kilometres to the project, swelling Flagship’s position by a hefty 132 per cent to about 66 square kilometres. The company says the new ground captures prospective strike extensions to its existing exploration target, which sits within a colossal porphyry mineral system stretching roughly 3.7km long and 1.2km wide. Flagship Minerals’ Whipsaw copper project sits just 17km west of Hudbay Minerals’ operating and expanding Copper Mountain mine in British Columbia. Whipsaw is already backed by 58 historical drill holes with standout hits, including 283.47 metres at 0.28 per cent copper equivalent from 70.1m, 193.7m at 0.30 per cent copper equivalent from 4.42m and 124.93m at 0.33 per cent copper equivalent from 26.3m. Notably, the project also features a sizeable JORC-compliant exploration target of between 510 million and 1.02 billion tonnes, grading between 0.2 and 0.4 per cent copper equivalent, hinting at the sort of scale that’s likely to get pulses quickening. The expansion comes as British Columbia puts its pro-mining “Look West Strategy” into overdrive, with the government actively looking to fast-track major project approvals. Recent examples include Skeena Resources’ Eskay Creek mine, which saw its application-to-decision timeline cut by 40 per cent alongside Centerra Gold’s Mount Milligan extension, which was approved 60 per cent faster than previous processes.



‘Our objective is straightforward: Advance Whipsaw in a capital-efficient manner for a spin-out to unlock value for Flagship shareholders.’ Flagship Minerals managing director Paul Lock Flagship says its own claims were granted in just over three months, a timeline that appears to back up the provincial government’s promise to revive its mining sector. That push already seems to be bearing fruit almost on Whipsaw’s doorstep, with Hudbay Minerals’ New Ingerbelle expansion at its Copper Mountain operation, just 17 kilometres away, securing key permits and breaking ground in recent months. New Ingerbelle is expected to deliver 750,000 tonnes of copper, 900,000 ounces of gold and 5.5 million ounces of silver over its mine life. The geological neighbourhood only adds to the intrigue in what can be fairly described as elephant country for copper. The ground separating Whipsaw from Copper Mountain is held by Collective Metals, whose exploration has already identified porphyry-style targets. Just 134 kilometres north, Teck’s giant Highland Valley operation underscores the region’s pedigree, containing a resource of over 2.2 billion tonnes grading 0.26 per cent copper. Flagship Minerals managing director Paul Lock said: “The additional tenure strengthens our position at Whipsaw and captures prospective extensions to what is already a very large mineralised system, with a very large drill supported JORC compliant Exploration Target. The approval process and timeline bodes well for the BC Government’s push for a mining revival, aiming to transform the province into a leading mining jurisdiction.” The market is also putting serious money behind emerging British Columbia copper stories. Amarc Resources, with a market value of C$228 million (A$229M), has Freeport-McMoRan funding its exploration. At the same time, the more advanced Northisle Copper and Gold, with a defined 1.2-billion-tonne resource, carries a market capitalisation of C$1.45 billion (A$1.46B).



Those numbers provide a good example of how the market can progressively revalue big copper systems as they are de-risked, which is pertinent given Flagship’s plans to spin Whipsaw out into a dedicated listed vehicle. Since Whipsaw currently has little to no value assigned to it in the company’s market cap, a spin-out could put the asset under a market spotlight of its own, allowing Flagship to maintain its focus on advancing its flagship 2.1-million-ounce Isidora gold project in Chile. With the new claims now locked in, the company plans to kick off low-cost LiDAR and drone magnetic surveys to help generate fresh drill targets. As it prepares to launch its new geophysical surveys over a much larger footprint, in a jurisdiction that is actively encouraging development, Flagship appears to be piecing together all the right ingredients for its Canadian copper aspirations. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

World.title: ‘Long story short, I’ve got breast cancer’: Comedian Judith Lucy reveals diagnosis
World.content:
Breaking CultureCelebrityBreast cancer ‘Long story short, I’ve got breast cancer’: Comedian Judith Lucy reveals diagnosis Kayla Olaya October 6, 2026 — 1:19pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Comedian Judith Lucy has revealed she has been diagnosed with breast cancer … in a way only she could. In a video uploaded to social media, Lucy matter-of-factly delivers the health update, sandwiched between quick quips about her newly released wellness book and recent faecal transplants. Judith Lucy reveals she has been diagnosed with breast cancer. Simon Schluter “Not so fun update from me,” Lucy says at the start of the Instagram video. “I got an email from BreastScreen Australia, telling me that my mammogram result was a bit weird. May I take this opportunity to say, ladies, for the love of God, keep up with your mammograms. “Long story short, I’ve got breast cancer.”



Lucy said three weeks ago she was going to “pick up yet two more syringes of yet another stranger’s turds” for her fecal transplants when she received the email. “I went on last Friday for a lumpectomy, and a doctor – I’m not making this up - called Doctor Fun found more cancer,” Lucy said. The cancer is “relatively non-aggressive”, Lucy shared, adding she is removing both her breasts by the end of this week via mastectomy – despite only one breast being cancerous. “Doctor Fun is amazing. I am in her debt, but we have gone from a lumpectomy to a mastectomy, which I am having Friday week,” she said.



“I said, while you’re there, let’s get rid of the other one because you know something. I have had 40 years of, if I do say so myself, large and spectacular breasts. You had your chance, fellas. “I think I’m quite fine with going bra-free for my last chapter, and my last chapter is going to be very long and healthy.” More to come

World.title: The real reason behind St Kilda’s steep asking price for Marshall
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLTrading and drafting The real reason behind St Kilda’s steep asking price for Marshall Michael Gleeson October 6, 2026 — 1:19pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

While he was lying on the couch watching Netflix or cleaning out his sock drawer, or indeed doing anything at all rather than going to his club’s best and fairest night, Rowan Marshall quietly finished 10th at the St Kilda awards function he was not at. Marshall avoided needing to pose for red carpet pics or speak disingenuously of his love and affection for a club he has felt neither from in the past year. (We’re not talking about his teammates, players always love their teammates.) Loading Marshall didn’t want to be at Moorabbin this year after the club brought Tom De Koning in over the top of him last October. We were told Marshall was fully on board with having a new stable partner. We now know he wasn’t. But then, as now, Marshall had a contract so he sucked it up and played the season. Played it well, too, to come tenth in the B&F. Interestingly, TDK was not in the top 10. This trade period Marshall is less inclined to suck it up. Monday night was a first statement.



Twelve months ago, St Kilda rejected Geelong’s overtures for Marshall and never stated what would persuade them to change their minds. This year they have at least put a price on a trade. They want Geelong’s first round pick and “a player”. Say what? OK, it’s an opening gambit, but sheesh, a first rounder and a player? It would be remarkable were that to be the eventual trade price. There is a logic to the ambit bid though, and it’s a logic that that ripples through deals involving Geelong, Carlton, Brisbane and GWS. St Kilda Saints ruckman Rowan Marshall. AFL Photos via Getty Images St Kilda needs to lose a Marshall to gain a Marshall. Rowan needs to leave so Sam can come in. The Saints want midfielder Sam Marshall, the Brisbane academy product who was taken at pick 25 in the 2024 draft. The Lions want a similar pick for him now and unfortunately the Saints don’t have one: their first pick is at eight (too much even for a club that gave up pick seven for Sam Flanders 12 months ago) and their next is 49.



Lions list boss Dom Ambrogio said on Monday: “[St Kilda] have got an awareness of what we are looking for, albeit it’s not in their hands at the moment in that they don’t hold the pick in the range we think is appropriate.” Whether “what we are looking for” and “what is appropriate” are the same thing in any trade is doubtful and normally depends on what colours you wear. In this case, what the Lions are looking for and thus what they hope is appropriate for Marshall is a pick in the 20s. So the Saints are trying to find a pick in that range. Losing one Marshall might buy them the draft capital to pass on for the other Marshall. Brisbane midfielder Sam Marshall. Getty The Cats are reluctant to part with their first pick (14) for a 30-year-old ruck, albeit a contracted one. Their next pick, the one they have offered for Rowan Marshall, is currently 34.



The problem is that the Cats’ pick 34 won’t satisfy Brisbane for Sam Marshall. Why not? It’s not far off the pick they want. Thirty-four seems fairly close for a player who played one game this year, is out of contract and has Essendon also keen on him – and thus able to take him for nothing in the pre-season if it came to it. But Brisbane want a pick in the 20s because they have a good academy player available (yes, another one. One out, one in). They need a pick to cover that bid. Academy player Caylen Murray is likely to be bid on somewhere in the mid-to-late-first round. Under new rules the two grand finalists have a 20 per cent loading on the points required to match a bid that comes in the first 18 in the draft for an academy player. And you can only use two picks to match any bid. Brisbane academy prospect Caylen Murray. via Getty Images So the Lions really need another pick in the 20s to be able to cover a bid on Murray. Pick 34 won’t cut it. So unless St Kilda can find another way of bringing in a pick in the 20s – another player going out? - the Saints will need more from Geelong for Rowan Marshall, to be able to pass it on to Brisbane. But Geelong don’t have one. Or do they?



Gryan Miers did a medical at West Coast on Friday before he flew overseas. It was a precaution in case the trade world moved while he was away. Given he partially tore his ACL this year and has not had surgery to repair it, the normal buyer beware caveat carries more heft. He’d rather stay at Geelong but is clearly open enough to West Coast’s interest to be doing a medical there. If the medical is clear enough and the Eagles want him, and Geelong is prepared to trade him (and that’s lot of ifs) what is Miers worth? A pick in the sweet spot with West Coast’s second round pick at 21? Bear in mind that when bids come for Dougie Cochrane and Cody Walker early in the draft, West Coast as one of the bottom five clubs will be compensated with an extra pick at the end of the first round. So they will have picks at what is now 21 and 24. Miers, anyone? Lachie Whitfield of the Giants could be on the move. Getty Carlton are in a similar pickle trying to satisfy GWS for Lachie Whitfield. The Blues have picks at 23 and 24 and have offered one for Whitfield, which seems about bang on market price for a 32-year-old being swept up in the Giants’ list renewal. But the Giants want more; they want a first round draft pick. They were also filthy not to get a first round or end-of-first-round pick as compensation for losing Toby Greene. They got pick 26 instead and really, that’s decent for a 33-year-old, albeit one on about $1 million a year. Unhelpfully for the Giants, pick 26 only further framed the idea that Carlton’s pick 23 is market rate for Whitfield.

World.title: ‘I never want to see it again – but I also want to book for tomorrow night’
World.content:
COMEDY

Creepy Boys | SLUGS

Meat Market, until October 17 This is Fringe at its purest – and this show comes with more content warnings than a film by Larry Clark. SLUGS was nominated for Best Comedy Show at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe last year, and rightly so. It’s delirious mayhem from Canadian artists S.E. Grummett and Sam Kruger. SLUGS is at Meat Market until October 17. Bokeh Media How often do you see the genitalia (some accompanied with googly eyes) of both performers, and see them threatening an audience member at gun-point, then offering another a very raunchy sex service that can’t be printed in these pages? Free candy is also extended to the crowd, so it’s not all R18+ (but it is 99 per cent of the time). There’s deliberately poorly performed puppetry (shout-out to a terribly voiced Joni Mitchell), and the two cosplaying as a horse. Essentially, it’s Play School on crack with a decent dollop of existential doom and dread woven in. If you’re a fan of comedic chaos with the capability of warping your mind, then I couldn’t recommend it more highly. If you prefer your comedy more middle of the road and TV friendly, then stay far, far away. SLUGS is a paradox of a show. It’s advertised as being about “nothing, nothing, nothing, nothing, nothing, nothing, nothing, nothing” but is somehow about everything. It’s breathtakingly stupid but ingeniously clever. I never want to see it again, but I also want to book again for tomorrow night.

★★★★★

Reviewed by Tyson Wray



CABARET

Mara Knezevic | Kauboj

The Motley Bauhaus – Cabaret Stage, until October 11 In the hands of a master storyteller such as singer-songwriter Mara Knezevic, a simple tale about a Croatian man’s life and ambition, becomes an enthralling and touching adventure. Two years after first staging Kauboj at Sydney Fringe Festival, the classically trained artist has brought her show to Melbourne. Kauboj is at The Motley Bauhaus until October 11. Benjamin Draisma We hear about a chef-slash-cowboy named Jakov, who lives in the fictional Dalmatian town of Božje Selo. It’s a migrant story of hope and disillusionment. Through spoken word and song, Jakov’s world – brimming with purpose, love, fear and failure – is deftly and vividly created. Electric guitarist Daniel Potaczala strums along. Nostalgia and hints of humour are seamlessly woven in. Knezevic’s soulful, evocative vocals tackle a mix of traditional folk, covers and originals. Tender original tunes Till I See You Again and Cecilia’s Lullaby enchant, while we’re asked to sing along to an upbeat Kauboj Café and Grill. Professionalism reigns as stage lights flicker and falter and the sound plays up for a few moments. It’s a delightful hour that passes quickly.

★★★★★

Reviewed by Donna Demaio



THEATRE

In Bed With My Brother | Philosophy of the World

Meat Market, until October 3 Affectionately known as the best worst band ever, The Shaggs were a trio of young sisters from Exeter, New Hampshire, whose astonishingly inept songs were later reappraised as genius by the likes of Kurt Cobain and Frank Zappa. Philosophy of the World. Rona Bar & Ofek Avshalom That’s the official story, at least. Here, another trio reviews the legacy forced on three women who never wanted their spot in the limelight, but who were made to perform and record by a domineering father. In other hands, this material would lend itself to satire and condescension, but UK outfit In Bed With My Brother treats The Shaggs with respect while simultaneously trashing most conventions of respectable theatre. If you like your performances truly unpredictable, this is your ticket. Bristling with barely containable energy and randomly erupting into violence, music or comedy, the work suggests that to truly redeem artists with no aesthetic merit requires us to rewrite the rules of art itself.

★★★★★

Reviewed by John Bailey



DANCE and PHYSICAL THEATRE

Emma J. Hawkins and Leisa Prowd | Exhibit

La Mama Courthouse, until October 4 Two short-statured women walk on stage, inviting the audience to stare. But how do we see them? Is it with the weight of the caricatures and tropes that come with bodies their size on a stage, or as they see themselves? Can they shed the limitations placed upon them by expectation, or are they restricted by our acceptance of what they can and cannot be? Exhibit is a compelling performance by Leisa Prowd and Emma J. Hawkins exploring the roles of viewer, audience, watcher and watched. Exhibit is at La Mama Courthouse until October 4. Darren Gill Hawkins and Proud are frequently controlled by other people’s narrow expectations – audiences, directors, casting agents – but in Exhibit claim the freedom to perform to their potential as leading ladies with complexity, emotional depth and charisma. Deeply funny, the comedy is not thrust upon them by infantalisation but found in the performers subverting expectation. Dance brings vitality and exuberance to the performance, conveying their tumultuous experiences with movement ranging from graceful interludes to urgent, rapidly repeated passages. As our invited gaze is subverted and audience becomes subject, an unsettling mood evolves and the performance moves from comedy to disquiet. It is not so easy to remain passive when we cannot dictate how and when we too are perceived.

★★★★

Reviewed by Lefa Singleton Norton



THEATRE

Jessie Ngaio | Dirt Church

Meat Market, until October 3 Dirt Church. Teague Leigh Imbuing cult theatre with a whole new meaning, this part-church sermon, part-variety act has just about everything you could want from a Fringe show: nudity, poetry, music, dance, glo-paint, eco-feminism, body positive queer manifestos, beautiful costumes forged from rubbish, exquisitely shot BDSM films, and … live worms. Also, thankfully, comedy – especially from the church’s first disciple, the delightfully filthy and golem-like “Spider Crotch”. Think ConFest meets end-of-school-camp play, but the camp is for adults only, and the writing is good. The many rituals in this religion centre around themes such as decomposition, rebirth and revelling in the miraculous beauty of nature, sex and art. We go from weird to earnest to hilarious and back again. A song about the future we’re leaving our children dampens the tone where most of the hour is otherwise playfully creative, constructive and hopeful. Highlights include a crass and absurd opening banger about birthing, and a contemplative descent into the earth inviting us to “consider the worms” – set to a vocal track reminiscent of Yello’s Oh Yeah. Fringe theatre at its best.

★★★★

Reviewed by Hannah Francis



COMEDY

Ruff as Gutz | Dune but Worse

Trades Hall, until October 24 You’re in for a memorable show when your usher hands you a knife on admission. New Zealand clown Sean Burnett Dugdale-Martin’s solo rendition of Frank Herbert’s epic Dune saga pulls off something unexpectedly grand in scale, including an interstellar battle featuring his entire audience. You’ll emerge unscathed but won’t forget the moment. Dune but Worse is at Trades Hall until October 24. Tyler Clarke I’m an Arrakis tourist at best, and if you don’t know your Atreides from your Harkonnens, this will be an experience as baffling as the famously difficult source material. Dune is hardcore SF, but Dugdale-Martin is equally well-read and irreverent. Their audience is in on the joke: All it takes is a mask of a grumpy Zendaya to prove that love and derision can occupy the same space in fandom. Watching a giant, blindfolded worm chase a random audience member around the room only drives home the ridiculousness of our devotions.

★★★★

Reviewed by John Bailey



CABARET

Briefs Factory | Briefs: The Works

Spiegel Haus Melbourne: Spiegeltent until October 18 On a small (cramped?), round stage, a troupe of saucy performers titillates through striptease, while showcasing impressive feats of physical prowess and core strength. Lovers of drag (replete with lip-syncing and banging tunes), circus acts and full-frontal nudity, this is a show for you. Briefs: The Works is at Spiegel Haus Melbourne: Spiegeltent until October 18. Aitor Santomé Select numbers are perfection. Glistening aerialist Dylan Rodriguez captivates and hula-hoop legend Jess Love is also a dazzling flying trapeze artist. Fez Faanana, who founded Briefs Factory in Brisbane 18 years ago, hosts the affair as alter-ego Shivannah. Biting quips, filthy lines and general silliness mostly work but frustratingly, occasional stumbles in delivery hinder both the message and flow. “Dirty laundry” confessions, extracted from the audience, are ribald, comedy nuggets. Prepare for the possibility of flung garments, including still-warm underwear, to strike you in the face. Or for a naked performer to plonk onto your lap. There’s plenty of celebration of self, with Shivannah wrapping up the show by urging those gathered to “look after each other”.

★★★★

Reviewed by Donna Demaio



COMEDY

Elliot Wood | Mrs Lovett’s Famous Meat Pies Grand Reopening Extravaganza

Trades Hall, until October 4 Fancy a bit of cannibalism with your comedy? Elliot Wood has you covered – and it’s no wonder why this show scored a Best Newcomer nomination at the Comedy Festival and has returned for an encore season. Mrs Lovett’s Famous Meat Pies Grand Reopening Extravaganza. Iz Zettl Two centuries on from the partnership with the demon barber Sweeney Todd in the penny dreadful series, Wood (literally) carves out an, ahem, deliciously camp and deranged version of Mrs Lovett. But didn’t she die? No, in Wood’s world she was cryogenically frozen rather than thrown into a furnace. She’s departed Fleet Street and comes to Melbourne to indulge in her favourite pastime: making meat pies filled with the human remains of Todd’s murder victims. Accompanied by a disturbingly muted assistant named Kitchenette, Lovett engages the crowd to help prepare her signature dishes. While audience participation is rife, Wood ensures that only the willing are brought to the stage (you’re offered a raffle ticket on arrival, and if your number is called and you’d prefer to stay in your seat, the show moves on seamlessly). The gags come rapid-fire and the wordplay is first-rate. One would be wise to not wear white, however: there is a splash zone. While the hour will give your stomach a workout, it’s a shame that the main cuisine on offer in the foyer of Trades Hall this year is almost all pies. You don’t quite leave with a craving for one.

★★★★

Reviewed by Tyson Wray



EXPERIMENTAL

Chamber Made | The Enormous Radio

The Substation, until October 10 A tiny audience is surrounded by a multitude of vintage radios, each tuning into spectral frequencies whose origin is never clear. Bird calls, cicada chirps and predatory growls dissolve into electronic chaos, while the mind strains to figure out whether these are field recordings put through digital filters, or human-made sounds expertly crafted to pass as the real thing. The Enormous Radio is at The Substation until October 10. Sarah Walker Roslyn Oades and Bob Scott’s aural installation is an uncanny meditation on the interconnectedness of the animal, the human and the technological. Most unsettling is when language enters the mix. At one point, I’d decided that the buzzing of a fly was definitely authentic – and then it began talking. Captions appear on screens to translate the half-comprehensible phrases, which range from menacing to comic (whales, it turns out, aren’t the amiable types you’d expect). It’s audio wizardry reminding us that humans and the things we create are all just another part of nature. There’s no agenda here, no narrative to follow, and it ends without fanfare. Just like life.

★★★★

Reviewed by John Bailey



THEATRE

Cat Finch and Rose Bishop, performed by Annie Lumsden | Ghostware

Festival Hub: Meat Market – Craft Room, until October 10 “Loose in the cloud” calls to mind something free-flowing and ethereal, but in the play, Ghostware, its connotations are far more sinister: Gertie (Annie Lumsden) is plagued by a version of her dead sister Bea’s consciousness that is permanently embedded in the digital ether. Thanks to a watertight contract, Bea is here to stay and what’s worse: she pays for herself by continually unfurling sponsored content on her grief-afflicted family. Ghostware is at Meat Market until October 10. Matthew Dunn Back after its debut at last year’s Fringe, Cat Finch and Rose Bishop’s tight one-hander masterfully conjures a time in which manufacturing has all but been outsourced and robotic essential workers are commonplace. That the world-building is so effective is due in large part to Lumsden, who expertly conveys Gertie’s interiority while inhabiting the flights and foibles of various characters – from her eccentric parents to the decrepit lawyer and young hacker she seeks in desperate attempts to rid herself of AI Bea. Amid a sea of baby-blue packing boxes, we watch as Gertie grapples with the spectres of loss, unfulfilled potential and acute unbelonging. Ghostware is a deeply felt, darkly humorous and strangely affecting play about the things we do to escape ourselves and others.

★★★★

Reviewed by Sonia Nair



THEATRE

Mary-Agnes O’Loughlin | Glimpses of Heaven

The Motley Bauhaus, until October 4 In Glimpses of Heaven, Mary-Agnes O’Loughlin draws inspiration (or should that be devastation?) from the battles with alcoholism, drug dependence and mental health issues of her own mother, comedic veteran Fiona O’Loughlin. Fiona’s struggles in the past are well-documented. She’s never been one to shy away from detailing her addiction and a 2013 suicide attempt (she credits Mary-Agnes for saving her life). Glimpses of Heaven. Ruby Healey A partly fictionalised story, the reality of Mary-Agnes’ truths about her upbringing are laid bare. She performs as Hannah, attending the apartment of her mother – an illustrious musician with chaotic habits (of whom Fiona herself provides the voiceovers) – to pack her belongings. All of the sentimental keepsakes elicit memories from a childhood with a mother constantly in the spotlight and turning a blind eye to the lowlights caused due to her compulsions. The show asks: is unconditional love possible when you’re watching a family member slowly killing themselves? Is any amount of fame and fortune amassed worth it if you seem destined to join the 27 Club, even if you may be a few years past the admission date? Under the directorial eye of another Australian comedy mainstay, Damian Callinan, there’s also humour to be found throughout the morbid storytelling intertwined with well-choreographed dance and music. Glimpses of Heaven is a tender, vulnerable exploration of the struggles with the concepts of familial love, intergenerational trauma and the catharsis found in forgiveness. While it must come recommended with the caveat of a strong trigger warning for anyone with a history of domestic distress, it’s a very impressive solo debut deserving of a main-stage season in future runs to come.

★★★★

Reviewed by Tyson Wray



THEATRE

Ryan Hamilton and Georgie Wolfe | F--- Your Funding

Festival Hub: Trades Hall - Solidarity Hall, until October 4 What if, over the course of a night, you could agitate for the arts to occupy a more central place in the political agenda and redress inequitable funding models? Such concerns reach an apotheosis at the 2026 Melba Awards, a fictional annual celebration of seriously high stakes in the play F--- Your Funding. Hosted by a venerated opera singer and opened by an imagined version of the Victorian arts minister, the night descends into chaos when two cultural terrorists hold them at gunpoint with a list of demands. F--- Your Funding. Jaimi Houston F--- Your Funding is at its most uproarious when it’s laying bare the arts sector’s greatest hypocrisies. A slide containing a list of morally vacuous donors? Tick. A politician lauding the cultural cachet of Melbourne while refusing to bolster the arts sector in any real, tangible way? Tick. As the play lurches wildly from farcical hijinks to sincere proselytising about the role of art in a whiplash-inducing manner, it simultaneously lampoons itself and us while paying homage to its intended audience. Leftists too busy preaching to the converted and fighting among one another to organise. Artists making work centred on their latest diagnoses. Clowns.

★★★★

Reviewed by Sonia Nair



DANCE

Caroline Meaden | Immacolata

Chunky Move Studios, until October 3 Immacolata. Caroline Meaden, Jeff Busby and William McBride This is a beautifully strange and melancholy solo dance vigil: a restless choreographic grisaille, delicate and disquieting. Caroline Meaden struts and frets, with crisp bird-like movements, then hesitates. Always there is hesitation in this work. Then an arm – or a hand or a leg – begins to wobble. It’s like a part of the body just turns to water. The dimly lit stage is furnished with only a clothes rack, some biscuit crumbs and a stool, but Meaden keeps mostly to its edges. She is pulled backwards or drawn into the corners, as if kept out of the empty centre by some unseen force. Immacolata tantalises with the mystery of its significance. What does it all mean? Is there a story behind its troubling silences? In fact, Meaden provides an accompanying essay, intended to be read after the performance, which does explain much of what we see – and gives the work’s air of sadness a touching specificity.

★★★★

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann



COMEDY

Holly Bohmer, Mario Hannah and Taylor Griffiths | Nosebleeds

The Improv Conspiracy, until October 18 Nosebleeds is at The Improv Conspiracy until October 18. Simon McCulloch and Mario Hannah The Nosebleeds, veterans of improv comedy, know it doesn’t take much to evoke the horror genre, even less to make fun of it. The trio, together for a decade, are back at Melbourne Fringe to take a proverbial (and literal) stab at the evergreen genre with an hour of uneven but charming sketches. Exorcisms become blind dates, séances turn into couples therapy, and haunted mansions turn nipples into weapons. Rather than looking to recent films, the self-described “comedian cinephiles” pull from an older vintage of horror. It’s Mel Brooks via Henry James. Holly Bohmer is the perfect wide-eyed governess with no fear of her homicidal employer, Mario Hannah is the ever-likeable himbo contacting the dead to learn more about the Titanic, and Taylor Griffiths, who delivers the night’s best punchlines, is uproarious as every manservant with a handlebar moustache or ghost child. But by the fourth Victorian-era conceit or ill-formed attempt at audience engagement, the show becomes static and its parodies rote. It’s a fun night out, but it’s not quite a scream.

★★★

Reviewed by Guy Webster



THEATRE

Gregory Nussen | QFWFQ

Trades Hall, until October 4 In this brave dissection of self, politics and art, Californian performer Gregory Nussen takes their cue (and title) from Italo Calvino’s metafictional work, If on a winter’s night a traveller. Centre stage is a writer’s desk piled with Calvino’s extended works, and we continue through a series of false starts as Nussen keeps attempting the play they’re “meant” to perform. QFWFQ. Sonya Katerina It’s a neat framing device for their autobiographical narrative, in which the preordained script of a rigid Jewish upbringing creates visceral and lasting internal conflict for a protagonist whose sexuality and gender identity don’t stick to the script. The most powerful moments draw an elegant through line between the cognitive dissonance of war and propaganda (both historical and current), and the terrifying and complex pursuit of self-actualisation and truth in a world where, too often, two plus two continues to equal five. There is plenty to like here, but the overall result is too many references and layers – some of them heavy-handed to begin with, then unnecessarily explained – which distract from its beating heart.

★★★

Reviewed by Hannah Francis



VISUAL ARTS and FILM

Youbi Lee | OBANG 오방

ArtPlay, until October 25 If you’re accustomed to picking up after a toddler, this interactive visual arts experience will make you feel right at home. OBANG 오방 combines the Korean term for five, O, with the word, BANG, referring to direction or room. The minimalist space is set up as a halmoni’s (grandmother’s) house, with individual stations representing the kitchen, bedroom, toilet and living room, alongside a partitioned area for the bathroom. OBANG 오방 is at ArtPlay until October 25. Darren Gill Familiar household elements ignite sensory play: a mini kitchenette, a bed, a clothing line and a blow-up bath. Tactile elements feed curiosity: plastic puddle decals, a dumpling steamer, silk manchester, a straw hanging and a wooden puzzle. The experience is low stimulation, with gentle traditional music and a wall projection adding an audiovisual dimension. The space is modest, which creates a safe and contained environment, but limits the number of families that can engage simultaneously, and the amount of time you can occupy an active toddler. As you leave, respect halmoni’s home by leaving the space as you found it, which is a good lesson for the young.

★★★

Reviewed by Vyshnavee Wijekumar



COMEDY

Blak Out: An Indigenous Comedy Showcase

Trades Hall, until October 4 Blak Out is an ideal comedy show to see early at Fringe. It offers a range of performers delivering a taste of what they offer, leaving the audience hungry to seek them out elsewhere at the festival. The featured comedians hail from all over the country, and with a mix of four performers each night there is a satisfying variety of styles. Blak Out: An Indigenous Comedy Showcase is at Trades Hall until October 4. When I attended, Wiradjuri/Kamilaroi performer Jacob Keed opened with a laconic storytelling style to ease the audience in, followed by Gamilaroi comic Ben Moodie. His material skewed darker with quick jabs that met their mark. Ngarrindjeri actor/producer/comedian Kimmie Lovegrove’s personal material offered a tempting preview of the material in her solo show, which will open later in Fringe. Kamilaroi performer Cameron Ribbons, the MC for the evening and the closing act, stole the show on this night by hitting a sweet spot of storytelling and punchy jokes. His re-enactment of crocodile spotting was the perfect crescendo.

★★★

Reviewed by Lefa Singleton Norton



DANCE

Weichen Cui | In Green, In White

Dancehouse, until October 3 The Chinese folk legend of Lady White Snake is forever shedding one skin for another. The most recent retellings shift the focus from White Snake’s mortal lover to her demonic servant, Green Snake, recasting the bond between mistress and maid in terms of enduring female friendship and homoerotic desire. In Green, In White is at Dancehouse until October 3. Georgia Moloney Choreographer Weichen Cui explores this queer transformation in a new duet with Jiawen Feng. At first, the performers are silhouetted behind separate screens, isolated, wearing costumes informed by tradition. As if reflecting the evolution of the story, the two figures are gradually brought together – culminating in a final serpentine tangle of limbs. There are interesting moments, such as the use of waacking to playfully disrupt a fan dance. But overall, the episodic structure feels slow and over-formal, arresting the flows of desire it seeks to release. It might also be a little long – compressed to half an hour, this duet could bring its strongest moments into more volatile contact.

★★★

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann



DANCE

Joyce Liu | INTERLINK_SYSTEM

Dancehouse, until October 3 Joyce Liu stands before us in the gloom, a tangle of red wires trailing from one arm, fingers twitching. Finally, we get it: she is actually controlling the soundscape, summoning jackhammer bursts and ominous bass drones from a body that barely seems to move. As the noise intensifies, four creatures wake inside a plastic greenhouse behind her. They claw at its walls, tearing them open. Free at last, the juddering young humanoids – all in their underwear – begin feverishly coupling in a sort of grotesque orgy-of-Doctor-Moreau. INTERLINK_SYSTEM is at Dancehouse, until October 3. Carlin Stephenson Liu – also director and choreographer – builds a convincingly creepy laboratory atmosphere, with smoke and wildly sweeping lights lending urgency to the action. There’s also some irony, even comedy, in the monstrous debauch – though it does go on and on. I do think, however, we could have stayed with that opening image of the human wired for sound a little longer, perhaps giving the idea of an interlinked system more room to unfold – before rushing into the bioengineered bacchanal.

★★★

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.
