World.title: FENZ responding to vegetation fire on Walter Peak, smoke visible from Queenstown
World.content:
Fire and Emergency is responding to a large vegetation fire at Walter Peak station on the shores of Lake Wakatipu.

Two helicopters with monsoon buckets were already at work to protect the Walter Peak homestead while other aircraft was on their way.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406332291112

Firefighters from Frankton and Glenorchy were being airlifted onto the fireground while crews from Mossburn were travelling by road.

Assistant District Commander Nic McQuillan said initial efforts were focused on protecting the homestead.

Supplied / Dave Noble

The fire was also spreading rapidly up the steep slopes of Mount Nicholas.

Smoke from the fire was being blown across the lake towards Jacks Point and Hanleys Farm, and was likely to move towards Queenstown.

Supplied / Dave Noble

Residents in areas affected by the smoke were told to keep doors and windows closed to avoid exposure.

The fire was reignited from a planned burn in the area last Wednesday.

Katie Todd

Walter Peak tour operator RealNZ said people had been evacuated and experiences cancelled.

"Following a controlled scrub burn last week, the site has reignited this afternoon in an area south of the Walter Peak Homestead. The Homestead and nearby treeline are not impacted at this stage, and Fire & Emergency NZ are responding to bring the fire under control," a RealNZ spokesperson said.

World.title: Homemade bomb found near new CRL train station
World.content:
Emergency services safely removed an improvised bomb after it was found near an Auckland train station on Monday.

NZ Defence Force (NZDF) staff had been alerted by police to an "item of concern" near the Maungawhau train station in Mt Eden.

The defence force's Explosive Ordinance Disposal team investigated the item, identifying it as an improvised explosive device.

An NZDF spokesperson said the device was removed from the area and disposed of safely.

"Anyone who discovers a potentially dangerous item should always exercise caution until the item is deemed safe by an expert," they said.

"If you do discover something that might be dangerous, remain clear of the item and contact New Zealand Police as soon as possible."

Acting detective senior sergeant Craig Burrow said police had found a stolen vehicle in Ellerslie which was removed and taken to a towing facility in Mt Eden.

"While being examined, a small, improvised explosive was discovered. This was rendered safe and destroyed."

There was no wider risk to the public at the time, Burrow said.

World.title: Specialist pain doctors call for free shingles vaccine for over-65s
World.content:
Audio player for " Calls for free shingles vaccinations for Kiwis over 65 " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/health/1749344%2Fspecialist-pain-doctors-call-for-free-shingles-vaccine-for-over-65s

Calls for free shingles vaccinations for Kiwis over 65 Morning Report Download MP3 5m

Specialist pain doctors are calling for the shingles vaccine to be free for everyone over 65.

Health NZ recommended the two-shot vaccine for anyone over 50 but it was only free if people got their first dose in the year they turned 65.

Otherwise it could cost up to $800.

The Faculty of Pain Medicine, part of the Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists, said whoever was in government next should change that as a priority.

Shingles is an often painful nerve condition caused by the same virus that causes chickenpox and which stays dormant in the body for decades.

Chair of the New Zealand National Committee of the college's faculty of pain medicine Charlotte Hill said one in three people would get shingles in their lives, rising to one in two over 85.

Up to a third of them developed a chronic nerve pain that could last for months or years.

It would be much better to prevent that condition from happening than to try and treat it, she said.

"Once post-herpetic neuralgia develops, it can be extremely difficult to treat," she said.

"The medicines we use for neuropathic pain can have significant side effects, particularly in older people, including sedation and dizziness, which can contribute to falls and threaten independence."

Hill told Morning Report New Zealand did not have the capacity to manage the chronic pain, and prevention would lower pressures on GPs and pain management services.

In the meantime, she encouraged anyone over 50 who could afford to to pay for a vaccination and for those who were 65 not to miss out on their chance.

Australia funded the vaccine for everyone over 65.

Pharmac said it had five applications to widen access to the shingles vaccine and four of those were on its "options for investment list," the list of medicines it would fund if it had the budget.

Pharmaceuticals director Geraldine MacGibbon said the agency's immunisation committee was actively considering extending funding for the vaccine Shingrix to immunocompromised people.

Funding for vaccines was often targeted at age groups where the vaccine would likely provide the most benefit.

The current age was set after advice the vaccine's effectiveness reduces with age, she said.

World.title: OFC Pro League final moves to Honiara for 2027 season
World.content:
Capacity crowd at the fourth round of this year's Oceania Football Confederation Professional League (OFC Pro League) has seen the 2027 final moved to Honiara.

This year's inaugural OFC Pro League final was held at Eden Park in Auckland, which closed off major parts of the grandstand and the retail area because of low crowd turnout.

In a statement on Tuesday, OFC confirmed the Solomon Islands would host the final of the 2027 OFC Pro League season.

"It follows on from scenes that saw Honiara's National Stadium packed with passionate fans during its successful hosting of circuit series four of the inaugural season earlier this year," the OFC said.

Honiara recorded capacity crowd on each of the match-days during the first season's round four competition. While confirming the final venue, OFC also revealed there will be a new finals format in 2027.

It will involve all eight clubs, kicking off on 25 May with the play-offs, followed by the quarterfinals on 29 May and the semifinals on 2 June.

The second season of Oceania's first-ever professional football competition kicks off on Friday, 22 January in Australia. Other round one matches will also be co-hosted by Papua New Guinea.

The first game of the new season will feature Vanuatu United FC and Solomon Kings FC.

Defending champions Auckland FC will begin their title defence in a rematch of the 2026 final against South Melbourne FC later the same evening.

Tahiti United will meet South Island United in the first game of match-day two in Port Moresby, followed by PNG's Hekari United and Fiji's Bula FC.

Vanuatu will host matches for the first time in round five, co-hosting with Fiji, while round three will have New Zealand and the Solomon Islands co-hosting as well.

The first New Zealand derby of the season will come in circuit round three in Aotearoa, as South Island United meet Auckland FC on Sunday, 7 March.

There will be five rounds of pool matches between 22 January and 8 May.

World.title: Fiji, Samoa and Tonga name 2026 Rugby League World Cup squads
World.content:
Fiji, Samoa and Tonga have named their men's squads for the 2026 Rugby League World Cup.

While the three teams look strong on paper, with star players included, the omission of some key players stood out when all three teams were announced.

The Fiji Bati squad announced on Tuesday does not include star forwards Tui Kamikamica, who has since retired after suffering a stroke four months ago, and Viliame Kikau, who is out because of an ankle injury.

Fullback Jahream Bula is out also due to post-season shoulder surgery.

Samoa will miss tough forward Payne Haas because of injury, along with Simi Sasagi, who is also out awaiting surgery.

Also missing are Queensland stars Jeremiah Nanai and Murray Taulagi, who have both missed the cut.

Tonga have opted to leave out veteran Roosters winger Daniel Tupou, who claimed his fourth National Rugby League grand final title on Sunday night, while one of the 24 named on Tuesday morning will still have to be omitted from the final 23.

New Bati leader

The absence of Kamikamica and Kikau means the Fiji Bati will have a new captain at the world meet.

Head coach Mick Potter, who took Fiji Bati to the semi-finals at the 2017 Rugby League World Cup, told the Fiji Sun a new captain will be named, as the squad started their preparation at the Uprising Resort in Deuba, which is about 45 minutes drive outside Suva.

With Kamikamica, who was Bati captain, and Kikau, who deputised at times, both unavailable, the likely choice would be veteran West Tigers captain and three-time premiership winner Apisai Koroisau.

Potter is likely to select a leadership team, with the focus on the team combining together to produce the results.

"The expectation is that they individually do their best and col-lectively they do their best," he told the Fiji Sun.

"I think that's what their country wants, what their family wants and what I want. I'm pretty confident they'll do that, and I don't think there'll be any stone left unturned in terms of preparation."

As of Monday evening, a total of 19 players were in camp. The remaining squad members are expected to join the team in Newcastle, Australia, on Sunday.

Flight changes had also affected the team, Potter said, with several play-ers going through changed flights.

"It was nearly like travelling to Europe as opposed to travelling to Fiji, just to get to Fiji, so they're all very tired," he said.

"We've got a good squad here and they need to keep training, other-wise they're going to get an injury. It's commendable that they do that in their own time."

Potter has moved on from the Fainu brothers, Latu, Samuela and Sione, who have not been allowed to play for Fiji because their documentation does not meet International Rugby League requirements.

The absences have forced Potter to reshuffle three positions, cre-ating opportunities for younger players.

Newcastle Knights prop Jacob Saifiti is free to play for the Bati, following the completion of his four-match ban for a high shot on Warriors winger Luke Laulilii in the team's NRL round 26 match.

The veteran prop is an important inclusion, especially with Kamikamica and Kikau both missing.

The Bati have been top performers at the World Cup and reached the semi-finals in 2008, 2013 and 2017 only to be knocked out by Australia on each occasion.

They will meet Cook Islands, Australia and New Zealand in pool play, in what is the toughest pool for the event.

Fiji Bati squad: Bayleigh Bentley-Hape, Waqa Blake, Kurt Donoghoe, Apenisa Driti, Kitione Kautoga, Elijah Keung, Apisai Koroisau, Josese Lanyon, Jordan Leiu, Joseph Litidamu, Kylan Mafoa, Taane Milne, Caleb Navale, Jimmy Ngutlik, Ronald Philitoga, Mitchell Prest, Emosi Ravosai, Jacob Saifiti, Solomone Saukuru, Sunia Turuva, Brandon Wakeham, Jordan Miller

Toa Samoa stars

A star-studded squad will take Toa Samoa to the 2026 Rugby League World Cup.

Captain and veteran forward Junior Paulo, PNG Chiefs bound Jarome Luai, Canterbury Bulldogs star Stephen Crichton, Penrith Panthers winger Brian To'o and Dolphins speedster Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow are some of the big names in the squad.

Sua Fa'alogo, Clayton Faulalo, Deine Mariner and Greg Marzhew, who is coming off a heartbreaking Grand Final loss to the Roosters, plus Warriors playmaker Chanel Harris-Tavita are some exciting names that will feature along the backline.

Samoa will play their first World Cup match next Friday, 16 October, against France.

Head coach Ben Gardiner told the media in Australia, following the squad announcement, the squad will play for the people of Samoa, with large crowds expected at all their matches, especially with battle against Tonga in their last pool game.

"One of the great things rugby league does is bring people together," Gardiner said.

"As we build towards our first World Cup game, we want to thank all Samoans around the world for their ongoing support. Your blessings and prayers are welcomed, whether you are in Samoa, elsewhere around the world, taking part in a parade or marching into the ground, we see you and thank you for your love and support.

"Our staff and players look forward to seeing our colours, flags and supporters over the coming five weeks. We encourage everyone to celebrate safely and positively, showing our men's and women's teams love and blessings from near and far.

"As we pull on the blue jersey in Rugby League Samoa's 40th anniversary year, we carry the pride and resilience of generations of players before us, while seeking to inspire the future of our game and our country."

Experience is something the Toa Samoa will have a lot of, with their backliners in Crichton bringing 16 international caps and 14 State of Origin appearances, To'o having already represented Samoa 20 times and NSW 17 times and Luai, who has 13 caps for the Toa and 12 State of Origin appearances.

Samoa's forward pack combines established international experience alongside Paulo, with Roosters NRL final winner Spencer Leniu adding to that.

Francis Manuleleua and Jermatime McEwen, who helped Newcastle to a Grand Final this year, are also in the squad as young guns.

Tabuai-Fidow's inclusion is particularly significant, with the Dolphins star having previously represented Australia.

Toa Samoa squad: Shawn Blore Anae Ulesese (Melbourne Storm), Stephen Crichton (Canterbury-Bankstown Bulldogs), Sua Fa'alogo (Melbourne Storm), Clayton Faulalo (Manly Warringah Sea Eagles), Chanel Harris-Tavita (Warriors), Benaiah Ioelu (Sydney Roosters), Connelly Lemuelu (Dolphins), Spencer Leniu (Sydney Roosters), Jarome Luai (Wests Tigers), Francis Manuleleua (Newcastle Knights), Deine Mariner (Brisbane Broncos), Ata Mariota (Canberra Raiders), Greg Marzhew (Newcastle Knights), Jermaine McEwen (Newcastle Knights), Francis Molo (Dolphins), Junior Paulo (Parramatta Eels), Pasami Saulo (Newcastle Knights), Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow (Dolphins), Izack Tago (Penrith Panthers), Jazz Tevaga (Wakefield Trinity), Brian To'o (Penrith Panthers), Enari Tuala (Canterbury-Bankstown Bulldogs), Ronald Volkman (Parramatta Eels)

Tonga's balanced team

Tonga Rugby League chairman Lord Fatafehi Fakafanua, who is also the country's prime minister, believes the squad named is well-balanced with a lot of firepower across the field.

The headache for the coaching team will be who will they leave out from the 24 named in Nuku'alofa on Tuesday.

Three Roosters players, who claimed the National Rugby League grand final on Sunday night, have made the cut, when Tonga's Crown Prince Tupouto'a 'Ulukalala revealed the squad make-up.

Tonga's head coach Kristian Woolf will take an exciting squad into the World Cup, with one final player still to be cut before their opening match against England on Saturday 17 October in Perth.

Manly provides the biggest contingent with four players, Haumole Olakau'atu, Lehi Hopoate, Taniela Paseka and Tolutau Koula. The Roosters and the New Zealand Warriors follow with three each, while the Dolphins, Sharks, Titans and Cowboys each have two representatives.

The only players from outside the NRL are Huddersfield Giants' Tuimoala Lolohea and Junior Amone who has most recently played in the Queensland Cup with Wynnum Manly.

Roosters trio Salesi Foketi, Siua Wong and Robert To'ia have all been named in the Tongan squad, two days after helping the Sdney club claim in the 2026 NRL title.

Veteran forward Jason Taumalolo, Newcastle Knights Tyson Frizell, Warriors Leka Halasima, Manly's Haumole Olakau'tau and Cronulla Sharks Addin Fonua-Blake are some star players included in the squad.

Dolphins coach and longtime Tonga coach Woolf will map out the side's campaign against England on October 17, with Lebanon and Samoa as their other pool opponents.

His club playmaker Isaiya Katoa, who was under injury worry, will provide a pin-point kicking and passing game for the side, with a lot of power and speed along the backline.

Lehi Hopoate, Jojo Fifita, Paul Alamoti, Dallin Watene-Zelezniak, Rob Toia, Tolu Koula and Sione Katoa can all run in at the centres or on the wing.

Upfront Foketi will join Olakau'atu and Kulikefu Finefeuiaki while Taumalolo, Moeaki Foutaika, Stefano Utoikamanu and Fonua-Blake will provide plenty of size and brutal strength up front.

Latu Fainu is the likely leading contender to partner Katoa, but Tuimoala Lolohea, Talatau Amone and even Koula are all options.

World.title: 'Cart before the horse': Fiji opposition slams Rabuka's pre-emptive referendum date
World.content:
Fiji's opposition is accusing the country's prime minister of political "strangulation" ahead of an upcoming election.

It comes after Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka pre-emptively announced a date for Fiji's first-ever national referendum on the island nation's constitution reform process on Monday - just two days after his coalition pushed through a major bill on its second reading to change the 2013 Constitution.

Parliamentary opposition leader Inia Seruiratu said that, by announcing a date for the referendum, Rabuka was "putting the cart before the horse".

Seruiratu described the move as "premature", as the Fijian parliament had not completed debating the Constitution (Amendment) Bill.

"The bill has only passed its second reading and has now been referred to a Special Select Committee for further scrutiny, public awareness and public submissions," he said in a statement on Tuesday.

"It is expected to return to parliament for its third reading in November. Until that process is completed, parliament has not given its final approval to the Bill.

"What then is the basis for announcing 9 December as the referendum date when Parliament has not even determined the final form of the Constitution Amendment Bill?"

Rabuka announced on Monday that the question to be put to the people had not yet been decided, but said it would only require a 'yes' or 'no' vote, even though the exact wording has not yet been determined.

He also told reporters that there was no Plan B if his bid fails during the bill's third reading next month.

"We can't have a contingency plan," he said in response to a question from a local reporter.

Rabuka said that he would write to the Electoral Commission to suspend all election-related campaigning.

More than 723,000 eligible Fijian voters still have not been told the date for the country's general election, but Rabuka has maintained that the timeline remains unchanged and the polls will go ahead by 6 February 2027 - the maximum deadline under the current constitution.

Since independence, Fiji has had four coups and four constitutions. Critics of the 2013 Constitution, including the Rabuka-led coalition, argue that it was imposed on the people by the previous Bainimarama administration.

The coalition has made it a priority to replace the document and roll back many of its defining features.

The constitutional debate takes place as the country grapples with several social and economic issues, including deteriorating health infrastructure, declining education standards, rising unemployment and poverty. The critics of the coalition say the government should focus on fixing the bread-and-butter issues first.

"Why should political parties be prevented from speaking to voters about the cost of living, health services, education, employment, infrastructure, governance and the many other issues upon which the government must be held accountable simply because the government has decided to pursue a referendum?" Seruiratu said.

"Announcing the referendum date beforehand creates the unfortunate impression that the timetable has already been determined irrespective of what the public or ultimately parliament may decide."

However, Justice Minister Siromi Turaga said the government was going to systematically inform the Fijian people about the bill.

"Government machinery will be activated to ensure every Fijian [has] a good understanding for what they're going to cast their [referendum] vote on," Turaga, who is also the acting Attorney-General, said.

Fiji's Electoral Commission said in a statement that it would - alongside the Fijian Elections Office (FEO) - proceed with the preparations for the national referendum, while continuing preparations for the general election.

World.title: Friend of missing Queenstown woman Erika Coelho remaining optimistic
World.content:
A close friend of a woman missing near Queenstown is not giving up hope that she will be found safe, as search crews continue to comb land around Coronet Peak.

Erika Rodrigues Coelho, 47, has not been seen or heard from since 18 September.

The Brazilian national's rental car was found at Skippers Saddle on 21 September. Police believe it was parked there some time in the afternoon or evening of 18 September.

Police have appealed for public help to identify a man seen on the summit track in the Mount Dewar area at 12.30pm on 18 September as part of their search for Coelho.

Brett Squire told RNZ Coelho's friends and family were extremely worried and distressed but "absolutely focused on Erika and her safe return".

Supplied

"In terms of the work that has been done so far by the police and search and rescue teams - I believe that they are all doing a very thorough job and we want to thank them all for their hard work and dedication to finding Erika," he said.

"While a couple of weeks has passed since Erika's disappearance, she is an incredibly strong woman, we are therefore remaining optimistic that this concludes (hopefully soon) with a good outcome."

The large-scale search for Coelho involved helicopters, drones, Coastguard crews, Land Search and Rescue volunteers and a search dog.

Queenstown Sergeant Terry Wood has previously said the man on the summit track could be a tourist.

"The man is described as of Asian complexion, in his 30s, average to taller in height. Slim build with short dark hair and clean shaven," he said.

"We would like to speak with him regarding our ongoing investigation for missing 47-year-old Erika Rodrigues Coelho near Queenstown."

World.title: Jaymie Graham named new North Melbourne AFL coach
World.content:
North Melbourne has named Fremantle assistant coach Jaymie Graham as the new coach for the AFL side.

A statement from club president Sonja Hood on Tuesday said Graham was the new senior coach, succeeding four-time premiership coach Alastair Clarkson, who was sacked by the Kangaroos earlier this year.

Graham spent five seasons at the Dockers as an assistant to Justin Longmuir.

The Kangaroos finished the 2026 season — Clarkson's fourth season in charge — in 14th spot with nine wins.

Speaking at his first press conference, Graham thanked the club for having faith in him.

Having missed out on a number of coaching opportunities before landing the North Melbourne job, he said he was nervous and proud to take charge of the Kangaroos.

"This opportunity came up, things happen for a reason. I feel I belong here already," he said.

"There's no ceiling on where we want to get to. There's clearly some talent on this list, but there's also some work to do."

Graham described himself as a "systems-based and relationships-based coach".

"People don't care how much you know, until they know how much you care."

Club CEO Jen Watt confirmed the panel tasked with finding the new coach had unanimously picked Grham.

Earlier, in the club statement, Hood told members Graham had "the resilience to handle the relentless toils of the football environment, carrying the exact kind of grit we value at North Melbourne.

"As a coach, Jaymie is a process-driven leader with a quiet, grounded presence, sharp attention to detail, and a clear football vision," she said.

"Outside of his exceptional character, he joins us with a proven skill set. He played a key role in West Coast's 2018 premiership success, and more recently he was the line coach for one of the competition's best forward lines at Fremantle as part of a high-performing program.

"He is widely respected across the industry as a developer of talent and a connector of people — someone who builds strong player relationships instantly and earns respect through his actions."

The announcement marks a change in direction, with a young untested AFL senior coach — who has been a caretaker or interim coach for three games in total at West Coast and Fremantle, after a period in charge of East Perth in the WAFL — after the end of the Clarkson era.

The Kangaroos were criticised for the tone of their press conference in early September announcing Clarkson's departure.

Alastair Clarkson leaves North North Melbourne president Sonja Hood and football boss Todd Viney explain why the club is parting ways with Alastair Clarkson with a year to run on his deal.

At the time, Hood said Clarkson's replacement needed to be "a coach who can coach for the modern game".

"It'll be a coach who knows what they're doing, and it'll be a coach who's the best fit for this football club," she said.

Football manager Todd Viney said in the press conference there were "still some gaping holes in our game plan".

Fremantle paid tribute to Graham in a statement, wishing him well for his new role and thanking him for his "five outstanding seasons" at the club.

"Jaymie has had a significant impact not only on our player group — but the entire football department and broader club," Fremantle executive general manager of football Joe Brierty said.

"It is well documented that Jaymie has had ambitions of becoming a senior coach in his own right one day, and we couldn't be prouder or happier for him to take an opportunity he's worked so hard for."

World.title: Mary Fowler withdraws from Matildas squad for Germany, Haiti games
World.content:
Matildas star Mary Fowler has been withdrawn from the Australian squad for two upcoming internationals, due to personal circumstances.

A release from Football Australia on Tuesday morning said the decision had been taken following discussions between Fowler, Manchester City and Matildas staff.

Fowler has been in solid form, coming on as a sub to spark a comeback win for Manchester City over WSL rivals Arsenal on Monday morning, Australian time.

Fowler's City still perfect in WSL Mary Fowler's landmark 100th game for Manchester City is a bright spot for the beleaguered club, with a big win over Arsenal keeping them with a perfect record on top of the WSL.

There was no talk of injury after the game.

Fowler's partner, Nathan Cleary, is recovering in Sydney after leg surgery.

The Penrith Panthers NRL star went into the preliminary final against Newcastle with a broken foot, before suffering a compound fracture and a dislocated ankle in a hip-drop tackle, requiring emergency surgery.

Fowler has been replaced in the Australian squad by Charlton Athletic midfielder Leah Davidson. Davidson has made four appearances for the Matildas since her international debut in 2024.

The Matildas are playing two international friendlies in Europe as they continue preparations towards next year's FIFA Women's World Cup.

Australia split a two-match series with Mexico in June, with one win each.

Now the Matildas will face Germany in Karlsruhe on Saturday morning, Australian time before taking on Haiti in France on October 13.

World.title: Live: Wantaway Saints star boycotts best and fairest as Cats eye AFL trade
World.content:
Hi Chris, Looking forward to another fun trade week and to be glued to this thread for a week straight. With the Lions, coming off the threepeat and having resigned Bailey, Morris, Zorko & Lester I can't imagine there would be much we are looking for but are there any players we have our eyes on? Also any update on if McKenna will play on? - Rachel

I can't imagine the Lions have too much coming in terms of incoming players.

The main point of action will be a few departures in the form of Keidean Coleman, Sam Marshall and Will McLachlan.

AFL.com.au's Cal Twomey reported earlier this morning that McLachlan has met with both Essendon and Melbourne.

Brisbane has so far tabled multiple contract offers for McLachlan.

The Coleman one is a bit more ambiguous. He has struggled with injuries over the last couple of years, but played 13 games this year, the most since 2023.

All indications are that Brisbane will play hardball on that one. It remains unclear where exactly Coleman would want to go, if he indeed does leave.

He has one more year left to run on his current deal with Brisbane.

Sam Marshall has requested a trade to St Kilda, and it has been reported that the Lions are interested in something close to the pick 25 they drafted him with in 2024.

World.title: Demon faces Djokovic in China final after Medvedev disqualified
World.content:
Alex de Minaur will face Novak Djokovic in the China Open final after the Serb's semifinal opponent, Daniil Medvedev, was disqualified ‌for hitting a loose ball into the crowd and causing a spectator to suffer an eye injury.

The Australian number one progressed from his semifinal after Poland's Hubert Hurkacz retired injured when trailing in the second set.

Djokovic was leading 7–5, 5–3 in Beijing and serving for the match when the incident happened.

After a forehand volley winner from Djokovic, the ball bounced off the advertising boards to Medvedev, who smacked a backhand that sailed into the stands.

A male spectator (obscured) was struck in the eye after Daniil Medvedev hit a ball into the stands during his China Open semifinal. (AP: Andy Wong)

It hit a spectator in the front row behind him.

The spectator clutched his left eye and appeared to be in ‌pain as he walked out, assisted by stadium staff.

"Terribly sorry to ‌the spectator, first ⁠of all," Medvedev told reporters. "I'm trying to get in touch with him, if he wants it. Hopefully I can apologise in person and see how he feels."

The Russian world number five said he did not cause the incident intentionally.

"The ball was bouncing back, so I tried to, like, just hit it anywhere, so it doesn't go out from the court. When I saw the result, I mean, I felt horrible because, again, I don't think I was ever close to such a situation."

Medvedev, 30, has a history of on-court behaviour issues. He was fined 6,000 euros ($9,600) after he smashed his racquet seven times during a 6–0, 6–0 loss to Matteo Berrettini at this year's Monte Carlo Masters.

"I was shocked, to be honest … I hope that person is not ‌badly injured," said Djokovic, who was disqualified from the US Open in 2020 under similar circumstances.

"On the other hand, I also feel sorry for Daniil because I know exactly how it feels to be disqualified in a big match … ‌I'm sure that Daniil didn't want to do this intentionally."

Alex de Minaur was a set up on Hubert Hurkacz in the China Open semifinal when Hurkacz was forced to withdraw due to injury. (Getty Iimages: Eurasia Sport/Hermann Chu)

De Minaur will be seeking to become the first person to beat Djokovic in 34 matches at the China Open. He has a 1–3 head-to-head record with the Serb.

The winner will leave Beijing ninth in the race to qualify for November's eight-man ATP Finals, with the gap to Medvedev in eighth reduced as the Russian will lose the 200 points he had gained in Beijing.

There are two ATP Masters 1000 events to come, in Shanghai and Paris, but ninth may be enough with Jannik Sinner's availability uncertain.

On Saturday, the world number one, who last played at Wimbledon, pulled out of Shanghai, which begins on Wednesday. The Italian has a knee problem.

De Minaur was up 6–4, 3–2 and 40–0 when Hurkacz retired with an apparent adductor injury after showing mobility problems.

The world number nine had broken a tentative Hurkacz in his opening two service games before holding to lead 4–0, then withstood a comeback to take the first set 6–4.

Another break in the third game of the second set helped de Minaur build a 3–1 lead. Hurkacz fought desperately to hold serve in the following game, surviving four break points and a marathon deuce game, but was unable to battle much longer.

In Tokyo, defending champion Carlos Alcaraz overcame early wobbles on his serve ‌to outclass fellow Spaniard Jaume Munar 5–7, 6–3, 6–1 ‌and reach the Japan Open final.

He will play Jiri Lehecka, who beat Valentin Vacherot 6-4, 6-2.

AAP/AP

World.title: Why NRL grand final 'freak' is making Wallabies lick their lips
World.content:
It was not just the 80,000 spectators crammed inside Sydney's Olympic stadium, nor the millions of TV viewers in Australia, who were left in awe of Mark Nawaqanitawase's performance in the NRL grand final.

Last night, across the Tasman in New Zealand, the Wallabies eagerly watched on as Nawaqanitawase added to his highlight reel by scoring two tries in the Sydney Roosters' nail-biting 19-18 victory over Newcastle.

Roosters win classic NRL grand final A Daly Cherry-Evans field goal proves the difference as the Sydney Roosters beat the Newcastle Knights 19-18 in the NRL grand final.

The fact that some of the Wallabies were Nawaqanitawase's ex-teammates helped explain the interest.

But knowing the dual international is switching codes once again, in time for next year's Rugby World Cup, also had Wallabies players licking their lips in anticipation.

"He'll be massive. He's just been a freak," Wallabies prop Allan Alaalatoa told reporters in Auckland today.

"What he's done in the last two years in league is probably unheard of.

"He's gone over there in the space of two years and pretty much done everything, and now he's coming back."

Following the Wallabies' disastrous Rugby World Cup campaign three years ago, Nawaqanitawase announced he would move to the NRL ahead of the 2025 season.

He was given clearance to join the Roosters earlier than scheduled, and made his NRL debut in the final round of the 2024 premiership.

Mark Nawaqanitawase (left) scored twice for the Roosters in the NRL grand final.

To suggest Nawaqanitawase made an impact in rugby league is an understatement.

He took the NRL by storm in his first full season, which was capped off when he debuted for Australia in last year's Ashes series in England.

Nawaqanitawase was selected in NSW's successful State of Origin squad this year and played a crucial role in helping the Roosters capture their first NRL premiership since 2019.

His athleticism and aerial skills on the wing contributed to an astonishing strike rate of 47 tries in as many NRL matches.

Nawaqanitawase has hit the pause button on his NRL career for now, having signed with Japanese rugby club Saitama Wild Knights on a two-year deal.

He will be available for Wallabies selection, although the 26-year-old is unlikely to feature in November's Nations Championship Tests against England, Scotland and Wales.

After impressing for the Wallabies in 11 Test appearances between 2022-23, he is expected to make a smooth transition once he returns to rugby.

Having him play alongside the likes of Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii and Max Jorgensen in a Wallabies' backline is a tantalising prospect; however, coach Les Kiss says there are "no promises and no guarantees".

Mark Nawaqanitawase played 11 Tests for the Wallabies before switching codes in 2024. (Getty Images: Aurelien Meunier)

Kiss is justified in declaring Nawaqanitawase will not walk straight back into the Wallabies squad.

But his presence will create competitive pressure among candidates for the Wallabies' wing spots ahead of the Rugby World Cup, which Australia is hosting.

"He'll just naturally start demanding more from other people because of the type of competition that is in the squad," said Alaalatoa, as the Wallabies prepare for Saturday's Bledisloe Cup Test at Eden Park.

"I think that only adds health to the group, and it brings the best out of people in his position because of the type of player that he is and what he's shown on some of the biggest stages in Australia.

"I think that is the type of value he'll add to our group."

Nawaqanitawase is set to debut for Saitama Wild Knights in the Japan Rugby League One competition in December.

Not surprisingly, his immediate focus is helping the Roosters celebrate the club's NRL and NRLW premiership victories.

World.title: Wiradjuri Aboriginal Rivers, Newcastle Yowies claim Koori Knockout glory
World.content:
The Wiradjuri Aboriginal Rivers have defeated the Bourke Warriors, 26-6, to claim their first Koori Knockout men's title.

Despite a nailbiting first half of Sunday's grand final, WAR came back strong in the second half and led their team to victory.

"For this club here, WAR, its more than footy", said WAR player Julian Christian.

"We've been close a couple of times over the years, we've lost against WAC (Walgett Aboriginal Connection) a couple of times in a grand final.

" This is so good, its so worth it. So worth it. "

Fans watch the finals of the Koori Knockout intensely. (ABC Newcastle: Piper Duffy)

As well as winning glory at the Knockout, WAR will now get to choose where the 2027 Knockout is played.

In the women's final, the Newcastle Yowies secured back-to-back titles, defeating the Redfern All Blacks 14-6.

The side featured a mixture of young talent, as well as experienced NRLW players including two-time premiership winner Caitlin Johnston.

She told NITV the win was dedicated to members of their community who recently passed.

"We've lost some very special people to us, so to take it back to back means quite a bit," Johnston said through tears.

" Newy's a community full of footballers ... to host the Knockout is pretty special, and then to win it puts the icing on the cake. "

Game day 'means everything'

About 40,000 fans spent their long weekend on Worimi Country at Raymond Terrace to attend the biggest sporting event of the Indigenous calendar.

Described as a modern-day corroboree, the tournament has been running since 1971, now bringing together almost 180 mens, women's and junior teams from across the state.

Bourke Warriors centre Colby Pellow and his wife Alex travelled more than 700 kilometres to play in the mammoth sporting event.

"Our community, it's only small, but we all get around this time of year," he said.

Colby Pellow and his wife Alex travelled from Bourke to attend the Knockout in Raymond Terrace. (ABC Newcastle: Emma Simkin )

Knockout veteran Josh Toole, who played for WAR, said the annual event brings mob together.

"I've played for a couple of different [Knockout] sides and it doesn't matter which side you go for it's that sense of community," he said.

"Also for Aboriginal people, we're big on footy, we love footy so there's a lot of passion."

Maddi Ireland led her Newcastle team to victory in the under 15s. (ABC Newcastle: Piper Duffy)

Young talent on display

Maddi Ireland spent her childhood watching her father take to the Knockout field year after year.

This year Ms Ireland, a Wiradjuri woman from Dubbo, took out the title for the Under 15's playing for her new team, the Newcastle Yowies.

"[It's] just good to do it for the culture, the mob, and my friends and the families around me," she said.

"'It's surreal honestly playing out on the field with all the crowd and mob around us supporting us.

"It just feels unreal out there," she said.

Ms Ireland said the win had inspired her to pursue bigger rugby league dreams of her own.

"One day I hope I can make NRLW, make my family proud and my culture," she said.

Families from across the state came to watch the annual Koori Knockout in Raymond Terrace. (ABC Newcastle: Piper Duffy)

World.title: Australia's Rugby League World Cup squad is a sign of the changing times
World.content:
The depths of Australia's star power means the Kangaroos will always name squads oozing with class and Kevin Walters's combination for this year's World Cup is no exception.

It's a side with major success stories, young and old and in-between.

James Tedesco's return three years after his last Test caps the 33-year old's resurrection and after he ran the ball to hell and back in the grand final to win the Clive Churchill Medal, there can be no doubt that, at an age where many players best days are only just a memory, he is once again the best fullback in the world.

Walker among six Kangaroos debutants The grand final sides feature in the Kangaroos squad for the Rugby League World Cup, with James Tedesco back in and Sydney's Sam Walker and Newcastle's Bradman Best among six debutants.

The inclusion of Dolphins flyer Jack Bostock, who will almost certainly see a Test debut in the World Cup opener given the side's shortage of wingers, heralds the start of a new generation wearing green and gold.

At 26, David Fifita is no longer a youngster in rugby league terms but his looming Australian debut is both a long time coming and well-earned following his strong finish to the year with Souths.

The one-time prodigy has longed seemed a player of limitless possibilities but only now, eight years after his NRL debut and three years since he last played for Queensland, will he get the chance to be a Kangaroo.

But the Australian squad also reveals the new truths about representative football, that the disconnect between State and Origin and Test matches is wider than ever before and may never be stitched back together again.

The disconnect between Origin and Test football has never been wider. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

It's a process that began with Origin's gradual but unmistakeable rise past Test football as rugby league's biggest stage then continued when a host of players chose to represent Pasifika nations over Australia while retaining their Origin eligibility.

The final change came earlier this year when the NRL allowed players to represent New Zealand or England and still being available for Origin selection.

Both of those eligibility changes reflect the changing face of rugby league and the people who play it and the game is better for them.

But it does require a reset of over a century's worth of thinking that interstate football is the pathway to national selection.

This has not been true for some years now, but there's a reason old habits have a hard time dying.

And while Australia will never be hard up for talent, some of the more eyebrow-raising picks prove this old adage is as antiquated as Kangaroo tours that travel to England by boat.

Robert Toia would have been a walk-up start for Australia but has chosen Tonga. (Getty Images: Izhar Khan)

Not one of the Queensland outside backs is in the side at all. Kalyn Ponga, Robert Toia, Jojo Fifita, Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow all would be, but they're playing for other nations while Selwyn Cobbo is injured.

That's how we end up with Brisbane's Kotoni Staggs, a fine centre who had a tough year, making the side despite being dropped by New South Wales for the Origin decider after a horror night in Game II at the MCG.

Latrell Mitchell missed the entire series through injury and has only started one match in the past five months but he's made it, while Tom Trbojevic is a likely starter on one wing despite not having played rep football for two years and not playing a match on the flank since 2018.

Tom Trbojevic will play his first Test match in two years. (AAP: Darren England)

Likewise of the 12 men who played in the forwards for New South Wales, only Blayke Brailey, Isaah Yeo, Liam Martin and Cameron Murray have made the squad.

Hudson Young and Payne Haas are both out with injury, but Haumole Olakau'atu and Addin Fonua-Blake will both line up for Tonga while Victor Radley is with England.

So Reuben Cotter makes the squad despite an underwhelming season with the Cowboys and a lacklustre series for Queensland.

His selection over Dolphins hardman Max Plath, who does a similar job with similar attributes whilst offering the same versatility and is coming off a far superior season for club and state, is perhaps the hardest pick to understand.

How Plath became Queensland's newest Origin hero The players who fill the spaces in between the stars are the secret to Queensland's Origin dominance and in Max Plath the Maroons have found yet another player who knows just how to do it.

Plath, along with Newcastle's Fletcher Sharpe and South Sydney's Tallis Duncan can count himself most aggrieved at missing out but it's hard to take up too much issue with Walters's squad, even if it's short of wingers.

This is the hand the Australian coach has been dealt for his final tournament before he departs to take over Super League side St Helens.

The eligibility changes and the fact that Test football misses out on players who pick up injuries during club seasons that are getting longer and longer all the time means sometimes his options are a bit more limited than he would have liked.

Australia are still the pick to win the World Cup and will be warm favourites in every game they play, beginning with their tournament opener against New Zealand next Thursday night in Sydney.

Walters is attempting to solve a puzzle no other Kangaroos coach has ever had to face and there is no one-size-fits-all philosophy in the battle between fitness, function and form when it comes to selecting a player.

But when numbers are scarce, and for the Kangaroos they're a lot shorter than they used to be, the first two are more important than the last.

World.title: Best is yet to come for Naufahu Whyte following NRL grand final victory
World.content:
The 2026 NRL grand final was the kind of game they'll talk about for years to come.

As it goes further into history and the old stories come out at reunions and in front bars and on podcasts, they'll talk about Kalyn Ponga's try, Newcastle's heroic defence, Mark Nawaqanitawase's whole deal and the big finish.

They'll talk about James Tedesco winning the Clive Churchill Medal and maybe someone will remember his exact number of running metres — an obscene 388.

But what's certain is that at least one person will argue, passionately and adamantly, that Naufahu Whyte was the best player on the field.

Tedesco wins Churchill Medal After skippering the Sydney Roosters to their first men's premiership in seven years, James Tedesco claims the Clive Churchill Medal as the player of the match in the grand final.

There's no wrong answer between Tedesco and Whyte, who were the Roosters' best in the 19-18 victory.

Together, they combined for 55 runs and add Whyte's metres gained (187) to Tedesco's total and they carried the ball for more than half a kilometre.

Where Tedesco had 12 tackle busts, two forced dropouts and a try assist, Whyte forced several errors with his brutal defence, affirmed his status as one of the best forwards in the game and created the ruck speed that helped lead to Nawaqanitawase's crucial second-half try.

Winning the award as a middle isn't easy either, because even though you never win a comp without a few good ones, they always seem to miss out.

Sam Burgess was the last middle forward to win the Churchill medal when he led South Sydney from the front in 2014. Before then, you have to go back to Brent Kite in 2008 to find the last front-rower to do it.

For his part, the 24-year-old was happy to defer to his skipper.

Whyte and Tedesco were the premiers' two best players in the grand final win. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"He deserves it; he's been doing it all year," Whyte said.

"I have big love for my captain and what he's done for the game. I'll say he's the best fullback in the game ever. That's my brother."

While Tedesco took home the medal, Whyte's own trophy cabinet has become cluttered in a short space of time.

His premiership ring will vie with the Dally M Prop Of The Year award he won last week for pride of place, but if Whyte keeps up this form, there's sure to be more to come.

Especially if Whyte is telling the truth when he says there's still major improvement in him despite dominating on the game's biggest stage on Sunday night.

"I know this isn't my best. It's far from it. I'm still just at the start of my career. There's a lot of work to put in," Whyte said.

"In the grand final, I had to take it next level. It's not easy winning a grand final, and the Knights were always going to show up, so I had to push myself.

"Taking carry after carry, that's what I'll do for my brothers. It's paid off for me so far.

NRL grand final live A Daly Cherry-Evans field goal proves the difference as the Sydney Roosters beat the Newcastle Knights 19-18 in the NRL grand final. Follow live.

"We came in confident we would get the job done, even down six, because that's the belief we have in each other, that's the belief we have in this team."

That belief proved crucial for the Tricolours as they claimed their first premiership since 2018-19, especially in coming back from 12-0 down with a Knights ambush eminently possible.

Whyte, who watches highlights of those games all the time, now has a version of it that he can not just replay but relive.

"Everything is going through my head and my heart now. I just want to embrace this moment and enjoy every part of it, because it's the best feeling ever," Whyte said.

"I screamed, had tears of joy; I was all over the place. All the hard work it took to get here — I'm speechless, brother, I really am."

Tech.title: Gemini Call for Me might tell your mom you’re running late
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google may be expanding its “Call for Me” AI feature beyond business calls so you can use it to send messages to friends and family. Android Authority reports finding a “Gemini Calling” introductory screen in an APK teardown with examples that include “Call Mom and tell her I will be 15 minutes late” and “Call John and ask if he is coming for dinner.”

Based on those examples, even with this expansion, Gemini would likely be limited to basic, text message-like calls. While Google’s AI might not automate an entire catch-up phone call with your relatives, it could deliver quick messages to people who prefer a phone call, miss texts often, or even still have a landline phone.

Android Authority also says it found “granular permissions” for Gemini actions in individual apps, including what appear to be settings for phone call permissions. These settings would allow users to pick and choose which app capabilities they want to allow Gemini to access, potentially giving users an option to opt out of receiving incoming automated calls from Gemini. However, as Android Authority notes, it’s also possible Google might not publicly release this expansion or the granular Gemini app settings.

Tech.title: Reverse-engineered games: All the news on video game decomps, recomps, VR and web and 3D ports
Tech.content:
It’s a wild time for retro gaming. Thanks to decompilations and recompilations of classic titles, those games are becoming unshackled from their proprietary code and original hardware to be ported to new devices or updated in ways to completely change the original game. Ever imagined skateboarding in Call of Duty? Or playing the original Halo right in your web browser, complete with multiplayer?

These are unofficial versions of games, so they may sit in a legal gray area. It seems unlikely that Nintendo, for example, is particularly happy about people finding ways to play The Legend of Zelda on non-Nintendo hardware. Many of these projects are also made with the assistance of AI, which, for some people, is a non-starter given ethical or environmental concerns surrounding the technology.

Tech.title: The Matic is the first robovac to get an FCC ban waiver, not that it needs it
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Well, sort of — because the Matic wasn’t banned to begin with.

Here’s what’s actually happening: On October 2nd, the FCC added the original Matic, model 4MA0001, and its charging dock model 4DK0008 to its ban waiver list. That allows the FCC to approve these radio products for import, marketing, and sale.

But the Matic doesn’t need a waiver, because its radios were already approved years ago. The FCC’s foreign drone, robot, and router bans only keep future products from getting imported into the United States, not existing ones whose radios have already been approved.

Besides, Matic’s products don’t get FCC approval to begin with — instead, Matic ships them with an off-the-shelf Intel AX210 Wi-Fi and Bluetooth chip that gets its own approval from the FCC. (It’s the same kind of Wi-Fi card you’ll find inside a desktop or laptop computer.) Matic also doesn’t need to worry about an import ban specifically, because Matic assembles its robots right here in Mountain View, California.

A waiver could theoretically help if Matic were to build new products outside the United States and try to import them here, except that the FCC hasn’t granted Matic a blanket approval on a brand of robot, like it did with Asus and Netgear’s routers. Instead, it specifically granted a waiver for the Matic models 4MA0001 and 4DK0008, which, again, have already made it through the FCC.

The waiver might not be completely symbolic. The FCC is currently trying to close lots of the loopholes that currently make its ban impotent, is weighing whether to make manufacturers disclose all the components in their gadgets, and is retroactively cracking down on some companies it sees as flaunting the rules. While Matic assembles its robots in the US, it admits it doesn’t yet source 65 percent of its components from US suppliers, the threshold for it to be seen as Made in the US, and perhaps one of those foreign components could trip it up if not for the waiver.

Even so, Matic already gets its “core compute platform” from Nvidia, co-founder and CEO Mehul Nariyawala tells The Verge, and sources other “critical components” from US companies “whenever possible.”

And unlike some of the other companies where the FCC has mysteriously granted a waiver, Matic is committing to more US manufacturing and onshoring.

“Up till 3 months ago, both our R&D offices and production facilities were in the same office in Mountain View, about 24,000 square feet,” Nariyawala tells The Verge. “We’ve turned that entire facility into production facility and moved our office to Menlo Park.”

He says Matic went from shipping 1,500 robots a year ago to 17,000 now, and is trying to find more and more US suppliers so it can use even fewer foreign parts.

“At the moment we might be the only floor cleaning robot built in America,” he says. “That is becoming one of the key value propositions for our product.”

Tech.title: This startup is issuing AI-generated acne prescriptions
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

People in Utah can now use AI to get a prescription for acne treatment. On Monday, healthcare startup Nolla Health announced that users in the state can scan their faces using its app, allowing its AI system to analyze acne severity and autonomously write a prescription, as reported earlier by Bloomberg.

The service is launching as a pilot program with gradually loosening physician oversight. Two physicians will approve each AI-generated prescription before they’re issued for the first 100 patients, but will start reviewing them only after they’re prescribed for up to 500 patients. “After that, physicians review a sample of at least 10% of prescriptions every month, plus every case involving an escalation or side effect,” Nolla Health says.

Several other healthcare companies are experimenting with AI-generated prescriptions in Utah, which started allowing AI systems to renew certain medications earlier this year. But Nolla Health says it’s the first in the country to issue initial prescriptions, rather than renewals. “The pilot is designed to complement, not replace, physicians,” Nolla Health writes in its press release. “By handling routine, low-acuity cases, Nolla Derm frees dermatologists to focus on complex, high-risk patients.”

The program will cost $4.99 / month, and only applies to Utah residents who are 18 years of age or older and have mild-to-moderate acne. Nolla Health says it will direct users to a physician if its AI system cannot “confidently select a treatment.” The startup’s AI can currently prescribe eight different skin treatments, according to Bloomberg.

Tech.title: All the drama around AI’s takeover of mathematics
Tech.content: This past year, OpenAI, Anthropic, and other labs have announced breakthroughs on numerous long-standing mathematical problems, in some cases pushing well beyond what researchers expected current systems to be capable of — including resolving one of the famous Millennium Prize problems. But in classic Silicon Valley style, AI labs are moving fast and breaking things, barreling through the discipline with all the grace of a runaway bulldozer. Results that might normally have been celebrated have instead sparked backlash. AI labs say they are learning from earlier mistakes. Whether those promises bear fruit remains to be seen.

Tech.title: Wikipedia operator says OpenAI’s ‘rogue’ bots may be linked to a May outage
Tech.content:
Wiki editing: We’ve identified edits to Wikimedia wikis that we believe are from AI agents operated by OpenAI. These edits were not published to pages with visibility to general readers; almost all of them were testing edits in “sandbox” areas of the wiki. It also included a few edits to the configuration for a citation tool, which we believe were potentially malicious edits that were intended to misuse this tool as a proxy for fetching data from remote services. While Wikipedia policies allow bots to edit when they are disclosed and approved by the community, none of those approvals were sought in these incidents.

Etherpad probing and use: Agents we believe to be operated by OpenAI made some unsuccessful attempts to compromise our public Etherpad, a note-taking tool we host as a community service. Agents unsuccessfully tried to use it to fetch data from other websites as a proxy. Other agents also likely operated by OpenAI took notes about their tasks, though this did not appear to turn into coordination.

Excessive data downloading: Agents we believe to be operated by OpenAI made millions of automated requests to our public APIs to access the knowledge on Wikimedia projects, crawled millions of pages (mainly from our projects Wikidata and Wikimedia Commons), and made hundreds of thousands of data queries to the Wikidata Query Service (WQDS). This traffic may have contributed to a partial outage on WQDS in May.

Tech.title: Hyundai CEO says only a ‘level playing field’ can minimize damage from China
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

There’s been a lot of doom and gloom from the auto industry lately when the subject of China comes up. Automaker CEOs, in particular, warn that allowing low-cost, high-tech Chinese electric vehicles to be sold in the US would effectively spell the end of their businesses.

Hyundai CEO José Muñoz is not as pessimistic as some of his counterparts. He says he’s confident the right mix of protectionist policies and improvements on the product side can keep China at bay. Even though his company is feeling the squeeze from China, Muñoz isn’t ready to throw in the towel. But he also acknowledges that China could flood the US with affordable imports without established protections in place.

“As long as there is a level playing field for everybody,” Muñoz said at the reveal of the new 2027 Hyundai Tucson in New York City last week. “That’s all we ask, right? We compete everywhere in the world, and then we have seen that in the markets where that position is respected, so it’s really good for us.”

Chinese automakers have expanded rapidly in Europe, gobbling up market share and damaging domestic brands like Volkswagen, Volvo, and Mercedes by offering vehicles at much lower prices. US automakers warn the same could be true for them if China were allowed to import its vehicles here.

“We compete everywhere in the world, and then we have seen that in the markets where that position is respected, so it’s really good for us.” — José Muñoz

Steep tariffs and laws that prohibit the sale of cars with software from China have basically made it impossible to sell Chinese vehicles in the US. But in recent months, the dam appears to be weakening. President Donald Trump has said several times that he would be open to Chinese automakers building manufacturing plants in the US if they hire American workers. And experts across the board believe it’s only a matter of time before China finds a way to sell its cars in the US.

But if Chinese brands eventually set up manufacturing inside North America or enter via partner channels, it’s not clear whether Hyundai has a defensive strategy ready. I asked Muñoz whether his company had begun to plan for the eventuality of Chinese imports available in the US market. He said it had not.

“We don’t develop strategies specifically because of the Chinese or because of other types of consumers, or other types of competitors,” he said. “We are always trying to do better.”

If Hyundai has any strategy, Muñoz added, it’s vertical integration: bringing down costs by making its tech and components. “This allows us to be more competitive,” he said. “Better quality over cost.”

“We don’t develop strategies specifically because of the Chinese or because of other types of consumers, or other types of competitors.”

Muñoz cited Hyundai’s $5.8 billion investment in Louisiana to produce green steel as an example of the company’s efforts to vertically integrate in the US. Hyundai expects the investment to provide better, more competitive, and more environmentally friendly steel. He says the same philosophy applies to software and other technologies that Hyundai wants to develop internally.

“So there is always room to do better,” he continued. “So if the Chinese competitor were to enter in the market, we would see what would happen, but I don’t know, I don’t have a crystal ball. I just look around, for example, Europe, and see what has happened, and then you may expect similar type of behaviors.”

Chinese vehicles sold in Europe are on average about 30 percent cheaper than comparable European-made rival models, even when factoring in EU import tariffs. The US has already fallen behind the rest of the world when it comes to EV adoption, after Trump and Republicans in Congress eliminated federal subsidies. In Europe, EVs account for over 20 percent of sales; in China, it’s over 60 percent. In the US, it’s less than 6 percent.

Political polarization certainly plays a role in depressing sales, as does inadequate charging infrastructure. But the lack of affordable electric models is regularly cited as the biggest barrier to adoption in the US. On that front, Muñoz thinks the US can still catch up.

“I think the American market is the most competitive in the world,” he said, noting that Hyundai still records robust EV sales here. That may be true, but the company’s hybrids are what’s keeping its EV business afloat. Hyundai has added hybrids to a wide range of vehicles, including its top-selling Tucson.

Unlike other automakers, Hyundai hasn’t retreated from EVs. It continues to sell its Ioniq 5 and Ioniq 9 here in the US, as well as a growing number of hybrids. In fact, the Hyundai Group recently surpassed Honda to claim second place in US hybrid sales behind Toyota.

Muñoz acknowledged that the US was still catching up to China’s dominance in EV batteries. Hyundai operates a battery manufacturing joint venture with SK On in Georgia near its massive Metaplant, where it builds all of its EVs and hybrids.

“Obviously if you don’t have the critical mass, the volume, it’s very difficult to be competitive,” he said. “One of the biggest pieces of cost is the battery. That is the key element, right? But there is a lot of production of batteries in the United States with some of the best global manufacturers. So I’m not concerned.”

Tech.title: OpenAI is adding text watermarking in ChatGPT and Codex
Tech.content:
Rolling out text watermarking in the EU. Over the coming weeks, we will introduce text watermarking to eligible ChatGPT and Codex users across all plans in the EU only. We are not making text watermarking a global default at launch. This regional approach gives us room to learn from real-world use and feedback.

Enabling opt-in watermarking for API customers. Starting today, API customers around the world will be able to opt in to watermarked text outputs for select models. This lets customers decide how watermarking fits their transparency obligations and the experiences they provide to users. We are also working with cloud partners to make watermarking available for OpenAI model outputs accessed through their services in the coming weeks.

Providing detector access to researchers and expert organizations. Approved researchers and expert organizations can apply starting today. In accordance with the Code of Practice, access will be initially granted on a case-by-case basis to support evaluation and improvement of text provenance. The tool will report whether it detects an OpenAI watermark, without identifying the user or revealing their prompts or conversations. Given the risk of missed watermarks and false positives, we are not making it publicly available at launch.

Tech.title: Lucid Motors’ EV output falls to lowest level in almost 2 years
Tech.content:
Lucid Motors built 2,954 electric vehicles (EVs) in the third quarter of this year, a 54% drop from a year ago, as the company purposely limits production to better meet demand for its EVs.

This was the third straight quarter in which the number of EVs Lucid built has declined. It’s also the lowest quarterly output since the first quarter of 2025, which was just after Lucid Motors started production of its second EV, the Gravity SUV.

Lucid delivered 3,806 EVs in the third quarter, roughly flat with the second quarter and down about 200 vehicles from the third quarter of 2025. The company has struggled to find buyers for either of its first two luxury EVs. In five of the last six quarters, it built more vehicles than it delivered.

Lucid’s new CEO, Silvio Napoli, has spent the last few months leading an effort to “simplify the company.” That effort has included laying off around 1,500 employees, streamlining the company’s leadership, and eliminating a second shift at its factory in Arizona in a bid to reach cost savings of $1.4 billion. Lucid also delayed the release of its third EV, the Cosmos. That model is supposed to be much cheaper, starting at under $50,000.

The third-quarter figures, released Monday afternoon, come just a few days after rival EV upstart Rivian posted its best quarter in history on the back of the R2, its new, more affordable SUV. Although Rivian didn’t break out specific delivery figures for the R2, the company shipped nearly 20,000 vehicles in the third quarter, the first full quarter with the R2 in production, up from 12,194 in the second quarter.

Lucid’s failure to find a large market of buyers for its EVs is even more stark when compared with the promises the company made when it went public in 2021. That year, Lucid Motors merged with a special purpose acquisition company and estimated it would ship as many as 90,000 EVs in 2024 alone. The company raised $4 billion in the transaction.

On Lucid’s second-quarter earnings call in August, Napoli spoke about why he thinks the company has failed to make a dent in the EV market.

“While there is no question that Lucid brought leading innovations and outstanding products to the market, we have disappointed on several fronts, and for far too long,” he said. “We have not executed consistently. We missed commitments, launched products before they were ready, underinvested in service, responded too slowly to quality issues, and allowed complexity to slow decisions down.”

The Cosmos’ lower price could, in theory, let Lucid access a wider market, but Napoli cautioned shareholders that rushing the new EV out could create more trouble.

“We will not repeat the mistakes of the past by bringing a product to market before it is ready,” Napoli said on the call.

Tech.title: OpenAI will start watermarking ChatGPT’s text in the EU
Tech.content:
OpenAI will start adding an invisible watermark to text generated by ChatGPT and Codex in the European Union to comply with the EU AI Act, the company said Monday in a blog post.

The EU AI Act’s transparency rules, which took effect on August 2, require AI companies to mark AI-generated content in a way other systems can identify.

OpenAI said the watermark will roll out over the coming weeks to eligible ChatGPT and Codex users on all plans, but only in the EU. Developers using OpenAI’s API anywhere in the world can turn it on for select models starting today; it’s off by default. OpenAI said it is not making text watermarking a global default at launch.

The watermark is not an actual symbol, but works by subtly shaping the model’s word choices, leaving a pattern readers can’t see, but a detector can pick up. Because it lives in the words themselves, it travels with the text when it’s copied and pasted. OpenAI said the watermark doesn’t identify the user, and that it saw no meaningful change in its models’ performance with it switched on.

OpenAI also published a technical report for its method, called textGrain, alongside the announcement. Co-written with researchers from the University of Pennsylvania and Yale, it walks through an example of using a secret key to sort next-word predictions to finish the sentence. Add hundreds of these nudges together, and the detector can spot AI-generated content using only the text and the key.

Can the watermark be removed by editing? OpenAI’s tests suggest yes. In one test, replacing 10% of words with synonyms dropped detection from about 92% to 66%. The company also said short passages, math answers, and translated text are harder to detect.

“These limitations contribute to our decision to provide initial detector access only to approved researchers and expert organizations, who can help us evaluate reliability and responsible uses,” said the company.

OpenAI also cautioned that a missing watermark “does not prove human authorship.” The text could be too short or too heavily edited, or it could come from another company’s AI.

“[Watermarks] can indicate that an OpenAI system generated or processed part of a passage, but not how much human judgment, editing, or creativity went into it,” the company said.

The announcement comes two months after Anthropic said it would watermark text generated by Claude, a move it’s applying worldwide. That decision drew backlash from some Claude users, who argued they had supplied “the instructions, context, decisions” while Claude was just “the tool.”

OpenAI had built a text watermark before but held off on releasing it, partly over concerns that users would switch to rivals that didn’t watermark, The Wall Street Journal reported in 2024.

Anthropic, Google, Meta, Microsoft, and OpenAI are among the companies that have committed to following the EU’s code of practice on AI-generated content.

Tech.title: Etched fields funding offers at $40B+ valuation, sources say
Tech.content:
Although it’s only been a couple of months since Etched raised $700 million at a $21 billion valuation, the AI chip startup is already being plied with investment offers at double or more its value, according to people familiar with the company.

Etched is reviewing incoming bids that range from $40 billion from top-tier investors to $50 billion from lesser-known backers, one person said. These fundraising talks are early, so terms of any deal, should one happen, may change. Etched declined to comment.

While this may seem like a fast timetable to raise another mega round, Etched is pursuing a particularly expensive segment of the AI industry: building full AI hardware systems powered by its own proprietary chips. The person familiar with these offers said that if it raises as much as its last round, this could give Etched a cushion of as much as 3.5 years of runway.

There are reasons why VCs are hot to own a piece of Etched. The four-year-old startup shows promise of challenging Nvidia. Not only did quant trading firm Jane Street lead the last $700 million round, it is also a customer that took delivery of an early system. Etched said in July that it had already secured $1 billion in customer orders, including the one from Jane Street, after manufacturing its test chip at a TSMC factory this summer.

Co-founder and COO Robert Wachen previously told TechCrunch that investors are so enthusiastic because Etched has designed two new components from scratch to speed up inference — the computing process that happens after a user submits a prompt.

The company claims its chips can process more tokens faster and at a lower cost than Nvidia’s. That’s the reason its processors have been so attractive to Jane Street, for whom a microscopic advantage in speed can yield massive profits.

The startup has also impressed investors with its ability to attract engineers from Nvidia, with roughly 15% of Etched’s 400-person workforce having previously worked at the chip giant, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Etched also operates a new 10-megawatt data center in Silicon Valley and established a facility in Taiwan to coordinate production near TSMC.

Co-founders Gavin Uberti and Chris Zhu famously met in an advanced math course at Harvard, while Wachen was Uberti’s roommate and they dropped out to pursue the company.

In terms of fast rounds at big leaps in valuations, Etched already has a history of them. The startup announced a $300 million round at a $10.3 billion valuation led by Sequoia in July. It announced the $700 million round at a $21 billion valuation in September. Back-to-back funding rounds, which essentially act as a single financing split into two tranches with separate valuations, are increasingly common among the buzziest startups.

Tech.title: After Factory’s public spat with Khosla, Menlo proudly invests
Tech.content:
Menlo Ventures partner Matt Murphy and his team announced Monday in a blog post that the firm has invested in AI coding startup Factory.

Menlo declined to comment on how much it invested but said the deal was part of Factory’s latest funding round announced last month at a $5 billion valuation. A source familiar with the deal told us the investment was significant to Menlo — not a token gesture — and that Menlo would have invested more had there been room on the cap table.

Ordinarily, something like this wouldn’t necessarily be news; startups often extend previous rounds to add new investors. But last week, Factory co-founder and CEO Matan Grinberg was embroiled in a very public airing of dirty laundry when he alleged that he had fired investor Chris Degnan of firm RPT Partners from his role as board advisor. Grinberg said he feared Degnan may have shared confidential information with Factory’s biggest competitor, Cognition. The accusation followed Degnan’s move to Cognition as its chief revenue officer.

A who’s who of the tech industry came out of the woodwork either to support Degnan and condemn Factory, or vice versa, but none was more surprising than Vinod Khosla. Khosla’s firm is an investor in both Factory and Cognition. But that didn’t stop the venerable VC from calling Factory a desperate “struggling second tier competitor,” and accusing Grinberg of lying about firing Degnan and impugning his character. Degnan disputed Grinberg’s story, saying he resigned and that he’d rebuffed a competing job offer from Grinberg.

So Menlo’s full-throated endorsement of Factory, which praised its founders, its tech, and its relationship with its customers, is more than a feather in Factory’s cap. It’s a statement that Factory is not in the state that Khosla implied it was.

Murphy famously bet his firm on Anthropic back when it appeared to be an also-ran to OpenAI and has been on a hot streak ever since, landing deals with Lovable and Legora, for instance. So now some VCs are calling Factory “the next Anthropic.“

Sequoia’s Shaun Maguire, also a Factory backer who came out on X in support of Grinberg last week, appears thrilled with Menlo’s endorsement, saying the firm is “on a tear.” Notably, Menlo is not an investor in competitor Cognition.

Tech.title: Reflection debuts Beam, an open-weight AI model to rival Chinese models at lower compute cost
Tech.content:
Reflection AI is officially unveiling Beam, its first frontier, open-weight AI model. The two-year-old, Brooklyn-based startup claims Beam matches the performance of leading Chinese open models on advanced reasoning benchmarks at dramatically lower costs, a claim that could heat up the race to build a Western answer to DeepSeek, Qwen, and Z.ai.

Reflection’s announcement confirms reporting from Axios over the weekend that the startup was close to a launch. The company shared new details in a lengthy blog post Monday, which described Beam as a text-only mixture-of-experts model trained on high-compute reinforcement learning to be effective at reasoning, coding, and agentic tasks at “a fraction of the token cost and inference time compute” of rivals.

Beam is a 501-billion-parameter model with 23 billion active parameters. It was pretrained on 23.8 trillion tokens and has a 1 million token context window. To compare, Z.ai’s GLM-5.2 has roughly 744 billion total parameters with 40 billion active.

Reflection’s performance claims haven’t been independently verified, but on advanced reasoning benchmarks, the company says Beam scores on par with Z.ai’s GLM-5.2 and outperforms today’s leading Western open models while using “3-4x less inference compute.” Reflection calls it a “workhorse model” for enterprises, the public sector, and developers.

Reflection is positioning itself against closed labs like Anthropic and OpenAI, against popular open models from Chinese developers, and against Western players like Mistral, Meta, and Cohere. Its most direct U.S. rival might be Inkling, the open model from Mira Murati’s Thinking Machines Lab released in July. Reflection’s own benchmarks show that Beam outscores Inkling on four coding tests where both report results, but Inkling is a multimodal model and Beam is text-only.

Reflection was founded in 2024 by two former Google DeepMind researchers and has raised roughly $4.7 billion from backers, including Nvidia, Sequoia Capital, and Lightspeed Venture Partners, per PitchBook. Its last round valued the company at a $25 billion pre-money valuation.
